title: Preface
content:
Preface The two earlier volumes used numbers as familiar objects. Their arithmetic and order were school facts, named where they were used and never proved. This volume proves them. It starts from Peano’s axioms for the natural numbers and builds the integers, the rationals and the real numbers, each out of the one before. At the end the real numbers form a complete ordered field, and any two complete ordered fields are the same up to exactly one isomorphism. Who it is for. The reader we have in mind has worked through Logic and Proof and Sets and Functions, or has their habits from elsewhere. That means negating a quantified statement, running an induction, and checking that a rule on equivalence classes does not depend on the representative chosen. The last of these is used in almost every chapter. The chapters point back to both volumes where they use a definition or a rule, so a reader who is unsure of a step can look it up. What it covers. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Chapter Title What it does ----------------------- ---------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 The Natural Numbers 
N as a Peano system: induction, the recursion theorem, addition and multiplication, order and well-ordering, any two Peano systems alike; a short closing section on where 
N comes from in set theory 2 The Integers 
Z as classes of pairs of natural numbers, well-defined operations, commutative rings, ordered rings and the rules for inequalities, division with remainder 3 The Rationals 
Q as classes of fractions, an Archimedean ordered field, and the gap in 
Q where \sqrt 2 should be 4 Ordered Fields and Sequences Limits and Cauchy sequences in an arbitrary ordered field, the Archimedean property, and a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit 5 The Real Numbers from Cauchy Sequences 
R as classes of rational Cauchy sequences, an ordered field in which every bounded set has a supremum 6 The Complete Ordered Field Is Unique Exactly one order-preserving isomorphism between any two complete ordered fields, and what Analysis on the Real Line takes from this volume ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Chapters 1–3 build the numbers that algebra needs, one chapter for each. Chapters 4 and 5 fill the gap that Chapter 3 found in 
Q: first the rules for sequences, proved without the number they aim at, then the numbers made from the sequences themselves. Chapter 6 shows that the construction does not matter. How to read it. The main line is Chapters 1–6; read them in order, since each uses the ones before it. Every section has Quick checks with folded answers; answer each one before you unfold it. The exercises of a section come in three groups, A to check understanding, B for practice and C to go deeper, and the last section of each chapter adds R items that reach back to earlier chapters. A chapter’s opening page lists what it needs, with links, and the time it takes. Second-reading folds, in most chapters, hold edge cases and longer justifications. They can stay closed on a first reading, but they are not optional, since later proofs may use what they contain. Results marked optional can be skipped, and nothing outside them depends on them. Time. About 120 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks) and about 180 hours for everything. Chapter by chapter, core and full: Chapter 1, 20 and 30 hours; Chapter 2, 20 and 25; Chapter 3, 15 and 25; Chapter 4, 25 and 40; Chapter 5, 25 and 35; Chapter 6, 15 and 25. The figures come from word counts and exercise counts, not from reader logs, and will be replaced by the median of logged hours once there are some. What comes next. Analysis on the Real Line does not need this volume. It starts from the axioms of a complete ordered field, the axioms this volume proves for its 
R, and Chapter 6 explains why it does not matter which model of them one has in mind. A reader who wants to know that those axioms describe something real, and only one thing, will find both answers here. Algebraic Preliminaries builds on Chapters 2, 5 and 6: the integers with division with remainder (its Chapter 1 takes up divisibility, prime factorization and congruences), the real numbers as a complete ordered field, and square roots in it, together with the ring and field rules of Chapters 2, 3 and 4 that come with them.

title: The Natural Numbers
content:
The Natural Numbers The two earlier volumes counted with the natural numbers and never asked what they are. Logic and Proof took induction as an axiom about numbers it did not build, and Sets and Functions described 
N as a subset of the school 
R and proved the recursion theorem there. A volume that builds the real numbers cannot start from a subset of 
R. This chapter takes one assumption instead: there is a Peano system, a set with a start 0, a step \mathrm{S}, and three demands on them (the start is not a step, the step never merges two numbers, and the only subset that contains the start and is closed under the step is everything). From that one assumption the chapter derives induction, the recursion theorem, addition and multiplication with their laws, the order, well-ordering, and powers. A reader may fear that the choice of Peano system matters. Section 1.4 shows it does not: any two Peano systems are alike in exactly one way, so every statement about one is a statement about the other, and the 
N of this chapter, the 
N of Logic and Proof and the 
N of Sets and Functions are identified by a citing rule that says which earlier results carry over. Section 1.5, short and without proofs, says where a Peano system comes from: sets are the raw material, the natural numbers form the least inductive set, and pairs are sets. The proofs belong to Axiomatic Set Theory. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 (induction and strong induction: @fd1:ax-induction, @fd1:thm-strong-induction), Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 (reductio: @fd1:def-rule-raa), Logic and Proof, Section 7.6 (non-standard models, for the comparison after the independence example: @fd1:exm-non-standard-naturals) and Logic and Proof, Chapter 8 (the catalogue of what a proof may not do, for the find-the-error exercises: @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). Sets and Functions, Chapter 1 (sets cut out by a property, ordered pairs and products: @fd2:def-set-builder, @fd2:def-ordered-pair, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set); Sets and Functions, Chapter 2 (functions, injective, surjective and bijective maps, composition, inverses: @fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-injective, @fd2:def-surjective, @fd2:def-bijective, @fd2:def-composition, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse); Sets and Functions, Chapter 3 (induction, the recursion theorem, well-ordering and the three proof boxes: @fd2:thm-induction, @fd2:thm-recursion, @fd2:thm-well-ordering, @fd2:lem-naturals-arithmetic, @fd2:exm-method-induction-step, @fd2:exm-method-least-element, @fd2:exm-method-smallest-counterexample); Sets and Functions, Chapter 4 (finite and infinite sets, for the citing rule of Section 1.4: @fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy); and Sets and Functions, Chapter 5 (partial orders: @fd2:def-partial-order). Time. About 20 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - Peano’s Axioms and Induction. What counting needs, and why the smallest closed subset of the school 
R does not do; a Peano system (M, e, s) and the assumption that one exists, which names its set 
N; the three clauses (P3), (P4), (P5) shown independent by three small structures, one of them two copies of 
N; induction in the set form and the statement form; and the predecessor, the proof that every natural number except 0 is a successor of exactly one, and that no number is its own successor. - The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication. A function on 
N defined by a start and a step, existing and unique, by the smallest closed set of pairs; the sum and product defined by recursion, the numerals, successor cancellation, and the laws of arithmetic (associativity, commutativity, distributivity) proved by induction on the recursion variable. - Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers. m \le n when n = m + j; the order and its compatibility with sum and product, cancellation in sums and products, and n - m for m \le n; a strict total order; every non-empty set has a least element; powers and the parity of n \cdot n. - All Peano Systems Are Alike. The categoricity theorem: any two Peano systems are isomorphic by exactly one isomorphism, which carries sum, product and order along; the identification of this 
N with the 
N of Logic and Proof and Sets and Functions, and the citing rule that lets a later chapter cite their results about 
N. - Where 
N Comes From. Seven axioms of set theory said in one line each, zero and the successor as sets, \omega as the least inductive set and why it is a Peano system, and pairs as sets. No proofs: they are in Axiomatic Set Theory. Named moves - Induction through a closed subset (@exm-method-closed-subset). To prove a property of every natural number, let A be the set of numbers that have it; show 0 \in A and that n \in A gives \mathrm{S}(n) \in A; then A = 
N by (P5). It is used for induction in Section 1.1, and in Section 1.4 to show that the map out of 
N is onto (apply (P5) to its image). (Section 1.1) - Fix the others, induct on the recursion variable (@exm-method-induct-on-recursion-variable). A law about a sum or product is proved by induction on the variable the definition is a recursion on, with the other variables fixed. It proves the laws of arithmetic in Section 1.2 and is reused in Section 1.3. (Section 1.2) - Translate \le into a sum. Replace m \le n by n = m + j for some j, and every order claim becomes a claim about sums, which Section 1.2 already controls. (Section 1.3) - Build by recursion, compare by induction (@exm-method-build-by-recursion). To compare two structures, build the map between them by the recursion theorem and prove it respects everything by induction. It proves categoricity in Section 1.4. Threads - Induction. Logic and Proof took it as an axiom, Sets and Functions kept that axiom for its 
N \subseteq 
R, and here it is clause (P5); Section 1.4 shows the three agree. - Recursion. The recursion theorem of Section 1.2 builds the sum, the product and the power, and Section 1.4 uses it to build the isomorphism between two Peano systems. Chapter 2 uses it again for multiples in a ring. - Well-ordering and least elements. Section 1.3 proves it for 
N; Section 2.4 extends it to sets of integers bounded below, and Section 2.5 uses it to find remainders. - The citing rule. Section 1.4 says which results of Logic and Proof and Sets and Functions may be cited about this 
N and why; every later chapter cites through it with @cor-omega-identification. Summary A Peano system is a set M with an element e and a function s \colon M 	o M such that e is not a value of s, s is injective, and the only subset of M that contains e and is closed under s is M (@def-peano-system). The chapter assumes one and calls its set 
N (@ax-natural-numbers); the last clause is induction (@thm-omega-induction), and every element but 0 has exactly one predecessor (@prp-peano-predecessor). A start and a step define exactly one function on 
N (@thm-omega-recursion), which defines the sum and the product (@def-omega-arithmetic); they satisfy cancellation (@cor-omega-successor-cancellation) and the usual laws (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws). The order m \le n when n = m + j (@def-omega-order) is compatible with the operations (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic), is a strict total order (@thm-omega-order), and every non-empty set has a least element (@thm-omega-well-ordering); powers and parity follow (@prp-omega-powers-parity). Any two Peano systems are isomorphic by exactly one isomorphism (@thm-peano-categoricity), which preserves sums, products and order (@prp-isomorphism-preserves-arithmetic), so the 
N of the earlier volumes may be identified with this one (@cor-omega-identification). Section 1.5 describes, without proofs, how set theory supplies a Peano system: \omega, the least inductive set, whose elements are the von Neumann numerals, with pairs built as sets. What is open: nothing here lets us subtract 5 from 3. Chapter 2 builds the integers from pairs of natural numbers to fix that. Terms - Peano system: a set with a start and a step satisfying (P3), (P4), (P5) (@def-peano-system). - natural number, 
N, 0, \mathrm{S}, successor: the elements, start and step of the assumed Peano system (@ax-natural-numbers). - predecessor: the one m with \mathrm{S}(m) = n, for n 
e 0 (@prp-peano-predecessor). - defined by recursion: determined by a start and a step (@thm-omega-recursion). - sum, product, numeral: the operations defined by recursion, and 1 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0), 2 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1), and so on (@def-omega-arithmetic). - \le, <: the order on 
N (@def-omega-order). - well-ordering: every non-empty subset has a least element (@thm-omega-well-ordering). - power: b^n defined by recursion on n (@prp-omega-powers-parity). - isomorphism of Peano systems: a bijection that carries start to start and step to step (@thm-peano-categoricity).

title: 1.1 Peano's Axioms and Induction
content:
Peano’s Axioms and Induction Sets and Functions, Chapter 3 took the natural numbers as a subset 
N of the familiar real numbers, and borrowed the arithmetic of 
R whenever it was convenient. This volume builds the integers, the rationals and the real numbers. If we started from the 
N inside 
R, the real numbers would rest on the real numbers. So we need 
N on its own. We make one assumption: there is a set with a start and a step that obey three rules. This section shows that each rule is needed, proves induction in the form we use, and proves that every natural number except 0 has exactly one predecessor. What counting needs Two descriptions of 
N come to mind at once, and neither will do. The first is 
N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}. It names four elements and then writes three dots, and the dots carry all the content. They say “keep going one at a time, and nothing else”, and to say what that means is exactly the job of a definition of 
N. The second is more careful: 
N is the smallest subset of 
R that contains 0 and is closed under x \mapsto x + 1. A smallest such subset exists, by @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set with start 0 and step x \mapsto x + 1, and the set form of @fd1:ax-induction shows that it is the 
N of Sets and Functions. Either way the description needs 
R. Since 
R is where this volume is going, it cannot be where 
N comes from. So we describe 
N by what counting has to do, not by where its elements live. Counting needs - (P1) a start: an element where counting begins; - (P2) a step: a rule sending each element to a next element of the same set. That is a set M, an element e \in M, and a function s \colon M 	o M. A start and a step are not enough, and here are three ways they fail to count. In each picture an arrow goes from x to s(x). A loop. Let M \coloneqq \{p, q, r\}, start at p, and step p \mapsto q \mapsto r \mapsto p. Counting comes back to its start: three steps after p we are at p again, as on a clock. A merge. Let M \coloneqq \{p, q, r\} again, start at p, and step p \mapsto q \mapsto r \mapsto q. Counting never returns to p, but two different elements, p and r, step to the same q. After r the count repeats q, and runs in a circle from there. An extra row. Take the counting numbers, and beside them a second copy with its own step, which the start never reaches. Every element still has one next element, no two elements step to the same one, and nothing steps back to the start. Yet starting at the start and stepping, we never meet the second copy. Counting cannot see those elements, and a description of the natural numbers must exclude them. Each failure is ruled out by one clause: the step never returns to the start; the step never sends two elements to the same one; and nothing is there that steps from the start cannot reach. The last clause needs care, since “reached by steps” is the three dots again. The way around it is the one @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set takes: speak of subsets. A subset that contains the start and is closed under the step contains everything the steps reach. If the only such subset is the whole set, nothing is left over. A Peano system is a set with a start and a step, where the step is one-to-one, never returns to the start, and reaches everything. [Peano system] A Peano system (M, e, s) consists of a set M, an element e \in M, and a function s \colon M 	o M, such that: - (P3) s(x) 
e e for every x \in M; - (P4) s is injective; - (P5) every subset A \subseteq M with e \in A and s(x) \in A for every x \in A is equal to M. In words: (P1) and (P2) are built into the data, since e \in M and s maps M into M. (P3) says the step never leads back to the start. (P4) says two different elements never step to the same element. (P5) is induction for M: a subset that contains the start and is closed under the step is everything, so every element of M is reached from e by steps. We write (M, e, s) and not (N, e, s), so that the letter never suggests 
N. The notation (M, e, s) lists the three pieces of data; it is not a set built from them (if one object is wanted, take the pair ((M, e), s) of @fd2:def-ordered-pair). The merge breaks (P4), since s(p) = q = s(r) with p 
e r. The extra row breaks (P5): the first copy contains the start, is closed under the step, and is not everything. The loop is the subject of the first Quick check. For the loop (M = \{p, q, r\}, e = p, s(p) = q, s(q) = r, s(r) = p), which of (P3), (P4), (P5) fail? Only (P3): s(r) = p = e. (P4) holds, since the three values s(p) = q, s(q) = r, s(r) = p are different. (P5) holds: a subset containing p and closed under s contains s(p) = q, then s(q) = r, so it is M. The one assumption The natural numbers are to be a Peano system. That is the whole of what we assume about them. [The Natural Numbers] There is a Peano system. We fix one Peano system for the rest of the volume and write it (
N, 0, \mathrm{S}). Its elements are the natural numbers, 0 is zero, and \mathrm{S}(n) is the successor of n. Spelled out, 
N is a set, 0 \in 
N, \mathrm{S} \colon 
N 	o 
N is a function, and: - (P3) \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 for every n \in 
N; - (P4) \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n) implies m = n; - (P5) every A \subseteq 
N that contains 0 and is closed under \mathrm{S} is 
N. Why believe the assumption? If the school real numbers are trusted, the 
N of Sets and Functions, with start 0 and step x \mapsto x + 1, is a Peano system; Section 1.4 checks this. And Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 1 builds a Peano system from sets alone, assuming nothing about numbers; Section 1.5 describes how. Which Peano system we fix does not matter: Section 1.4 proves that any two are copies of each other, matched by exactly one bijection that sends start to start and step to step. From here on, every fact about 
N is proved from @ax-natural-numbers. We do not borrow the order, the subtraction or the arithmetic of 
R. Addition and multiplication are not defined yet; Section 1.2 defines them. Even the numeral 1 is not available until then, and the element after 0 is written \mathrm{S}(0). Why these three clauses and no others? Each one does work that the other two cannot do: for each clause there is a structure satisfying the other two and failing it. [Each axiom is needed] Show that each of the following structures (M, e, s), with s \colon M 	o M, satisfies two of (P3), (P4), (P5) and fails the third. 1. M \coloneqq \{0\}, e \coloneqq 0, s(0) \coloneqq 0. 2. M \coloneqq \{0, \mathrm{S}(0)\}, e \coloneqq 0, s(0) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0), s(\mathrm{S}(0)) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0). 3. (Two copies of 
N.) Let a 
e b be two objects, M \coloneqq 
N 	imes \{a, b\}, e \coloneqq (0, a), and s(n, t) \coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), t) for n \in 
N and t \in \{a, b\}. (i) Fails (P3): s(0) = 0 = e. (P4) holds: M has one element, so two inputs with equal outputs are equal. (P5) holds: a subset of \{0\} containing e = 0 is \{0\}. (ii) Here 0 
e \mathrm{S}(0) by (P3) for 
N, so M has two elements. Fails (P4): s(0) = s(\mathrm{S}(0)) with 0 
e \mathrm{S}(0). (P3) holds: both values are \mathrm{S}(0) 
e 0 = e. (P5) holds: if A \subseteq M has 0 as an element and is closed under s, then s(0) = \mathrm{S}(0) \in A, so A = M. (iii) First, s is a function M 	o M. Each element of M is (n, t) for some n \in 
N and t \in \{a, b\} (@fd2:def-cartesian-product), and for exactly one such pair (@fd2:def-ordered-pair), so the formula names one value; and (\mathrm{S}(n), t) \in M, since \mathrm{S} maps 
N into 
N. (P3) holds. If s(n, t) = (0, a), then (\mathrm{S}(n), t) = (0, a) gives \mathrm{S}(n) = 0 (@fd2:def-ordered-pair), against (P3) for 
N. (P4) holds. If s(n, t) = s(n', t'), then (\mathrm{S}(n), t) = (\mathrm{S}(n'), t') gives t = t' and \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(n'), so n = n' by (P4) for 
N. Hence (n, t) = (n', t'). (P5) fails. Let A \coloneqq 
N 	imes \{a\}. It contains e = (0, a), and it is closed under s, since s(n, a) = (\mathrm{S}(n), a) \in A. But (0, b) \in M is not in A, because its second coordinate is b 
e a. So A 
e M. The picture shows (iii), with an arrow from each element to its image under s. This is the extra row of the start of the section. The element (0, b) has no arrow coming in, and it is not e. The top row is a copy of 
N, and so is the bottom row; but the bottom row cannot be reached from e. (P3) and (P4) cannot prevent this, and (P5) is the clause that says “nothing else”. (P5) speaks of every subset of M, and that is what lets it exclude every kind of extra row. A first-order induction schema speaks only of subsets defined by formulas, and Logic and Proof, Section 7.6 showed (@fd1:exm-non-standard-naturals) that the sentences true in 
N also hold in a structure with an element beyond every numeral; its closing remark promised the comparison made here. Exercise C2 builds an extra row in which, unlike (0, b) above, every element has an arrow coming in. Induction in the form we use (P5) is induction, stated about subsets of a Peano system. For 
N we record it in the two forms the rest of the volume cites: a set form, and a form about properties. [Induction on 
N] 1. (Set form.) Let A \subseteq 
N. If 0 \in A, and \mathrm{S}(n) \in A for every n \in A, then A = 
N. 2. (Property form.) Let P(n) be a property of natural numbers, possibly with other variables as parameters. If P(0) holds and, for every n \in 
N, P(n) implies P(\mathrm{S}(n)), then P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. (a) This is (P5) of @def-peano-system for the Peano system (
N, 0, \mathrm{S}) of @ax-natural-numbers. (b) Let A \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : P(n) \} (@fd2:def-set-builder). Then 0 \in A, because P(0) holds. Let n \in A. Then P(n), so P(\mathrm{S}(n)) by hypothesis, and \mathrm{S}(n) \in 
N because \mathrm{S} maps 
N into 
N; hence \mathrm{S}(n) \in A. By (a), A = 
N, which says that P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. Compare part (b) with the principle of induction, @fd1:ax-induction. Read with \mathrm{S}(n) in place of n + 1, the two statements are the same, and Section 1.2 shows that n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n) once addition is defined. The difference lies in their status. In Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, induction was taken on trust, for an 
N that came with the school arithmetic attached. Here (P5) is part of the one assumption, and arithmetic is not assumed at all: Section 1.2 builds it, and proves its laws by this theorem. Both halves of the hypothesis are needed. The set 
N \setminus \{0\} is closed under \mathrm{S}, by (P3), and it is not 
N. The set \{0\} contains 0 and is not closed under \mathrm{S}, since \mathrm{S}(0) 
e 0. Let P(n) be “n = 0”. Does the base case hold? Does the step hold? What does @thm-omega-induction (b) conclude? The base case holds: P(0) says 0 = 0. The step fails at n = 0: P(0) holds, while P(\mathrm{S}(0)) says \mathrm{S}(0) = 0, which is false by (P3). So the theorem concludes nothing, and indeed P fails at \mathrm{S}(0). Every natural number except 0 has one predecessor Sets and Functions used that n - 1 \in 
N for every natural number n 
e 0 (@fd2:lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)), with the subtraction done in 
R. Our 
N has no subtraction. Yet Sections 1.2–1.4 split, again and again, into the cases “n = 0” and “n = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k”. For that we need every n 
e 0 to be a successor, and of exactly one k. The fact holds in every Peano system, and the proof is no harder there; Exercises B3 and C2 use it in that generality. [Predecessors in a Peano System] Let (M, e, s) be a Peano system. 1. For every x \in M with x 
e e there is exactly one y \in M with s(y) = x. 2. s(x) 
e x for every x \in M. [Scratch work] For (a), “at most one” is (P4): if s(y) = x = s(y'), then y = y'. “At least one” is the real question. Of the three clauses, only (P5) can prove that every element of M has a given property, and (P5) speaks of subsets. So we must choose a subset A of M and show A = M. That choice is the new point. Inside an abstract M nothing can be computed: there is no subtraction that would produce y from x. The first candidate is the set of values of s, \{ z \in M : z = s(y) 	ext{ for some } y \in M \}. It fails at the start, since e is not a value, by (P3). The cure is the shape of @fd2:lem-naturals-arithmetic (c): carry “z = e or …”. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Givens Goal ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------- (M, e, s) a Peano system; x \in M, x 
e e some y \in M with s(y) = x A \coloneqq \{ z \in M : z = e 	ext{ or } z = s(y) 	ext{ for some } y \in M \} A = M; then x \in A and x 
e e give y (P5) for A e \in A; and z \in A \Rightarrow s(z) \in A, since s(z) is a value of s ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The step never uses z \in A, as in @fd2:exm-predecessor-no-hypothesis. Both parts apply (P5) to a subset chosen for the purpose: (a) to e together with the values of s, and (b) to the set where s(x) 
e x. In (b), unlike (a), the step uses its hypothesis, through (P4). (a) Let x \in M with x 
e e. At most one: if s(y) = x and s(y') = x, then y = y' by (P4). At least one: let A \coloneqq \{ z \in M : z = e 	ext{ or } z = s(y) 	ext{ for some } y \in M \} (@fd2:def-set-builder). Then e \in A, by the first alternative. Let z \in A. Then s(z) \in M is the value of s at z, so s(z) \in A, by the second alternative with y \coloneqq z. By (P5), A = M. Hence x \in A; since x 
e e, the second alternative holds, and x = s(y) for some y \in M. (b) Let A' \coloneqq \{ x \in M : s(x) 
e x \}. Then e \in A', since s(e) 
e e by (P3). Let x \in A', so that s(x) 
e x. If s(s(x)) = s(x), then (P4), applied to the inputs s(x) and x, gives s(x) = x, a contradiction. So s(s(x)) 
e s(x), that is, s(x) \in A'. By (P5), A' = M. This proves the proposition. For 
N, part (a) says that every natural number n 
e 0 is \mathrm{S}(k) for exactly one k \in 
N; this k is the predecessor of n. Part (b) says that no natural number is its own successor. The two proofs make the same move with one difference. In (a) the closure step proves s(z) \in A outright, whatever z is; in (b) it needs x \in A', and (P4) turns the hypothesis s(x) 
e x into the conclusion s(s(x)) 
e s(x). The move has a name. [Method: induction through a closed subset] Template. (1) Name A \coloneqq \{ x \in M : P(x) \}. (2) Show e \in A. (3) Take x \in A and show s(x) \in A, using P(x) if needed. (4) Conclude A = M by (P5). If P fails at e, carry “x = e or P(x)” (the shape of @fd2:lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)). When to use it. title: 1.2 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content:
The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication The natural numbers now have a zero, a successor map and induction (@thm-omega-induction), and nothing else: no addition, no multiplication. Sets and Functions, Section 3.3 had the same need and met it with @fd2:thm-recursion, a theorem that turns two equations into a function. Its proof built partial solutions on the sets \{0, \dots, n\} and compared them using the order of the real numbers. The natural numbers of @ax-natural-numbers have no order yet; the order is defined in the next section, from the addition of this one. So this section proves the recursion theorem by a construction that needs no order at all: it takes the smallest set of pairs that the two equations force, and shows that this set is the graph of a function. Then it defines addition and multiplication as school does, and proves the laws of arithmetic by one move and its consequences. Recursion on ℕ A starting value and a rule for the next value determine exactly one function on 
N. [Recursion Theorem on 
N] Let X be a set, let a \in X, and let g \colon 
N 	imes X 	o X be a function. Then there is exactly one function f \colon 
N 	o X such that f(0) = a \quad 	ext{and} \quad f igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } n \in 
N . This is the statement of @fd2:thm-recursion, with 
N the Peano system of @ax-natural-numbers and \mathrm{S}(n) in place of n + 1. The set 
N 	imes X is the Cartesian product of @fd2:def-cartesian-product. As before, a is the starting value and g turns the stage n and the current value into the next value; the conclusion has an existence half and a uniqueness half. [Scratch work] Uniqueness will be an induction: two solutions agree at 0, and the second equation passes agreement from n to \mathrm{S}(n). Existence is the hard half. “Define f by the two equations” names f on both sides of the second one, so it is not yet a definition. A definition must produce an object, and the object a function is made of is its graph (@fd2:def-function). So ask what the graph must contain. It must contain the pair (0, a). Whenever it contains a pair (n, x), meaning f(n) = x, it must also contain (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, x)). That is a description of a closed set: in 
N 	imes X, take the starting element (0, a) and the step (n, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, x)), which maps 
N 	imes X into itself because g takes its values in X. By @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set there is a smallest closed subset; call it R. It contains exactly what the equations force and nothing more. The question is whether R is a graph: does each n have exactly one partner x with (n, x) \in R? ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- R is the smallest closed subset of 
N 	imes X each n has exactly one x with (n, x) \in R induction on n base: the only pair at 0 is (0, a); step: the only pair at \mathrm{S}(n) is (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, x_n)), where x_n is the partner of n an extra pair (n, y) \in R R \setminus \{(n, y)\} is still closed, against “smallest” ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The last row is the gap the proof closes. A smallest closed set has no spare elements: if one pair could be removed without breaking closure, the smaller set would be closed, and R would lie inside it. Removing a pair is safe only if no step produces it from a pair that stays. That is where (P3) and (P4) enter. Before reading on: where is each of them used? Step 1 (uniqueness). Let f, f' \colon 
N 	o X both satisfy the two equations, and let P(n) be “f(n) = f'(n)”. P(0) holds, since f(0) = a = f'(0). If P(n) holds, then f igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) = g igl(n, f'(n) igr) = f' igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) , so P(\mathrm{S}(n)) holds. By @thm-omega-induction (b), P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. The two functions have the same domain and codomain, so f = f' by @fd2:prp-function-equality. Step 2 (the set of pairs). Call a subset C \subseteq 
N 	imes X closed if (0, a) \in C and (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, x)) \in C for every (n, x) \in C. The step sends 
N 	imes X into itself, since \mathrm{S}(n) \in 
N and g(n, x) \in X. By @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set there is a closed set R \subseteq 
N 	imes X that lies inside every closed set. Step 3. For every n \in 
N there is exactly one x \in X with (n, x) \in R. We use @thm-omega-induction (b) on n. Base case. (0, a) \in R, since R is closed. Suppose (0, b) \in R with b 
e a, and let R' \coloneqq R \setminus \{(0, b)\}. Then (0, a) \in R', because (0, a) 
e (0, b) (@fd2:def-ordered-pair). Let (m, x) \in R'. Then (m, x) \in R, so (\mathrm{S}(m), g(m, x)) \in R; and this pair is not (0, b), because \mathrm{S}(m) 
e 0 by (P3). So it lies in R', and R' is closed. Hence R \subseteq R', which is false, since (0, b) \in R and (0, b) 
otin R'. So a is the only partner of 0. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N, and suppose n has exactly one partner x_n in R. Since (n, x_n) \in R and R is closed, (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, x_n)) \in R. Suppose (\mathrm{S}(n), y) \in R with y 
e g(n, x_n), and let R' \coloneqq R \setminus \{(\mathrm{S}(n), y)\}. Then (0, a) \in R', because \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 by (P3). Let (m, x) \in R'; then (\mathrm{S}(m), g(m, x)) \in R. If this pair were (\mathrm{S}(n), y), then \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), so m = n by (P4); then (n, x) \in R, so x = x_n by the induction hypothesis; and then y = g(m, x) = g(n, x_n), against the choice of y. So (\mathrm{S}(m), g(m, x)) \in R', and R' is closed. As in the base case, R \subseteq R' is false. So g(n, x_n) is the only partner of \mathrm{S}(n), which proves the claim. Step 4 (the function). R is a subset of 
N 	imes X in which each n \in 
N has exactly one partner, so f \coloneqq (R, X) is a function 
N 	o X by @fd2:def-function, and f(n) is the partner of n. Since (0, a) \in R, f(0) = a. For n \in 
N, (n, f(n)) \in R, so closure gives (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, f(n))) \in R, that is, f(\mathrm{S}(n)) = g(n, f(n)). This proves existence, and with Step 1, the theorem. Each Peano axiom has a visible job in the proof. (P3) appears in the base case of Step 3, where no step can produce a pair with first coordinate 0, and again in its inductive step, where it keeps (0, a) in R'. (P4) appears in the inductive step: a pair that steps to first coordinate \mathrm{S}(n) has first coordinate n, where the induction hypothesis applies. (P5) enters through @thm-omega-induction, in Steps 1 and 3. No choice is made: R is the one smallest closed set, and each partner is the only one. From now on a definition “f(0) \coloneqq a, f(\mathrm{S}(n)) \coloneqq g(n, f(n))” on 
N is legitimate whenever a \in X and g \colon 
N 	imes X 	o X is a function, and f is defined by recursion. For X = 
N, a = 0 and g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(x)), which pairs of R have first coordinate 0, 1 or 2? (Here 1, 2, 3, 4 stand for \mathrm{S}(0), \mathrm{S}(1), \mathrm{S}(2), \mathrm{S}(3).) (0, 0), since R contains the starting pair; then (1, 2), since g(0, 0) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0)) = 2; then (2, 4), since g(1, 2) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(2)) = 4. There are no others with these first coordinates, by the claim of Step 3. In the inductive step of the claim, why does R' \coloneqq R \setminus \{(\mathrm{S}(n), y)\} still contain (0, a)? Which axiom is used? (P3): \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0, so the removed pair has a different first coordinate from (0, a) and is not (0, a) (@fd2:def-ordered-pair). The hypothesis that g takes its values in X cannot be dropped. Let X = \{0\}, a = 0, and g(n, x) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0) for n \in 
N, x \in X, so that g maps 
N 	imes X into 
N but not into X. Any f \colon 
N 	o X with the two equations would need f(\mathrm{S}(0)) = g(0, f(0)) = \mathrm{S}(0), and \mathrm{S}(0) 
otin X since \mathrm{S}(0) 
e 0 by (P3); so no such f exists. The proof breaks at Step 2: this step does not map 
N 	imes X into itself, so @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set does not apply. Addition and multiplication With the theorem, addition is the old school definition made official. To add n to m, start at m and take n successor steps: m + 0 is m, and m + \mathrm{S}(n) is one step further than m + n. Multiplication is repeated addition in the same way. Adding n to m is taking n successor steps from m. [Addition and Multiplication on 
N] 1. For each m \in 
N, let A_m \colon 
N 	o 
N be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with X = 
N, a = m and g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(x). The sum of m and n is m + n \coloneqq A_m(n). Thus, for all m, n \in 
N, m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n) . 2. For each m \in 
N, let M_m \colon 
N 	o 
N be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with X = 
N, a = 0 and g(n, x) = x + m. The product of m and n is m \cdot n \coloneqq M_m(n), also written mn. Thus, for all m, n \in 
N, m \cdot 0 = 0, \qquad m \cdot \mathrm{S}(n) = m \cdot n + m . 3. The numerals are 1 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0), 2 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1), 3 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2), and so on. For every n \in 
N, n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n); in particular 1 + 1 = 2 and k + 2 = (k + 1) + 1 for every k \in 
N. In words: (a) and (b) are the two clauses we would write for a school definition, and the theorem guarantees that they define exactly one function A_m, respectively M_m, for each m. The laws of arithmetic Every law of arithmetic that Sets and Functions, Chapter 3 took from the real numbers must now be proved, and the only tools are the four defining equations and induction. The equations are lopsided: they say what happens when the second argument goes up by one, and nothing about the first. So in every induction in the proof of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws we fix all variables but one and induct on the variable that the recursion runs on, the second argument of + or \cdot. [Scratch work] Take the first law that school arithmetic uses without a thought: 0 + n = n. The defining equations do not give it. They give m + 0 = m, with the 0 in the second place, and 0 + n has its 0 in the first. Which variable to induct on? The equations speak about 0 and successors in the second place, and in 0 + n that place is held by n. So induct on n: then the base case is a defining equation, and the step can open 0 + (n + 1) with the other one. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------- m + 0 = m and m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 for all m, n 0 + n = n for every n \in

N] For all k, m, n \in

Each induction is @thm-omega-induction (b), applied to the property stated in the clause, with the other variables fixed. “Def” refers to the equations of @def-omega-arithmetic, “IH” to the induction hypothesis. So P(n + 1) holds, and by @thm-omega-induction (b), P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. (b), (d)–(g) follow by the same move, in the order of the table in the fold below. “Def” refers to the equations of @def-omega-arithmetic, “IH” to the induction hypothesis. The second half of (d) and the last part of (e) are derived from earlier clauses without induction; for the first half of (d) the variable is k, the recursion variable of m(n + k). This proves the theorem. The laws (a)–(g) are the rules of school arithmetic, now proved from @ax-natural-numbers. The next section defines the order from addition and proves its properties with these laws. Do not assume 0 + n = n. It is clause (a) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, proved by induction; the defining equation is n + 0 = n. For the same reason, inducting on m in m + n = n + m gets stuck: the step would need (m + 1) + n, and the definition says nothing about a sum whose first argument is a successor until (a) is proved. The order of the table is forced by the lopsided definition. Commutativity, which lets us move a successor from the second place to the first, comes only after the two facts in (a) that move it by hand; once it is available, (e) and (f) follow the same way for multiplication. The step is m igl(n + (k + 1) igr) = m igl((n + k) + 1 igr) = m(n + k) + m = (mn + mk) + m = mn + (mk + m) = mn + m(k + 1) , by Def of +, Def of \cdot, IH, associativity (c), and Def of \cdot again. Why does the uniqueness half need only an induction, while existence needs the set R? 3. Name the move, and the variable, for proving 0 \cdot n = 0. 4. State the idea of the existence proof in two sentences. (a) (P3) is used in the base case of the claim of Step 3: no step produces a pair with first coordinate 0, since \mathrm{S}(m) 
e 0, so a second pair (0, b) could be removed without breaking closure. It is used again in the inductive step, where \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 keeps (0, a) in R'. (P4) is used in the inductive step: a pair that steps to first coordinate \mathrm{S}(n) has first coordinate n, where the induction hypothesis applies. (b) Uniqueness compares two functions that are given, value by value, and comparing values at n + 1 through the values at n is exactly an induction on n. Existence asks for a function that is not given; induction proves statements and builds nothing. So existence needs an object first, the set R, and induction then proves a statement about it (the claim of Step 3). (c) Fix the others, induct on the recursion variable (@exm-method-induct-on-recursion-variable). There are no others to fix; the recursion variable of 0 \cdot n is n. Base: 0 \cdot 0 = 0 by Def. Each n has exactly one partner in it, because a second partner could be removed without breaking closure, so the set is the graph of the required function. B. By (a), 0 + 3 = \mathrm{S}(0 + 2) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0 + 1)) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0 + 0))) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0))) = 3. Then 3 + 3 = \mathrm{S}(3 + 2) = \mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(3 + 1) igr) = \mathrm{S}\Bigl(\mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(3 + 0) igr)\Bigr) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(3))) = 6 . So 3 \cdot 2 = 6. For 2 \cdot 3, by (b), 2 \cdot 3 = 2 \cdot 2 + 2, and 2 \cdot 2 = 4 by the Quick check above. Then 4 + 2 = \mathrm{S}(4 + 1) = \mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(4 + 0) igr) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(4)) = 6 . So 2 \cdot 3 = 6 = 3 \cdot 2, as (f) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws predicts; but the two computations took different routes, and neither used a law. N and induct on k. Base case: m(n + 0) = mn = mn + 0 = mn + m \cdot 0. Inductive step: suppose m(n + k) = mn + mk. Then m igl(n + (k + 1) igr) = m igl((n + k) + 1 igr) = m(n + k) + m = (mn + mk) + m = \underline{\hspace{6em}} . Justify each equality you add. The completion is (mn + mk) + m = mn + (mk + m) = mn + m(k + 1) , where the first equality is associativity, (c) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, and the second is the defining equation m(k + 1) = mk + m of @def-omega-arithmetic (b), read from right to left. This is the statement for k + 1, so by @thm-omega-induction (b) it holds for every k \in 
N. (This is clause (d) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, already proved; the exercise practices the move.) [B3: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. All letters stand for natural numbers, and you may use @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws. 1. If m + n = 0, then m = n = 0. 2. If mn = m, then n = 1. 3. m \cdot (n + 1) = m \cdot n + n. 4. If m + n = m, then n = 0. 5. If n \cdot n = n, then n = 0. (a) True. Suppose n 
e 0. Then n = \mathrm{S}(k) = k + 1 for some k \in 
N (@prp-peano-predecessor (a), and (c) of @def-omega-arithmetic), and m + n = m + (k + 1) = (m + k) + 1

e 1, since 1 = \mathrm{S}(0)

Step: suppose the property for m, and let (m + 1) + n = m + 1. By law (a), (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1, so (m + n) + 1 = m + 1, and @cor-omega-successor-cancellation gives m + n = m. By the hypothesis, n = 0. (e) False. Take n = 1: 1 \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 0 + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1, by Def and law (a), but 1 
e 0. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: addition is commutative] From the two defining equations of addition, m + 0 = m and m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1, and @thm-omega-induction alone, prove that m + n = n + m for all m, n \in 
N. Prove every auxiliary fact you need. [Hint 1] The definition says what happens when the second argument is 0 or a successor. To use it on n + m, you need to know the same for the first argument: prove two lemmas first. [Hint 2] Start with the first lemma, 0 + n = n, by induction on n; the base is the first equation with m = 0. Then find the second lemma, about (m + 1) + n, yourself. All inductions are by @thm-omega-induction (b). Lemma 1: 0 + n = n for every n. Induct on n. Base: 0 + 0 = 0, by the first equation. Step: if 0 + n = n, then 0 + (n + 1) = (0 + n) + 1 = n + 1, by the second equation and the hypothesis. Lemma 2: (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1 for all m, n. Fix m and induct on n. Base: (m + 1) + 0 = m + 1 = (m + 0) + 1, by the first equation twice. Step: if (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1, then (m + 1) + (n + 1) =  igl((m + 1) + n igr) + 1 =  igl((m + n) + 1 igr) + 1 =  igl(m + (n + 1) igr) + 1 , by the second equation, the hypothesis, and the second equation read from right to left inside the outer + 1. Main induction. Fix m and induct on n for “m + n = n + m”. Base: m + 0 = m = 0 + m, by the first equation and Lemma 1. Step: if m + n = n + m, then m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 = (n + m) + 1 = (n + 1) + m , by the second equation, the hypothesis, and Lemma 2 (with n in the role of m and m in the role of n), read from right to left. Hence m + n = n + m for all m, n \in 
N. Marking scheme. A second route inducts on m in the main induction with n fixed; it needs the same two lemmas, and its base and step map to the same 2 + 2 points. A third route proves associativity and 1 + n = n + 1 (each by induction on n, from the equations and 0 + n = n) and then closes the step as m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 = (n + m) + 1 = n + (m + 1) = n + (1 + m) = (n + 1) + m; those two lemmas together earn the 3 points. title: 1.3 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content:
Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers Sets and Functions, Chapter 3 ordered the natural numbers by the order of the real line, and proved from that order and induction that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least element (@fd2:thm-well-ordering). The natural numbers of @ax-natural-numbers lie on no line. They do have addition, though, and addition already says when one number comes before another: m comes before n when we can count up from m to n. This section takes that as the definition of the order, ties it to the arithmetic of the previous section, proves that it is a total order and a well-ordering, and records the facts about powers and parity that later sections cite. Counting up from m to n The first idea is to copy Sets and Functions: m \le n when n - m \ge 0. On 
N this says nothing yet. There is no subtraction, and “\ge 0” is the very order we are trying to define. What we do have is the sum. In school, 2 \le 5 because three more steps lead from 2 to 5; that statement uses only +. m \le n when n is reached from m by adding a natural number. [Order on 
N] For m, n \in 
N, we write m \le n if n = m + j for some j \in

N. There it was derived from @fd1:ax-induction directly; here the route goes through well-ordering, which was itself proved from @thm-omega-induction. The proof is the move of @fd2:exm-method-smallest-counterexample: a least failure, below which everything holds. As in Logic and Proof, the hypothesis at n = 0 is vacuous (no k < 0, since k \le 0 forces k = 0 by @thm-omega-order (c)), so it hands us P(0) outright. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: considers the set of failures (or argues by contradiction from a failure) and makes it a set. - 3: applies @thm-omega-well-ordering, with the set non-empty, to obtain a least failure a. - 3: shows P(k) for every k < a, using that a is least and the order facts. - 2: applies the hypothesis at a and reaches the contradiction. Fatal errors (0 for the step): citing @fd1:thm-strong-induction (a statement about the natural numbers of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, not proved from @ax-natural-numbers) instead of proving the result; taking a least element of a set not shown to be non-empty. A route by @thm-omega-induction (b) on “P(k) for every k < n” earns the same points: 2 for the property Q(n): "P(k) for every k < n"; 2 for the vacuous base (no k < 0, by @thm-omega-order (c)); 4 for the step (P(n) from the hypothesis, then k < n + 1 gives k \le n by @thm-omega-order (b), so k < n or k = n); 2 for deducing P(n) from Q(n + 1). [C2: Find the error] Here is an attempted proof that any two natural numbers are comparable. The proof is meant to replace the totality step in the proof of @thm-omega-order, so it may cite only results stated before that theorem. Is the conclusion true? Is the proof correct? If not, give the first line that fails, the error, and a counterexample to the step. Claim. For all m, n \in 
N: m \le n or n \le m. (1) Fix m; we use @thm-omega-induction (b) on n, for the property “m \le n or n \le m”. (2) For n = 0: 0 \le m, since m = 0 + m. (3) Suppose that m \le n or n \le m. (4) If n = m + j, then n + 1 = m + (j + 1), so m \le n + 1. (5) If n \le m, then n + 1 \le m, because n < n + 1 and nothing lies strictly between n and n + 1. (6) So m \le n + 1 or n + 1 \le m. (7) By induction, the claim holds. The conclusion is true: it is the totality proved inside @thm-omega-order, and it follows from trichotomy, @thm-omega-order (a). The proof is not correct. The failing line is (5), and it fails for two independent reasons. First, n \le m includes the case n = m, where the conclusion n + 1 \le n is false (the Quick check after @prp-omega-order-arithmetic). This is a missing case, entry (N7) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Counterexample to the step: m = n = 0. The hypothesis of line (3) holds, since 0 \le 0, and so does n \le m; but n + 1 = 1 \le 0 is false, since 0 < 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)). Second, even when n < m, the stated reason does not give n + 1 \le m without comparing m with n + 1: “nothing lies strictly between n and n + 1” excludes n < m < n + 1, and one still needs that m < n + 1, m = n + 1 or n + 1 < m. That is trichotomy, and @thm-omega-order (b), which the reason quotes, was itself proved from trichotomy, that is, from the claim being proved. So the line rests on a fact not available at that point of the proof of @thm-omega-order: entry (N9). Repair. Replace (5) by two cases. If n = m, then m \le n + 1, since n + 1 = m + 1. If n < m, then m = n + j with j 
e 0 (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)), so j = j' + 1 for some j', and m = (n + 1) + j' by @def-omega-arithmetic (a) and @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a); this uses no comparison. Lines (1)–(4), (6) and (7) are correct; fixing m is harmless, since the step never needs the property for another m. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and that the proof is not correct. - 3: names line (5) as the failing line, with either defect: the case n = m, or the hidden comparison of m with n + 1. - 2: classifies the error as (N7), a missing case, or as (N9), a line resting on an unavailable fact (the claim itself). - 2: gives a counterexample to the step, such as m = n = 0 (a case with n = m; the (N9) defect alone has none, since the conclusion of (5) is true when n < m). - 1: gives a repair through m = n + j with j 
e 0. Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; blaming line (1).

title: 1.4 All Peano Systems Are Alike

All Peano Systems Are Alike Section 1.1 fixed one Peano system and called it (
N, 0, \mathrm{S}). It is not the only one. The natural numbers of Sets and Functions, Chapter 3, sitting inside the familiar real numbers, form another; the numbers from 1 on, (
N \setminus \{0\}, 1, \mathrm{S}), form a third; and Axiomatic Set Theory builds a fourth out of sets alone (Section 1.5 describes how). So a question is left: does the choice matter? This section answers no. Any two Peano systems are copies of each other, by exactly one matching, and that matching also carries +, \cdot and < across. Then it says how the later chapters read what Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, and Sets and Functions, Chapters 3 and 4 proved about natural numbers. Two Peano systems, and what “alike” should mean Here is a second Peano system, inside 
N itself: (
N \setminus \{0\}, 1, \mathrm{S}), the natural numbers from 1 on, with the same successor. Exercise C1 of Section 1.1 asked for the check; here it is, in three lines. - \mathrm{S} maps 
N \setminus \{0\} into itself, since \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 by (P3) for 
N. - (P3) holds with e = 1: if \mathrm{S}(n) = 1 = \mathrm{S}(0), then n = 0 by (P4) for 
N, and 0 
otin 
N \setminus \{0\}. (P4) holds because \mathrm{S} is injective on all of 
N. - (P5) holds: if A \subseteq 
N \setminus \{0\} contains 1 and is closed under \mathrm{S}, then \{0\} \cup A contains 0 and is closed under \mathrm{S} (as \mathrm{S}(0) = 1 \in A), so it is 
N by @thm-omega-induction (a), and A = 
N \setminus \{0\}. Its starting point is 1, not 0, yet it counts the same way: n \mapsto \mathrm{S}(n) pairs 0, 1, 2, \dots with 1, 2, 3, \dots, sends start to start, and turns one step into one step. That is the right meaning of “alike”. For Peano systems (M, e, s) and (M', e', s'), call a bijection \psi \colon M 	o M' an isomorphism if \psi(e) = e' \quad 	ext{and} \quad \psi igl(s(x) igr) = s' igl(\psi(x) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } x \in M . In words: \psi renames the elements, sends start to start, and stepping then renaming is the same as renaming then stepping. Being equinumerous is not enough. The bijection 	au \colon 
N 	o 
N that exchanges 1 and 2 and fixes every other number satisfies 	au(0) = 0, but 	au(\mathrm{S}(0)) = 	au(1) = 2, while \mathrm{S}(	au(0)) = \mathrm{S}(0) = 1. So 	au is a bijection from a Peano system to itself that is not an isomorphism: it does not respect the successor. Categoricity, below, is a statement about isomorphisms, and it says much more than “same size”. The categoricity theorem The theorem says that every Peano system is an isomorphic copy of 
N, and so any two are copies of each other, in only one way. [Categoricity of the Peano Axioms] Let (M, e, s) be a Peano system. 1. There is exactly one function \varphi \colon 
N 	o M with \varphi(0) = e and \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n)) for every n \in 
N. 2. This \varphi is a bijection. 3. For any two Peano systems (M, e, s) and (M', e', s') there is exactly one bijection \psi \colon M 	o M' with \psi(e) = e' and \psi(s(x)) = s'(\psi(x)) for every x \in M. Try it first (ten minutes): given a Peano system (M, e, s), which map 
N 	o M would you build, with which theorem, and how would you show that it is onto? [Scratch work] The attempt meets three obstacles, one for each part. ① Which map. It is forced: 0 must go to e, then 1 to s(e), then 2 to s(s(e)), and so on. But “and so on” is not a definition. @thm-omega-recursion turns it into one, with X = M, starting value e and step x \mapsto s(x); it gives existence and uniqueness at once. ② Onto. We know nothing about the elements of M one by one, so we cannot show “each x \in M is s(\dots s(e))” directly. What we have is (P5) for M, which speaks about subsets. So look at the image of \varphi: it contains e and is closed under s, and (P5) does the rest, by @exm-method-closed-subset. ③ One-to-one. Prove “\varphi(m) = \varphi(n) \Rightarrow m = n” by induction on n. If m is fixed before the induction, the hypothesis at n speaks about that one m, while the step needs it at the predecessor of m. So “for every m” goes inside the property. The base and the step then use (P3) and (P4) for M: a successor is never e, and equal successors have equal predecessors. For (c), compose: go back from M to 
N along \varphi^{-1}, then forward to M' along \varphi'. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Givens Goal -------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (M, e, s) a Peano system \varphi \colon 
N 	o M, \varphi(0) = e, \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n)), bijective @thm-omega-recursion with X = M, a = e, g(n, x) = s(x) (a): such a \varphi exists, and only one the image \varphi(
N) contains e and is closed under s onto, by (P5) for M Q(n): for every m, \varphi(m) = \varphi(n) \Rightarrow m = n one-to-one: base by (P3), step by (P4) for M ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Before reading on: which axiom of M gives surjectivity, and which give injectivity? (a) Let g \colon 
N 	imes M 	o M be g(n, x) \coloneqq s(x), a function because s is. By @thm-omega-recursion with X = M and a = e, there is exactly one \varphi \colon 
N 	o M with \varphi(0) = e and \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = g(n, \varphi(n)) = s(\varphi(n)) for every n \in 
N. (b), onto. Let B \coloneqq \varphi(
N) \subseteq M, the image of 
N under \varphi (@fd2:def-image). Then e = \varphi(0) \in B. If x \in B, say x = \varphi(n) with n \in 
N, then \mathrm{S}(n) \in 
N, since \mathrm{S} maps 
N into 
N, and s(x) = s(\varphi(n)) = \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) \in B. So B contains e and is closed under s, and (P5) for M gives B = M. Hence \varphi is surjective (@fd2:def-surjective). (b), one-to-one. Let Q(n) be “for every m \in 
N, if \varphi(m) = \varphi(n), then m = n”. We prove Q(n) for every n \in 
N by @thm-omega-induction (b). Base case. Let m \in 
N with \varphi(m) = \varphi(0) = e. Suppose m 
e 0. Then m = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in 
N (@prp-peano-predecessor (a)), and \varphi(m) = s(\varphi(k)) 
e e by (P3) for M, a contradiction. So m = 0. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N with Q(n), and let m \in 
N with \varphi(m) = \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n)). If m = 0, then s(\varphi(n)) = \varphi(0) = e, against (P3) for M. So m 
e 0, and m = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in 
N (@prp-peano-predecessor (a)). Then s(\varphi(k)) = \varphi(m) = s(\varphi(n)), so \varphi(k) = \varphi(n) by (P4) for M, and k = n by Q(n), applied to k in the place of m. Hence m = \mathrm{S}(k) = \mathrm{S}(n), which is Q(\mathrm{S}(n)). So \varphi is injective (@fd2:def-injective), and with the first half it is a bijection (@fd2:def-bijective). (c) Let \varphi \colon 
N 	o M and \varphi' \colon 
N 	o M' be the maps of (a) for the two systems; both are bijections by (b). By @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \varphi has an inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon M 	o 
N, and we set \psi \coloneqq \varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1} (@fd2:def-composition). The two equations \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \id_M and \varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = \id_
N of @fd2:def-inverse-function also say that \varphi is an inverse of \varphi^{-1}, so \varphi^{-1} is a bijection by @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Hence \psi is a bijection as a composite of bijections (@fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)). \psi has the two properties. Since \varphi(0) = e, we have \varphi^{-1}(e) = 0, so \psi(e) = \varphi'(0) = e'. Let x \in M and n \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}(x), so x = \varphi(n). Then s(x) = \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)), so \varphi^{-1}(s(x)) = \mathrm{S}(n), and \psi igl(s(x) igr) = \varphi' igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = s' igl(\varphi'(n) igr) = s' igl(\psi(x) igr) . Uniqueness. Let \chi \colon M 	o M' be any function with \chi(e) = e' and \chi(s(x)) = s'(\chi(x)) for every x \in M. Then \chi \circ \varphi \colon 
N 	o M' satisfies (\chi \circ \varphi)(0) = \chi(e) = e' and (\chi \circ \varphi) igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = \chi igl(s(\varphi(n)) igr) = s' igl((\chi \circ \varphi)(n) igr) for every n \in 
N. By the uniqueness in (a), for the system M', \chi \circ \varphi = \varphi'. So for every x \in M, \chi(x) = \chi(\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(x))) = \varphi'(\varphi^{-1}(x)) = \psi(x), and \chi = \psi by @fd2:prp-function-equality. This proves the theorem. The proof used one pattern three times: a map out of 
N came from the recursion theorem, two maps out of 
N were shown equal by the uniqueness half of that theorem, and every property of the map came from an induction or from (P5). It deserves a name. [Method: build by recursion, compare by induction] Template. (1) To make a map out of 
N, give its value at 0 and say how the value at \mathrm{S}(n) comes from the value at n; @thm-omega-recursion builds the map, and only one. (2) To show two maps out of 
N equal, check that both satisfy the same two equations, and cite the uniqueness. (3) To prove a property of the map (onto, one-to-one, preserving an operation), induct on n, or apply (P5) to its image. When to use it. Maps between Peano systems; operations defined by recursion; recognizing a formula as the map a recursion defines. The usual failure. “And so on” in place of the theorem, entry (N13) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Citing uniqueness when the equations differ (another start or another step). Fixing m outside Q(n), as ③ of the scratch work warned. The uniqueness in (c) is stronger than stated: no function at all, bijective or not, other than \psi respects e and s. Functions f, g \colon 
N 	o 
N satisfy f(0) = g(0) = 3, f(n + 1) = f(n) + 2 and g(n + 1) = g(n) + 2 for every n. Which step of @exm-method-build-by-recursion gives f = g? What is f(2)? Step (2): both satisfy the equations of @thm-omega-recursion with X = 
N, a = 3 and step h(n, x) = x + 2, so they are equal by its uniqueness. From the equations, f(1) = 3 + 2 = 5 and f(2) = 5 + 2 = 7. Step (2) also finds the map of the theorem without computing it. For the Peano system (
N \setminus \{0\}, 1, \mathrm{S}) of the first subsection, the map n \mapsto \mathrm{S}(n) sends 
N into 
N \setminus \{0\} by (P3), sends 0 to \mathrm{S}(0) = 1, the starting point, and its value \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) at \mathrm{S}(n) is the step s = \mathrm{S} applied to its value \mathrm{S}(n) at n. By the uniqueness in @thm-peano-categoricity (a), \varphi(n) = \mathrm{S}(n) = n + 1 (@def-omega-arithmetic (c)). In particular \varphi(3) = 4; step by step, \varphi(0) = 1, \varphi(1) = \mathrm{S}(1) = 2, \varphi(2) = 3, \varphi(3) = 4. Each axiom of M has a job in (b), and the structures of @exm-peano-axioms-independent show each job failing. These are not Peano systems, so the theorem does not apply to them. But for each of them @thm-omega-recursion, with X = M, a = e and g(n, x) = s(x) exactly as in the proof of (a), still gives exactly one \varphi \colon

title: 1.5 Where \( \nN \) Comes From
content:
Where 
N Comes From Section 1.1 assumed one thing: that a Peano system exists (@ax-natural-numbers). Why should we believe it? Inside the real numbers there is one, the set 
N_{
R} of Sets and Functions (@cor-omega-identification (a)); but that answer presupposes 
R, an object far richer than the one it is meant to support. Axiomatic Set Theory gives a better answer: it builds a Peano system out of sets alone. This section describes that construction, without proofs. Nothing later in the book depends on it. Sets as the raw material Sets and Functions used sets as a working language. Its Section 1.2 stated a short list of working rules (W1)–(W6) that say which sets exist: a set may be cut out of a given set by a property (@fd2:def-set-builder), finitely many objects may be listed, sets have unions, the subsets of a set form a set (@fd2:def-power-set), pairs from two sets form a product, and the number sets are sets. It did not derive these rules from more basic principles, and it took numbers and pairs as given objects. Two questions were left open: where these rules come from, and whether everything else, numbers and pairs included, is a set too. Set theory answers both questions with a list of axioms. The construction below uses seven of them, each of which can be said in one line: - Extensionality. Two sets with the same elements are equal (@fd2:def-set-equality, now an axiom). - Empty set. There is a set with no elements, written \emptyset. - Pairing. For any sets a, b there is a set \{a, b\} whose elements are exactly a and b. - Union. For any set \mathcal{S} of sets there is a set  igcup \mathcal{S} of the elements of its members; with pairing it gives a \cup b. - Power set. For any set X there is a set \powerset{X} of all its subsets. - Specification. For any set A and any property, the elements of A with that property form a set. - Infinity. Some set contains \emptyset and is closed under one particular step, the successor below. Axiomatic Set Theory states the rest of the list (replacement, foundation and choice) and proves everything this section only describes. Two features of the list matter for us. First, every axiom but extensionality says that some set exists. All of them except the empty set and infinity build their set out of sets already given; infinity is the one axiom that hands us a set no finite chain of building steps reaches. Second, there is nothing on the list except sets: no numbers, no points, no pairs as separate objects. So if natural numbers are to exist in this world, they must be particular sets. The question is which ones. The answer is a matter of choice, not discovery. We need a set \omega, an element of it to call zero and a function on it to call the successor, such that the three satisfy (P3), (P4) and (P5) of @def-peano-system. By @thm-peano-categoricity, any two such choices are copies of each other, so it does not matter much which one we make. It only has to be made from the empty set by the operations on the list. Zero and the successor as sets There is only one set we are given outright, so it plays zero. For the successor we need a step that always produces something new, and the axioms offer a natural one: add the set itself as a new element. From here through Exercise B2, 0 and \mathrm{S} stand for these sets, except in a sentence that names 
N, 
N_{
R} or 
R, where they keep their usual meanings; elsewhere in the section, and in the rest of the book, they mean what they meant before: 0 \coloneqq \emptyset , \qquad \mathrm{S}(x) \coloneqq x \cup \{x\} . The right-hand side is a set by pairing (with a = b = x) and union. The first few numerals then come out as follows:  egin{aligned} 1 &= \mathrm{S}(0) = \emptyset \cup \{\emptyset\} = \{0\} , \ 2 &= \mathrm{S}(1) = \{0\} \cup \{1\} = \{0, 1\} , \ 3 &= \mathrm{S}(2) = \{0, 1\} \cup \{2\} = \{0, 1, 2\} . \end{aligned} The pattern is the point of the choice: each numeral is the set of the numerals before it. So n has exactly n elements, and “m comes before n” can be read as m \in n. Thus 2 \in 3, and also 2 \subseteq 3, since every element of 2 is an element of 3. This reading is a feature of this construction, not of the natural numbers. In 
N_{
R} the question “is 2 \in 3?” has no meaning, and a warning in Section 1.4 records that no theorem of this book asks it. These sets are called the von Neumann numerals. Write 3 using only \emptyset and braces. Is 1 \subseteq 3? Is 3 \in 1? 3 = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\}. Yes, 1 \subseteq 3: the only element of 1 = \{0\} is 0, and 0 \in 3. No, 3 
otin 1: the only element of 1 is \emptyset, and 3 
e \emptyset, since 3 has elements. The least inductive set We now want a set holding all the numerals and nothing else. The other axioms build 0, then 1, then 2, one at a time, each in finitely many steps. A set holding all of them at once is what the axiom of infinity is for, and its “particular step” is \mathrm{S}. A set I is inductive if \emptyset \in I and \mathrm{S}(x) \in I whenever x \in I. The axiom of infinity says that an inductive set exists. It says nothing more, and in particular it does not say that its inductive set holds only numerals. The cure is the move of @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set, with I as the ambient set, \emptyset as the starting element and \mathrm{S} as the step. The inductive subsets of I form a set, cut out of \powerset{I} by specification, and their intersection is the smallest inductive subset of I. Axiomatic Set Theory checks that it lies inside every inductive set, not only inside those contained in I, and so does not depend on which I the axiom supplied. This least inductive set is called \omega. Is (\omega, \emptyset, \mathrm{S}) a Peano system? The three axioms fare differently. - (P5) is leastness itself. A subset of \omega that contains \emptyset and is closed under \mathrm{S} is inductive, so it contains the least inductive set \omega; hence it is \omega. - (P3) is immediate. Every \mathrm{S}(x) has x as an element, and \emptyset has none, so \mathrm{S}(x) 
e \emptyset. - (P4) is the real work. From x \cup \{x\} = y \cup \{y\} we want x = y, and for arbitrary sets this needs care. For elements of \omega it holds because each n \in \omega has two properties that the pattern above suggests: an element of an element of n is an element of n, and n 
otin n. Axiomatic Set Theory proves both by induction on \omega, and (P4) follows from them. With all three in hand, (\omega, \emptyset, \mathrm{S}) is a Peano system. By @thm-peano-categoricity it is a copy of (
N, 0, \mathrm{S}), by exactly one isomorphism, which carries the von Neumann numeral n to the natural number n. So the assumption @ax-natural-numbers is not a new article of faith: it follows from the axioms for sets. A reader who trusts them may read @ax-natural-numbers as a theorem. An inductive set need not be \omega. The axiom of infinity supplies some inductive set, which may hold much else. In the same way, 
R contains 0 and is closed under x \mapsto x + 1, and
