title: The Integers
content:
The Integers In the natural numbers, “subtract 5 from 3” has no answer. The school integers answer it by a stroke of the pen: add negative numbers, and trust that everything still works. This chapter builds them instead, with no new assumption. A pair (a, b) of natural numbers records the difference a - b without performing it, two pairs record the same difference when a + d = b + c, and an integer is a class of such pairs. The quotient set of Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 makes this a set, and the number of pairs per integer is infinite, so nothing about an integer may depend on which pair we use to write it. That is the danger of the whole chapter. A formula that looks fine on pairs can give different answers for two pairs of the same class, and then it is no operation on integers. Section 2.2 proves one lemma that tells us what to check, and the check is done once, one argument at a time. With the operations in hand, Section 2.3 names the structure they form, a commutative ring, and checks every law by pushing it down to the natural numbers. Section 2.4 adds the order, from one choice, the set of positive elements, and proves the rules for inequalities that every later chapter uses. Section 2.5 closes with division with remainder and the even-odd split. At the end 
Z is an ordered ring in which every set bounded below has a least element, and it is still not a field. What you need. Chapter 1: induction and the recursion theorem on 
N (@thm-omega-induction, @thm-omega-recursion), with the citing rule of Section 1.4 for results of the earlier volumes (@cor-omega-identification), the arithmetic and order of 
N (@def-omega-arithmetic, @cor-omega-successor-cancellation, @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic, @thm-omega-order), well-ordering (@thm-omega-well-ordering), and parity (@prp-omega-powers-parity). Sets and Functions: ordered pairs, products, functions and their equality (@fd2:def-ordered-pair, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality); equivalence relations, classes, quotient sets and the partition theorem, with the method for checking a rule on representatives, from its Section 5.2 (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-equivalence-class, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition, @fd2:exm-method-well-definedness, @fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map); the least-element method (@fd2:exm-method-least-element); for Section 2.4’s C1 only, finite and infinite sets from its Section 4.1 (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @fd2:prp-subset-finite); and, for Section 2.5 only, the school facts about division and parity that it compares with (@fd2:thm-division-algorithm, @fd2:thm-even-or-odd, @fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime). Logic and Proof: the square of an even integer (@fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even), for a comparison in Section 2.5. Time. About 20 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 25 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Integers as Classes of Pairs. Why 3 - 5 needs a new kind of number; pairs of natural numbers with (a, b) \sim (c, d) when a + d = b + c, checked to be an equivalence relation; 
Z as the quotient set; pictures of the classes on a staircase; and the normal form, by which every class contains exactly one pair of the form (n, 0) or (0, n). - Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers. The lemma on functions defined on classes through representatives, with its one-argument-at-a-time check; the sum, product and negative of integers, shown well defined; rules that look like functions and are not; and the copy of 
N inside 
Z, which turns the class [(a, b)] into the difference a - b. - Commutative Rings; the Integers Are One. The ring and field axioms; the integers a commutative ring with 1 
e 0, every law checked by the move that reduces it to the level below; the algebra that follows from the axioms alone. - Ordered Rings and the Rules for Inequalities. Ordered rings and fields; an order from a positive set; the order of 
Z; the rules for inequalities, including multiplication by a positive and by a negative element; multiples; least and greatest elements of sets of integers; and a ring that cannot be ordered. - Division with Remainder. Divisibility on the constructed integers and its rules; division with remainder, existence and uniqueness, with the existence proof by a least element; and even and odd integers, exactly one of the two. Named moves - Check on representatives, one argument at a time (@exm-method-one-argument-at-a-time, with @fd2:exm-method-well-definedness and @thm-well-defined-on-classes). Change one representative with the other fixed; each change is one identity at the level below. A formula symmetric in its two inputs gets the second change free. (Section 2.2) - Reduce to the level below (@exm-method-reduce-to-level-below). Write a law about classes on representatives; the two sides become the same pair, or two related pairs, by an identity in 
N. (Section 2.3) - Turn the comparison into one positive element (@exm-method-one-positive-element). To compare a and b, look at b - a and ask whether it is in the positive set. (Section 2.4) - Order from a positive set (@prp-order-from-positives). Say which elements are positive, check (P1) and (P2), and read off every rule for inequalities. (Section 2.4) - Least element (@fd2:exm-method-least-element). A set of integers bounded below has a least element; it finds the remainder in Section 2.5 and the integer part in Chapter 3. (Sections 2.4 and 2.5) Threads - Well-definedness, the level below and positive sets. Section 2.1 makes integers from pairs of naturals, Section 3.1 makes rationals from pairs of integers, and Chapter 5 makes real numbers from classes of sequences of rationals, each time by the lemma and the check of Section 2.2, the move of Section 2.3 and the order of Section 2.4. - Least elements. Chapter 1 proves it for 
N, Section 2.4 for sets of integers bounded below, Section 2.5 uses it for the remainder, and Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 takes it up for divisibility and the Euclidean algorithm. - The copy of 
N. Section 2.2 identifies n with [(n, 0)]; every later chapter writes 
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q without further comment. Summary A pair (a, b) of natural numbers records the difference a - b, and the relation a + d = b + c is an equivalence relation (@prp-integer-pairs-equivalence); its classes form 
Z (@def-integers-as-classes), and each class has a normal form (n, 0) or (0, n) (@prp-integer-normal-form). A rule defined on classes through representatives is a function when it passes the check of @thm-well-defined-on-classes; the sum, product and negative do (@def-integer-operations, @prp-integer-operations-well-defined), and n \mapsto [(n, 0)] copies 
N into 
Z (@prp-naturals-embed-integers). 
Z is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @thm-integers-commutative-ring), and the algebra of a ring follows (@prp-ring-algebra). The positive classes make 
Z an ordered ring (@def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-order-from-positives, @def-integer-order, @thm-integers-ordered-ring) with the usual rules for inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules); a set of integers bounded below has a least element (@prp-integer-least-element). Divisibility has its usual rules (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers), division with remainder exists and is unique (@thm-integers-division-remainder), and every integer is even or odd and not both (@cor-integers-even-odd). What is open: 
Z is not a field, since 2x = 1 has no solution. Chapter 3 repeats the construction with pairs of integers to supply quotients. Terms - integer: a class [(a, b)] of pairs of natural numbers under a + d = b + c (@def-integers-as-classes). - normal form: the one pair (n, 0) or (0, n) in a class (@prp-integer-normal-form). - well defined, induced function: a rule on classes that does not depend on the representatives, and the function it gives (@thm-well-defined-on-classes). - commutative ring, field: a set with addition and multiplication satisfying the laws (F1)–(F7), (F9), and also 1 
e 0 and (F8) for a field (@def-commutative-ring-and-field). - ordered commutative ring, ordered field: a ring or field with a relation < satisfying (O1)–(O4) (@def-ordered-ring-and-field). - positive set: a subset P closed under sums and products, with every element exactly one of positive, zero or negative (@prp-order-from-positives). - discreteness: no integer lies strictly between n and n + 1 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring). - multiple n \cdot a: a added n times, defined by recursion (Section 2.4). - divides, prime: a \mid b when b = ka for an integer k; p is prime when p \ge 2 and its only positive divisors are 1 and p (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers). - quotient, remainder: the q and r with a = qn + r and 0 \le r < n (@thm-integers-division-remainder). - even, odd: a = 2q or a = 2q + 1 (@cor-integers-even-odd).

title: 2.1 The Integers as Classes of Pairs
content:
The Integers as Classes of Pairs Chapter 1 took the natural numbers to be a Peano system and built on it addition, multiplication and the order, with the laws of arithmetic and well-ordering; by Section 1.4 any two Peano systems are alike, and from here on 
N is that system (@cor-omega-identification, with the citing rule of Section 1.4). In 
N the equation 5 + x = 3 has no solution: 5 \le 5 + x for every x \in 
N by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), while 3 < 5 by the same result, as 5 = 3 + 2 with 2 
e 0. So 5 + x = 3 would give 5 \le 3 < 5, hence 5 < 5, which @thm-omega-order (a) rules out. This section builds a larger set 
Z, out of 
N alone, with the one tool of Sets and Functions, Section 5.2: the quotient of a set by an equivalence relation. What we use about the natural numbers Every fact about 
N in this section and the next is one of the following results of Chapter 1, cited where a proof uses it. The defining equation n + 0 = n and the evaluation of numeral sums and comparisons such as 2 + 3 = 5 and 0 
e 2 rest on @def-omega-arithmetic and @thm-omega-order and are not cited each time. - Defining equations (@def-omega-arithmetic (a), (b)): n + 0 = n, m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n), n \cdot 0 = 0; the numerals 1 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0), 2 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1), …, with n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n) (@def-omega-arithmetic (c)). - Laws of arithmetic (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws): + and \cdot are commutative and associative, \cdot distributes over +, and 0 + n = n, 1 \cdot n = n, 0 \cdot n = 0. - Cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b), (f)): m + k = n + k gives m = n, and so does mk = nk with k 
e 0. - Order (@thm-omega-order (a)): < is a strict total order, so exactly one of m < n, m = n, n < m holds. - Order and addition (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), (c)): m \le n if and only if n = m + j for some j \in 
N, and m < n if and only if this holds with j 
e 0; adding preserves <. - Small facts and well-ordering: 0 < 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)); nothing lies strictly between n and \mathrm{S}(n) (@thm-omega-order (b)); every non-empty subset of 
N has a least element (@thm-omega-well-ordering). That is the whole list for now. Nothing about the integers or the rationals of school enters a proof: from here on they are the sets this chapter and the next build, and their familiar properties become theorems. A naive attempt The school picture of an integer is “a natural number with a sign”: +3, -2, 0. It is tempting to take that literally and let an integer be a pair (s, n) with a sign s \in \{0, 1\} (read 0 as “plus” and 1 as “minus”) and a size n \in 
N. Two things go wrong at once. First, zero gets two names, (0, 0) and (1, 0): a “plus zero” and a “minus zero”. Either both stay, and every theorem must treat them as the same, or one is banned, and every definition must check that it never produces the banned one. Second, addition needs cases. Adding +m and -n should give +(m - n) when n \le m and -(n - m) when m < n, where m - n is the subtraction of @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), defined on 
N only when n \le m. There are four sign patterns for a sum, and two of them split again by the order of the sizes. A proof that addition is associative would split by the signs of all three terms and then by the order of their sizes, and every case would subtract in 
N in its own direction. The trouble in both is the same: the definition performs a subtraction that 
N can only do one way round. The construction below never performs it. It records the subtraction as a pair, and lets an equivalence relation decide when two recorded subtractions should count as equal. Pairs that record a difference Think of a pair (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N as a note saying “a minus b”, to be computed later or never. The note (3, 5) is legitimate even though 3 - 5 is not a natural number. Many notes say the same thing: (3, 5), (0, 2) and (10, 12) all describe “two less than nothing”, which school calls -2. When do two notes (a, b) and (c, d) describe the same thing? School would write a - b = c - d, and then add b + d to both sides to get a + d = b + c. That last equation is the one we keep, because it uses only addition, which 
N has for all inputs. The computation with minus signs is a heuristic, borrowed from school to find the definition; the definition does not depend on it. An integer is a difference you have not computed yet. [The Integers] For (a, b), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N, let (a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff a + d = b + c . The set of integers is the quotient set 
Z \coloneqq (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim} of @fd2:def-quotient-set, and an integer is an element of 
Z. The class of the pair (a, b) is written [(a, b)]: [(a, b)] = \{ (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N : (c, d) \sim (a, b) \} . In words: two pairs are related when their cross sums agree, the first coordinate of each added to the second coordinate of the other. The relation is a subset of (
N 	imes 
N) 	imes (
N 	imes 
N), described by a property (@fd2:def-relation, @fd2:def-cartesian-product). An integer is one whole class: the set of all pairs that record the same difference. The notation [(a, b)] is the class notation [x] of @fd2:def-equivalence-class with x = (a, b); no new bracket is introduced. Well-definedness. @fd2:def-quotient-set is stated for an equivalence relation. Until \sim is shown to be one, the definition of 
Z is a plan, not a definition. The next proposition supplies the missing check, and it is placed directly after the definition for that reason. An integer is a set of pairs. It is not a natural number with a sign, and it is not a pair. Sets and Functions, Chapter 1 adopted the convention that a pair is not a number (after @fd2:def-ordered-pair). The same care is needed here: [(0, 2)] is the set \{ (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), \dots \}, and the school -2 is what those pairs have in common. The construction takes “what they have in common” to be the set of them. [The Relation Behind the Integers] The relation \sim of @def-integers-as-classes is an equivalence relation on 
N 	imes 
N (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). This is the check of @fd2:exm-method-relation-properties: three clauses, each unwound to an equation in 
N. Reflexivity and symmetry are rearrangements of one equation, by commutativity. Transitivity has two hypotheses, a + d = b + c and c + f = d + e, and a goal a + f = b + e in which c and d do not appear. In school one would subtract them. In 
N we add the two equations, so that c + d appears on both sides, and then remove it by cancellation. Before reading on: which line uses cancellation in 
N, and why is it more direct than subtracting c + d? We check (Eq1)–(Eq3) of @fd2:def-equivalence-relation. Let (a, b), (c, d), (e, f) \in 
N 	imes 
N. (Eq1) a + b = b + a by commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b)), so (a, b) \sim (a, b). (Eq2) Suppose (a, b) \sim (c, d), that is, a + d = b + c. By commutativity, c + b = b + c = a + d = d + a, and c + b = d + a says (c, d) \sim (a, b). (Eq3) Suppose (a, b) \sim (c, d) and (c, d) \sim (e, f), that is, a + d = b + c \quad 	ext{and} \quad c + f = d + e . Adding the two equations gives (a + d) + (c + f) = (b + c) + (d + e). By associativity and commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c)), the left side is (a + f) + (c + d) and the right side is (b + e) + (c + d), so (a + f) + (c + d) = (b + e) + (c + d) . By cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) with k = c + d, a + f = b + e. That is (a, b) \sim (e, f). This proves that \sim is an equivalence relation. The answer to the prompt is the last line of (Eq3). Subtracting c + d would need a check that the difference exists in 
N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)), and reading the difference off uses uniqueness, itself proved by cancellation. Cancellation removes c + d for every value, with no check. So 
Z = (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim} is now defined, and by @fd2:thm-classes-partition its elements partition 
N 	imes 
N: every pair lies in exactly one integer, and [(a, b)] = [(c, d)] if and only if a + d = b + c. Which classes contain (4, 0), (0, 4) and (4, 4)? Is any pair in two of them? Each pair lies in its own class, and (4, 4) \sim (0, 0) (cross sums 4 + 0 = 4 + 0), so [(4, 4)] = [(0, 0)], the class of zero. The three classes are distinct: for (4, 0) and (0, 4) the cross sums are 4 + 4 
e 0 + 0; for (4, 0) and (0, 0), 4 + 0 
e 0 + 0; for (0, 4) and (0, 0), 0 + 0 
e 4 + 0. Distinct classes are disjoint (@fd2:thm-classes-partition), so no pair lies in two of them. Pictures of classes The quarter plane 
N 	imes 
N is a grid of lattice points, and the classes are easy to see in it. [Three classes, listed and drawn] List the elements (x, y) with x \le 4 of each of the classes [(3, 5)], [(0, 0)] and [(4, 1)], and describe each class as a set of lattice points. The class [(3, 5)]. A pair (x, y) lies in it when x + 5 = y + 3. This holds if and only if y = x + 2. Indeed, if y = x + 2, then y + 3 = x + (2 + 3) = x + 5 by associativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c)). Conversely, x + 5 = (x + 2) + 3, so x + 5 = y + 3 gives (x + 2) + 3 = y + 3, and cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) gives y = x + 2. So [(3, 5)] = \{ (x, x + 2) : x \in 
N \} , and, since the natural numbers x \le 4 are exactly 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (@thm-omega-order (c)), the elements with x \le 4 are (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 6). The class [(0, 0)]. Here the condition is x + 0 = y + 0, that is, x = y, since n + 0 = n (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)). So [(0, 0)] = \{ (x, x) : x \in 
N \}, the diagonal, and, likewise, the elements with x \le 4 are (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4). The class [(4, 1)]. The condition x + 1 = y + 4 holds if and only if x = y + 3, by the same two steps as for [(3, 5)]. So [(4, 1)] = \{ (y + 3, y) : y \in 
N \}. Its elements with x \le 4 are (3, 0) and (4, 1) only: x = y + 3 = 3 + y gives 3 \le x (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)); with x \le 4 = \mathrm{S}(3), x is 3 or 4, since no natural number lies strictly between 3 and \mathrm{S}(3) (@thm-omega-order (b)); and then y + 3 = 3 = 0 + 3 or y + 3 = 4 = 1 + 3, so y is 0 or 1 by cancellation. Each of these three classes is the set of lattice points on one diagonal line y = x + k or x = y + k of the quarter plane, starting on an axis and running up and to the right. The picture shows the three classes as three diagonals: [(3, 5)] solid with filled dots, [(0, 0)] dashed with open dots, [(4, 1)] dotted with squares. Every pair lies in exactly one class (@fd2:thm-classes-partition), so no two of these diagonals share a lattice point; after the normal form below we see that every class is a diagonal of this kind, so every lattice point lies on exactly one of them. The class [(0, 0)] is the degenerate case: it is the integer zero, and it is the only class whose line passes through the origin. A non-example by minimal change. Replace the sums in the definition by products: on 
N 	imes 
N, let (a, b) \approx (c, d) mean ad = bc. This is still reflexive (ab = ba) and symmetric (ad = bc gives cb = da), both by commutativity of \cdot (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (f)). It is not transitive: (1, 1) \approx (0, 0), \qquad (0, 0) \approx (2, 1), \qquad 	ext{but} \qquad (1, 1) 
ot\approx (2, 1) , since 1 \cdot 0 = 1 \cdot 0, 0 \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 2 and 1 \cdot 1 
e 1 \cdot 2. The clause that fails is (Eq3), and the line of the proof above that has no counterpart is cancellation. Additive cancellation holds for every k; multiplicative cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (f)) needs k 
e 0, and the pair (0, 0) supplies a middle factor that is 0. When Section 3.1 builds fractions with this product relation, it excludes zero second coordinates for exactly this reason. Why this definition Why cross sums. “a - b = c - d” cannot be the definition, because a - b is defined in 
N only when b \le a. The cross-sum equation a + d = b + c says the same thing whenever both differences exist, and it makes sense for every two pairs. Why whole classes. Each class has a simplest pair, one with a coordinate 0, as the next proposition shows. One could define 
Z as the set of these simplest pairs instead. But then the sum of (3, 0) and (0, 5) would have to be brought back to a simplest pair, (0, 2), by a subtraction in 
N in the right direction: the case analysis of the naive attempt returns. With classes, any representatives may be combined, and the equivalence relation absorbs the bookkeeping. The price is the check of the next section: a definition through representatives must not depend on which ones were used. The class of (0, 0) is the diagonal; it will be the zero of 
Z. The first result about the new set says that each class has exactly one simplest name. [Normal Form of an Integer] 1. Every class [(a, b)] \in 
Z contains exactly one pair of the form (n, 0) or (0, n) with n \in 
N (the pair (0, 0) has both forms and counts once). Precisely, for each (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N exactly one of the following holds: - a = b + k for some k 
e 0, and then [(a, b)] = [(k, 0)]; - a = b, and then [(a, b)] = [(0, 0)]; - b = a + k for some k 
e 0, and then [(a, b)] = [(0, k)]. 2. For all m, n \in 
N: if [(m, 0)] = [(n, 0)], then m = n; and if [(0, m)] = [(0, n)], then m = n. The three cases are the three cases of trichotomy for a and b, and @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) turns each inequality into an equation with a non-zero k. In each case one line of arithmetic shows that (a, b) is related to the simplest pair. For “exactly one pair”, two simplest pairs of the same form are handled by (b), so we prove (b) first. Two of opposite forms, (k, 0) and (0, l) with k, l 
e 0, would need k + l = 0, which the order forbids. (b) Suppose [(m, 0)] = [(n, 0)]. By @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), (m, 0) \sim (n, 0), that is, m + 0 = 0 + n. Since m + 0 = m (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)) and 0 + n = n (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)), m = n. Likewise [(0, m)] = [(0, n)] gives 0 + n = m + 0, so n = m. (a), the three cases. Let (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N. By @thm-omega-order (a), exactly one of b < a, a = b, a < b holds. By @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), b < a holds if and only if a = b + k for some k 
e 0, and a < b if and only if b = a + k for some k 
e 0. So exactly one of the three listed conditions holds. In each case the stated equality of classes follows from @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), once the two pairs are shown to be related: - if a = b + k, then a + 0 = a = b + k (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)), so (a, b) \sim (k, 0); - if a = b, then a + 0 = b + 0, so (a, b) \sim (0, 0); - if b = a + k, then a + k = b = b + 0 (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)), so (a, b) \sim (0, k). In particular every class contains a pair of the form (n, 0) or (0, n). (a), only one such pair. Let C be a class containing two such pairs p and p'. Since both lie in C, [p] = C = [p'] by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). If p = (m, 0) and p' = (n, 0), then m = n by (b), so p = p'; likewise if both have the form (0, \cdot). This covers every case in which one of the pairs is (0, 0), since (0, 0) has both forms. There remains p = (k, 0) and p' = (0, l) with k 
e 0 and l 
e 0. Then p \sim p' says k + l = 0 + 0 = 0. Since l 
e 0, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) gives k < 0; and since k = 0 + k (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)) with k 
e 0, it also gives 0 < k. By transitivity k < k, which @thm-omega-order (a) rules out. So this case cannot occur, and the pair is unique. So every integer has a normal form: it is [(n, 0)] for a unique n \in 
N, or [(0, n)] for a unique n \in 
N with n 
e 0. In the picture, every class is a diagonal: (x, y) \sim (n, 0) means x + 0 = y + n, that is, x = y + n, and (x, y) \sim (0, n) means x + n = y + 0, that is, y = x + n (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)), so [(n, 0)] = \{ (y + n, y) : y \in 
N \} \quad 	ext{and} \quad [(0, n)] = \{ (x, x + n) : x \in 
N \} . The normal form is where the class’s diagonal meets an axis. The next section reads [(n, 0)] as the natural number n and [(0, n)] as its negative; this is how the description of Sets and Functions, Section 3.1, “an integer is a natural number or the negative of one”, becomes a theorem about the constructed 
Z. Find the normal forms of [(17, 9)] and [(9, 17)], and a third pair in each class. Since 17 = 9 + 8, [(17, 9)] = [(8, 0)] and [(9, 17)] = [(0, 8)] (@prp-integer-normal-form (a)). Third pairs: (18, 10) and (10, 18), since 17 + 10 = 9 + 18 gives both (17, 9) \sim (18, 10) and (9, 17) \sim (10, 18). A property of a class must not be read off one representative. “The integer [(a, b)] is small when a \le 3” sounds like a property of integers and is not one: [(3, 3)] = [(5, 5)], the first pair has a = 3 \le 3, and the second has a = 5. The class is “small” or not according to the name we happened to use. The property “[(a, b)] is positive when b < a” looks the same and happens to be safe: if (a, b) \sim (a', b') and b < a, then b' < a'. That needs a proof, and Section 2.4 gives it before it calls any integer positive. Is (2, 7) \sim (10, 15)? Is (2, 7) \sim (15, 10)? Yes: the cross sums are 2 + 15 = 17 and 7 + 10 = 17. No: the cross sums are 2 + 10 = 12 and 7 + 15 = 22, and 12 
e 22. In school terms, (2, 7) and (10, 15) both record “five less”, while (15, 10) records “five more”. The normal forms agree: 7 = 2 + 5 and 15 = 10 + 5, so [(2, 7)] = [(0, 5)] = [(10, 15)], while [(15, 10)] = [(5, 0)], a different class by @prp-integer-normal-form (a). The set 
Z exists, and each element has a simplest name. It has no arithmetic yet. The next section defines the sum and product of two integers by formulas on representatives, and the warning above is the question it must answer for each formula. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the relation \sim and the set 
Z of @def-integers-as-classes in symbols. 2. Which pairs with a coordinate equal to 0 lie in [(6, 9)]? 3. Why does the proof of @prp-integer-pairs-equivalence cancel c + d rather than subtract it? 4. True or false, with a reason: [(1, 1)] = [(5, 5)]. (a) For (a, b), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N: (a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff a + d = b + c; and 
Z \coloneqq (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim} = \{ [(a, b)] : (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N \}. (b) Only (0, 3). A pair (x, 0) in the class would need x + 9 = 0 + 6 = 6 (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)); but 9 \le x + 9 by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) (with @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b) to write x + 9 = 9 + x), and 6 < 9, so x + 9 = 6 would give 9 \le 6 < 9, and then 9 < 9, which @thm-omega-order (a) excludes. A pair (0, y) needs 0 + 9 = y + 6, that is, 3 + 6 = y + 6, so y = 3 by cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)). This agrees with @prp-integer-normal-form (a): 9 = 6 + 3, so [(6, 9)] = [(0, 3)], and the class has exactly one pair with a coordinate 0. (c) Subtraction in 
N is defined only when the number subtracted is at most the other (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). Here c + d is at most both sides, so subtracting would be possible, but only after that check, and reading off the differences uses the uniqueness in (a), which is itself proved by cancellation. Cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) holds for every k \in 
N with no check, so the proof uses it directly. (d) True. (1, 1) \sim (5, 5) because 1 + 5 = 1 + 5, so the classes are equal by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). Both are the zero class [(0, 0)]. B. Practice [B1: Three look-alike relations] On 
N 	imes 
N, determine which of the following relations are equivalence relations. For each one, decide which of (Eq1)–(Eq3) hold. Justify your answer. 1. (a, b) \approx_1 (c, d) if and only if a + c = b + d. 2. (a, b) \approx_2 (c, d) if and only if a + 2d = 2b + c. 3. (a, b) \approx_3 (c, d) if and only if a + d \le b + c. (a) Symmetric, but neither reflexive nor transitive. Symmetric: a + c = b + d gives c + a = d + b by commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b)). Not reflexive: (0, 1) \approx_1 (0, 1) would need 0 + 0 = 1 + 1, that is, 0 = 2, which is false. Not transitive: (0, 1) \approx_1 (1, 0) since 0 + 1 = 1 + 0, and (1, 0) \approx_1 (0, 1) since 1 + 0 = 0 + 1; transitivity would give (0, 1) \approx_1 (0, 1), which we just saw is false. Notice that every pair is related to something, since (a, b) \approx_1 (b, a) by commutativity. A symmetric relation in which every element is related to something still need not be reflexive: “x related to y, so y related to x, so x related to x” uses transitivity, and that is what fails here. (b) An equivalence relation. (Eq1) a + 2b = 2b + a. (Eq2) a + 2d = 2b + c gives c + 2b = 2d + a, by commutativity. (Eq3) Suppose a + 2d = 2b + c and c + 2f = 2d + e. Adding, and rearranging by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c), (a + 2f) + (2d + c) = (2b + e) + (2d + c) , and cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) gives a + 2f = 2b + e. In school terms the pair (a, b) records a - 2b, and the relation says a - 2b = c - 2d. (c) Reflexive and transitive, not symmetric. (Eq1) a + b \le b + a, since the two sides are equal. (Eq3) First, for x, y, u, v \in 
N, x \le y and u \le v give x + u \le y + v: by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), y = x + i and v = u + j for some i, j \in 
N, so y + v = (x + u) + (i + j) by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c), and (a) again gives x + u \le y + v. Now let a + d \le b + c and c + f \le d + e. Adding and rearranging, (a + f) + (c + d) \le (b + e) + (c + d) . If b + e < a + f, then (b + e) + (c + d) < (a + f) + (c + d) by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (c), contradicting the display by trichotomy (@thm-omega-order (a)). So a + f \le b + e, by trichotomy again. Not symmetric: (0, 1) \approx_3 (0, 0) since 0 + 0 \le 1 + 0, that is, 0 \le 1; but (0, 0) \approx_3 (0, 1) would need 0 + 1 \le 0 + 0, that is, 1 \le 0, which is false since 0 < 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)). [B2: A class in set-builder form] Let (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N. Describe the class [(a, b)] by a set-builder expression, in the two cases b \le a and a \le b. Hence describe [(7, 2)] and [(2, 7)]. Case b \le a. Write a = b + k with k \in 
N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). We claim [(a, b)] = \{ (y + k, y) : y \in 
N \} . A pair (x, y) lies in [(a, b)] when x + b = y + a, that is, x + b = (y + k) + b by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c), (b). By cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) this holds if and only if x = y + k; the converse direction is substitution. So the elements of the class are exactly the pairs (y + k, y), y \in 
N. Case a \le b. Write b = a + k (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). In the same way, (x, y) \sim (a, b) means x + (a + k) = y + a, which by rearranging and canceling a holds if and only if y = x + k. So [(a, b)] = \{ (x, x + k) : x \in 
N \}. The two descriptions agree when a = b (then k = 0), as they must. For the examples, 7 = 2 + 5, so [(7, 2)] = \{ (y + 5, y) : y \in 
N \}, and [(2, 7)] = \{ (x, x + 5) : x \in 
N \}. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the relation that builds 
Z] Let \sim be the relation of @def-integers-as-classes on 
N 	imes 
N. 1. Prove that \sim is an equivalence relation. 2. Prove that if (a, b) \sim (a', b') and (c, d) \sim (c', d'), then (a + c, b + d) \sim (a' + c', b' + d'). 3. Say in one sentence what (b) means for a rule that adds two integers by adding representatives coordinatewise. Name the property of 
N behind each step. (a) This is @prp-integer-pairs-equivalence; here is the proof once more. Reflexive: a + b = b + a by commutativity. Symmetric: if a + d = b + c, then c + b = d + a by commutativity. Transitive: let a + d = b + c and c + f = d + e. Adding the two equations and rearranging by associativity and commutativity gives (a + f) + (c + d) = (b + e) + (c + d), and cancellation of c + d (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) gives a + f = b + e. (b) The hypotheses are a + b' = b + a' and c + d' = d + c'. Adding them, (a + b') + (c + d') = (b + a') + (d + c') . By associativity and commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c)), the left side is (a + c) + (b' + d') and the right side is (b + d) + (a' + c'). So (a + c) + (b' + d') = (b + d) + (a' + c') , which is the cross-sum equation for (a + c, b + d) \sim (a' + c', b' + d'). (c) The class of (a + c, b + d) does not depend on which representatives of [(a, b)] and [(c, d)] were used, so “add representatives coordinatewise, then take the class” is well defined: it assigns exactly one integer to each pair of integers. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: reflexive and symmetric, each citing commutativity of + in 
N. - 3: transitivity: combines the two hypotheses into one equation with a common summand on both sides (by adding them, or by substituting one into the other) and removes that summand by cancellation in 
N, named as such. - 2: in (b), combines the two hypotheses (by adding them, or by substituting both into a rearranged sum). - 2: in (b), rearranges by associativity and commutativity to the cross-sum equation for the two sums. - 1: (c) concludes that the coordinatewise sum is well defined on classes. A proof of (b) that changes one argument at a time (first (a, b) to (a', b') with (c, d) fixed, then the other) and joins the two by transitivity earns the four points of (b) if each step is justified. Fatal errors (0 for the step): subtracting in 
N (for instance “subtract d from both sides”) without showing that the difference exists; proving only reflexivity and symmetry and calling the relation an equivalence relation.

title: 2.2 Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers
content:
Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers Section 2.1 built 
Z as the set of classes of \sim on 
N 	imes 
N, and gave each integer a normal form (@prp-integer-normal-form). The integers cannot yet be added. Every operation on classes will be defined by a formula on representatives, and Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 showed what can go wrong: a formula that gives two answers for one class (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map). This section proves, once and for all, the lemma that says when such a formula defines a function. It then uses the lemma for the sum, product and negative of integers, and finds a copy of 
N inside 
Z. Definitions through representatives In Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 the addition of 
Z/n was defined by [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b], and @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic checked that the right side depends only on the classes, not on the integers a and b used to name them. In @fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map the same kind of formula, [a]_6 \mapsto [a]_4, gave one class two values, and so defined no function. The same situation will recur throughout this volume: for 
Z in this section, for 
Q in Section 3.1, and for 
R later in this volume. Each time, a set is a quotient X/{\sim}, and something is defined on it by a formula on elements of X. Rather than repeat the argument of @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic for every formula, we separate it into two parts: a general lemma, proved here once, which turns a check on representatives into a function on classes; and the check itself, which is different for each formula and is all that remains to do each time. A rule “[x] \mapsto something computed from x” is called well defined when representatives of the same class always give the same result. The lemma below says that being well defined is enough, in three settings: a map from one quotient to another, a binary operation on a quotient, and a property of classes. The lemma A rule on classes is a function as soon as equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs. [Functions on Classes] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X, and \approx an equivalence relation on a set Y. Classes are taken for \sim in X and for \approx in Y. 1. Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function such that, for all x, x' \in X, x \sim x' implies f(x) \approx f(x'). Then there is exactly one function F \colon X/{\sim} 	o Y/{\approx} with F([x]) = [f(x)] for every x \in X. 2. Let g \colon X 	imes X 	o X be a function such that, for all x, x', y, y' \in X,  egin{aligned} x \sim x' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) , \ y \sim y' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x, y') . \end{aligned} Then there is exactly one function G \colon (X/{\sim}) 	imes (X/{\sim}) 	o X/{\sim} with G([x], [y]) = [g(x, y)] for all x, y \in X. 3. Let S \subseteq X be such that, for all x, x' \in X, x \sim x' and x \in S imply x' \in S. Let  ar S \coloneqq \{ [x] : x \in S \} \subseteq X/{\sim}. Then, for every x \in X, [x] \in  ar S if and only if x \in S. In words: (a) says that a map on elements that respects the two relations passes to a map on classes; (b) says that a binary operation that respects \sim in each argument separately passes to an operation on classes; (c) says that a property that respects \sim can be asked of a class, and the answer is the answer for any of its representatives. Clause (a) will give the negative of an integer, (b) its sum and product, and (c) the positive integers in Section 2.4. Clause (a) is @fd2:exm-method-well-definedness turned into a theorem: steps (1)–(3) of that method are its hypothesis, and step (4) is the graph built below. A function is a graph with exactly one output for each input (@fd2:def-function). The obvious graph is the set of all pairs ([x], [f(x)]). It has at least one output for each class, because every class is some [x]. The only danger is two outputs for one class, coming from two representatives x and x' of it; @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) turns “same class” into x \sim x', the hypothesis turns that into f(x) \approx f(x'), and @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) turns it back into “same output”. For (b) the same plan works, once the two one-argument hypotheses are chained into one statement about both arguments by transitivity. (a) Let G_F \coloneqq \{ (C, D) \in (X/{\sim}) 	imes (Y/{\approx}) : C = [x] 	ext{ and } D = [f(x)] 	ext{ for some } x \in X \} , a set by specification (@fd2:def-set-builder). We check the two clauses of @fd2:def-function. (Fn1): every C \in X/{\sim} is [x] for some x \in X (@fd2:def-quotient-set), and then (C, [f(x)]) \in G_F. title: 2.3 Commutative Rings; the Integers Are One

Commutative Rings; the Integers Are One Sections 2.1 and 2.2 built 
Z with well-defined operations +, \cdot and -. Why was it built at all? 
N already adds and multiplies by all the usual laws but one: it has no negatives, since 1 + x = x + 1 
e 0 for every x \in 
N (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), @cor-omega-successor-cancellation). This section collects the laws of school algebra into one definition, a commutative ring, checks them for 
Z by reducing each to a law of 
N, and derives the consequences that hold in every commutative ring. The laws of a ring Expanding brackets or moving a term across an equation uses a short list of laws: sums and products may be reordered and regrouped, 0 and 1 do nothing, every element has a negative, and products distribute over sums. The list holds in 
Z, it will hold in 
Q, and a result proved from the list alone holds wherever the list does. It deserves a name. A commutative ring is a set where you may add, subtract and multiply by the usual rules; a field is one where you may also divide by anything non-zero. [Commutative Ring, Field] A commutative ring is a set R with two functions, addition + \colon R 	imes R 	o R and multiplication \cdot \colon R 	imes R 	o R (written a \cdot b = ab), such that clauses (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of the following list hold; clause (F8) is used only for fields. 1. a + b = b + a for all a, b \in R. 2. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) for all a, b, c \in R. 3. There is an element 0 \in R with a + 0 = a for every a \in R. 4. For every a \in R there is an element -a \in R with a + (-a) = 0. 5. (ab)c = a(bc) for all a, b, c \in R. 6. ab = ba for all a, b \in R. 7. There is an element 1 \in R with a \cdot 1 = a for every a \in R. 8. For every non-zero a \in R there is an element a^{-1} \in R with a a^{-1} = 1. 9. a(b + c) = ab + ac for all a, b, c \in R. A field is a commutative ring in which, in addition, 1 
e 0 and (F8) holds. We write a - b \coloneqq a + (-b), and in a field a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1} for b 
e 0. In words: (F1)–(F4) say that addition is commutative and associative, with a neutral element 0 and negatives; (F5)–(F7) say the first three things about multiplication; (F9) links the two and lets us expand brackets. (F8) asks for inverses of non-zero elements only, and only in a field. The notations -a and a^{-1} anticipate that these elements are unique, which we prove below. These are the axioms (F1)–(F9) of the linear-algebra companion, Chapter 0, and of the ordered fields of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, in the same numbering, except that there (F7) includes 1 
e 0. Examples. - 
Z, with the operations of @def-integer-operations: the next theorem. - The zero ring R \coloneqq \{0\}, with 0 + 0 \coloneqq 0, 0 \cdot 0 \coloneqq 0 and 1 \coloneqq 0. Every axiom other than (F8) is an equation in R, and every such equation reads 0 = 0. So R is a commutative ring, with 1 = 0, and not a field. This degenerate ring is why several results below assume 1 
e 0. A non-example by minimal change. The set 
N, with its addition and multiplication from Chapter 1, satisfies (F1)–(F3), (F5)–(F7) and (F9), by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws and @def-omega-arithmetic (a). That one missing clause, (F4), is why 
Z had to be built. Why these clauses. No axiom says that ab = 0 forces a = 0 or b = 0: that is true in 
Z but fails in other commutative rings (the warning below), so it must be proved where it holds. The condition 1 
e 0 is kept out of the ring axioms, so that the zero ring is a ring, and put into the field axioms, so that \{0\}, where (F8) holds vacuously, is not a field. A commutative ring may have zero divisors: non-zero a, b with ab = 0. The integers modulo 6 of Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 (built there from the school integers, with well-defined operations by @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic) form a commutative ring: each of (F1)–(F7) and (F9) passes from the school integers to classes through representatives, a check we do not need and do not carry out here. In this ring [2] 
e [0] and [3] 
e [0], yet [2][3] = [6] = [0]. So “ab = 0, hence a = 0 or b = 0” is not a consequence of the ring axioms (F1)–(F7) and (F9). In a field it is, since b = a^{-1}(ab) when a 
e 0 (Section 4.1). In an ordered ring it is a theorem, proved in Section 2.4 from the order axioms. The integers form a commutative ring To prove a law for classes, compute both sides through representatives; the two pairs of natural numbers are then equal or related, and the classes agree. The Integers Form a Commutative Ring 
Z, with the addition, multiplication and negation of @def-integer-operations, is a commutative ring, with zero [(0, 0)] and one [(1, 0)], and in it 1 
e 0. [Scratch work] Take (F9), the law with the most terms. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- x, y, z \in 
Z x(y + z) = xy + xz x = [(a, b)], y = [(c, d)], z = [(e, f)]: every class has a representative (@fd2:def-quotient-set) two classes, each computed by @def-integer-operations from these representatives left: (a(c + e) + b(d + f), \ a(d + f) + b(c + e)); right: ((ac + bd) + (ae + bf), \ (ad + bc) + (af + be)) equal pairs, or related pairs distribute in 
N, then regroup four terms the same pair: the classes are equal ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The operations are functions (@prp-integer-operations-well-defined), so any representatives may be used. Only (F4) will need \sim; only (F5) is long. By @prp-integer-operations-well-defined, + and \cdot are functions

N. By @def-integer-operations, each side of each axiom is the class of the pair shown in the table. “Equal” means the same pair of natural numbers, by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws and @def-omega-arithmetic (a), (b). “Related” means related by \sim (@def-integers-as-classes: (p, q) \sim (r, s) means p + s = q + r), so the classes agree by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Axiom left side, as a pair right side, as a pair why the classes agree -------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------ -------------------------------------------------------- (F1) x + y = y + x (a + c, b + d) (c + a, d + b) equal: + is commutative on

Then (xy)z = [(ge + hf, gf + he)], and in 
N  egin{aligned} ge + hf &= ace + bde + adf + bcf, \ gf + he &= acf + bdf + ade + bce . \end{aligned} On the other side, yz = [(ce + df, cf + de)], and x(yz) is the class of the pair whose coordinates are  egin{aligned} a(ce + df) + b(cf + de) &= ace + adf + bcf + bde, \ a(cf + de) + b(ce + df) &= acf + ade + bce + bdf . \end{aligned} Both first coordinates are sums of ace, adf, bcf, bde, and both second coordinates of acf, ade, bce, bdf, so the pairs are equal (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b)–(g)). Finally, 1 
e 0: if [(1, 0)] = [(0, 0)], then 1 = 0 by @prp-integer-normal-form (b). But 0 < 1 in 
N (@thm-omega-order (d)), and < is irreflexive (@thm-omega-order (a)), so 1 
e 0. This proves the theorem. Seven of the eight rows end in “equal”. Only (F4) needs \sim: the pair (a + b, b + a) records “(a + b) - (b + a)”, which is zero, without performing the subtraction, and that is the whole point of passing to classes. The proof used one move eight times. It has a name. [Method: reduce to the level below] Template. To prove a law about classes whose operations are defined on representatives: (1) write each element as a class [p]; (2) compute each side by the defining formulas, with any representatives, since the operations are well defined; (3) compare the two representatives at the level below, by its laws: equal, or related; (4) conclude that the classes are equal (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)). When to use it. Laws in 
Z, with 
N below; any structure whose operations are formulas in a known ring (Exercise C1 below). The usual failure. Claiming equal pairs where only \sim holds (the row (F4)); computing with representatives before the operation is known to be a function; using a law of 
Z inside the computation in 
N, which is circular. The zero and one of this ring are [(0, 0)] = \iota(0) and [(1, 0)] = \iota(1) (@prp-naturals-embed-integers), so after the identification of Section 2.2 they are the elements 0 and 1 of 
N. With a - b \coloneqq a + (-b), the formula [(a, b)] = \iota(a) + (-\iota(b)) of @prp-naturals-embed-integers reads [(a, b)] = a - b for a, b \in 
N: the subtraction the pair recorded is now performed in 
Z. Which class is the negative of [(2, 7)]? Show by reducing to 
N that no other class [(c, d)] satisfies [(2, 7)] + [(c, d)] = [(0, 0)]. -[(2, 7)] = [(7, 2)] (@def-integer-operations). Now suppose [(2 + c, \ 7 + d)] = [(0, 0)]. By @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) and @def-integers-as-classes, (2 + c) + 0 = (7 + d) + 0, so 2 + c = 7 + d = 2 + (5 + d). Hence c + 2 = (5 + d) + 2 by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), and c = 5 + d by cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)). Then c + 2 = (5 + d) + 2 = d + 7, that is, (c, d) \sim (7, 2), and [(c, d)] = [(7, 2)] (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)). @prp-ring-algebra (a) below proves the same uniqueness in every commutative ring, from (F1)–(F7) and (F9) alone. What the definition does not list must be derived, and the derivations work in every commutative ring at once. [Algebra in a Commutative Ring] Let R be a commutative ring, and let a, b \in R. 1. The elements 0 and 1 of (F3) and (F7) are unique, the element -a of (F4) is unique, and -(-a) = a. 2. a \cdot 0 = 0. 3. (-a)b = a(-b) = -(ab) and (-a)(-b) = ab. 4. (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, where x^2 \coloneqq xx and 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1. To show that something equals 0, or -(ab), show that it satisfies the defining equation of that element and let uniqueness, part (a), finish. (a) Suppose 0 and 0' both satisfy (F3). Then 0' = 0' + 0 = 0 + 0' = 0, by (F3) for 0, (F1), and (F3) for 0'. Likewise, if 1 and 1' both satisfy (F7), then 1' = 1' \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 1' = 1, by (F7) and (F6). Next, suppose a + b = 0 and a + c = 0. Then  egin{aligned} b &= b + 0 = b + (a + c) = (b + a) + c \ &= (a + b) + c = 0 + c = c + 0 = c , \end{aligned} by (F3), the second hypothesis, (F2), (F1), the first hypothesis, (F1) and (F3). So -a is the only element whose sum with a is 0. Finally, (-a) + a = a + (-a) = 0 by (F1) and (F4), so a satisfies the defining equation of -(-a), and uniqueness gives -(-a) = a. (b) Let z \coloneqq a \cdot 0. By (F3) and (F9), z = a(0 + 0) = a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0 = z + z. Adding -z to both sides, 0 = z + (-z) = (z + z) + (-z) = z +  igl(z + (-z) igr) = z + 0 = z , by (F4), the equation z = z + z, (F2), (F4) and (F3). So a \cdot 0 = 0. (c) By (F6) and (F9), ab + (-a)b = b igl(a + (-a) igr) = b \cdot 0 = 0, the last step by (b). So (-a)b satisfies the defining equation of -(ab), and (a) gives (-a)b = -(ab). By (F6) also a(-b) = (-b)a = -(ba) = -(ab). Hence (-a)(-b) = - igl(a(-b) igr) = - igl(-(ab) igr) = ab, using the first identity, the second, and (a). title: 2.4 Ordered Rings and the Rules for Inequalities

Ordered Rings and the Rules for Inequalities Section 2.3 made 
Z a commutative ring and proved the rules for equations from (F1)–(F9). Inequalities need the same treatment. In school, -3 < -2 is read off a number line; here there is no line, only classes of pairs. This section lists four order axioms, shows that an order is the same thing as a set of positive elements, orders 
Z, and derives the rules for inequalities in every ordered ring. Each rule will come from one observation: a < b is a statement about the single element b - a. Ordered rings The integers carry an order tied to the operations: adding the same number to both sides keeps an inequality, and a product of positives is positive. We want every rule for inequalities to follow from a short list of axioms, as for equations. The list is the order axioms (O1)–(O4) of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, with “field” relaxed to “commutative ring”. An ordered ring is a ring with a strict order that adding respects, in which a product of positives is positive. [Ordered Ring, Ordered Field] An ordered commutative ring is a commutative ring R (@def-commutative-ring-and-field) together with a relation < on R such that, for all a, b, c \in R: 1. (trichotomy) exactly one of a < b, a = b, b < a holds; 2. (transitivity) if a < b and b < c, then a < c; 3. (addition) if a < b, then a + c < b + c; 4. (multiplication) if 0 < a and 0 < b, then 0 < ab. An ordered field is a field that is an ordered commutative ring. We write b > a for a < b, and a \le b for “a < b or a = b” (likewise b \ge a). An element a is positive if a > 0, negative if a < 0, and non-negative if a \ge 0. In words: any two elements compare in exactly one way, so a < a never holds; comparisons chain; we may add the same element to both sides; and (O4), the only clause about multiplication, speaks only of positive elements. The degenerate case: the zero ring \{0\} with the empty relation is an ordered commutative ring. Only the middle option of (O1) holds, and (O2)–(O4) are vacuous. There 1 = 0, so any rule concluding 1 > 0 must assume 1 
e 0. Checking (O1)–(O4) directly means handling pairs of elements. It is easier to say which elements are positive and let a < b mean that b - a is positive. The next proposition says which “positive sets” give an order, and that every order arises so. We call the move order from a positive set. [Order from a Positive Set] Let R be a commutative ring and P \subseteq R a subset such that: 1. if a, b \in P, then a + b \in P and ab \in P; 2. for every a \in R, exactly one of a \in P, a = 0, -a \in P holds. Define a < b to mean b - a \in P. Then (R, <) is an ordered commutative ring (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), and P = \{ a \in R : a > 0 \}. Conversely, if (R, <) is an ordered commutative ring, then P \coloneqq \{ a \in R : a > 0 \} satisfies (P1) and (P2), and for all a, b \in R, a < b holds if and only if b - a \in P. The labels (P1), (P2) are local; they are not the clauses of a partition (Sets and Functions, Section 5.2) or Peano’s axioms (Chapter 1). Each order axiom is a statement about one difference. (O1) is (P2) applied to b - a, since -(b - a) = a - b. (O2) is closure under sums, since (c - b) + (b - a) = c - a. (O3) holds since (b + c) - (a + c) = b - a. (O4) is closure under products. The algebra is uniqueness of negatives. We first record three identities in R, for a, b, c \in R:  egin{gathered} -(b - a) = a - b , \qquad (c - b) + (b - a) = c - a , \ (b + c) - (a + c) = b - a . \end{gathered} For the first, (b - a) + (a - b) = (b + (-b)) + ((-a) + a) = 0 by (F1), (F2), (F4), and @prp-ring-algebra (a) gives the identity. The second is regrouping by (F1)–(F4). For the third, (a + c) + ((-a) + (-c)) = 0 likewise, so -(a + c) = (-a) + (-c) by @prp-ring-algebra (a), and the c’s cancel. Also -0 = 0 (as 0 + 0 = 0), so a - 0 = a; and b - a = 0 if and only if b = a: one direction is (F4), and b - a = 0 gives b = (b - a) + a = 0 + a = a. Now let P satisfy (P1), (P2), and let a < b mean b - a \in P. (O1) Apply (P2) to b - a: exactly one of b - a \in P, b - a = 0, -(b - a) \in P holds. By the facts above, these say a < b, a = b and a - b \in P, that is, b < a. So exactly one of the three holds. (O2) If b - a \in P and c - b \in P, then c - a = (c - b) + (b - a) \in P by (P1). (O3) If b - a \in P, then (b + c) - (a + c) = b - a \in P. (O4) Since a - 0 = a, we have 0 < a if and only if a \in P. So 0 < a and 0 < b give a, b \in P, hence ab \in P by (P1), that is, 0 < ab. The same equivalence says P = \{ a \in R : a > 0 \}. Conversely, let (R, <) be an ordered commutative ring and P \coloneqq \{ a : a > 0 \}. If a < b, then a + (-a) < b + (-a) by (O3), that is, 0 < b - a. If 0 < b - a, then 0 + a < (b - a) + a = b by (O3), that is, a < b. This is the last claim. For (P1), let a, b > 0. Then 0 + b < a + b by (O3), so 0 < b < a + b and a + b > 0 by (O2); and ab > 0 by (O4). For (P2), let a \in R. By (O1) exactly one of 0 < a, a = 0, a < 0 holds, and by the last claim a < 0 holds exactly when 0 - a = -a is in P. This proves the proposition. So an order on a commutative ring is the same thing as a positive set. For 
Z, the natural one is the classes [(a, b)] with b < a. Section 2.1 warned that “b < a” is a statement about one representative; we now check that it is a statement about the class. The order of the integers [Order on the Integers] Let S \coloneqq \{ (a, b) \in

Then n - m > 0 (@prp-order-from-positives), so n - m \ge 1, and adding m by (O3) gives n \ge 1 + m. This proves the theorem. With the identification of Section 2.2, (a) says that the order of

(O2)–(O4) still hold, by the axioms for < and the cases of equality (for (O4), ab = 0 when a factor is 0, by @prp-ring-algebra (b)). But (O1) fails at a = b = 0: both “0 \le 0” and “0 = 0” hold. The axioms describe a strict order. - Reverse the order: a \prec b means b < a. (O1)–(O3) hold, by the same axioms for <. But (O4) fails: 0 \prec -1, since 0 - (-1) = 1 = [(1, 0)] \in P_{

otin P_{

Q once Section 3.2 orders it. One of them needs multiples first. Multiples. Let R be a commutative ring and a \in R. By @thm-omega-recursion, with X = R, starting value 0 and g(n, y) = y + a (and n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n), @def-omega-arithmetic (c)), there is exactly one function

If a \le b and c \le d, then a + c \le b + d, and the conclusion is strict if one of the hypotheses is strict. 3. If a < b and c > 0, then ac < bc. 4. If a < b and c < 0, then ac > bc. 5. If a
