A positive element plus a non-negative one is positive: by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), with the strict hypothesis 0 < b(d - c), we get 0 = 0 + 0 < b(d - c) + (b - a)c = bd - ac, where 0 + 0 = 0 is (F3). By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), ac < bd. The hypotheses a \ge 0 and c \ge 0 are exactly what make the two summands non-negative; the warning shows what goes wrong without them. Which positive element shows that a < b gives a + a < b + b? The element b - a, taken twice: (b + b) - (a + a) = (b - a) + (b - a) by the ring laws (regrouping by (F1), (F2), with -(a + a) = (-a) + (-a) as in the proof of @prp-order-from-positives). It is a sum of two positive elements, so it is positive by (P1) for the positive set (@prp-order-from-positives, converse), and a + a < b + b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). Is 
Z a field? No: 1 + 1 is non-zero (it is > 1 > 0, where 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in 
Z by @thm-integers-commutative-ring) and has no inverse. Suppose (1 + 1)x = 1. Since (1 + 1)x = x(1 + 1) = x + x by (F6), (F9) and (F7), this says x + x = 1. If x \le 0, then x + x \le 0 < 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (e). If x > 0, then x \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), so x + x \ge 1 + 1 > 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (e). Both contradict x + x = 1 by (O1). Least elements, and a ring that cannot be ordered The natural numbers are well ordered (@thm-omega-well-ordering); the integers are not, since x - 1 < x for every x. But a set of integers bounded below can be shifted into 
N. [Least and Greatest Elements of Sets of Integers] Let S \subseteq 
Z be non-empty. If S has a lower bound b \in 
Z (that is, b \le s for every s \in S), then S has a least element. If S has an upper bound c \in 
Z, then S has a greatest element. This is @fd2:cor-well-ordering-integers on the constructed 
Z, by the same shift into 
N, with @thm-omega-well-ordering in place of @fd2:thm-well-ordering. Let b be a lower bound and T \coloneqq \{ s - b : s \in S \}, a non-empty set. For s \in S, s \ge b gives s - b \ge 0 by (O3), so T \subseteq \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} = 
N by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). By @thm-omega-well-ordering, T has an element m with m \le t for every t \in T, in the order of 
N and so in that of 
Z (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (a)). Then m = s_0 - b for some s_0 \in S, so m + b = s_0 \in S; and for s \in S, s - b \ge m gives s \ge m + b by (O3). So m + b is least in S. If c is an upper bound, then -S \coloneqq \{ -s : s \in S \} has the lower bound -c (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so by the first part it has a least element, which is -s_1 for some s_1 \in S, by the definition of -S. For s \in S, -s_1 \le -s gives s \le s_1, by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or by -(-s) = s (@prp-ring-algebra (a)) when -s_1 = -s. So s_1 is greatest in S. This proves the proposition. Both hypotheses are needed: 
Z has no least element, and neither has \emptyset, which every integer bounds. The rules of @prp-ordered-ring-rules also show that some rings carry no order at all. [A field with two elements that cannot be ordered] Let R \coloneqq \{0, 1\}, two distinct elements, with addition and multiplication given by the tables  egin{array}{c|cc} {+} & 0 & 1 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \qquad\qquad  egin{array}{c|cc} \cdot & 0 & 1 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array} Check that R satisfies (F1)–(F9), so that it is a field, and show that no relation < on R makes it an ordered commutative ring. The axioms. (F1), (F6): both tables are symmetric. (F3), (F7): the row of 0 in the first table and of 1 in the second repeat the headings. (F4): -0 = 0 and -1 = 1, since 1 + 1 = 0. (F8): 1 has inverse 1, since the second table gives the product of 1 and 1 as 1. And 1 
e 0. The three laws with three variables can be checked over the eight triples (a, b, c), or by cases. From the tables, 0x = 0 and 1x = x, and x + y = 1 exactly when exactly one of x, y is 1. (F2): both sides are 1 exactly when an odd number of a, b, c (one or three) are 1. (F5): both sides are 1 exactly when a = b = c = 1. (F9): if a = 0, both sides are 0; if a = 1, both sides are b + c. So R is a field. No order. If < made R an ordered commutative ring, then, as 1 
e 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) would give 2 \cdot 1 > 0. But 2 \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 = (0 + 1) + 1 = 0 by the definition of multiples, and 0 > 0 is forbidden by (O1). The argument uses only 1 
e 0 and n \cdot 1 = 0 for some n \ge 1. So no commutative ring with 1 
e 0 in which n \cdot 1 = 0 for some n \in 
N, n \ge 1, can be ordered. The integers modulo n \ge 2 of Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 are such rings (their ring laws taken for granted, as in the warning after @def-commutative-ring-and-field), since n \cdot [1] = [n] = [0]; Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 rebuilds them on the constructed 
Z. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let R be an ordered commutative ring. 1. Here is a proof that if a < 0 < b, then ab < a^2 + b^2. Name the axiom, rule or result that justifies each of the five steps. (1) ab < 0b. (2) 0b = 0. (3) a^2 > 0 and b^2 > 0. (4) a^2 + b^2 > 0 + 0 = 0. (5) ab < a^2 + b^2. 2. True or false: “R has no zero divisors.” Give a reason. 3. True or false: “1 > 0 in every ordered commutative ring.” Give a reason. 4. Use the method of @exm-method-one-positive-element to show: if a < b and c \le 0, then ac \ge bc. (a) (1) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with a < 0 and b > 0. (2) @prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6). (3) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as a, b 
e 0 by (O1). (4) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict, and (F3). (5) (O2). (b) True, by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f); a general commutative ring may have zero divisors (the warning after @def-commutative-ring-and-field). (c) False: in the zero ring with the empty relation, 1 = 0. It is true when 1 
e 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). (d) By the method, compute the difference ac - bc. By (F9), (F6) and @prp-ring-algebra (c), ac - bc = (a - b)c; and a - b = -(b - a) (the first identity in the proof of @prp-order-from-positives), so (a - b)c = (-(b - a))c = (b - a)(-c) by @prp-ring-algebra (c). Here b - a > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). If c < 0, then -c > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), as 0 - c = -c), and the product is > 0 by (O4). If c = 0, then -c = 0 and the product is 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b). So ac - bc \ge 0: either bc < ac by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or ac - bc = 0, that is, ac = bc. In both cases bc \le ac, that is, ac \ge bc. B. Practice [B1: The wrong positive set] Let P' \coloneqq \{ [(a, b)] : a < b \} \subseteq 
Z. Show that membership in P' does not depend on the representative, that P' satisfies (P2) of @prp-order-from-positives, and that it does not satisfy (P1). Which part of (P1) fails? Independence of representatives. If (a, b) \sim (a', b') and b = a + k with k 
e 0, then b' + a = a + b' = b + a' = (a + k) + a' = (a' + k) + a (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c)), so b' = a' + k by cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)), and a' < b' by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a). By @thm-well-defined-on-classes (c), [(a, b)] \in P' if and only if a < b. (P2). For x = [(a, b)]: x \in P' iff a < b; x = 0 iff a = b (as in the proof of @thm-integers-ordered-ring); -x \in P' iff b < a. By trichotomy in 
N (@thm-omega-order (a)), exactly one holds. (P1) fails for products. [(0, 1)] \in P', but, by @def-integer-operations with a = c = 0 and b = d = 1 in [(ac + bd, \ ad + bc)], [(0, 1)][(0, 1)] = [(1, 0)] , and [(1, 0)] 
otin P', since 1 < 0 is false. The sum half of (P1) holds, as in the proof of @thm-integers-ordered-ring. So P', the negative integers, fails only closure under products; it would define the reversed order, which breaks exactly (O4). [B2: Prove or disprove] Prove or disprove. 1. In every ordered commutative ring, a < b implies a^2 < b^2. 2. In every ordered commutative ring with 1 
e 0, a^2 + 1 > 0. 3. In 
Z, if x > 0 and xy = x, then y = 1. 4. In every ordered commutative ring, a < b and c < d imply a - d < b - c. 5. In 
Z, x < y implies x + 1 < y. (a) False. In 
Z, -3 < 1, but (-3)^2 = 9 and 1^2 = 1, and 9 > 1. The true version needs a \ge 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). (b) True. First, a^2 \ge 0: if a = 0, then a^2 = 0 \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b); otherwise a^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e). Next, 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), since 1 
e 0. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), with the strict hypothesis 0 < 1, 0 = 0 + 0 < a^2 + 1, using (F3). (c) True. By (F9), (F7) and @prp-ring-algebra (c), x(y - 1) = xy + x(-1) = xy - x, and xy - x = x - x = 0 by the hypothesis and (F4). Since x > 0, x 
e 0 by (O1). So y - 1 = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f), and y = (y - 1) + 1 = 1 by (F1)–(F4). (d) True. From c < d, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) gives -d < -c. Adding this to a < b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict, gives a + (-d) < b + (-c), that is, a - d < b - c. (e) False. Take x = 0 and y = 1: then x < y (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in 
Z by @thm-integers-commutative-ring), but x + 1 = 1, and 1 < 1 is ruled out by (O1). Discreteness gives only x + 1 \le y (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)). C. Going deeper [C1: Ordered rings with 1 
e 0 are infinite] 1. Prove the sum law of @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) in full: for every ordered commutative ring R, every a \in R and all m, k \in 
N, (m + k) \cdot a = m \cdot a + k \cdot a. State the property you induct on and justify every equality. 2. Deduce that every ordered commutative ring with 1 
e 0 is infinite (@fd2:def-infinite). 3. The set \{0, 1, 2\} with addition and multiplication “modulo 3”, given by the tables below, is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 (you may take this for granted). Show that it cannot be ordered.  egin{array}{c|ccc} {+} & 0 & 1 & 2 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \qquad\qquad  egin{array}{c|ccc} \cdot & 0 & 1 & 2 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 0 & 2 & 1 \end{array} [Hint 1] For (b): what does (h) say about k \mapsto k \cdot 1? [Hint 2] Suppose R has m elements; consider k \mapsto k \cdot 1 on \{1, \dots, m + 1\}. (a) Fix R, a \in R, m \in 
N, and use @thm-omega-induction (b) on k, for P(k): “(m + k) \cdot a = m \cdot a + k \cdot a”. Base: (m + 0) \cdot a = m \cdot a = m \cdot a + 0 = m \cdot a + 0 \cdot a, by @def-omega-arithmetic (a), (F3) and 0 \cdot a = 0. Step: assume P(k). Then  egin{aligned} (m + (k + 1)) \cdot a &= ((m + k) + 1) \cdot a = (m + k) \cdot a + a \ &= (m \cdot a + k \cdot a) + a = m \cdot a + (k \cdot a + a) \ &= m \cdot a + (k + 1) \cdot a , \end{aligned} by associativity in 
N (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c)), the recursion for multiples, P(k), (F2), and the recursion again. So P(k + 1) holds, and P(k) holds for every k. (b) Let 1 
e 0 in R, and suppose R has m elements for some m \in 
N (@fd2:def-finite). Let f \colon \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o R, f(k) \coloneqq k \cdot 1. If k < l, then k \cdot 1 < l \cdot 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), so k \cdot 1 
e l \cdot 1 by (O1): f is injective. But \{1, \dots, m + 1\} has m + 1 > m elements (by its identity map), so @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) forbids an injection into R. This contradiction shows that R is infinite (@fd2:def-infinite). (c) By the definition of multiples and the tables, 1 \cdot 1 = 0 + 1 = 1, 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 and 3 \cdot 1 = 2 + 1 = 0. An order would give 3 \cdot 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), since 1 
e 0, that is, 0 > 0, against (O1). (Alternatively, (b) applies to this finite ring.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) states the induction property with m and a fixed and k the induction variable. - 2: (a) base case, citing m + 0 = m, 0 \cdot a = 0 and (F3). - 2: (a) inductive step, with associativity in 
N, the recursion, the hypothesis and (F2) each named. - 2: (b) shows that k \mapsto k \cdot 1 is injective, citing (h) and (O1). - 2: (b) derives the contradiction from @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) with m + 1 > m elements (or any correct count). - 1: (c) computes 3 \cdot 1 = 0 and concludes. Fatal errors (0 for the step): inducting on m and k at once without fixing one; using 1 > 0 without 1 
e 0; in (b), “the multiples are all different, so there are infinitely many” with no finiteness result cited (@fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @fd2:prp-subset-finite with 
N infinite, or equivalent). A route for (b) composing the inverse of a bijection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o R with f earns the same 4 points. So does a route that shows k \mapsto k \cdot 1 is an injection 
N 	o R (2 points, as above), so that its image is an infinite subset of R, and concludes with @fd2:prp-subset-finite (2 points).

title: 2.5 Division with Remainder
content:
Division with Remainder Two facts about the integers of school, taken as known, were proved in the previous volume: every integer is even or odd, and not both (Sets and Functions, Section 1.1, @fd2:thm-even-or-odd), and division with remainder (Sets and Functions, Section 3.2, @fd2:thm-division-algorithm). The integers are now the set of classes built in Section 2.1. Is [(0, 7)], the class that school calls -7, still odd, and could some integer be even and odd at once? Nothing proved so far says. This section answers by proving division with remainder again, on the constructed 
Z: the proof is that of Sets and Functions, Section 3.2, with each school fact replaced by a result of this chapter. Divisibility comes first, since uniqueness of the remainder rests on it. Throughout, 
Z is the ordered ring of @thm-integers-ordered-ring, with 
N \subseteq 
Z and 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). Numerals 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, 3 \coloneqq 2 + 1, and so on, are the natural numbers of those names, as in Section 2.2; a sum or product of numerals may be computed in 
N, because the embedding of @prp-naturals-embed-integers preserves + and \cdot, and a sign is moved by @prp-ring-algebra (c), as in (-4) \cdot 5 = -(4 \cdot 5) = -20. Divisibility on the constructed integers The definition of divisibility needs nothing that the ring 
Z lacks. We restate it, and the definition of a prime, from Sets and Functions, Section 1.1, with 
Z now the ring of Chapter 2. Divisibility (@fd2:def-divides). Let a, b \in 
Z. Then a divides b, written a \mid b, if there exists k \in 
Z with b = ka. Then a is a divisor of b, and b is a multiple of a. We write a 
mid b when a does not divide b. Prime (@fd2:def-prime). An integer p is prime if p \ge 2 and the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p. A prime factor of an integer n is a prime p with p \mid n. Divisibility is a question about existence: is b some integer times a? Some instances. 3 \mid -12, since -12 = (-4) \cdot 3. -4 \mid 0, since 0 = 0 \cdot (-4). Even 0 \mid 0 holds, since 0 = 1 \cdot 0: the definition asks for some k, and here every k works. On the other hand 5 
mid 12. That is a statement that no k \in 
Z has 12 = 5k, and to prove it we need the theorem on division with remainder below. The rules below are short consequences of the ring laws and the order. [Rules for Divisibility in 
Z] Let a, b, c, x, y \in 
Z. 1. a \mid 0, 1 \mid a and a \mid a. If 0 \mid a, then a = 0. 2. If a \mid b and b \mid c, then a \mid c. 3. If a \mid b and a \mid c, then a \mid bx + cy. 4. If a \mid b, then (-a) \mid b and a \mid (-b). 5. If a \mid b, a > 0 and b > 0, then a \le b. 6. If a, b \in 
N, a \mid b and b \mid a, then a = b. 7. If a \mid 1, then a = 1 or a = -1. 8. If a 
e 0, then exactly one of a, -a lies in 
Z_{>0}. Parts (a)–(d) are identities in the commutative ring 
Z: write each hypothesis as an equation b = ka and rearrange. Part (e) is the one that needs the order. If b = ka with a, b > 0, the factor k cannot be zero or negative, so by discreteness it is at least 1, and multiplying a by something at least 1 cannot make it smaller (the method of @exm-method-one-positive-element). Parts (f) and (g) then follow from (e), and (h) is (P2) for the positives of 
Z. We use the ring laws (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring) without further mention. Parts (a)–(d) are one-line identities and (h) restates (P2); their proofs are written out in the fold. After it come (e), which needs the order and discreteness, and the two parts built on it, (f) and (g). (a) 0 = a \cdot 0 = 0 \cdot a by @prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6), so a \mid 0 with k = 0. Also a = a \cdot 1 by (F7), so 1 \mid a with k = a; and a = 1 \cdot a, so a \mid a with k = 1. If 0 \mid a, then a = k \cdot 0 = 0 for some k \in 
Z, by @prp-ring-algebra (b). (b) Let b = ka and c = lb with k, l \in 
Z. Then c = l(ka) = (lk)a by (F5), so a \mid c. (c) Let b = ka and c = la. Then bx + cy = (ka)x + (la)y = (kx)a + (ly)a = (kx + ly)a by (F5), (F6) and (F9), and kx + ly \in 
Z. So a \mid bx + cy. (d) Let b = ka. By @prp-ring-algebra (c), (-k)(-a) = ka = b, so (-a) \mid b; and (-k)a = -(ka) = -b, so a \mid (-b). (e) Let a 
e 0. By the converse part of @prp-order-from-positives, applied to the ordered ring 
Z, the set \{ x \in 
Z : x > 0 \} satisfies (P2), so exactly one of a > 0, -a > 0 holds. That set is 
Z_{>0} by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). (e) Let b = ka with k \in 
Z, a > 0 and b > 0. We show first that k > 0. If k = 0, then b = 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), against b > 0. If k < 0, then ka < 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (multiplying k < 0 by a > 0), again against b > 0. So k > 0, and by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c), with 0 < k) 1 \le k. If k = 1, then b = a. If 1 < k, then k - 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so (k - 1)a > 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), that is, b - a = ka + (-1)a = (k - 1)a > 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (c), (F7) and (F9)), and a < b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). In both cases a \le b. (f) Let a, b \in 
N with a \mid b and b \mid a. If a = 0, then 0 \mid b, so b = 0 = a by (a). If b = 0, then a = 0 in the same way. Otherwise a, b \in 
N are non-zero, hence positive (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and (e) gives a \le b and b \le a. Since \le is a total order (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), it is antisymmetric, and a = b. (g) Let a \mid 1, say 1 = ka. Then a 
e 0: otherwise 1 = k \cdot 0 = 0, against 1 
e 0 in 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring). By (h), one of a, -a is positive; call it e. Then e \mid 1, by (d) if e = -a. Since 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), part (e) gives e \le 1; and e > 0 gives 1 \le e by discreteness. So e = 1. If e = a, then a = 1; if e = -a, then a = -(-a) = -1 by @prp-ring-algebra (a). This proves the proposition. Part (f) is the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N, @fd2:prp-divides-partial-order of Sets and Functions, Section 5.1, now proved on 
N \subseteq 
Z for the constructed integers. On all of 
Z it fails: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, by (d), yet 2 
e -2. Which hypothesis of (e) fails for a = 3, b = 0, and is the conclusion a \le b true there? 3 \mid 0 by (a), and a = 3 > 0, but b = 0 is not positive. The conclusion 3 \le 0 is false. Every integer divides 0, so no bound of the form a \le b can hold for b = 0; that is the reason for the hypothesis b > 0. Division with remainder Now the substitute for division. Given a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, we want to write a as a multiple of n plus something small, and we want “small” to make the answer unique. The obvious attempt subtracts n from a until what is left lies in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}, adding n instead when a is negative. That is a process; the theorem replaces it by a least element. [Division with Remainder in 
Z] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. 1. There are unique q, r \in 
Z with a = qn + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . The integers q and r are the quotient and the remainder of a on division by n. This is @fd2:thm-division-algorithm, and the proof is that volume’s: the method of @fd2:exm-method-least-element, with S the non-negative integers of the form a - kn, and @prp-integer-least-element in place of the school least-element principle. The least one, r, lies below n, or else r - n would be a smaller one. Uniqueness is @fd2:exm-method-uniqueness: two remainders differ by a multiple of n and by less than n, and @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) forbids a positive multiple of n below n. What is new is only that every step is now a theorem about the constructed 
Z. Read the proof of @fd2:thm-division-algorithm with these replacements: - the closure of 
Z under +, -, \cdot (@fd2:prp-integers-closed (a)) → @thm-integers-commutative-ring, with the identities a - an = a(1 - n) and r - n = a - (q + 1)n from the ring laws and @prp-ring-algebra; - “a positive integer is at least 1” (@fd2:prp-integers-closed (b)) → discreteness, @thm-integers-ordered-ring (c); - @fd2:cor-well-ordering-integers → @prp-integer-least-element; - the step “a positive multiple of n is at least n” → @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e); - the school rules for inequalities, and cancelling n 
e 0 from qn = q'n → @prp-ordered-ring-rules. With these, the proof of Sets and Functions, Section 3.2 goes through step for step on the constructed 
Z; the fold below writes it out. (a) Existence. Let R \coloneqq \{ a - kn : k \in 
Z \} \cap \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} . We show R 
e \emptyset. If a \ge 0, take k = 0: a - 0 \cdot n = a - 0 = a \ge 0, by (F6), @prp-ring-algebra (b) and -0 = 0 (0 + 0 = 0 and @prp-ring-algebra (a)). If a < 0, take k = a: then a - an = a + a(-n) = a(1 - n) by @prp-ring-algebra (c), (F7) and (F9). Since n > 0, discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)) gives 1 \le n. If n = 1, then a(1 - n) = a \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b). If 1 < n, then -n < -1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so 1 - n < 0 by (O3); multiplying a < 0 by 1 - n < 0 reverses the inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)), so a(1 - n) > 0 \cdot (1 - n) = 0. In every case R has an element. The set R \subseteq 
Z is non-empty and has the lower bound 0, so by @prp-integer-least-element it has a least element r. Write r = a - qn with q \in 
Z. Then a = qn + r and r \ge 0. Suppose r \ge n. Then r - n \ge 0: if r = n, then r - n = 0 by (F4); if r > n, then r - n > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). Also r - n = a - qn - n = a + (-1)(qn) + (-1)n = a + (-1) igl((q + 1)n igr) = a - (q + 1)n, since -x = (-1)x for every x (@prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F7)) and by (F9), so r - n \in R. But -n < -0 = 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), since n > 0), so r - n < r by (O3). This contradicts the choice of r as least. Hence r < n. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with q, q', r, r' \in 
Z, 0 \le r < n and 0 \le r' < n. Suppose r 
e r'. Exchanging (q, r) and (q', r') changes neither the hypotheses nor the goal, so we may suppose r' < r. Adding -r' - qn to both sides of qn + r = q'n + r' gives r - r' = q'n - qn = (q' - q)n , by (F1)–(F4), and by @prp-ring-algebra (c) with (F9) for the last step, so n \mid r - r'. Here r - r' > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), and n > 0, so @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) gives n \le r - r'. But adding r - r' to 0 \le r' gives r - r' \le (r - r') + r' = r (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), and r < n; so r - r' < n, a contradiction. Hence r = r'. Then qn = q'n (add -r to both sides of qn + r = q'n + r), so (q - q')n = qn - q'n = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F9), and since n 
e 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f) gives q - q' = 0. Hence q = (q - q') + q' = q', by (F1)–(F4). For n = 0 the statement fails: no r satisfies 0 \le r < 0. Exercise B1 handles n < 0. Uniqueness is what turns the theorem into a test for divisibility: n \mid a if and only if the remainder of a on division by n is 0. Indeed, if a = kn, then a = kn + 0 is a division with remainder, and by uniqueness it is the only one; conversely a = qn + 0 says n \mid a. For instance 12 = 2 \cdot 5 + 2 with 0 \le 2 < 5, so the remainder is 2 
e 0, and 5 
mid 12. Find the quotient and the remainder of a = -23 on division by n = 4. q = -6 and r = 1: (-6) \cdot 4 + 1 = -24 + 1 = -23, and 0 \le 1 < 4. By uniqueness this is the only such pair. The equation -23 = (-5) \cdot 4 - 3 is also true, but -3 is not a remainder, since it fails 0 \le r < 4; the warning below says why that matters. “The remainder” means the r with 0 \le r < n. The equation -17 = (-3) \cdot 5 - 2 is true, but -2 is not the remainder of -17 on division by 5; the remainder is 3. If negative “remainders” were allowed, uniqueness would fail at once: -17 = (-3) \cdot 5 + (-2) = (-4) \cdot 5 + 3. Even and odd Recall that an integer a is even if a = 2k for some k \in 
Z, and odd if a = 2k + 1 for some k \in 
Z (@fd2:def-parity, as in @fd2:thm-even-or-odd), now read on the constructed 
Z. With n = 2, the theorem answers the opening question. [Even and Odd Integers] 1. Every a \in 
Z is even or odd, and not both. More precisely, either a = 2q for exactly one q \in 
Z and a is not of the form 2k + 1, or a = 2q + 1 for exactly one q \in 
Z and a is not of the form 2k. 2. If a \in 
Z and a^2 is even, then a is even. Divide by 2. The remainder lies in \{0, 1\}, by discreteness, and it is unique, so each integer has exactly one of the two forms. For (b), square the odd form and read off the remainder. (a) Since 2 = 1 + 1 > 0, the theorem with n = 2 gives unique q, r \in 
Z with a = 2q + r and 0 \le r < 2. Then r \in \{0, 1\}: if r 
e 0, then 0 < r, so 1 \le r by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)); and if moreover 1 < r, then 2 = 1 + 1 \le r by discreteness again, against r < 2. If a = 2k and a = 2k' + 1 for some k, k' \in 
Z, then (k, 0) and (k', 1) would be two pairs as in the theorem, and 0 
e 1 contradicts its uniqueness. The same uniqueness shows that q is the only integer with a = 2q + r. (b) Suppose a is not even. By (a), a = 2q + 1 with q \in 
Z. Then a^2 = (2q + 1)^2 = 4q^2 + 4q + 1 = 2(2q^2 + 2q) + 1 , by @prp-ring-algebra (d) and (F5), (F6), (F9), so a^2 is odd, and by (a) it is not even. This proves (b) by contraposition. So -7 = (-4) \cdot 2 + 1 is odd and not even, as school says, and now by proof. Part (a) is @fd2:thm-even-or-odd on the constructed 
Z, and part (b) is @fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even, whose proof used (a) and the computation above as school facts. For a \in 
N, (a) is also @prp-omega-powers-parity (d) of Chapter 1. [Looking ahead] Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 builds on this section: greatest common divisors and Bézout’s identity, primes and unique factorization, and arithmetic modulo n, all on the constructed 
Z. Chapter 3 of this volume builds the rationals as classes of fractions, and its integer part of a/n is the quotient found here. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Find the quotient and the remainder on division by n = 6 of a = 47, of a = -47 and of a = 0. 2. Where is n > 0 used in the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a)? 3. True or false, with a reason: 0 \mid 0. 4. True or false, with a reason: for all a, b \in 
Z, if a \mid b and b \mid a, then a = b. (a) 47 = 7 \cdot 6 + 5, so (q, r) = (7, 5). -47 = (-8) \cdot 6 + 1, since -48 + 1 = -47, so (q, r) = (-8, 1). 0 = 0 \cdot 6 + 0, so (q, r) = (0, 0). In each case 0 \le r < 6, so by uniqueness these are the quotient and remainder. Note (-8, 1), not (-7, -5). (b) Twice. For a < 0, the element a - an = a(1 - n) of R is non-negative because 1 - n \le 0, which comes from n \ge 1, that is, from n > 0 and discreteness. And the contradiction “r - n < r” needs -n < 0, that is, n > 0. (c) True: 0 = 1 \cdot 0, so k = 1 witnesses 0 \mid 0 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). (d) False: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d)), but 2 
e -2. The statement is true for a, b \in 
N (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (f)). B. Practice [B1: Negative divisors] Let a, n \in 
Z with n < 0. Prove that there are unique q, r \in 
Z with a = qn + r and 0 \le r < -n. Since n < 0, -n > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so -n \in 
Z_{>0}. Existence. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) applied to a and -n, there are q_0, r \in 
Z with a = q_0(-n) + r and 0 \le r < -n. Let q \coloneqq -q_0. Then q_0(-n) = (-q_0)n = qn by @prp-ring-algebra (c), so a = qn + r. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with 0 \le r, r' < -n. By @prp-ring-algebra (c), qn = (-q)(-n) and q'n = (-q')(-n), so a = (-q)(-n) + r = (-q')(-n) + r' are two divisions of a by -n. The uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) gives r = r' and -q = -q', hence q = -(-q) = -(-q') = q' by @prp-ring-algebra (a). [B2: Three in a row] Let a \in 
Z. Prove that exactly one of a, a + 1, a + 2 is divisible by 3. At least one. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a), a = 3q + r with 0 \le r < 3, and r \in \{0, 1, 2\} by discreteness, as in the proof of @cor-integers-even-odd. If r = 0, then 3 \mid a. If r = 1, then a + 2 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1). If r = 2, then a + 1 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1). At most one. Suppose 3 \mid a + i and 3 \mid a + j with 0 \le i < j \le 2. By @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c) (with x = 1, y = -1), 3 \mid (a + j) - (a + i) = j - i, and j - i \in \{1, 2\} is positive. By @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), 3 \le j - i \le 2, which is false. So no two of the three are divisible by 3. (Equivalently: the remainders of a, a + 1, a + 2 on division by 3 are r, and then the other two of 0, 1, 2, and uniqueness of remainders allows only one of them to be 0.) C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: remainders of squares] 1. Prove that for every a \in 
Z, the remainder of a^2 on division by 4 is 0 or 1. 2. Deduce that no integer whose remainder on division by 4 is 3 is a sum x^2 + y^2 of two squares of integers. Name the result behind each step. (a) By @cor-integers-even-odd (a), a = 2q or a = 2q + 1 for some q \in 
Z. In the first case a^2 = (2q)(2q) = 4q^2 = q^2 \cdot 4 + 0, by the ring laws (F5), (F6) and 4 = 2 \cdot 2, computed in 
N. In the second, a^2 = (2q + 1)^2 = 4q^2 + 4q + 1 = (q^2 + q) \cdot 4 + 1 , by @prp-ring-algebra (d) and the ring laws (F5), (F6), (F9). Since 4 is a non-zero natural number, 4 > 0 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and both remainders, 0 and 1, satisfy 0 \le r < 4, so by the uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) they are the remainders of a^2 on division by 4. (b) Let x, y \in 
Z. By (a), x^2 = 4k + s and y^2 = 4l + t with k, l \in 
Z and s, t \in \{0, 1\}. Then x^2 + y^2 = 4(k + l) + (s + t) , \qquad s + t \in \{0, 1, 2\} , by (F1), (F2) and (F9). So 0 \le s + t \le 2 < 4, and by uniqueness s + t is the remainder of x^2 + y^2 on division by 4. It is not 3, so no sum of two squares has remainder 3. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: splits into the two cases a = 2q, a = 2q + 1, citing @cor-integers-even-odd (a). - 3: expands both squares and writes each in the form q' \cdot 4 + r, with the identities justified by the ring laws. - 2: checks 0 \le r < 4 and invokes uniqueness to conclude that r is the remainder. - 3: for (b), adds the two forms, checks 0 \le s + t \le 2 < 4, and concludes by uniqueness (or by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) applied to the difference) that the remainder is s + t 
e 3. Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling a value outside 0 \le r < 4 a remainder; concluding in (b) that the remainder is s + t without checking 0 \le s + t < 4 or an equivalent divisibility argument. A proof that divides a by 4 instead, with four cases a = 4m + j, j \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, earns the first 2 points for the case split (citing @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) and discreteness) and the rest as above. R. Review [R1] Let f \colon 
N 	o 
N satisfy f(0) = 0 and f(n + 1) = f(n) + 2n + 1 for every n \in 
N. Prove that f(n) = n \cdot n for every n. By @thm-omega-recursion, with g(n, x) = x + 2n + 1, exactly one such f exists, so the question is about a definite function. We prove f(n) = n \cdot n by induction on n (@thm-omega-induction). Base. f(0) = 0 = 0 \cdot 0, by @def-omega-arithmetic (b). Step. Suppose f(n) = n \cdot n. Then f(n + 1) = (n \cdot n + 2n) + 1. On the other side, with \mathrm{S}(n) = n + 1 (@def-omega-arithmetic (c)),  egin{aligned} (n + 1)(n + 1) &= (n + 1) \cdot n + (n + 1) \ &= (n \cdot n + n) + (n + 1) = (n \cdot n + (n + n)) + 1 , \end{aligned} by @def-omega-arithmetic (b) applied to (n + 1) \cdot \mathrm{S}(n), then @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (e) for (n + 1) \cdot n = n \cdot n + n, and @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c) to regroup. Finally 2n = (1 + 1)n = 1 \cdot n + 1 \cdot n = n + n, by 1 + 1 = 2 (@def-omega-arithmetic (c)) and @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (d), (e). So f(n + 1) = (n + 1)(n + 1), and the claim holds for every n. This is Chapter 1’s move of fixing everything else and inducting on the recursion variable, as in the proof of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws. [R2] Decide which of the following maps 
Z 	o 
Z are injective and which are surjective: 1. x \mapsto -x; 2. x \mapsto 2x; 3. x \mapsto x^2. (a) Bijective. Since -(-x) = x (@prp-ring-algebra (a)), equal values -x = -y give x = -(-x) = -(-y) = y, and every y is the value at -y. (b) Injective, not surjective. If 2x = 2y, then 2(x - y) = 2x - 2y = 0 by (F9) and @prp-ring-algebra (c); and 2 
e 0, since 2 = 1 + 1 > 0. So x - y = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f), and x = y. Not surjective: 1 = 2x would make 1 even, but 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, and no integer is both (@cor-integers-even-odd (a)). (c) Neither. Not injective: (-1)^2 = 1 = 1^2 (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), and -1 
e 1, since -1 < 0 < 1 (shown below) gives -1 < 1 by (O2), and (O1) forbids equality. Not surjective: x^2 \ge 0 for every x (x^2 = 0 for x = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), and x^2 > 0 otherwise by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), while -1 < 0 (1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), so -1 < -0 = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)). So -1 is not a value. The methods are those of @fd2:exm-method-injectivity and @fd2:exm-method-surjectivity: for injectivity, start from equal values and reach equal inputs; for surjectivity, solve for the input, or show that a target is never reached. [R3] Prove that for every a \in 
Z: if 3 \mid a^2, then 3 \mid a. By contraposition, as in @fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even. Suppose 3 
mid a. Since 3 is a non-zero natural number, 3 > 0 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), so division by 3 (@thm-integers-division-remainder (a)) gives a = 3q + r with 0 \le r < 3, so r \in \{0, 1, 2\} by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), as in the proof of @cor-integers-even-odd; and r 
e 0, since otherwise a = 3q and 3 \mid a. By @prp-ring-algebra (d) and the ring laws,  egin{aligned} r = 1 &: \quad a^2 = 9q^2 + 6q + 1 = 3(3q^2 + 2q) + 1 , \ r = 2 &: \quad a^2 = 9q^2 + 12q + 4 = 3(3q^2 + 4q + 1) + 1 . \end{aligned} In both cases 0 \le 1 < 3, so the remainder of a^2 on division by 3 is 1 
e 0, and 3 
mid a^2 by the divisibility test after @thm-integers-division-remainder. This proves the contrapositive.

title: The Rationals
content:
The Rationals Chapter 2 built 
Z, an ordered commutative ring in which 2x = 1 has no solution. This chapter supplies the missing quotients by the move that built 
Z: a pair (p, q) with q > 0 records “p divided by q” without performing it, two pairs are identified when ps = rq, and a rational number is a class of such pairs. Addition and multiplication are defined on representatives and checked to be well defined, and each field law becomes an identity in 
Z, already proved. Sets and Functions, Section 3.1 took 
Q = \{ m/n : m \in 
Z, \ n \in 
Z_{>0} \} as a definition; here it is a theorem about the constructed set. The order comes from one choice: a class is positive when a representative has a positive numerator. The Archimedean property then follows from the construction, with no supremum anywhere. The last section asks what 
Q still lacks. No rational squares to 2, and the set of rationals with square below 2 is bounded above but has no supremum in 
Q. A sequence of rationals, 2, 3/2, 17/12, \dots, closes in on the gap from above. Chapters 4 and 5 turn sequences of this kind into the real numbers. What you need. Chapter 2, all of it, and from Chapter 1 only induction, recursion and well-ordering on 
N; Sets and Functions, Chapters 2, 3 and 5, chiefly Section 5.2; a few results of Logic and Proof. From Chapter 2: classes of pairs and the lemma on rules defined on classes (@def-integers-as-classes, @thm-well-defined-on-classes), the operations of 
Z and the copy of 
N in it (@def-integer-operations, @prp-naturals-embed-integers); commutative rings and fields with their algebra (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @thm-integers-commutative-ring, @prp-ring-algebra), from Section 2.3; ordered rings, orders from a positive set, the order of 
Z, the rules for inequalities and least elements of sets of integers bounded below (@def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-order-from-positives, @def-integer-order, @thm-integers-ordered-ring, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-integer-least-element), from Section 2.4; division with remainder and parity (@thm-integers-division-remainder, @cor-integers-even-odd), from Section 2.5. From Chapter 1: @cor-omega-identification, by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion) apply to 
N, and well-ordering (@thm-omega-well-ordering), which Section 3.2 contrasts with 
Q_{>0}. From Sets and Functions: equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-equivalence-class, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition) and the method box for well-definedness (@fd2:exm-method-well-definedness), from Section 5.2; upper bounds and suprema (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum), from Section 5.3; functions and their equality (@fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality), from Chapter 2; and the smallest-counterexample method with its instance on lowest terms (@fd2:exm-method-smallest-counterexample, @fd2:lem-lowest-terms), from Chapter 3. Review exercise R2 uses the countability results of Sets and Functions, Chapter 4 (@fd2:thm-product-countable, @fd2:cor-product-countable, @fd2:prp-countable-subset, @fd2:prp-countable-image, @fd2:thm-integers-rationals-countable). From Logic and Proof: the negation laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan, @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication), for Exercise A1 of Section 3.2 and review exercise R3, and the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for the find-the-error exercises. Section 3.3 compares its proof with the parity proof that \sqrt 2 is irrational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational) and does not use it. Time. About 15 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 25 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Rationals as Classes of Fractions. Pairs (p, q) with q > 0 identified by cross-multiplication, 
Q as their quotient set, a sum and a product checked on representatives (the second argument free by symmetry), rules that look like functions and are not, the proof that 
Q is a field, and the copy of 
Z inside it that turns the class [(p, q)] into the quotient p/q. - The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property. The positive rationals as the classes with a positive numerator, and why negative denominators would break this; 
Q an ordered field with the comparison formula p/q \le r/s \iff ps \le rq; reciprocals reversing order and the midpoint of two rationals; every rational below a natural number, proved from the construction, with its form 1/n < \varepsilon; and the integer part  loor{x}. - The Gaps in the Rationals. No rational squares to 2, proved by descent on a least denominator rather than by parity; the set \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \}, bounded above with no supremum in 
Q, each candidate refuted by an explicit rational; and the rational sequence 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots that closes in on the gap from above. The review exercises return to Chapter 2 and to Sets and Functions and Logic and Proof. Named moves The chapter introduces no new method box; the first four moves below were taught earlier and are run here on new data, and the last is new to this chapter. - Check on representatives, one argument at a time (@fd2:exm-method-well-definedness, with @thm-well-defined-on-classes). Change one representative with the other fixed; each change is one identity at the level below. A formula symmetric in its two inputs gets the second change free. (Section 3.1) - Reduce to the level below (Section 2.3). Write a law about classes on representatives; the two sides become the same pair, or two related pairs, by an identity in 
Z. (Section 3.1) - Order from a positive set (@prp-order-from-positives). Say which elements are positive, check (P1) and (P2), and read off every rule for inequalities. (Section 3.2) - Descent on a least denominator (@fd2:exm-method-smallest-counterexample). Take a counterexample with the least denominator and build one with a smaller denominator. (Section 3.3) - Refute a supremum candidate by an explicit rational. Given a rational s claimed to be the supremum, produce from s an element of the set above it or an upper bound below it. (Section 3.3, the scratch work for @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2) Threads - Classes of pairs. Section 2.1 made integers from pairs of natural numbers, Section 3.1 makes rationals from pairs of integers, and Chapter 5 makes real numbers from classes of sequences of rationals, by the same route. - The integer part. Section 3.2 defines  loor{x}; for a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0},  loor{a/n} is the quotient of Section 2.5 (Exercise B3 of Section 3.2), and Section 4.2 builds the integer part in every Archimedean ordered field. - 1/n < \varepsilon. The corollary of Section 3.2 is the form of the Archimedean property that the limit arguments of Chapters 4 and 5 use, with \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. - The sequence 2, 3/2, 17/12, \dots Section 3.3 computes it; Section 4.6 proves it Cauchy in 
Q with no limit in 
Q; Chapter 5 opens with it, as the first sequence of rationals that should converge and does not in 
Q. Summary A rational number is a class of pairs (p, q) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} under ps = rq (@def-rationals-as-classes), and the sum and product defined on representatives are well defined (@prp-rational-operations-well-defined). With them 
Q is a field (@thm-rationals-field) containing a copy of 
Z, and every rational is m/n with m \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-embed-rationals). Declaring a class positive when its numerator is positive makes 
Q an ordered field whose order extends that of 
Z (@def-rational-order, @thm-rationals-ordered-field). Every rational lies below a natural number (@thm-rationals-archimedean), so for each \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} some 1/n is smaller (@cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon), and every rational has an integer part (@prp-rational-integer-part). No rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two), and \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} is bounded above with no supremum in 
Q (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). What is open: 
Q is an Archimedean ordered field with gaps. Can the gaps be filled, and by what? Chapter 4 develops limits in an ordered field to say what “closing in on a gap” means, and Chapter 5 fills the gaps. Terms - denominator, numerator: q and p in a representative (p, q) of a rational number (@def-rationals-as-classes). - integer part:  loor{x}, the one integer m with m \le x < m + 1 (@prp-rational-integer-part). - order on 
Q: x < y when y - x is positive (@def-rational-order). - positive rational: a class [(p, q)] with p > 0; the set P_{
Q} = 
Q_{>0} (@def-rational-order). - rational number: a class [(p, q)] of pairs in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} under ps = rq (@def-rationals-as-classes).

title: 3.1 The Rationals as Classes of Fractions
content:
The Rationals as Classes of Fractions Chapter 2 built 
Z and made it an ordered commutative ring, but not a field: 2x = 1 has no solution in 
Z (Quick check in Section 2.4). This section repairs that defect with the move of Section 2.1, used a second time. There a pair (a, b) recorded “a - b” without performing it; here a pair (p, q) records “p divided by q” without performing it. We define 
Q as a set of classes of such pairs, give it addition and multiplication through representatives, check that they are well defined, and prove that 
Q is a field containing a copy of 
Z. Fractions as pairs Before reading on. The pairs (1, 2) and (2, 4) are different elements of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, yet both should name one half. Which condition on two pairs (p, q) and (r, s) says “same quotient”, using only operations that 
Z already has? At school, 	frac12, 	frac24 and 	frac36 are “the same number”, and the test for sameness is cross-multiplication: 	frac pq = 	frac rs when ps = rq. The test is the useful part. It mentions only multiplication of integers, which we have, and not division, which we do not. So we keep the test and let a rational number be what the equivalent fractions have in common: the class of all of them. A rational number is a quotient you have not computed yet: the set of all fractions that would compute to it. Signs need a decision. The fractions 	frac{1}{-2} and 	frac{-1}{2} name the same number, and allowing both would put a sign in two places. We require the denominator to be positive, so that a sign can sit only in the numerator. This is the convention Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 already used for its fractions, and Section 3.2 below will profit from it: there, the order of 
Q is read off a single inequality between integers. Recall that 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \}, by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). On 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, let (p, q) \sim (r, s) mean ps = rq. We reuse the symbol \sim of Section 2.1; which relation is meant is always clear from the pairs, natural numbers there and an integer with a positive integer here. [Cross-Multiplication Is an Equivalence Relation] The relation \sim on 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} given by (p, q) \sim (r, s) \iff ps = rq is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). Reflexivity and symmetry are just reflexivity and symmetry of =: with this form of the test, (p, q) \sim (p, q) reads pq = pq. For transitivity we are given ps = rq and ru = ts, and want pu = tq. Multiply the first equation by u and use the second to replace ru: this gives (pu)s = (tq)s. We cannot divide by s, but 
Z has no zero divisors, so a factor s 
e 0 can be canceled. Let (p, q), (r, s), (t, u) \in 
Z 	imes

Z,  egin{aligned} (p + 2q)(2q') &= 2pq' + 4qq' , \ (p' + 2q')(2q) &= 2p'q + 4qq' , \end{aligned} and the right-hand sides are equal since pq' = p'q. (The function is x \mapsto [(p, 2q)] + [(1, 1)], half of x plus one, by @def-rational-operations.) (b) False. Conversely, write x = [(p_0, q_0)] (@fd2:def-quotient-set); then (p, q) \in x means (p, q) \sim (p_0, q_0) (@fd2:def-equivalence-class), so [(p, q)] = [(p_0, q_0)] = x by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). By @fd2:def-quotient-set, x = [(p_0, q_0)] for some pair, and (p_0, q_0) \in x by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (a), so q_0 \in D_x and D_x is non-empty. Every element of D_x is positive, so 0 is an integer lower bound. By @prp-integer-least-element, D_x has a least element, and it is unique, by antisymmetry of \le (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). Existence and uniqueness of N. Let N be the function whose graph is \{ (x, \min D_x) : x \in 
Q \} \subseteq 
Q 	imes

Any function with the property must take the value \min D_x at every x, so it equals N (@fd2:prp-function-equality). Unlike the rule in (a), N is defined from the class x itself, not from a chosen representative, so there is nothing to check for well-definedness. (c) 6/4 = [(6, 4)] by @prp-integers-embed-rationals (a). A pair (p, q) lies in this class if and only if 4p = 6q. - q = 1 is impossible: it needs 4p = 6. e 6, by (O1). - q = 2 works: 4 \cdot 3 = 12 = 6 \cdot 2, so (3, 2) \in [(6, 4)]. Since 1 is the only element of
