(10 points) - 2: (a) exhibits two representatives of one class with different denominators. - 2: (b) defines the set of denominators of x from the class, and shows it non-empty. - 2: (b) gets a least element from @prp-integer-least-element, with the lower bound named. - 2: (b) explains why this defines exactly one function (one value per class; any such function has those values). - 2: (c) shows 4p = 6 has no integer solution and exhibits (3, 2). Fatal errors (0 for the step): defining N([(p, q)]) as “q divided by a common factor” (the formula uses a representative, and lowest terms come only in Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 1); in (c), “4p = 6 has no solution since p = 3/2” (uses division in 
Q to decide a question about 
Z without the discreteness argument). [C2: Find the error] Here is a proof that multiplication on 
Q is well defined. Is the conclusion true? Is the proof correct? If not, name the first line that fails, the error, and give a counterexample to the step. (1) Let (p, q) \sim (p', q'), and let (r, s) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}. (2) Then [(p, q)] = [(p', q')]. (3) So [(p, q)] \cdot [(r, s)] = [(p', q')] \cdot [(r, s)]. (4) That is, [(pr, qs)] = [(p'r, q's)], so the product does not depend on the first representative. (5) The second argument is handled in the same way. The conclusion is true: it is @prp-rational-operations-well-defined. The proof is not correct. The failing line is (3). Line (2) is correct: it is (1) restated by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), and says that (p, q) and (p', q') name the same class. Line (3) then multiplies that class by [(r, s)], using the multiplication of 
Q. But that multiplication is exactly what is being shown to exist: until it is known to be well defined, “[(p, q)] \cdot [(r, s)]” has no meaning, or rather means “[(pr, qs)], computed from the representative (p, q)”, and whether this depends on the representative is the claim. The line cites the goal, which is circular: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Counterexample to the step. The inference “[(p, q)] = [(p', q')], so F(p, q) = F(p', q')” fails for formulas F in representatives. With F(p, q) \coloneqq p + q, the same lines “prove” that [(p, q)] \mapsto p + q is a function on 
Q, since “p + q is a function of the class [(p, q)]”. It is not: (1, 2) \sim (2, 4) and 1 + 2 
e 2 + 4 (@exm-ill-defined-fraction-sum (a)). Repair. Replace (2)–(3) by an identity in 
Z: from pq' = p'q, (pr)(q's) = (pq')(rs) = (p'q)(rs) = (p'r)(qs), so (pr, qs) \sim (p'r, q's). Do the same for the second argument, and conclude with @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b). Lines (1), (4) and (5) are correct as stated, once (3) is replaced. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and that the proof is not correct. - 3: names line (3) as the failing line and explains that it uses the multiplication of 
Q, which is being defined. - 2: names the error as circular, entry (N9). - 2: gives a counterexample to the step (any formula in representatives that is not constant on classes, such as p + q). - 1: gives the repair through the integer identity (pr)(q's) = (p'r)(qs). Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; blaming line (1) or (2), which only restate the hypothesis. [C3: Non-zero denominators] Let Y \coloneqq 
Z 	imes (
Z \setminus \{0\}), and for (p, q), (r, s) \in Y let (p, q) \approx (r, s) mean ps = rq. Show that \approx is an equivalence relation on Y, and that I \colon 
Q 	o Y/{\approx} , \qquad I igl([(p, q)] igr) \coloneqq [(p, q)]_{\approx} , is a well-defined bijection. Equivalence relation. The proof of @prp-rational-pairs-equivalence works on Y with two changes: the pairs are taken in Y instead of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, and the line deriving s 
e 0 from s > 0 is dropped, since in Y the middle denominator s is non-zero by definition. That is the only property of the denominators the proof uses. Well defined. Since q > 0, q 
eq 0 by (O1), so (p, q) \in Y and the inclusion is a function. Apply @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a) to the inclusion (p, q) \mapsto (p, q) from 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} to Y: if (p, q) \sim (p', q'), then pq' = p'q, which says (p, q) \approx (p', q'). Injective. If [(p, q)]_{\approx} = [(p', q')]_{\approx}, then (p, q) \approx (p', q') by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), so pq' = p'q, so (p, q) \sim (p', q') and [(p, q)] = [(p', q')]. Surjective. Let [(p, q)]_{\approx} \in Y/{\approx}, with q 
e 0. By (O1), q > 0 or q < 0. If q > 0, the class is I([(p, q)]). If q < 0, then -q > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so -q \in 
Z_{>0} by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b), and (-p, -q) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}; and (p, q) \approx (-p, -q), since p(-q) = -(pq) = (-p)q by @prp-ring-algebra (c); so [(p, q)]_{\approx} = [(-p, -q)]_{\approx} by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), and the class is I([(-p, -q)]). So I is a bijection: the two constructions have “the same” rational numbers, matched by I.

title: 3.2 The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property Section 3.1 made 
Q a field (@thm-rationals-field). It did not give 
Q an order, and the school number line cannot supply one. We order 
Q the way Section 2.4 ordered 
Z: name the positive elements, check (P1) and (P2) of @prp-order-from-positives, and read off every rule for inequalities. Then we prove, from the construction and with no supremum anywhere, that every rational lies below a natural number; Chapters 4 and 5 use its form 1/n < \varepsilon at every turn. Finally every rational gets an integer part. Which fractions are positive Throughout, a rational is written as in Section 3.1. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), every x \in 
Q is p/q for some p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}, where p/q is the class [(p, q)], and p/q = r/s if and only if ps = rq. The integers sit inside 
Q as m = m/1, and the natural numbers inside the integers. The order of 
Z came from its positive set P_{
Z} (@def-integer-order), and @prp-order-from-positives turned closure under + and \cdot, together with a trichotomy, into all of (O1)–(O4). We do the same for 
Q, so the whole question is: which fractions should count as positive? A first guess from school is “numerator and denominator have the same sign”. But in 
Q the denominator is always positive. That was the decision recorded with @def-rationals-as-classes, and here it pays: the sign of a fraction is the sign of its numerator. A fraction with a positive denominator is positive exactly when its numerator is. [The Order on 
Q] Let P_{
Q} \coloneqq  igl\{ [(p, q)] : (p, q) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} 	ext{ and } p > 0  igr\} . For x, y \in 
Q, we write x < y if y - x \in P_{
Q}. As in @def-ordered-ring-and-field, x > y means y < x, and x \le y means x < y or x = y. In words: a rational is in P_{
Q} if it has a representative (p, q) with p > 0, the inequality being the order of 
Z; and x < y means that the difference y - x, computed in the field 
Q, lies in P_{
Q}. Well-definedness. The definition says “has a representative with p > 0”. To use it we want more: that every representative of a class in P_{
Q} has a positive numerator, so that the test can be run on whichever representative is at hand. This is the situation of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (c), with X = 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} and S = \{ (p, q) \in X : p > 0 \}. Its hypothesis asks: if (p, q) \sim (p', q') and p > 0, is p' > 0? It is, and the reason is the sign of the denominators. Suppose pq' = p'q with q, q' \in 
Z_{>0} and p > 0. Since q, q' > 0 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), (O4) gives pq' > 0, so p'q > 0. If p' = 0, then p'q = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)); if p' < 0, then p'q < 0 \cdot q = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), since q > 0. Both contradict p'q > 0 by trichotomy, so p' > 0. Now @thm-well-defined-on-classes (c) gives, for every (p, q) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, [(p, q)] \in P_{
Q} \iff p > 0 . {#eq-positive-test} Examples. The class 3/4 = 6/8 lies in P_{
Q}, with both numerators positive, as @eq-positive-test says it must; -6/8 does not. Zero does not: 0 = 0/7, and 0 > 0 fails. That matters for (P2), which asks for exactly one of x \in P_{
Q}, x = 0, -x \in P_{
Q}. Non-example by minimal change. Allow negative denominators: let Y \coloneqq 
Z 	imes (
Z \setminus \{0\}) with the same cross-multiplication, written \approx. It is still an equivalence relation, since the proof of @prp-rational-pairs-equivalence used only s 
e 0. Now (1, 1) \approx (-1, -1), and the test "the numerator is positive" passes on one representative and fails on the other: the hypothesis of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (c) fails, at the step "q > 0" of the check above. The comparison of two fractions breaks the same way. For (0, 1) and (1, 1), the test "ps < rq" asks whether 0 < 1, which is true; for (0, 1) and (-1, -1) it asks whether 0 < -1, which is false, because multiplying by a negative denominator reverses an inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)). Comparing numerators alone is not comparing fractions. The rationals 1/2 and 2/5 have 1 < 2, yet 1/2 > 2/5, since 1/2 - 2/5 = 1/10 \in P_{
Q}. Only after bringing both to the same positive denominator do the numerators decide: that is the comparison formula below. Which of [(-2, 3)], [(0, 5)], [(4, 6)] lie in P_{
Q}? Why can one not ask whether [(2, -3)] lies in P_{
Q}? By @eq-positive-test, only [(4, 6)] does: its numerator 4 is positive, while -2 > 0 and 0 > 0 both fail. The symbol [(2, -3)] names no element of 
Q: the denominator -3 is not in 
Z_{>0}, so (2, -3) is not in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} and has no class. (The rational one might mean is -2/3 = [(-2, 3)], which is not in P_{
Q}.) The rationals form an ordered field The payoff is that the order of 
Q has every property of the order of 
Z, together with a formula that compares two fractions with one integer inequality. The Rationals Form an Ordered Field With the order of @def-rational-order, 
Q is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), and P_{
Q} = \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0 \}. Moreover: 1. (The comparison formula.) For p, r \in 
Z and q, s \in 
Z_{>0},  rac{p}{q} <  rac{r}{s} \iff ps < rq ; in particular p/q > 0 if and only if p > 0. 2. For m, n \in 
Z, j(m) < j(n) if and only if m < n. @prp-order-from-positives reduces everything to (P1) and (P2), and @eq-positive-test turns each into a statement about numerators in 
Z: the level below, as in Section 2.3. For p, r > 0, a sum p/q + r/s has numerator ps + rq, positive because s and q are. The comparison formula is the same computation run on a difference. Before reading on: where is q > 0 used? By @thm-rationals-field, 
Q is a field, in particular a commutative ring. We check (P1) and (P2) of @prp-order-from-positives for P = P_{
Q}. (P1) Let x, y \in P_{
Q}, say x = [(p, q)] and y = [(r, s)] with q, s \in 
Z_{>0}. By @eq-positive-test, p > 0 and r > 0; and q, s > 0 by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). By @def-rational-operations, x + y = [(ps + rq, \, qs)] , \qquad xy = [(pr, \, qs)] , with qs \in 
Z_{>0}. By (O4) in 
Z, ps > 0 and rq > 0, so ps + rq > 0 + 0 = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b); and pr > 0 by (O4). By @eq-positive-test, x + y \in P_{
Q} and xy \in P_{
Q}. (P2) Let x = [(p, q)] \in 
Q. Then -x = [(-p, q)] (@def-rational-operations). By @thm-rationals-field, the zero of 
Q is [(0, 1)], and x = 0 if and only if p = 0. By @eq-positive-test, x \in P_{
Q} if and only if p > 0, and -x \in P_{
Q} if and only if -p > 0, which by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) means p < 0. By (O1) in 
Z, exactly one of p > 0, p = 0, p < 0 holds, so exactly one of x \in P_{
Q}, x = 0, -x \in P_{
Q} holds. By @prp-order-from-positives, the relation x < y \iff y - x \in P_{
Q}, which is the relation of @def-rational-order, satisfies (O1)–(O4), and P_{
Q} = \{ x : x > 0 \}. A field that is an ordered commutative ring is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field). (a) Let p, r \in 
Z and q, s \in 
Z_{>0}. By @def-rational-operations and @prp-ring-algebra (c),  rac{r}{s} -  rac{p}{q} = [(r, s)] + [(-p, q)] = [(rq + (-p)s, \, sq)] = [(rq - ps, \, qs)] . So p/q < r/s holds if and only if this class lies in P_{
Q}, that is (by @eq-positive-test, since qs \in 
Z_{>0}), if and only if rq - ps > 0, which by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) means ps < rq. For the special case, compare 0 = 0/1 with p/q: the formula gives 0/1 < p/q if and only if 0 \cdot q < p \cdot 1, that is, p > 0. (b) j(m) = m/1 and j(n) = n/1 (@prp-integers-embed-rationals), so by (a), j(m) < j(n) if and only if m \cdot 1 < n \cdot 1, that is, m < n. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: three times. In the well-definedness check, q and q' carry the sign from p to p'; in (P1), ps, rq > 0; and in (a), the difference has denominator qs > 0. The non-example above shows the first and the third failing without it. Since p/q = r/s exactly when ps = rq (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)), the comparison formula has a version with \le: for q, s \in 
Z_{>0},  rac{p}{q} \le  rac{r}{s} \iff ps \le rq . {#eq-comparison-le} By (b) and @thm-integers-ordered-ring (a), a comparison of two integers means the same in 
N, 
Z and 
Q, so we never say where it is made. Every rule of @prp-ordered-ring-rules holds in 
Q, and 
Q_{>0} \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0 \} is P_{
Q}. One rule is new with fields, because rings have no inverses: taking reciprocals reverses the order of positive elements. [Reciprocals Reverse Order] Let F be an ordered field and a, b \in F. 1. If a > 0, then a^{-1} > 0. 2. If 0 < a < b, then 0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}, that is, 0 < 1/b < 1/a. For (a), turn a^{-1} into a product we can sign: a^{-1} = a \cdot (a^{-1})^2, a positive element times a non-zero square. For (b), multiply a < b by the positive element a^{-1} b^{-1}: it cancels a on the left and b on the right, and swaps which reciprocal stands on which side. (a) Let a > 0. Then a 
e 0, so a^{-1} exists, and a^{-1} 
e 0 by the Quick check after the uniqueness of inverses in Section 2.3. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (a^{-1})^2 > 0. Now a \cdot (a^{-1})^2 = (a a^{-1}) a^{-1} = 1 \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} , and the left side is a product of two positive elements, so a^{-1} > 0 by (O4). (b) Let 0 < a < b. Then b > 0 by (O2), so a^{-1} > 0 and b^{-1} > 0 by (a), and c \coloneqq a^{-1} b^{-1} > 0 by (O4). Multiplying a < b by c > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives b^{-1} = (a a^{-1}) b^{-1} = ac < bc = (b b^{-1}) a^{-1} = a^{-1} . Since 1/b = 1 \cdot b^{-1} = b^{-1} (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), this is 0 < 1/b < 1/a. Find non-zero a, b \in 
Q with a < b and 1/a < 1/b. Which hypothesis of @prp-reciprocal-order (b) fails? Take a = -1 and b = 1. Then 1/a = -1, since (-1)(-1) = 1, and 1/a = -1 < 1 = 1/b. The hypothesis 0 < a fails: (b) is about positive elements only. Between two rationals In 
Z every integer has a next one: there is no integer strictly between m and m + 1 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)). In 
Q the opposite holds. Let 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) and (b), 1 > 0 and 2 > 0, so 1/2 > 0 by @prp-reciprocal-order (a). Now let a < b in 
Q. Adding a, and then b, by (O3), a + a < a + b < b + b , and a + a = (1 + 1)a = 2a, b + b = 2b by distributivity. Multiplying by 1/2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives a <  rac{a + b}{2} < b . So between two distinct rationals there is always a third, their midpoint. Applied with a = 0: for every x > 0, also 0 < x/2 < x. Hence 
Q_{>0} has no least element. In particular, well-ordering is a property of 
N (@thm-omega-well-ordering) that 
Q_{>0} does not share. Between any two rationals lies another, but that does not mean every rational has a neighbor “right next to it”. It means the opposite: no rational x has a next one, since any candidate y > x is beaten by the midpoint of x and y. Phrases like “the rational just after 0” name nothing. Find the midpoint of 1/3 and 1/2, and confirm with the comparison formula that it lies strictly between them. 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6 by @def-rational-operations ([(1 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3, \, 6)]), and (5/6) \cdot (1/2) = 5/12. By @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a): 1/3 < 5/12 because 1 \cdot 12 = 12 < 15 = 5 \cdot 3, and 5/12 < 1/2 because 5 \cdot 2 = 10 < 12 = 1 \cdot 12. The Archimedean property Here is a statement so familiar that it seems not to need proof: every rational number is smaller than some natural number. For the real numbers it is a genuine theorem. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 obtains it from the least upper bound axiom, and there are ordered fields in which 
N is bounded above. For the constructed 
Q it is true for a simpler reason: every rational is a quotient of integers, and integers are as discrete as natural numbers. [The Rationals Are Archimedean] For every x \in 
Q there is n \in 
N with x < n. Try it first (ten minutes): given x = p/q with q \in 
Z_{>0}, which natural number beats it? Do not forget negative p. The first candidate is p + 1, on the grounds that dividing by q \ge 1 “makes things smaller”, so p/q \le p < p + 1. An attempt meets two obstacles. Dividing by q \ge 1 makes a negative number larger: -3/2 > -3. And p + 1 is not a natural number when p \le -2. Both disappear if we split on the sign of p. A fraction with p \le 0 is at most 0, and 1 beats it. For p > 0 the school intuition is right and provable: q \ge 1 gives p \le pq, which the comparison formula reads as p/q \le p. Let x \in 
Q. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), x = p/q with p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. Case 1: p \le 0. By @eq-comparison-le, p/q \le 0/1, since p \cdot 1 \le 0 \cdot q. So x \le 0 < 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), and n \coloneqq 1 \in 
N works. Case 2: p > 0. Then p \in 
N by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). Since q > 0, discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c), with 0 < q) gives 1 \le q. Multiplying by p > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), or equality if q = 1) gives p \cdot 1 \le p \cdot q. By @eq-comparison-le this says p/q \le p/1 = p. Finally p < p + 1 by (O3), since 0 < 1. So x \le p < p + 1, and n \coloneqq p + 1 lies in 
N, because 
N is closed under addition. Hence x < n. In both cases x < n for some n \in 
N, as claimed. The n found depends on the representative, and any one will do. The proof uses only x = p/q, the comparison formula, and the ordered ring 
Z (discreteness, 
N = \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \}); no supremum appears. For the real numbers the same conclusion needs completeness. The form in which later chapters of this volume use the property is about reciprocals: 1/n eventually falls below any positive rational. [Small Reciprocals in 
Q] For every \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \varepsilon. Moreover every m \in 
Z with m \ge n then also satisfies 1/m < \varepsilon. In symbols,  orall \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists n \in 
Z_{>0} \ \  orall m \in 
Z_{>0} \ \  igl( m \ge n \Rightarrow 1/m < \varepsilon  igr) . Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @prp-reciprocal-order (a), 1/\varepsilon > 0. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is n \in 
N with 1/\varepsilon < n. Then n > 0, so n \in 
Z_{>0} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). By @prp-reciprocal-order (b) with 0 < 1/\varepsilon < n,  rac{1}{n} <  rac{1}{1/\varepsilon} = \varepsilon , where 1/(1/\varepsilon) = \varepsilon is (a^{-1})^{-1} = a for a = \varepsilon, the Quick check after the uniqueness of inverses in Section 2.3. If m \ge n, then either m = n, or 0 < n < m and 1/m < 1/n by @prp-reciprocal-order (b); in both cases 1/m \le 1/n < \varepsilon. The order of the quantifiers is the point: \varepsilon is given first, and n is chosen after it and depends on \varepsilon (Exercise A1 (e) swaps them). Chapter 4 uses the corollary in exactly this form, with \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. The integer part By @thm-rationals-archimedean, every rational lies below an integer. With the least-element property of 
Z, it pins every rational between two consecutive integers. [Integer Part of a Rational] For every x \in 
Q there is exactly one m \in 
Z with m \le x < m + 1. It is called the integer part of x and written  loor{x}. The integer just above x should be the least integer exceeding x. So look at the set of integers that exceed x: @thm-rationals-archimedean makes it non-empty, and applied to -x it bounds the set below, so @prp-integer-least-element hands us its least element. One less than that is the integer part. Uniqueness is discreteness: two candidates one unit apart cannot both fit below x and above x - 1. Let x \in 
Q, and let S \coloneqq \{ k \in 
Z : x < k \}. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is n \in 
N \subseteq 
Z with x < n, so S 
e \emptyset. Applying @thm-rationals-archimedean to -x gives n' \in 
N with -x < n', that is, -n' < x (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)). Every k \in S then has -n' < x < k, so the integer -n' is a lower bound of S. By @prp-integer-least-element, S has a least element l. Let m \coloneqq l - 1 \in 
Z, so that l = m + 1. Existence. x < l = m + 1, since l \in S. And m 
otin S: otherwise l \le m = l - 1 < l, so l < l, against (O1). So x < m fails, and m \le x by totality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). Uniqueness. Let m, m' \in 
Z both satisfy the condition, and suppose m < m'. By discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), m + 1 \le m'. Then m' \le x < m + 1 \le m', so m' < m', against (O1). By symmetry m' < m is impossible too, so m = m' by (O1). The comparisons in this proof mix integers and rationals (x < k); by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) the two orders agree on 
Z. For a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0},  loor{a/n} is the quotient in Section 2.5’s division of a by n (Exercise B3). Compute  loor{-7/3}. Then find the least n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < 3/1000.  loor{-7/3} = -3: by @eq-comparison-le, -3 = -3/1 \le -7/3 because (-3) \cdot 3 = -9 \le -7, and -7/3 < -2 because -7 < -6 = (-2) \cdot 3 (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)). Not -2: the rule “drop the fraction” gives  loor{x} for x \ge 0, but not for negative non-integers such as -7/3. For n \in 
Z_{>0}, the comparison formula gives 1/n < 3/1000 if and only if 1 \cdot 1000 < 3n. Since 3 \cdot 333 = 999 < 1000 and 3 \cdot 334 = 1002 > 1000, the least such n is 334 (for n \le 333, 3n \le 999). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-rationals-ordered-field and about @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon. 1. Where in the proof (including the well-definedness check before it) is q > 0 used? What goes wrong without it? 2. Why does (P2) need “exactly one” of x \in P_{
Q}, x = 0, -x \in P_{
Q}, and not just “at least one”? 3. Run the comparison formula on -2/3 and -3/5: which is larger? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 5. Write @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon (its first sentence) in symbols. Then write the version with the two quantifiers swapped, negate it, and decide which of the two versions is true. (a) Three times: in the well-definedness check, q, q' > 0 turn p > 0 into p' > 0; in (P1), ps > 0 and rq > 0 need s > 0 and q > 0; in (a), the difference r/s - p/q has denominator qs > 0, so its sign is the sign of its numerator. Without it, the non-example after @def-rational-order shows both failures: (1, 1) \approx (-1, -1) gives two verdicts for one class, and “ps < rq” gives 0 < 1 for (0, 1), (1, 1) but 0 < -1 for (0, 1), (-1, -1). (b) “At least one” would allow a non-zero x with both x and -x positive, and then x < 0 and 0 < x at once, against (O1). The “at most one” half is what makes the order antisymmetric; @prp-order-from-positives uses it to get trichotomy (O1). (c) By @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a), -2/3 < -3/5 if and only if (-2) \cdot 5 < (-3) \cdot 3, that is, -10 < -9, which is true. So -3/5 is the larger. (d) By @prp-order-from-positives it is enough to show that the positive set is closed under + and \cdot and satisfies the trichotomy (P2). Each of these, run on representatives with positive denominators, is a statement about integer numerators, which holds because 
Z is an ordered ring. (e) The corollary:  orall \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \exists n \in 
Z_{>0} \ \ 1/n < \varepsilon. Swapped: \exists n \in 
Z_{>0} \  orall \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ 1/n < \varepsilon, “one n works for every \varepsilon”. By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (the bounded form of @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation), applied twice, its negation is  orall n \in 
Z_{>0} \ \ \exists \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ 
eg (1/n < \varepsilon) . This negation is true: given n \in 
Z_{>0}, take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/n, which lies in 
Q_{>0} by @prp-reciprocal-order (a), and 1/n < 1/n fails by (O1). So the swapped version is false, and the corollary (proved above) is true. The n must be allowed to depend on \varepsilon. B. Practice [B1: A rational of the form a + 1/n] 1. Let a, b \in 
Q with a < b. Prove that there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with a < a + 1/n < b, and that every m \in 
Z with m \ge n works too. 2. Find the least such n for a = 1/3 and b = 1/2. (a) Let \varepsilon \coloneqq b - a. Then \varepsilon > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \varepsilon, and 1/m < \varepsilon for every m \ge n. Fix such an m (for instance m = n). Adding a (O3): a + 1/m < a + (b - a) = b. And 1/m > 0 by @prp-reciprocal-order (a), since m > 0; adding a gives a < a + 1/m. (b) Here b - a = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6, and for n \in 
Z_{>0} the comparison formula gives 1/n < 1/6 if and only if 6 < n. So the least n is 7, and a + 1/7 = 1/3 + 1/7 = 10/21. Check: 1/3 < 10/21 since 21 < 30, and 10/21 < 1/2 since 20 < 21. For n = 6, a + 1/6 = 1/2 = b, which is not strictly below b. [B2] Compute  loor{22/7},  loor{-22/7},  loor{0} and  loor{-1/100}, and check each against the defining inequalities of @prp-rational-integer-part. We use @eq-comparison-le and the comparison formula with denominators 1 for the integers. -  loor{22/7} = 3: 3 \le 22/7 since 3 \cdot 7 = 21 \le 22, and 22/7 < 4 since 22 < 28 = 4 \cdot 7. -  loor{-22/7} = -4: -4 \le -22/7 since -28 \le -22, and -22/7 < -3 since -22 < -21. -  loor{0} = 0: 0 \le 0 < 1. -  loor{-1/100} = -1: -1 \le -1/100 since -100 \le -1, and -1/100 < 0 since -1 < 0. The first two show that  loor{-x} 
e - loor{x} in general:  loor{22/7} = 3, but  loor{-22/7} = -4, not -3. [B3: The quotient is the integer part] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, and let q, r be the quotient and remainder of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a), so a = qn + r with 0 \le r < n. Prove that q =  loor{a/n}, and hence r = a - n  loor{a/n}. From the hypothesis, 0 \le r < n; adding qn (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)) gives qn \le a < qn + n . These are inequalities between integers, and by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) and @prp-integers-embed-rationals they hold in 
Q as well, with the same sums and products. In 
Q, n > 0, so n^{-1} > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). Multiplying by n^{-1} preserves strict inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and equalities, so q = qn \cdot n^{-1} \le a \cdot n^{-1} < (qn + n) \cdot n^{-1} = q + 1 . That is, q \le a/n < q + 1, with q \in 
Z. By the uniqueness in @prp-rational-integer-part, q =  loor{a/n}, and then r = a - qn = a - n  loor{a/n}. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. 1. If x, y \in 
Q and 0 < x < y, then 1/x - 1/y < y - x. 2. For every x \in 
Q_{>0} there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < x < n. 3. Every non-empty S \subseteq 
Q that has a positive lower bound has a least element. 4. For every x \in 
Q,  loor{x + 1} =  loor{x} + 1. (a) False. Take x = 1/2 and y = 1. Then 0 < x < y, but 1/x - 1/y = 2 - 1 = 1 and y - x = 1/2, and 1 > 1/2. (b) True. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is n_1 \in 
N with x < n_1. By @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon there is n_2 \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < x for every m \in 
Z with m \ge n_2. Let n be the larger of n_1 and n_2 (totality, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). Then n \ge n_2 > 0, so n \in 
Z_{>0} and 1/n < x; and x < n_1 \le n. (c) False. The set S \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : 1 < x \} is non-empty (2 \in S) and has the positive lower bound 1. For x \in S, the midpoint (1 + x)/2 lies strictly between 1 and x (the midpoint paragraph of this section), so it is in S and smaller than x. No element of S is least. A positive lower bound does not help: 
Q is not 
Z. (d) True. Let m \coloneqq  loor{x}, so m \le x < m + 1. Adding 1 (O3) gives m + 1 \le x + 1 < (m + 1) + 1, with m + 1 \in 
Z. By the uniqueness in @prp-rational-integer-part,  loor{x + 1} = m + 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: 
Q is Archimedean] Prove, from the construction of 
Q and the results of this chapter before @thm-rationals-archimedean (and not from any fact about the real numbers), that for every x \in 
Q there is n \in 
N with x < n; and deduce that for every \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < \varepsilon. The theorem. Let x \in 
Q. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), x = p/q with p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. If p \le 0, then p \cdot 1 \le 0 \cdot q, so x = p/q \le 0/1 = 0 by the comparison formula (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a), with equality by @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)). Hence x \le 0 < 1, and n = 1 works. If p > 0, then p \in 
N (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and q \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), since q > 0. Multiplying 1 \le q by p > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), or equality if q = 1) gives p \le pq, which by the comparison formula says p/q \le p/1. So x \le p < p + 1, and n \coloneqq p + 1 \in 
N works. The corollary. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} be given. Then 1/\varepsilon > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), and the theorem gives n \in 
N with 1/\varepsilon < n; in particular n > 0, so n \in 
Z_{>0}. By @prp-reciprocal-order (b), 1/n < 1/(1/\varepsilon) = \varepsilon. The n depends on \varepsilon, which was fixed first. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: writes x = p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0}, citing the representation of rationals. - 2: the case p \le 0: x \le 0 < 1, justified by the comparison formula. - 3: the case p > 0: q \ge 1 by discreteness of 
Z, and p/q \le p by the comparison formula (or an equivalent inequality argument from the ordered-field rules). - 1: exhibits n \in 
N (for instance p + 1) and checks x < n. - 3: the corollary: \varepsilon fixed first, n > 1/\varepsilon from the theorem, reciprocals reverse order. Fatal errors (0 for the step): no separate treatment of p < 0 (there “p/q \le p” fails once q \ge 2, as -3/2 > -3 shows, and p + 1 
otin 
N once p \le -2); using a supremum, the real numbers, or “the decimal expansion of x”. A route through @prp-rational-integer-part is circular here (its proof uses the theorem) and earns nothing for the theorem’s 7 points; the corollary’s 3 points, deduced from the theorem as stated, can still be earned. [C2: The comparison, on representatives] The comparison formula of @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a) was proved through the positive set. Prove directly that the relation “ps < rq” on pairs in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} does not depend on the representatives: if (p, q) \sim (p', q') and (r, s) \sim (r', s'), then ps < rq if and only if p's' < r'q'. Here is the start. We change one argument at a time. First argument: let (p, q) \sim (p', q') and ps < rq; we must show p's < rq'. … Name the move, then complete it. The move is check on representatives, one argument at a time: change the first pair with the second fixed, then the second with the first fixed, and join the two by transitivity of \iff. First argument. Let pq' = p'q and ps < rq. Multiply by q' > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)): psq' < rqq'. The left side is (pq')s = (p'q)s = (p's)q, and the right side is (rq')q. So (p's)q < (rq')q. If p's \ge rq', then multiplying by q > 0 would give (p's)q \ge (rq')q (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), or equality), against (O1). So p's < rq'. Since \sim is symmetric, the same argument with the roles of (p, q) and (p', q') exchanged gives the converse: ps < rq \iff p's < rq'. Second argument. Let rs' = r's, and fix (p', q'). If p's < rq', multiply by s' > 0: p'ss' < rq's', and rs' = r's turns the right side into (r's)q' = (r'q')s. So (p's')s < (r'q')s, and canceling s > 0 as above gives p's' < r'q'. By symmetry again, p's < rq' \iff p's' < r'q'. Join. Chaining the two equivalences, ps < rq \iff p's < rq' \iff p's' < r'q' . This proves the claim. By @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a) both sides also mean p/q < r/s; the point of the exercise is that the integer relation alone is already independent of the representatives, and positivity of q, q', s, s' is used at every multiplication and cancellation. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move (check on representatives, one argument at a time, joined by transitivity of \iff). - 3: first argument: multiplies ps < rq by q' > 0, uses pq' = p'q to reach (p's)q < (rq')q, cancels q > 0 (by contradiction via trichotomy), and gets the converse from symmetry of \sim. - 3: second argument: the same with s' > 0, rs' = r's and cancellation of s > 0, with the converse by symmetry. - 2: chains ps < rq \iff p's < rq' \iff p's' < r'q' and says where positivity of q, q', s, s' is used. Fatal errors (0 for the step): multiplying or canceling by a denominator without using its sign; proving only one direction of an equivalence without invoking symmetry; using p/q < r/s (the comparison formula of @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)) instead of working on the integer relation. [C3: Find the error] Here is an argument for @thm-rationals-archimedean. Is the conclusion true? Is the argument correct? If not, name the first line that fails, say what makes it illegal, and give a counterexample to the step. (1) Let x \in 
Q, and write x = p/q with p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. (2) Then q \ge 1, by discreteness of 
Z. (3) So x = p/q \le p, since dividing by a number at least 1 cannot increase it. (4) Hence n \coloneqq p + 1 is a natural number with n > x. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-rationals-archimedean. The argument is not correct. The failing line is (3). It cites the general “fact” that p/q \le p whenever q \ge 1. That is neither proved in this chapter nor true, so the line rests on nothing: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. What is true, and what the proof of the theorem uses, is the special case p \ge 0. Counterexample to the step. p = -3, q = 2: then q \ge 1, but x = -3/2 > -3 = p. Indeed the comparison formula gives -3/1 < -3/2, because (-3) \cdot 2 = -6 < -3 = (-3) \cdot 1. There is no counterexample to the conclusion. A second failing line. Line (4) also fails for p \le -2: then p + 1 \le -1, which is not in 
N = \{ n \in 
Z : n \ge 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). For p = -1, n = 0 happens to work, because x < 0; but the stated reason “x \le p” still fails there once q \ge 2. Repair. Split on the sign of p, as the proof of @thm-rationals-archimedean does: for p \le 0, x \le 0 < 1; for p > 0, line (3) is correct, with the comparison formula as its reason (p \cdot 1 \le p \cdot q). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and the argument is not correct. - 3: names line (3), and the unproved general claim “p/q \le p for q \ge 1” (entry (N9)) as what makes it illegal. - 2: gives a counterexample to the step with p < 0 and q \ge 2, checked by the comparison formula. - 1: notes that line (4) fails as well for p \le -2. - 2: repairs the argument by a case split on the sign of p. Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; offering a counterexample to the conclusion. [C4: Division from the integer part] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) directly from @prp-rational-integer-part, without the least-element argument of the proof in Section 2.5: put q \coloneqq  loor{a/n} and r \coloneqq a - qn, and show that 0 \le r < n. Say where n > 0 is used. By @prp-rational-integer-part, q \coloneqq  loor{a/n} \in 
Z satisfies q \le a/n < q + 1 in 
Q, where a/n = a \cdot n^{-1} and n 
e 0 in 
Q. Since n > 0, multiplying by n preserves the strict inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and the equality case, so qn \le (a \cdot n^{-1}) \cdot n = a < (q + 1)n = qn + n . Subtracting qn (that is, adding -qn, (O3)) gives 0 \le a - qn < n. Here r \coloneqq a - qn is an integer, and by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) and @prp-integers-embed-rationals (j preserves sums and products, so j(a) - j(q)j(n) = j(a - qn)) the inequalities 0 \le r < n, proved in 
Q, hold in 
Z. So a = qn + r with 0 \le r < n. The hypothesis n > 0 is used when multiplying by n: for n < 0, multiplication reverses inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)), and the same q would give qn \ge a > qn + n, so n < r \le 0 instead. (This exercise is practice with a result already proved; nothing later rests on it.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: states q \le a/n < q + 1 from @prp-rational-integer-part. - 3: multiplies by n > 0, treating both the strict inequality and the equality case. - 2: subtracts qn to get 0 \le a - qn < n. - 1: moves the inequalities back to 
Z for the integer r = a - qn. - 2: says where n > 0 is used, with the reversed inequalities when n < 0. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder or its least-element proof (circular here); multiplying the inequalities by n without using n > 0.

title: 3.3 The Gaps in the Rationals
content:
The Gaps in the Rationals The rationals now have everything Section 3.2 asked of them: they form an ordered field (@thm-rationals-ordered-field), every rational lies below a natural number (@thm-rationals-archimedean), and no two rationals are neighbors, since their midpoint lies between them. Is anything missing? School geometry suggests an answer. The diagonal of a square with side 1 has a length whose square is 2, and no fraction seems to measure it. That picture is motivation only. This section proves the two facts behind it from the construction: no rational squares to 2, and the set of rationals whose square is below 2 has no least upper bound in 
Q. We also build a sequence of rationals that closes in on the gap from above without ever landing in it. A later chapter of this volume fills the gap. No rational squares to two Throughout, x^2 \coloneqq x \cdot x, and 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, 4 = 2 \cdot 2 and so on are the natural numbers of these names, read in 
Q through the identifications of Sections 2.2 and 3.1; their sums, products and comparisons may be computed in 
N (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals, @thm-integers-ordered-ring (a), @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b)). Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 proved by parity that \sqrt 2 is irrational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), for the school rationals. Parity is available for the constructed 
Z too (@cor-integers-even-odd), and Exercise C1 allows it. Here we take a route that needs only the order and the least elements of 
Z, and that adapts to other non-squares (Exercise C2). No Rational Squares to Two There is no x \in 
Q with x^2 = 2. Work backwards from a supposed square root x = p/q. This is the smallest-counterexample method (@fd2:exm-method-smallest-counterexample) run on denominators, as in @fd2:lem-lowest-terms; here no lowest terms are needed, only a least denominator. From x^2 = 2 we get 2 - x = x^2 - x = x(x - 1), so x =  rac{2 - x}{x - 1} =  rac{2 - p/q}{p/q - 1} =  rac{2q - p}{p - q} . Since 1 < x < 2 (as 1^2 < 2 < 2^2), the new denominator p - q is positive and smaller than q. So no fraction for x can have a least positive denominator, while @prp-integer-least-element says some fraction must. The written proof checks the descent with integers only: it never divides, and it verifies (2q - p)^2 = 2(p - q)^2 by expanding. Before reading on: using only integers, why is the new denominator q' \coloneqq p - q positive, and why is q' < q? Suppose, for a contradiction, that x \in 
Q and x^2 = 2. Then x 
e 0, since 0^2 = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)) and 2 > 0. By (O1), x > 0 or x < 0; let y \coloneqq x in the first case and y \coloneqq -x in the second. Then y > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)) and y^2 = x^2 = 2, because (-x)(-x) = x x (@prp-ring-algebra (c)). By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), y = a/b with a \in 
Z and b \in 
Z_{>0}, and a > 0 by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a). By @def-rational-operations, y^2 = a^2/b^2, and 2 = 2/1, so y^2 = 2 says a^2 \cdot 1 = 2 b^2 (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)). Hence the set D \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Z_{>0} : p^2 = 2q^2 	ext{ for some } p \in 
Z_{>0} \} contains b, so it is non-empty, and 0 is a lower bound of it. By @prp-integer-least-element, D has a least element q. Choose p \in 
Z_{>0} with p^2 = 2q^2. q < p. Suppose p \le q. Since p, q \ge 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) gives p^2 < q^2 if p < q, and p^2 = q^2 if p = q; so p^2 \le q^2, that is, q^2 + q^2 \le q^2, and adding -q^2 (O3) gives q^2 \le 0. But q 
e 0, so q^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e). This contradicts (O1), so p \le q fails, and q < p by totality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). p < 2q. Suppose 2q \le p. Since 2q, p \ge 0, (g) (or equality, if 2q = p) gives (2q)^2 \le p^2, that is, 2q^2 + 2q^2 = 4q^2 \le 2q^2, so 2q^2 \le 0. But 2q^2 > 0 by (O4). As before, p < 2q. Descent. Let p' \coloneqq 2q - p and q' \coloneqq p - q, integers. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), p < 2q gives p' > 0, and q < p gives q' > 0; so p', q' \in 
Z_{>0} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). Adding -q to p < 2q (O3) gives q' = p - q < q. Expanding with @prp-ring-algebra (c) and (d),  egin{aligned} p'^2 - 2q'^2 &= (4q^2 - 4pq + p^2) - (2p^2 - 4pq + 2q^2) \ &= 2q^2 - p^2 = 0 . \end{aligned} So p'^2 = 2q'^2 with p' \in 
Z_{>0}, that is, q' \in D. But q' < q, and q is the least element of D. This contradiction shows that no x \in 
Q has x^2 = 2. The answer to the prompt: q' = p - q > 0 because q < p, and q' < q because p < 2q. These are the two inequalities “1 < x < 2” of the Idea, written for integers. The hypothesis p^2 = 2q^2 is used in each of the three steps, and the minimality of q only once, in the final contradiction. Run the descent on p = 2, q = 1, a pair with p^2 = 4q^2. Then c > 0 and c^2 < k^2 = n by (g), so c \in A_n, and c > w \ge v, so v is not an upper bound. Hence k \le v for every upper bound v, and k is the supremum. Case k^2 < n < (k + 1)^2. Then n \ge 2, since n = 1 = 1^2 is the other case; so 1 \in A_n. (i) No rational squares to n. Suppose x^2 = n with x \in

Z_{>0}, with q least among all such denominators (@prp-integer-least-element). Multiplying k^2 < n < (k + 1)^2 by q^2 > 0 gives (kq)^2 < p^2 < ((k + 1)q)^2, so kq < p < (k + 1)q by (g). Let p' \coloneqq nq - kp , \qquad q' \coloneqq p - kq . Then 0 < q' < q. For p', expand: q \cdot p' = nq^2 - kpq = p^2 - kpq = p(p - kq) > 0 by (O4); since q > 0, p' \le 0 would give q p' \le 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), so p' > 0. Finally, expanding, p'^2 - n q'^2 = (k^2 - n)(p^2 - nq^2) = 0 , so q' is a smaller admissible denominator, a contradiction. (ii) No supremum. The proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 (a) goes through with n in place of 2, using (i) where it used @thm-no-rational-square-two, and A_n contains 1 and is bounded above by n. For s \in 
Q_{>0}, let t(s) \coloneqq  rac{s^2 + n}{2s} , \qquad u(s) \coloneqq  rac{2ns}{s^2 + n} . Clearing denominators as before gives the four identities  egin{aligned} t(s)^2 - n &=  rac{(s^2 - n)^2}{4s^2} , & s - t(s) &=  rac{s^2 - n}{2s} , \ u(s) - s &=  rac{s(n - s^2)}{s^2 + n} , & n - u(s)^2 &=  rac{n(s^2 - n)^2}{(s^2 + n)^2} . \end{aligned} So A_n has a supremum in 
Q exactly when n is the square of a natural number. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: produces k \in 
N with k^2 \le n < (k + 1)^2, from a least element. - 2: the case n = k^2: checks (S1) and (S2) for k. - 3: the case k^2 < n: no rational squares to n, by a descent with a least denominator (or another correct route), including a proof that the new numerator is positive. - 2: the two maps (or any explicit rationals) and the two cases, as in the proof for 2. - 1: states the answer: exactly the squares of natural numbers. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a square root of n, or the floor of one, as if it existed; deducing nq - kp > 0 from kq < p < (k + 1)q alone, which fails for n = 5, k = 2, q = 10, p = 28. R. Z} 	ext{ or } x = 0) \iff d \le c. Hence either b \le a and d \le c, and then f(a, b) = (a, b) \sim (c, d) = f(c, d); or a < b and c < d, and then f(a, b) = (b, a), f(c, d) = (d, c), and b + c = a + d says (b, a) \sim (d, c). Since x \ge 0 if and only if b \le a, and -[(a, b)] = [(b, a)] (@def-integer-operations), the function sends x to x if x \ge 0 and to -x if x < 0: it is the familiar x \mapsto \abs{x}. [R2] Show that the set 
Q, as constructed in this chapter, is countable. The tools are the results on countable sets of Sets and Functions, Chapter 4, which run on 
N by the citing rule after @cor-omega-identification (group (i) for @fd2:prp-countable-subset and @fd2:prp-countable-image; group (ii), citable in review exercises, for @fd2:thm-product-countable and @fd2:cor-product-countable (a)).
