Z is countable by @fd2:prp-countable-subset, and the product of two countable sets is countable (@fd2:cor-product-countable (a)). 
Q is countable. The map (p, q) \mapsto [(p, q)], from 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} to 
Q, is surjective (@fd2:def-quotient-set), so 
Q is countable by @fd2:prp-countable-image. The conclusion is @fd2:thm-integers-rationals-countable for the constructed 
Q; that theorem, about the school rationals, is not used. [R3] Let A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} and s \in 
Q. Write “s is a supremum of A in 
Q” in symbols, with bounded quantifiers. Then write its negation, moving 
eg inward as far as it goes and naming the law used at each step. The proof that A has no supremum in 
Q has two cases; which half of the negation does each case establish, and with which witness? By @fd2:def-order-supremum, “s is a supremum of A” is the conjunction of (S1) and (S2):  igl(  orall x \in A \ \ x \le s  igr) \ \wedge \  orall v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) 	o s \le v  igr) . Its negation is, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan (d), 
eg  igl(  orall x \in A \ \ x \le s  igr) \ \vee \ 
eg  orall v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) 	o s \le v  igr) . By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a), the first disjunct becomes \exists x \in A \ 
eg(x \le s), that is, \exists x \in A \ \ s < x (totality of \le, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a) and then @fd1:prp-negated-implication, the second becomes \exists v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) \wedge 
eg(s \le v)  igr) , that is, there is an upper bound v of A with v < s. In words: s fails to be the supremum when some element of A lies above s, or some upper bound lies below s. In the proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2, Case 1 (s^2 < 2) establishes the first disjunct, with witness x = u(s) = 4s/(s^2 + 2). Case 2 (s^2 > 2) establishes the second, with witness v = t(s) = (s^2 + 2)/(2s). (The proof itself needs no negation law: it derives a contradiction from (S1) in Case 1 and from (S2) in Case 2.) [R4] Is there a rational number x with x^3 = 2, where x^3 \coloneqq x^2 \cdot x? Prove your answer. No. The tool is descent on the denominator, as in @thm-no-rational-square-two, run with parity. Parity. Every integer is 2m or 2m + 1 for some m \in 
Z, and not both (@cor-integers-even-odd (a)). An odd cube is odd: (2m + 1)^3 = 2(4m^3 + 6m^2 + 3m) + 1 . Descent. Suppose x \in 
Q and x^3 = 2. Then x > 0: x = 0 gives x^3 = 0, and x < 0 gives x^2 > 0 and x^3 = x^2 \cdot x < 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c)). So x = p/q with p, q \in 
Z_{>0} and p^3 = 2q^3 (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), @def-rational-operations). Take q least among such denominators (@prp-integer-least-element), with its p. Since p^3 = 2q^3 has the even form, p is not odd (its cube would be odd), so p = 2m with m \in 
Z, and m > 0 because p > 0 (m \le 0 would give 2m \le 0). Then 2q^3 = 8m^3, and canceling the non-zero factor 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), q^3 = 2(2m^3). So q is not odd either: q = 2l with l \in 
Z_{>0}. Then 8m^3 = 2 \cdot 8l^3, so m^3 = 2l^3, and l < l + l = q. So l is a smaller admissible denominator, with m \in 
Z_{>0}: a contradiction. Why the look-alike fails. The substitution p' \coloneqq 2q - p, q' \coloneqq p - q of the square-root proof came from x = (2 - x)/(x - 1), which used x^2 = 2. For cubes the same algebra fails: expanding, (2q - p)^3 - 2(p - q)^3 = -3p^3 + 12p^2 q - 18pq^2 + 10q^3 , which is not a constant multiple of p^3 - 2q^3 (it has a p^2 q term), so this identity gives no way to derive p'^3 = 2q'^3 from p^3 = 2q^3, and the descent has no smaller pair to move to. Parity, by contrast, works for every power: “even cube, so even base” is the same argument for squares and cubes.

title: Ordered Fields and Sequences in an Ordered Field
content:
Ordered Fields and Sequences in an Ordered Field In 
Q the numbers 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots crowd together, and their squares crowd toward 2; yet Chapter 3 proved that no rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two). Chapter 5 will make the missing number out of sequences like this one. Before it can, we must say what “crowd together” means when the only yardsticks are rationals, and prove the rules for such sequences without presupposing the number they are aiming at. This chapter does that once, for an arbitrary ordered field F, with every tolerance \varepsilon taken from F itself. It adds to the inequality rules of Chapter 2 what limits need (halving, fractions, the absolute value and the triangle inequality), places a copy of 
N and of 
Q inside every ordered field, and names the Archimedean property, which 
Q has and an ordered field need not have. Then come limits (uniqueness, boundedness, the limit laws, limits and order) and Cauchy sequences (convergent implies Cauchy, Cauchy implies bounded, sums and products, and the sign of a Cauchy sequence that is not null). Chapter 5 applies all of it with F = 
Q. The chapter ends at the gap it was written for. The sequence above is Cauchy in 
Q and has no limit in 
Q, so in 
Q “Cauchy” does not imply “convergent”. If you have met limits in a course on 
R, most statements here will look familiar. What is new is that they are proved in any ordered field, from the axioms alone. Watch where the Archimedean property is needed (each use names it), and note that completeness never appears: no supremum, no monotone convergence theorem and no Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem is used, as Section 4.6 checks. What you need. Chapters 1–3, chiefly Sections 2.3, 2.4, 3.2 and 3.3; Logic and Proof, Chapters 2–8, chiefly Chapter 6; and Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–5. From Chapter 2, Sections 2.3 and 2.4: commutative rings and fields, ordered rings and fields and the rules for inequalities (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-ring-algebra, @prp-ordered-ring-rules, @prp-order-from-positives), the integers as an ordered ring with least elements of sets bounded below (@thm-integers-commutative-ring, @thm-integers-ordered-ring, @prp-integer-least-element), and the two-element field that cannot be ordered (@exm-finite-ring-not-orderable). From Sections 2.2, 3.1 and 3.2: the copies of 
N in 
Z and of 
Z in 
Q (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals), 
Q as an ordered field with reciprocals reversing order (@thm-rationals-ordered-field, @prp-reciprocal-order), and the Archimedean property of 
Q, its form 1/N < \varepsilon, and the integer part (@thm-rationals-archimedean, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon, @prp-rational-integer-part), whose method review exercise R1 of Section 4.6 reuses. From Section 3.3: no rational squares to 2, and the Newton sequence with the term-wise facts proved there (@thm-no-rational-square-two, @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2), which Sections 4.3, 4.5 and 4.6 use; and the set of rationals with square below 2, which has no rational supremum (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2), named in Section 4.6 only. From Chapter 1: the citing rule of Section 1.4 (@cor-omega-identification), by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, @thm-omega-recursion) apply to 
N; the arithmetic and order of 
N (@def-omega-arithmetic, @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, @thm-omega-order, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic); and the powers of Section 1.3 (@prp-omega-powers-parity), which Section 4.2 compares with powers in F and Exercise B2 of Section 4.6 uses as indices. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 6: the negation laws (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication), used to negate the definitions of limit, Cauchy sequence and Archimedean field, and the statement “eventually keeps one sign” in review exercise R3; and the argument that numbers arbitrarily close are equal (@fd1:prp-arbitrarily-close-equal), which Section 4.3 reruns in F. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan), which R3 also uses; from its Chapter 8, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for the find-the-error exercises C2 of Section 4.3 and C3 of Section 4.5. From Sets and Functions: sequences as functions (@fd2:def-function), from Chapter 2; total orders (@fd2:def-partial-order) and finite maxima (@fd2:prp-finite-max), from Sections 5.3 and 3.3. A few items reach further. Exercise C1 of Section 4.2 uses finite and infinite sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets) from Sets and Functions, Section 4.1. Section 4.6 names suprema (@fd2:def-order-supremum) without using them. One example, the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of Section 4.2, uses school algebra of polynomials, which Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 4 builds; it appears only in examples, remarks, warnings and exercises, and no proof of a numbered result cites it. Nothing from Analysis on the Real Line is used, and no fact about 
R. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 40 hours for everything. Roadmap - Working in an Ordered Field. The standing setup of an arbitrary ordered field F, the fraction rules of a field and the absence of zero divisors, halving a tolerance and the midpoint, comparing reciprocals and multiplying non-negative inequalities, and the absolute value with the triangle and reverse triangle inequalities, ending in the form \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon \iff a - \varepsilon < x < a + \varepsilon that the rest of the chapter uses. - The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property. The elements n \cdot 1_F and powers in F, which add, multiply and compare as in 
N; the unique embedding \iota_F of 
Q into every ordered field, strictly increasing and order-reflecting; the Archimedean property as a property of F, with its reciprocal form 1/(n \cdot 1_F) < \varepsilon; the integer part and the density of the rationals in an Archimedean field; and 
Q(t), an ordered field that is not Archimedean. - Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field. Sequences indexed from 0 and “eventually”, the limit with tolerances from F and its negation, first limits in 
Q and the divergence of ((-1)^n) in every ordered field, null and bounded sequences, 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 as a restatement of the Archimedean property, changing finitely many terms, uniqueness of limits, and the boundedness of convergent sequences. - The Algebra and Order of Limits. Null times bounded is null, terms near a non-zero limit stay away from 0, the limit laws for sums, multiples, products and quotients, and weak inequalities passing to the limit, with the squeeze; no result of the section uses the Archimedean property. - Cauchy Sequences. Terms close to one another instead of to a point, convergent sequences Cauchy and Cauchy sequences bounded, sums and products of Cauchy sequences, the sign theorem (a Cauchy sequence that is not null eventually stays at least some c > 0 above 0, or at least c below it), sign stability under null differences, reciprocals, and a sequence of rationals whose steps shrink to 0 and which is not Cauchy. - A Cauchy Sequence with No Rational Limit. The Newton sequence for \sqrt 2 is decreasing with overshoot e_n \le 1/(4n), Cauchy in 
Q, and convergent to no rational, since a limit L would satisfy L^2 = 2; the section then lists what the chapter did not prove (suprema, monotone convergence, Bolzano–Weierstrass), each of which fails in 
Q, and the review exercises return to the integer part of a rational, to induction, and to the negation laws of Logic and Proof, Chapter 6. Named moves - Split \varepsilon. To make a sum of k small terms smaller than \varepsilon, give each term the tolerance \varepsilon/k, and combine the finitely many thresholds by a maximum. It proves the sum law in Section 4.4 and the sum of two Cauchy sequences in Section 4.5; Exercise B3 of Section 4.4 and Exercise C1 of Section 4.5 leave part of it to you. - Bound, then shrink. In a product, replace the factor you cannot control by a bound fixed in advance, then make the other factor small enough to absorb the bound. The bound comes from the whole sequence, before \varepsilon is named. It proves the product law in Section 4.4 and the product of two Cauchy sequences in Section 4.5. - Fix the bad \varepsilon. “Not null” says: some \varepsilon is missed beyond every threshold. It hands you one \varepsilon, to keep for the rest of the proof; ask the Cauchy condition for a threshold with \varepsilon/2 first, and only then take a term beyond it that misses \varepsilon. This is the sign theorem of Section 4.5. - Locate the missing limit. Suppose a limit L exists, and use the limit laws and uniqueness to find an equation that L must satisfy; if the field has no solution, there is no limit. In Section 4.6 the equation is L^2 = 2.

title: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content:
Working in an Ordered Field Section 2.4 proved the rules for inequalities from the order axioms, and Section 3.2 added the one rule that needs division: reciprocals reverse order. A limit argument asks for a few more. It halves a tolerance, so it needs 0 < \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon; it subtracts fractions, so it needs 1/b - 1/d = (d - b)/(bd); and above all it measures how far apart two numbers are, so it needs the absolute value and the triangle inequality. Each of these is a few lines from the rules we have. This section proves them once, in an arbitrary ordered field, and the rest of the chapter uses them on nearly every page. The standing setup Throughout this chapter, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field): a field with a relation < satisfying (O1)–(O4). The rationals are one, by @thm-rationals-ordered-field, and for most of the chapter they are the one that matters: the next chapter applies these results first with F = 
Q, to build the real numbers from Cauchy sequences of rationals, and then again with F = 
R, once 
R is shown to be an ordered field. We state results for a general F because the proofs never use anything about 
Q beyond (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4), and saying so on the page makes it checkable. From here on we use the field rules and the rules for inequalities of Sections 2.3, 2.4 and 3.2 without naming them, as in school algebra. A step is cited only where it needs care: multiplying or dividing an inequality, which needs the sign of the factor; taking reciprocals, which reverses order (@prp-reciprocal-order); and a weak inequality, which hides an equality case. Such a step cites its rule once in each proof. In a field 1 
e 0, so 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). We write F_{>0} \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x > 0 \} , \qquad F_{\ge 0} \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x \ge 0 \} , so that 
Q_{>0} of Section 3.2 is the case F = 
Q. Recall that a/b \coloneqq a b^{-1} for b 
e 0, so 1/b = b^{-1}, and that 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 and x^2 \coloneqq x x (@prp-ring-algebra (d)). Fractions School algebra adds fractions by cross-multiplying and subtracts reciprocals by a common denominator. Both are identities in any field, and the second is how we will compare 1/b_n with 1/b in Section 4.4. The only point needing care is that a product of non-zero elements is non-zero, so that bd may stand in a denominator. [Fraction Rules in a Field] Let F be a field (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), and let a, b, c, d \in F with b 
e 0 and d 
e 0. 1. b^{-1} is the only element y with b y = 1, and (b^{-1})^{-1} = b. Moreover bd 
e 0 and (bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}. 2. \dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad + bc}{bd} and \dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}. 3. \dfrac{1}{b} - \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{d - b}{bd}. 4. For all x, y \in F: if xy = 0, then x = 0 or y = 0. Everything rests on one move from Section 2.3: to identify an element, show it satisfies the defining equation of the element you want and let uniqueness finish. The product b^{-1} d^{-1} satisfies the defining equation of (bd)^{-1}; once bd is known to be a legal denominator, (b) and (c) are bookkeeping. (a) Suppose by = 1. Then y = 1 \cdot y = (b^{-1} b) y = b^{-1} (b y) = b^{-1} \cdot 1 = b^{-1} . This is the uniqueness argument of @prp-ring-algebra (a), run with multiplication. Next, b^{-1} 
e 0: otherwise 1 = b b^{-1} = b \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), against 1 
e 0. So (b^{-1})^{-1} exists, and since b^{-1} b = b b^{-1} = 1, the element b satisfies its defining equation; uniqueness gives (b^{-1})^{-1} = b. Now (bd)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) = (b b^{-1})(d d^{-1}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 . If bd = 0, the left side would be 0 \cdot (b^{-1} d^{-1}) = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), so 1 = 0, which is false in a field. Hence bd 
e 0, and the display says that b^{-1} d^{-1} satisfies the defining equation of (bd)^{-1}; by uniqueness, (bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}. (b) By (a), bd 
e 0, so both right-hand sides are defined. For the product, by (a),  egin{aligned}  rac{a}{b} \cdot  rac{c}{d} &= (a b^{-1})(c d^{-1}) = (ac)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) \ &= (ac)(bd)^{-1} =  rac{ac}{bd} . \end{aligned} For the sum, first \dfrac{ad}{bd} = (ad)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) = (a b^{-1})(d d^{-1}) = \dfrac{a}{b}, and likewise \dfrac{bc}{bd} = \dfrac{c}{d}. Then distributivity gives  egin{aligned}  rac{a}{b} +  rac{c}{d} &= (ad)(bd)^{-1} + (bc)(bd)^{-1} \ &= (ad + bc)(bd)^{-1} =  rac{ad + bc}{bd} . \end{aligned} (c) Apply the sum rule of (b) with a = 1 and c = -1. Since (-1) d^{-1} = -(d^{-1}) by @prp-ring-algebra (c), the left side is 1/b + (-1)/d = 1/b - 1/d, and the numerator on the right is 1 \cdot d + b(-1) = d - b. (d) Let xy = 0, and suppose x 
e 0. Then y = 1 \cdot y = (x^{-1} x) y = x^{-1} (xy) = x^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0. So x = 0 or y = 0. This proves the lemma. In an ordered field, (d) is also @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f). The point of (d) here is that it needs no order: a field has no zero divisors. The commutative ring of integers modulo 6, in the warning after @def-commutative-ring-and-field, has them ([2][3] = [0] with [2] 
e [0] 
e [3]), so by (d) it is not a field. Halving and comparing The commonest move in a limit proof is to give each of two terms half the tolerance. That needs \varepsilon/2 to be positive, smaller than \varepsilon, and to add up to \varepsilon with itself. The next proposition collects these facts with two comparisons we will need as often. [Halves and Comparisons in an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field. 1. \le is a total order on F (@fd2:def-partial-order), and its strict part is <. 2. 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 > 0. For every \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, 0 <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} < \varepsilon \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . For all a, b \in F with a < b, a < \dfrac{a + b}{2} < b. 3. For a, b \in F_{>0}: if a \le b, then \dfrac{1}{b} \le \dfrac{1}{a}. 4. For a, b, c, d \in F: if 0 \le a \le b and 0 \le c \le d, then ac \le bd. Each part is one or two of the rules of Sections 2.4 and 3.2 in sequence. The only care needed is with \le, which hides an “or”: each non-strict hypothesis splits into an equality case and a strict case, and the strict rules apply only to the second. (a) This is @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i). (b) Since 1 > 0, (O3) gives 2 = 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1, and 2 > 0 by (O2). So 2 
e 0, and 2^{-1} > 0 by @prp-reciprocal-order (a). For \varepsilon > 0, \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} > 0 by (O4), and  egin{aligned}  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} &= \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} \cdot 1 + \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} \cdot 1 \ &= (\varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1})(1 + 1) = \varepsilon (2^{-1} \cdot 2) = \varepsilon . \end{aligned} Adding \varepsilon/2 to 0 < \varepsilon/2 by (O3) gives \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. For the midpoint, let a < b. By (O3), a + a < a + b and a + b < b + b, and a + a = a(1 + 1) = 2a, b + b = 2b. Multiplying by 2^{-1} > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives a < (a + b)/2 < b, since (2a) 2^{-1} = a (2 \cdot 2^{-1}) = a. (c) If a = b, then 1/b = 1/a. Otherwise 0 < a < b, and 1/b < 1/a by @prp-reciprocal-order (b). In both cases 1/b \le 1/a. (d) First, ac \le bc: if a = b or c = 0, the two sides are equal (for c = 0 both are 0); otherwise a < b and c > 0, and ac < bc by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c). Next, bc \le bd, by the same argument with the roles of the factors exchanged: c \le d, and b \ge 0 since 0 \le a \le b (transitivity, part (a)). By transitivity of \le (part (a)), ac \le bd. Part (b) is used whenever a proof splits a tolerance: the sum of two quantities, each below \varepsilon/2, is below \varepsilon. The midpoint is the same fact read for two points: between any two elements of F lies a third. Part (d) is how a product of two small, or two bounded, quantities is estimated. The non-negativity in (d) cannot be dropped. In 
Q, take a = c = -2 and b = d = 0: then a \le b and c \le d, but ac = 4 and bd = 0, and 4 \le 0 is false. Before multiplying two inequalities, check that both sides are non-negative. Absolute value To say that x is close to a, we want one element of F measuring the gap between them, whichever of the two is larger. In school this is \abs{x - a}, and \abs{x} is sometimes written \sqrt{x^2}. That formula needs a square-root function, and an ordered field has none in general: no rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two). The square x^2 has the two square roots x and -x, and picking the non-negative one is already a definition by cases. So we define the absolute value by cases, using only the order. The absolute value of x is x with its sign made non-negative. [Absolute Value in an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field. For x \in F, the absolute value of x is \abs{x} \coloneqq  egin{cases} x & 	ext{if } x \ge 0 , \ -x & 	ext{if } x < 0 . \end{cases} For x, y \in F, the element \abs{x - y} is the distance from x to y. The two cases do not overlap and cover F, by trichotomy (O1), so \abs{x} is a well-defined element of F, and x \mapsto \abs{x} is a function F 	o F. Examples. In 
Q, \abs{3/4} = 3/4 and \abs{-3/4} = 3/4, the second because -3/4 < 0 and -(-3/4) = 3/4. The distance from 1/3 to 1/2 is \abs{1/3 - 1/2} = \abs{-1/6} = 1/6. The degenerate case is \abs{0} = 0. Part (a) below shows that 0 is the only element with absolute value 0, so the distance from x to y is 0 exactly when x = y. A non-example by minimal change. Replace the definition by x \mapsto x^2. This map is also non-negative, zero only at 0, and multiplicative, so it passes (a) and the product rule of (b) below. It fails the triangle inequality (e): in 
Q, with x = y = 1, the “size” of x + y would be 2^2 = 4, while the sizes of x and y add up to 1 + 1 = 2. A measure of size must not grow faster than its argument, and that is the clause the square breaks. [Rules for the Absolute Value] Let F be an ordered field, and let x, y, z, r \in F. 1. \abs{x} \ge 0, and \abs{x} = 0 if and only if x = 0. 2. \abs{-x} = \abs{x}, \abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y} and \abs{x}^2 = x^2; if x 
e 0, then \abs{1/x} = 1/\abs{x}. 3. -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}. 4. \abs{x} \le r if and only if -r \le x \le r; and \abs{x} < r if and only if -r < x < r. 5. (Triangle inequality.) \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, and \abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}. 6. (Reverse triangle inequality.)  igl| \abs{x} - \abs{y}  igr| \le \abs{x - y}. Parts (a)–(d) are case checks on the sign of x (and of y). The triangle inequality then needs no cases: by (c), x and y are each trapped between \pm their absolute values; adding the two traps traps x + y between \pm (\abs{x} + \abs{y}), and (d) reads that as the inequality. The reverse triangle inequality is the triangle inequality applied to x = (x - y) + y and to y = (y - x) + x. (a) If x \ge 0, then \abs{x} = x \ge 0. If x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), since -0 = 0. So \abs{x} \ge 0 always, and \abs{x} = 0 only in the first case with x = 0; conversely \abs{0} = 0. (b) Negation. If x > 0, then -x < 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so \abs{-x} = -(-x) = x = \abs{x}. If x = 0, both sides are 0. If x < 0, then -x > 0, so \abs{-x} = -x = \abs{x}. Product. If x \ge 0 and y \ge 0, then xy \ge 0 (by (O4), or @prp-ring-algebra (b) if a factor is 0), so \abs{xy} = xy = \abs{x}\abs{y}. If x \ge 0 and y < 0, then -y > 0 and \abs{x}\abs{y} = x(-y) = -(xy); and -(xy) \ge 0 by the first case, so xy \le 0 and \abs{xy} = -(xy) (if xy = 0, both readings give 0). The case x < 0 \le y is the same with the roles exchanged. If x < 0 and y < 0, then xy = (-x)(-y) > 0 by (O4), so \abs{xy} = xy = (-x)(-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Square. \abs{x}^2 is x x or (-x)(-x), and both are x^2. Reciprocal. Let x 
e 0. By the product rule, \abs{x} \, \abs{1/x} = \abs{x \cdot x^{-1}} = \abs{1} = 1, and \abs{x} 
e 0 by (a). So \abs{1/x} satisfies the defining equation of \abs{x}^{-1}, and @lem-field-fraction-rules (a) gives \abs{1/x} = 1/\abs{x}. (c) If x \ge 0, then -\abs{x} = -x \le 0 \le x = \abs{x}, using @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) for -x \le 0. If x < 0, then -\abs{x} = -(-x) = x, and x < 0 < -x = \abs{x}. In both cases -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}. (d) (\Rightarrow) Let \abs{x} \le r. By (c), x \le \abs{x} \le r. By (c) and (b) applied to -x, -x \le \abs{-x} = \abs{x} \le r, and negating reverses the inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or equality), so -r \le x. (\Leftarrow) Let -r \le x \le r. If x \ge 0, then \abs{x} = x \le r. If x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x \le r, by negating -r \le x. The strict version is the same argument with < in place of \le at the steps that involve r: for instance x \le \abs{x} < r gives x < r by transitivity. (e) By (c), -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} and -\abs{y} \le y \le \abs{y}. Adding (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), - igl(\abs{x} + \abs{y} igr) \le x + y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} , the left end because -(u + v) = (-u) + (-v). By (d) with r \coloneqq \abs{x} + \abs{y}, \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. For the second form, apply the first to x - z = (x - y) + (y - z). (f) By (e), \abs{x} = \abs{(x - y) + y} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y}, so \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y} by (O3) (or equality). Exchanging x and y, and using \abs{y - x} = \abs{-(x - y)} = \abs{x - y} from (b), gives \abs{y} - \abs{x} \le \abs{x - y}. So -\abs{x - y} \le -(\abs{y} - \abs{x}) by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) (or equality), and -(\abs{y} - \abs{x}) = \abs{x} - \abs{y}, since -(u + v) = (-u) + (-v); that is, -\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} - \abs{y}. By (d),  igl| \abs{x} - \abs{y}  igr| \le \abs{x - y}. This proves the proposition. The form of (d) that the rest of the chapter uses is about a distance. Apply the strict half of (d) to x - a with r = \varepsilon, and add a throughout; adding -a goes back, so the step is reversible: \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon \iff a - \varepsilon < x < a + \varepsilon . In words: x lies within \varepsilon of a exactly when it lies strictly between a - \varepsilon and a + \varepsilon. In Section 4.3 the role of x is played by the terms a_n of a sequence and a is a candidate limit. Example. In 
Q, which x satisfy \abs{x - 1/2} < 1/4? By the display above, exactly those with 1/2 - 1/4 < x < 1/2 + 1/4, that is, 1/4 < x < 3/4. So 2/3 qualifies and 3/4 does not: the inequality is strict, and \abs{3/4 - 1/2} = 1/4. Is \abs{a} - \abs{b} \le \abs{a - b} for all a, b \in F? Is \abs{a - b} \le \abs{a} - \abs{b} for all a, b \in F? The first: yes. By (f) and (c), \abs{a} - \abs{b} \le  igl| \abs{a} - \abs{b}  igr| \le \abs{a - b}. The second: no. In 
Q, take a = 0 and b = 1: then \abs{a - b} = \abs{-1} = 1, while \abs{a} - \abs{b} = -1, and 1 \le -1 is false. For which x \in 
Q do both \abs{x - 1} < 2 and \abs{x + 1} < 2 hold? By the display above, \abs{x - 1} < 2 says -1 < x < 3, and \abs{x + 1} = \abs{x - (-1)} < 2 says -3 < x < 1. Both hold exactly when -1 < x < 1. The triangle inequality is the tool of the whole chapter. In its second form it says that a detour through a third point y cannot shorten the way from x to z. Run backwards, it turns two small distances, from x to y and from y to z, into one small distance from x to z. That is the move of almost every proof in Sections 4.3–4.5. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let F be an ordered field. 1. Here is a proof that 0 < 1/2 < 1 in F: (1) 1 > 0; (2) 2 = 1 + 1 > 1 > 0; (3) 0 < 1/2 < 1/1 = 1. Name the rule behind each of the three steps. 2. True or false in every ordered field: “if a < b, then a^2 < b^2”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in 
Q. 3. True or false in every ordered field: “if \abs{a} < \abs{b}, then a < b”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in 
Q. 4. True or false in every ordered field: “x^2 + 1 > 0 for every x”. Give a reason, or a counterexample in 
Q. (a) (1) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), since 1 
e 0 in a field. (2) 1 + 1 > 0 + 1 = 1 by (O3) (or @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict), then 2 > 0 by (O2). (3) @prp-reciprocal-order (b), applied to 0 < 1 < 2; and 1/1 = 1 \cdot 1^{-1} = 1, since 1 is its own inverse (1 \cdot 1 = 1, and @lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). (b) False. In 
Q, -2 < 1, but (-2)^2 = 4 > 1 = 1^2. The true statement needs a, b \ge 0: @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). (c) False. In 
Q, a = 1 and b = -2 give \abs{a} = 1 < 2 = \abs{b}, but a = 1 > -2 = b. (d) True. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), x^2 > 0 if x 
e 0, and x^2 = 0 if x = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)); so x^2 \ge 0. Also 1 > 0. Hence x^2 + 1 > 0 + 0 = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict in the second summand. B. Practice [B1: Two companions of (c) and (d)] Let F be an ordered field. 1. Prove that if 0 \le a < b and 0 < c \le d, then ac < bd. 2. Prove that for a, b \in F_{>0}, a \le b if and only if 1/b \le 1/a. Name the rule behind each step. (a) Since 0 \le a < b, b > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i). First, ac < bc: a < b and c > 0, so @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) applies. Next, bc \le bd: if c = d the two sides are equal; otherwise c < d and b > 0, so cb < db by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), that is, bc < bd by (F6). Combining ac < bc \le bd by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i) gives ac < bd. (b) (\Rightarrow) is @prp-ordered-field-halves (c). (\Leftarrow) Let 1/b \le 1/a. Both are positive, by @prp-reciprocal-order (a). Applying @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) to the positive elements 1/b \le 1/a gives 1/(1/a) \le 1/(1/b), and 1/(1/a) = (a^{-1})^{-1} = a, 1/(1/b) = b by @lem-field-fraction-rules (a). So a \le b. [B3: Two more triangle inequalities] Prove that for all a, b, c in an ordered field, 1. \abs{a + b + c} \le \abs{a} + \abs{b} + \abs{c}; 2.  igl| \abs{a} - \abs{b}  igr| \le \abs{a + b}. (a) By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e) twice, \abs{(a + b) + c} \le \abs{a + b} + \abs{c} \le (\abs{a} + \abs{b}) + \abs{c}, the second step by adding \abs{c} to \abs{a + b} \le \abs{a} + \abs{b} (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). Conclude by transitivity (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). (b) Apply @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f) to a and -b:  igl| \abs{a} - \abs{-b}  igr| \le \abs{a - (-b)}. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{-b} = \abs{b}, and a - (-b) = a + b by @prp-ring-algebra (a). This is the claim. C. Going deeper [C1: A field that cannot be ordered] 1. Prove that in an ordered field no x satisfies x^2 = -1. 2. Deduce that if a field contains an element i with i^2 = -1, then no relation < makes it an ordered field. [Hint 1] Which sign does a square have, and which sign does -1 have? [Hint 2] Show first that x^2 \ge 0 for every x, splitting on whether x = 0. (a) Let F be an ordered field and x \in F. If x = 0, then x^2 = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)); if x 
e 0, then x^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So x^2 \ge 0. On the other hand 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in a field), so -1 < 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). If x^2 = -1, then 0 \le x^2 = -1 < 0, so 0 < 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i), against (O1). (b) If some relation < made the field an ordered field, then (a) would forbid i^2 = -1. So no such relation exists. The complex numbers of Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 contain such an i, so they form a field that cannot be ordered. Compare @exm-finite-ring-not-orderable, where the obstacle was 1 + 1 = 0; here it is that -1 is a square. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: shows x^2 \ge 0 for every x (cases x = 0, x 
e 0), or rules out x = 0 for the x with x^2 = -1 and then shows x^2 > 0, giving the rule for each step. - 2: shows -1 < 0 from 1 > 0 (from 1 
e 0 and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), or the standing setup of Section 4.1) and from negation reversing order. - 2: derives the contradiction with trichotomy (O1) or irreflexivity. - 2: (b) states that any order would make (a) apply, so none exists. Fatal errors: using strictness on x^2 > 0 without ruling out x = 0; asserting 1 > 0 with no reason; using 
R or \sqrt{\ }. [C2: Maximum and minimum through the absolute value] For a, b in an ordered field F, let \max\{a, b\} be b if a \le b and a otherwise, and \min\{a, b\} be a if a \le b and b otherwise. 1. Prove that \max\{a, b\} =  rac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2} , \qquad \min\{a, b\} =  rac{a + b - \abs{a - b}}{2} . 2. Deduce that \abs{x} = \max\{x, -x\} for every x \in F. (a) Case a \le b. Then a - b \le 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or equality), so \abs{a - b} = b - a: by the second clause of @def-absolute-value-ordered-field if a - b < 0, and because both sides are 0 if a = b. Hence  rac{a + b + \abs{a - b}}{2} =  rac{a + b + b - a}{2} =  rac{2b}{2} = b = \max\{a, b\} , and likewise \dfrac{a + b - (b - a)}{2} = \dfrac{2a}{2} = a = \min\{a, b\}, using b + b = 2b and (2b) 2^{-1} = b as in the proof of @prp-ordered-field-halves (b). Case b < a. Then a - b > 0, so \abs{a - b} = a - b, and the two formulas give (2a)/2 = a = \max\{a, b\} and (2b)/2 = b = \min\{a, b\}. (b) By (a) with a = x and b = -x: \max\{x, -x\} =  igl(x + (-x) + \abs{2x} igr)/2 = \abs{2x}/2. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{2x} = \abs{2}\abs{x} = 2\abs{x}, since 2 > 0. So \max\{x, -x\} = \abs{x}.

title: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property In an ordered field F we can form 1, 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1, and so on. They look like the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, \dots, but they are elements of F, and two questions need answers before the next section can use them as thresholds. Do they behave like natural numbers, adding, multiplying and comparing as 
N does? And does every element of F lie below one of them? For 
Q, Section 3.2 answered the second question with yes (@thm-rationals-archimedean). This section answers the first for every ordered field, and goes further: a whole copy of 
Q sits inside F, in exactly one way. The second question has the answer no in general. Fields where the answer is yes are called Archimedean, and in them every element has an integer part and the rationals are dense. The natural numbers in an ordered field Section 2.4 defined, in any commutative ring R and for any a \in R, the multiples n \cdot a for n \in 
N (just before @prp-ordered-ring-rules): 0 \cdot a = 0 and (n + 1) \cdot a = n \cdot a + a. With a = 1 they are the elements 0, 1, 1 + 1, \dots of the opening paragraph. We give them a name, together with powers, which this chapter needs for estimates such as 2^k \ge k + 1. [Natural Numbers and Powers in an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field, with unit element 1_F. 1. For n \in 
N, n \cdot 1_F \in F is the multiple of 1_F of Section 2.4: the map 
N 	o F, n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F, is the unique function with 0 \cdot 1_F = 0 , \qquad (n + 1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F \quad 	ext{for every } n \in 
N . 2. For x \in F, the powers x^k (k \in 
N) are given by @fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b), with X = F, starting value 1_F and step (k, y) \mapsto y x: x^0 \coloneqq 1_F , \qquad x^{k+1} \coloneqq x^k x \quad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N . The subscript in 1_F is there because two fields will often be in play, F and 
Q, each with its own 1; where only one field is in play the subscript is dropped. For natural numbers n, k, the power n^k \in 
N is the one of Section 1.3, defined (just before @prp-omega-powers-parity) by the same recursion with X = 
N: n^0 = 1 and n^{k+1} = n^k n. So 2^k may mean a natural number or an element of F; part (c) of the next proposition says the two readings match. Examples. 1 \cdot 1_F = 0 \cdot 1_F + 1_F = 0 + 1_F = 1_F, and 2 \cdot 1_F = 1_F + 1_F, the element written 2 in Section 4.1. Also x^1 = 1_F x = x and x^2 = x x, which is the square of @prp-ring-algebra (d). The degenerate case: 0 \cdot 1_F = 0, and 0^0 = 1_F by the first equation, a convention the recursion imposes and nothing below questions. Keep the field axioms and drop the order. In the two-element field of @exm-finite-ring-not-orderable, the same recursion gives 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = 0 = 0 \cdot 1. So the map n \mapsto n \cdot 1 is not injective there, and the elements 0 \cdot 1, 1 \cdot 1, 2 \cdot 1, \dots are not a copy of 
N. The next proposition shows that the order axioms prevent this. [The Natural Numbers inside an Ordered Field] Let F be an ordered field, and let m, n, k \in 
N. 1. (m + n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F and (mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F). 2. If m < n, then m \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F. Hence n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F is injective, and n \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F > 0 whenever n \ge 1. 3. (n^k) \cdot 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^k. In particular (2^k) \cdot 1_F = (2 \cdot 1_F)^k, the k-th power in F of 2 = 1 + 1. 4. In 
Q, n \cdot 1_{
Q} = j(\iota(n)), the image of n under the embeddings @prp-naturals-embed-integers and @prp-integers-embed-rationals. With the identifications 
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q, this says n \cdot 1_{
Q} = n. The sum law in (a) and part (b) are rules for multiples (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)); the product law and (c) are inductions following the recursion defining the left side. The product law is the only step with content: multiplying by n + 1 is multiplying by n and adding one more copy, and the sum law and distributivity turn that into the same step on the right. Part (d) compares two functions on 
N that satisfy the same recursion, and the uniqueness half of the recursion theorem makes them equal. (a) The sum law is @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) with R = F and a = 1_F. For the product law, fix m and use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on n, for P(n): “(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)”. Base: m \cdot 0 = 0 by @def-omega-arithmetic (b), so the left side is 0 \cdot 1_F = 0, and the right side is (m \cdot 1_F) \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b). Step: assume P(n). By @def-omega-arithmetic (b) and (c), m(n + 1) = mn + m. Hence  egin{aligned}  igl(m(n + 1) igr) \cdot 1_F &= (mn) \cdot 1_F + m \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F) + (m \cdot 1_F) 1_F \ &= (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F + 1_F) = (m \cdot 1_F) igl((n + 1) \cdot 1_F igr) , \end{aligned} by the sum law, P(n), distributivity, and the recursion of (a) in @def-naturals-in-ordered-field. So P(n + 1) holds, and P(n) holds for every n. (b) Since 1_F 
e 0 in a field, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) gives m \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F whenever m < n. If m 
e n, then m < n or n < m by trichotomy in 
N (@thm-omega-order (a)), so m \cdot 1_F 
e n \cdot 1_F by (O1): the map is injective. Finally 1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F (the examples above), and for n > 1, 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F; so n \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F for every n \ge 1, and 1_F > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e). (c) Fix n and induct on k. Base: n^0 = 1, so (n^0) \cdot 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^0. Step: if (n^k) \cdot 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^k, then, since n^{k+1} = n^k n, (n^{k+1}) \cdot 1_F =  igl((n^k) \cdot 1_F igr)(n \cdot 1_F) = (n \cdot 1_F)^k (n \cdot 1_F) = (n \cdot 1_F)^{k+1} , by the product law of (a), the hypothesis, and @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). The special case is n = 2, with 2 \cdot 1_F = 1_F + 1_F. Part (d) is proved in the fold below. (d) Let f(n) \coloneqq j(\iota(n)) \in 
Q. The zero and one of 
Z are \iota(0) and \iota(1) (@thm-integers-commutative-ring), and j sends them to the zero and one of 
Q (@prp-integers-embed-rationals). So f(0) = 0, and, since \iota and j preserve sums (@prp-naturals-embed-integers (a), @prp-integers-embed-rationals), f(n + 1) = j igl(\iota(n) + \iota(1) igr) = j(\iota(n)) + j(\iota(1)) = f(n) + 1_{
