N with a < (m + 1)/2^k < b. 3. Carry out the construction of (b) for a = 1/3, b = 1/2, taking k least with 1/(k + 1) < b - a. Hint: follow the proof of @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field, with 2^k in place of n. (a) Read 2^k as (2^k) \cdot 1_{
Q} = (2 \cdot 1_{
Q})^k (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (c), (d)). We use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on k for P(k): “(2^k) \cdot 1_{
Q} \ge (k + 1) \cdot 1_{
Q}”. Base: 2^0 = 1 = 0 + 1, so both sides are 1 \cdot 1_{
Q}. Step: assume P(k). Then  egin{aligned} (2^{k+1}) \cdot 1_{
Q} &=  igl((2^k) \cdot 1_{
Q} igr)(2 \cdot 1_{
Q}) \ge  igl((k + 1) \cdot 1_{
Q} igr)(2 \cdot 1_{
Q}) \ &= (2k + 2) \cdot 1_{
Q} \ge (k + 2) \cdot 1_{
Q} , \end{aligned} by @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a) and 2^{k+1} = 2^k \cdot 2; then @prp-ordered-field-halves (d), all factors being non-negative by @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b); then (a) again with (k + 1) 2 = 2k + 2 (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws); and finally @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), since k + 2 \le 2k + 2. This is P(k + 1). (b) By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal with F = 
Q and \varepsilon \coloneqq b - a > 0, there is k \in 
N with 1/(k + 1) < b - a (take k + 1 \ge N). By (a) and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), 1/2^k \le 1/(k + 1) < b - a. Let m \coloneqq  loor{2^k a} (@prp-rational-integer-part), so that m \le 2^k a < m + 1. Then 2^k a < m + 1 \le 2^k a + 1, so a <  rac{m + 1}{2^k} \le a +  rac{1}{2^k} < b , dividing by 2^k > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), @prp-reciprocal-order (a)) and using 1/2^k < b - a with (O3). (c) b - a = 1/6. For k \in 
N, 1/(k + 1) < 1/6 if and only if 6 < k + 1, so the least k is 6, with 2^6 = 64. Then 2^6 a = 64/3, and  loor{64/3} = 21, since 21 \cdot 3 = 63 \le 64 < 66 = 22 \cdot 3. So (m + 1)/2^k = 22/64 = 11/32. Check: 1/3 < 11/32 since 32 < 33, and 11/32 < 1/2 since 22 < 32. (The bound 1/2^k \le 1/(k + 1) is far from sharp: k = 3 already gives 3/8.) C. Going deeper [C1: Many rationals, and rational approximation] Throughout, F is an Archimedean ordered field. 1. Let x < y in F. Prove that the set S \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Q : x < \iota_F(q) < y \} is infinite (@fd2:def-infinite). 2. Let x \in F and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that there is q \in 
Q with \iota_F(q) \le x < \iota_F(q + 1/n). [Hint 1] For (a), apply @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field twice; for (b), apply @prp-integer-part-ordered-field to a multiple of x. [Hint 2] For (a): let r, s \in 
Q with x < \iota_F(r) < \iota_F(s) < y; it is enough to find infinitely many rationals strictly between r and s. For (b): let m be the integer part of (n \cdot 1_F) x. (a) By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is s \in 
Q with x < \iota_F(s) < y, and, applied to x < \iota_F(s), there is r \in 
Q with x < \iota_F(r) < \iota_F(s). Then r < s, since \iota_F reflects order (@thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field). For k \in 
Z_{>0}, let s_k \coloneqq r +  rac{s - r}{k + 1} \in 
Q . Since k + 1 > 1 > 0, 0 < 1/(k + 1) < 1 (@prp-reciprocal-order), so 0 < (s - r)/(k + 1) < s - r (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), and r < s_k < s by (O3). As \iota_F is strictly increasing, x < \iota_F(r) < \iota_F(s_k) < \iota_F(s) < y, so s_k \in S. If k < l, then 1/(l + 1) < 1/(k + 1) (@prp-reciprocal-order (b), @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), so s_l < s_k: the map k \mapsto s_k is injective. Suppose S were finite, with m elements for some m \in 
N (@fd2:def-finite). The map \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o S, k \mapsto s_k, would be injective, against @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a). So S is infinite. (b) Let c \coloneqq n \cdot 1_F > 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)) and let m be the integer part of c x (@prp-integer-part-ordered-field): \iota_F(m) \le c x < \iota_F(m + 1). Multiplying by c^{-1} > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed on the left) gives \iota_F(m) c^{-1} \le x < \iota_F(m + 1) c^{-1}. Let q \coloneqq m/n. Since c = \iota_F(n) and \iota_F respects products, \iota_F(m) c^{-1} = \iota_F(m/n) = \iota_F(q) and \iota_F(m + 1) c^{-1} = \iota_F igl((m + 1)/n igr) = \iota_F(q + 1/n), using (m + 1)/n = m/n + 1/n (@lem-field-fraction-rules (b) in 
Q). So \iota_F(q) \le x < \iota_F(q + 1/n). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) obtains two rationals r < s inside the interval, by density twice, with r < s justified (order reflected). - 2: (a) exhibits infinitely many distinct rationals between r and s (any explicit injective family, or an induction producing one more each time), each checked to lie strictly between. - 2: (a) concludes that S is infinite from an injection, citing a finiteness result (pigeonhole or subsets of finite sets). - 2: (b) applies the integer part to (n \cdot 1_F) x. - 2: (b) divides by n \cdot 1_F > 0 and identifies the bounds as \iota_F(q), \iota_F(q + 1/n). Fatal errors (0 for the step): using density in an arbitrary ordered field (the Archimedean hypothesis must be named); “infinitely many because the construction never stops” with no finiteness argument; dividing by n \cdot 1_F without its sign. [C2: Where the proof for the rationals breaks] In 
Q(t) (@exm-rational-function-field): 1. Show that the set \{ n \cdot 1 : n \in 
N \} is bounded above. 2. The proof of @thm-rationals-archimedean shows that every rational lies below a natural number. Which step of that proof has no analogue for the element t of 
Q(t)? Prove that it has none. (a) By @exm-rational-function-field, n \cdot 1 < t for every n \in 
N, so t is an upper bound. (b) The first step: “write x = p/q with p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}”. The rest of the proof (the case split on the sign of p, discreteness of 
Z, the comparison formula) works for any element of the form \iota_F(p)/\iota_F(q) of an ordered field F, in particular of 
Q(t). But t is not of this form. Indeed, \iota_{
Q(t)}(p)/\iota_{
Q(t)}(q) = \iota_{
Q(t)}(p/q) by @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field; if t = \iota_{
Q(t)}(r) with r \in 
Q, then @thm-rationals-archimedean gives n \in 
N with r < n, so t = \iota_{
Q(t)}(r) < \iota_{
Q(t)}(n) = n \cdot 1, against (a). So t is not the image of any rational, and the proof has nothing to start from. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a), t is an upper bound, cited. - 3: (b) names the representation x = p/q as the step that fails. - 3: (b) shows that t = \iota(r) would give t < n \cdot 1 by @thm-rationals-archimedean. - 2: (b) the contradiction with (a). Fatal errors (0 for the step): blaming the comparison formula or discreteness.

title: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field In 
Q the fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, \dots “tend to 1”. Sections 4.1 and 4.2 supplied the tools to say what that means without leaving 
Q: an absolute value to measure distance, and the Archimedean property to make 1/(n + 1) small. This section defines the limit of a sequence in an arbitrary ordered field, with tolerances taken from that field. It then proves that a sequence has at most one limit, and that a convergent sequence is bounded. Chapter 5 applies these results with F = 
Q, at a stage when no other number system is available. On the way it isolates the method behind the limit proofs of the chapter: estimate the distance, find a threshold, then write the proof forwards. Throughout, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), and F_{>0} = \{ x \in F : x > 0 \} is its set of positive elements, as in Section 4.1; for F = 
Q this is 
Q_{>0}. As agreed after @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field, we write n for n \cdot 1_F, so 1/(n + 1) \coloneqq 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1_F) exists and is positive (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), @prp-reciprocal-order (a)). Sequences A list 1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots is a rule that assigns a term to each position, and a rule of that kind already has a name: a function on 
N. [Sequence; Eventually] A sequence in F is a function a \colon 
N 	o F (@fd2:def-function). Its value at n is written a_n and called the n-th term; the sequence is written (a_n)_{n \in 
N}, or (a_n), and \{ a_n : n \in 
N \} is its set of values. A property P(n) of natural numbers holds eventually if there is N_0 \in 
N such that P(n) holds for every n \in 
N with n \ge N_0. Examples. - In 
Q: a_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1), with terms 1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots. - In any F: a_n \coloneqq n, that is, n \cdot 1_F, with terms 0, 1, 2, \dots; and a_n \coloneqq (-1)^n, with the powers of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field, with terms 1, -1, 1, \dots. The second sequence has infinitely many terms but only two values: its set of values is \{ 1, -1 \}. A sequence is ordered and may repeat; its set of values forgets both. - The degenerate case: a constant sequence a_n \coloneqq c for a fixed c \in F. It matters because every definition below must give the expected answer on it. - A sequence may be defined by recursion (@fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega as @thm-omega-recursion through @cor-omega-identification (b)). The Newton sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, x_0 = 2 and x_{n+1} = (x_n^2 + 2)/(2x_n), is a sequence in 
Q; Section 4.6 studies it. Non-example by minimal change. The formula n \mapsto 1/n defines no sequence: at n = 0 it asks for 1/0, and 0 has no inverse. Everything else about the first example survives the change, and only “a function on all of 
N” fails. This is why the book’s sequences start at n = 0 and why we write 1/(n + 1). “Eventually” absorbs any finite beginning. In 
Q, “1/(n + 1) < 1/10” holds eventually, from N_0 = 10 on, although it fails for n \le 9; “(-1)^n = 1” does not hold eventually, since it fails at every odd n. Two eventual properties hold together eventually: if P(n) holds for n \ge N_0 and Q(n) for n \ge N_1, then both hold for n \ge \max\{N_0, N_1\}, the larger of the two numbers, which exists by trichotomy in 
N (@thm-omega-order (a)). The same goes for any finite number of properties, taking the larger number one comparison at a time. For infinitely many properties it fails: “1/(n + 1) < 1/(k + 1)” holds eventually for each k \in 
N, from N_0 = k + 1 on, but no single N_0 serves every k, since k = N_0 fails at n = N_0. The limit of a sequence We want a precise sense in which 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, \dots “tends to 1” in 
Q. The first idea is “the terms get closer and closer to 1”. Here is why it fails. With a_n \coloneqq (n + 1)/(n + 2), 1 - a_n =  rac{1}{n + 2} , \qquad 2 - a_n =  rac{n + 3}{n + 2} = 1 +  rac{1}{n + 2} . Both distances shrink at every step, so the terms get “closer and closer” to 2 as well. What singles out 1 is that the distance to 1 falls below any tolerance we name, and stays below it, while the distance to 2 never falls below 1. The tolerances must come from F itself, since in 
Q there is nothing else to measure with. Every tolerance in F is eventually met. [Limit of a Sequence in an Ordered Field] Let (a_n) be a sequence in F and a \in F. The sequence converges to a in F, written a_n 	o a, if for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0} there exists N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \in 
N with n \ge N. In symbols,  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon  igr) . Then a is a limit of (a_n). The sequence is convergent if it converges to some a \in F, and divergent otherwise. In words (we say a limit until @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field): the first clause hands us an arbitrary tolerance \varepsilon, a positive element of F. The second says that some index N can be found, and it may depend on \varepsilon. The third says that from N on, every term lies within \varepsilon of a: the inequality holds eventually. The absolute value is that of @def-absolute-value-ordered-field, and by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d) the condition on each term reads \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon \iff a - \varepsilon < a_n < a + \varepsilon . The domain of \varepsilon is part of the definition. For F = 
Q, \varepsilon is a rational number, and “a_n 	o a in 
Q” mentions nothing outside 
Q. Negating the definition, quantifier by quantifier (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation for the bounded quantifiers, @fd1:prp-negated-implication for the implication), and using that 
eg(x < \varepsilon) means x \ge \varepsilon in the totally ordered F (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)): a_n 
ot	o a means \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n - a} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . One bad tolerance, and beyond every threshold a term that misses it. A sequence is divergent when this holds for every a \in F. [First Limits] Decide, from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, which of these converge, and to what. 1. A constant sequence a_n = c in any ordered field F. 2. a_n = 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. 3. a_n = (n + 1)/(n + 2) in 
Q. 4. a_n = (-1)^n in any ordered field F. (a) a_n 	o c. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0} and take N \coloneqq 0. For every n, \abs{a_n - c} = \abs{0} = 0 < \varepsilon. Here N does not depend on \varepsilon at all: the degenerate case. (b) a_n 	o 0. The field 
Q is Archimedean (@def-archimedean-ordered-field, by @thm-rationals-archimedean). Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. For n \ge N also n + 1 \ge N, so \abs{a_n - 0} = 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon, where the absolute value drops because 1/(n + 1) > 0. The N depends on \varepsilon, and Archimedes is what supplies it. (c) a_n 	o 1. By the computation above the definition, \abs{a_n - 1} = 1/(n + 2). Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, take the N of (b). For n \ge N, n + 2 > n + 1 \ge N, so 1/(n + 2) < \varepsilon. (d) Divergent, in every ordered field. By the recursion for powers, (-1)^{n+1} = (-1)^n (-1) = -(-1)^n (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), and \abs{(-1)^n} = 1 for every n, by induction with @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b). Hence \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} = \abs{-2 a_n} = 2 \abs{a_n} = 2 for every n. Suppose a_n 	o a for some a \in F. Take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1 and its N, and let n \coloneqq N, so that n and n + 1 are both \ge N. The three-point triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) gives 2 = \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} \le \abs{a_{n+1} - a} + \abs{a - a_n} < 1 + 1 = 2 , so 2 < 2, against (O1). So no a \in F is a limit. The bad tolerance is \varepsilon = 1: two consecutive terms are 2 apart and cannot both lie within 1 of one point. For a_n = 1/(n + 1) in 
Q and \varepsilon = 1/100, which N \in 
N satisfy “\abs{a_n} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N”? Exactly the N \ge 100. By the comparison formula (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)), 1/(n + 1) < 1/100 if and only if 100 < n + 1, that is, n \ge 100. So every N \ge 100 works, and an N \le 99 fails at n = N itself, where 1/(N + 1) \ge 1/100. The definition asks only for some working N; any larger one works too. Each clause of the definition is needed; the fold below shows what goes wrong when one is changed. a_n 	o a does not say that some term equals a: 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), and no term is 0. Nor does it say that \abs{a_n - a} decreases: a_n \coloneqq (1 + (-1)^n)/(n + 1) in 
Q has 0 \le a_n \le 2/(n + 1), so \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon as soon as 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon/2, and it tends to 0; yet its terms run 2, 0, 2/3, 0, 2/5, \dots, up and down, hitting 0 at n = 1, 3, 5, \dots. Non-example by minimal change. Keep the sequence a_n = (n + 1)/(n + 2) and change the candidate limit from 1 to 2. The distance \abs{a_n - 2} = 1 + 1/(n + 2) still shrinks at every step, and still the definition fails, at its first clause: for \varepsilon \coloneqq 1, every term has \abs{a_n - 2} > 1, so no N exists. This is the negation displayed above, with \varepsilon = 1 and n = N for every N. - Strict or not. Replacing \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon by \abs{a_n - a} \le \varepsilon gives the same notion: given \varepsilon, apply the weak form to \varepsilon/2, and \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). - Every n \ge N, not some. With “some n \ge N” the sequence (-1)^n would “converge” both to 1 and to -1: beyond any N there are terms equal to each. - The order of the quantifiers. With \exists N before  orall \varepsilon, the condition says that a_n = a for every n \ge N: for each such n, \abs{a_n - a} lies below every element of F_{>0}, so it is not itself positive, and it is 0 by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a). (Exercise A1 (b) asks for the details.) Then 1/(n + 1) would have no limit in 
Q. - Tolerances from F. In a field with more elements than 
Q, “every rational tolerance is eventually met” can be strictly weaker than “every tolerance in F is eventually met”. The fold after @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean (“Rational tolerances are not enough in 
Q(t)”) shows this happen. Two kinds of sequence get their own names, because they recur throughout the rest of the chapter. [Null Sequence] A sequence (a_n) in F is null if a_n 	o 0. [Bounded Sequence] A sequence (a_n) in F is bounded if there exists M \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N. Such an M is a bound for (a_n). Examples. In 
Q, (1/(n + 1)) is null and bounded by 1; in every F, ((-1)^n) is bounded by 1 and not null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)); a constant sequence c is bounded by \abs{c} + 1, which is positive even when c = 0. Non-example. In 
Q the sequence (n) is not bounded: for any M \in 
Q_{>0}, Archimedes (@thm-rationals-archimedean) gives n \in 
N with M < n = \abs{n}. The bound is required to be positive only for convenience, so that we may divide by it; any M \ge 0 that works can be replaced by M + 1. Proving a limit from the definition In @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field the distance \abs{a_n - a} was 1/(n + 1) or 1/(n + 2), and Archimedes supplied N at once. Usually the distance is messier, and the threshold has to be found before the proof can be written. [A limit found by working backwards] Prove from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field that a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{n^2 + 1}{2n^2 + 3} 	o \dfrac{1}{2} in 
Q. [Scratch work] The goal has the shape  orall \varepsilon \, \exists N \,  orall n \ge N. So the proof starts “Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}”, names an N, and checks every n \ge N. Finding N is the work, done backwards from the distance. One fraction:  rac{n^2 + 1}{2n^2 + 3} -  rac{1}{2} =  rac{-1}{2(2n^2 + 3)} , so the distance is 1/(2(2n^2 + 3)). Solving 1/(2(2n^2 + 3)) < \varepsilon for n exactly would need a square root. But no proof needs the least N, only some N; so we replace the distance by something larger and simpler. Since 2(2n^2 + 3) - (n + 1) = 4n^2 - n + 5 > 0 for every n, the distance is at most 1/(n + 1), and “1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon eventually” is Archimedes. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} N with \abs{a_n -  rac12} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N \abs{a_n -  rac12} =  rac{1}{2(2n^2 + 3)} N with  rac{1}{2(2n^2 + 3)} < \varepsilon for n \ge N  rac{1}{2(2n^2 + 3)} \le  rac{1}{n + 1} for every n N with  rac{1}{n + 1} < \varepsilon for n \ge N @prp-archimedean-reciprocal: N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon for m \ge N n \ge N gives n + 1 \ge N: the gap is closed --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The proof runs the table upwards: given \varepsilon, choose N, check n \ge N. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal (
Q is Archimedean, @thm-rationals-archimedean) choose N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. Bring the difference to one fraction: a_n -  rac{1}{2} =  rac{2(n^2 + 1) - (2n^2 + 3)}{2(2n^2 + 3)} =  rac{-1}{2(2n^2 + 3)} , so the distance is 1/(2(2n^2 + 3)). We bound it by 1/(n + 1). For n \ge 1, n^2 = n \cdot n \ge n \cdot 1 = n (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d), applied to 0 \le 1 \le n and 0 \le n \le n), so 2(2n^2 + 3) - (n + 1) = 4n^2 - n + 5 \ge 3n + 5 > 0 ; for n = 0 the left side is 5 > 0. So 0 < n + 1 < 2(2n^2 + 3), and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) gives 1/(2(2n^2 + 3)) \le 1/(n + 1). For n \ge N, n + 1 \ge N, so \abs{a_n -  rac12} \le 1/(n + 1) < \varepsilon. Archimedes entered only in choosing N; the algebra of the distance holds in every ordered field. The proof has a shape worth fixing as a method. [Method: proving a limit from the definition] Template. (1) Bring the distance \abs{a_n - a} to one fraction. (2) Bound it, for all n \ge n_0, by C/(n + 1) with C \in F_{>0}, enlarging numerators and shrinking denominators. (3) If F is Archimedean, take N' from @prp-archimedean-reciprocal with 1/m < \varepsilon/C for m \ge N', and let N \coloneqq \max\{N', n_0\}. (4) Write forwards: let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}; let N be as in (3); let n \ge N; then \abs{a_n - a} \le C/(n + 1) < \varepsilon. When to use it. The candidate limit is known, the distance has a formula, and F is Archimedean (as 
Q is, @thm-rationals-archimedean); in a general F, step (3) needs another source of thresholds (Section 4.4). The usual failure. Writing the backward computation as the proof: that proves the converse, entry (N5) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Choosing N before \varepsilon, or letting it depend on n. [A limit with an oscillating numerator] Prove from the definition that a_n = \dfrac{2n + (-1)^n}{n + 1} 	o 2 in 
Q. The steps are numbered as in @exm-method-limit-from-definition. (1) a_n - 2 = \dfrac{(-1)^n - 2}{n + 1}. (2) (-1)^n is 1 or -1 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)), so \abs{(-1)^n - 2} is 1 or 3, and \abs{a_n - 2} \le 3/(n + 1) for every n (n_0 = 0, C = 3). (3) Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/3 > 0; choose N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon/3 for every m \ge N (@prp-archimedean-reciprocal). (4) For n \ge N, n + 1 \ge N, so \abs{a_n - 2} \le 3/(n + 1) < 3 \cdot \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon. The distance itself goes up and down: 1, 3/2, 1/3, 3/4, 1/5, \dots. Step (2) replaced it by 3/(n + 1), which decreases, and only the bound had to be pushed below \varepsilon. In the proof just given, take \varepsilon = 1/10. Which N does step (3) produce if N is taken least? What is the least N that works in the definition itself? 1/m < 1/30 exactly when m \ge 31, so step (3) gives N = 31. In the definition: at even n the distance 1/(n + 1) is below 1/10 once n \ge 10; at odd n the distance 3/(n + 1) is below 1/10 exactly when n + 1 > 30. At n = 29 the distance is 3/30 = 1/10, not below it; from n = 30 on every term qualifies. So the least N is 30, and the proof’s larger N costs nothing. Archimedes and the sequence 1/(n + 1) In 
Q, 1/(n + 1) 	o 0 came straight from Archimedes. In a general ordered field, the two statements turn out to be the same. [Archimedes as a Null Sequence] The sequence  igl( 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1_F)  igr)_{n \in 
N} is null in F if and only if F is Archimedean. One direction is @prp-archimedean-reciprocal read as a limit. For the other, a field that is not Archimedean has an element x above every n \cdot 1_F; then every 1/(n + 1) is at least 1/x, and 1/x is a tolerance that is never met. (\Leftarrow) Let F be Archimedean and \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is N \in 
Z_{>0} (depending on \varepsilon) with 1/(m \cdot 1_F) < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. For n \ge N also n + 1 \ge N, so \Bigl\lvert  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} - 0 \Bigrvert =  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon , where the absolute value drops because the term is positive. So the sequence is null. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose F is not Archimedean. Negating @def-archimedean-ordered-field (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, and @prp-ordered-field-halves (a) for 
eg(x < n \cdot 1_F) \iff x \ge n \cdot 1_F), there is x \in F with x \ge n \cdot 1_F for every n \in 
N. In particular x \ge 1 \cdot 1_F = 1 > 0, so \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/x \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). For every n \in 
N, 0 < (n + 1) \cdot 1_F \le x (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), so @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) gives \Bigl\lvert  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} - 0 \Bigrvert =  rac{1}{(n + 1) \cdot 1_F} \ge  rac{1}{x} = \varepsilon . So for this \varepsilon no N works, even with n = N, and the sequence is not null. So in 
Q(t), the field of @exm-rational-function-field, which is not Archimedean, 1/(n + 1) does not tend to 0: the tolerance 1/t is never met. The same example shows why tolerances must come from F. In 
Q(t), every rational tolerance is eventually met by 1/(n + 1). Write \iota for the embedding \iota_F of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field. Since \iota respects products, \iota(1) = 1 and \iota(n + 1) = (n + 1) \cdot 1, we have ((n + 1) \cdot 1) \cdot \iota(1/(n + 1)) = \iota(1) = 1, so the term 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1) is \iota(1/(n + 1)). Given q \in 
Q_{>0}, @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b) gives N with 1/(n + 1) < q in 
Q for every n \ge N, and \iota, being strictly increasing, carries this to \iota(1/(n + 1)) < \iota(q). Yet the sequence is not null in 
Q(t). For F = 
Q the two readings coincide, because there every tolerance is rational. Changing finitely many terms Whether a sequence converges, and to what, depends only on its terms from some point on. Two forms of this are used constantly: altering finitely many terms, and dropping the first k. [Only the Tail Matters] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be sequences in F, and a \in F. 1. If there is N_0 \in 
N with a_n = b_n for every n \ge N_0, then a_n 	o a if and only if b_n 	o a; in particular (a_n) is null if and only if (b_n) is; and (a_n) is bounded if and only if (b_n) is. 2. For k \in 
N, the shifted sequence (a_{n+k})_{n \in 
N} converges to a if and only if (a_n) does. For limits, a threshold for one sequence becomes a threshold for the other once it is pushed past N_0, or moved by k. For bounds, the finitely many terms before N_0 are absorbed by a finite maximum. (a) Limits. Suppose a_n 	o a, and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Choose N with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N, and let N' \coloneqq \max\{N, N_0\}. For n \ge N', b_n = a_n and \abs{b_n - a} = \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon. So b_n 	o a. The hypothesis is symmetric in the two sequences, so the converse follows by exchanging them. The case a = 0 is the statement about null sequences. Bounds. Suppose \abs{a_n} \le M for every n, with M \in F_{>0}. If N_0 = 0, the two sequences are equal. Otherwise let M' \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{b_0}, \dots, \abs{b_{N_0 - 1}}, M \} , the maximum of finitely many elements of F, which exists by @fd2:prp-finite-max (its proof works in any ordered field, as Sets and Functions, Section 5.3 remarks). Then M' \ge M > 0. For n < N_0, \abs{b_n} \le M' because \abs{b_n} is one of the listed elements; for n \ge N_0, \abs{b_n} = \abs{a_n} \le M \le M'. So M' bounds (b_n). The converse is the same with the sequences exchanged. (b) Suppose a_n 	o a, and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, with N as in the definition. For n \ge N, also n + k \ge N, so \abs{a_{n+k} - a} < \varepsilon. Hence (a_{n+k})_n converges to a, with the same N. Conversely, suppose a_{n+k} 	o a, and let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, with N such that \abs{a_{m+k} - a} < \varepsilon for every m \ge N. Let n \ge N + k. Then n = m + k for the natural number m \coloneqq n - k, and m \ge N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), (c)). So \abs{a_n - a} = \abs{a_{m+k} - a} < \varepsilon, and N + k is a threshold for (a_n). This proves the proposition. The shift clause is about convergence only; it is used to start a sequence later, for instance to read a formula such as 1/n, which needs n \ge 1, as the shift by 1 of a sequence indexed from 0. One more reformulation moves every limit to 0. [Limits Through Null Sequences] For a sequence (a_n) in F and a \in F: a_n 	o a if and only if the sequence (a_n - a) is null. For every n, \abs{(a_n - a) - 0} = \abs{a_n - a}. So the two conditions of @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, for (a_n) with limit a and for (a_n - a) with limit 0, say word for word the same thing, with the same N for each \varepsilon. A sequence has at most one limit If “the terms are eventually within every tolerance of a” is to name the number the sequence tends to, it must single out one a. It does. [Uniqueness of Limits] Let (a_n) be a sequence in F and a, b \in F. If a_n 	o a and a_n 	o b, then a = b. Try it first (ten minutes): suppose a_n 	o a and a_n 	o b with a 
e b. Which \varepsilon makes the two tails collide? The natural first choice is \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{a - b}, positive because a 
e b; it is the choice that worked in @fd1:prp-arbitrarily-close-equal. Beyond both thresholds a term a_n is within \abs{a - b} of a and of b, and the triangle inequality through a_n yields only \abs{a - b} < 2\abs{a - b}: true, and no contradiction. The two tolerances add. So give each half: with \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{a - b}/2, the same chain ends in \abs{a - b} < \abs{a - b}. Let a_n 	o a and a_n 	o b, and suppose, for a contradiction, that a 
e b. Then a - b 
e 0, so \abs{a - b} > 0 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)), and \varepsilon \coloneqq  rac{\abs{a - b}}{2} \in F_{>0} by @prp-ordered-field-halves (b); it depends only on a and b. Since a_n 	o a, there is N_1 with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1; since a_n 	o b, there is N_2 with \abs{a_n - b} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_2. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. Then both inequalities hold at this n, and the three-point triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), with \abs{a - a_n} = \abs{a_n - a} by part (b) of the same proposition, gives \abs{a - b} \le \abs{a - a_n} + \abs{a_n - b} < \varepsilon + \varepsilon = \abs{a - b} . So \abs{a - b} < \abs{a - b}, against (O1). This contradiction shows a = b. Since a convergent sequence has exactly one limit, we may speak of the limit and write it \lim a_n, or \lim_{n 	o \infty} a_n. So \lim a_n = a means the same as a_n 	o a. In 
Q, @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field gives \lim 1/(n + 1) = 0 and \lim (n + 1)/(n + 2) = 1, while \lim (-1)^n names nothing. Convergent sequences are bounded A convergent sequence cannot run off: from some index on, its terms are trapped near the limit, and only finitely many terms come before that index. Convergent Sequences Are Bounded Every convergent sequence in F is bounded. Use the definition once, with the tolerance 1: from some N on, \abs{a_n} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a}. The terms before N are finitely many, so one of them, or \abs{a} + 1, is the largest absolute value in sight. Let a_n 	o a. Applying @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field with \varepsilon \coloneqq 1 \in F_{>0} gives N \in 
N with \abs{a_n - a} < 1 for every n \ge N. For such n, the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), with x = a_n - a and y = a) gives \abs{a_n} = \abs{(a_n - a) + a} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a} . If N = 0, let M \coloneqq \abs{a} + 1. Otherwise let M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{a} + 1 \} , which exists by @fd2:prp-finite-max in the totally ordered F (as in the proof of @prp-tail-change-ordered-field). In both cases M \ge \abs{a} + 1 \ge 1 > 0, by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), so M \in F_{>0}. For n < N, \abs{a_n} \le M because \abs{a_n} is one of the listed elements; for n \ge N, \abs{a_n} < \abs{a} + 1 \le M. So M bounds (a_n). The bound M depends on the whole sequence, through a, N and the first N terms, but on no tolerance: it is one element of F, fixed once. Section 4.4 uses exactly that, in the product of two limits. The converse fails: ((-1)^n) is bounded by 1 and divergent (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write “a_n 
ot	o a” in symbols, and name the law used at each step. 2. What does \exists N \in 
N \  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \  orall n \in 
N \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon  igr) say about (a_n)? Does (1/(n + 1)) satisfy it in 
Q, with a = 0? 3. For a_n = (2n + 1)/(n + 1) in 
Q, find the least N that works in @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field for the limit 2 and \varepsilon = 1/50. (a) Start from 
eg  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \exists N \in 
N \  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon). The bounded negation laws (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a), then (b), then (a)) move 
eg past the three quantifiers, turning each  orall into \exists and the \exists into  orall. That leaves 
eg(n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon), which is n \ge N \wedge 
eg(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon) by @fd1:prp-negated-implication. Finally 
eg(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon) is \abs{a_n - a} \ge \varepsilon, by trichotomy in F (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). The result: \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n - a} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . (b) It says that a_n = a for every n \ge N: the sequence is eventually constant, equal to a. Indeed, fix n \ge N. Then \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. If a_n 
e a, then \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{a_n - a} is in F_{>0} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)) and gives \abs{a_n - a} < \abs{a_n - a}, against (O1); so a_n = a. Conversely, a sequence with a_n = a for every n \ge N satisfies the formula, since \abs{a_n - a} = \abs{0} = 0 < \varepsilon. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) does not satisfy it: no term equals 0. It converges to 0, but its N must depend on \varepsilon. The quantifier order is the whole difference. (c) a_n - 2 =  igl( 2n + 1 - 2(n + 1)  igr)/(n + 1) = -1/(n + 1), so \abs{a_n - 2} = 1/(n + 1). By the comparison formula, 1/(n + 1) < 1/50 if and only if n + 1 > 50, that is, n \ge 50. So N = 50 works, and every N \le 49 fails at n = 49 (which is \ge N), where \abs{a_{49} - 2} = 1/50. The least N is 50. B. Practice [B1: Limits from the definition] Prove from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, following @exm-method-limit-from-definition, that in 
Q: 1. \dfrac{3n + 2}{n + 4} 	o 3; 2. \dfrac{n + 5}{n^2 + 1} 	o 0. Say where the Archimedean property is used. (a) (1) \dfrac{3n + 2}{n + 4} - 3 = \dfrac{-10}{n + 4}, so the distance is 10/(n + 4). (2) 0 < n + 1 < n + 4, so 1/(n + 4) < 1/(n + 1) (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)), and the distance is < 10/(n + 1). (3) Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, choose N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon/10 for m \ge N (@prp-archimedean-reciprocal). (4) For n \ge N, n + 1 \ge N, so the distance is < 10/(n + 1) < \varepsilon. (b) (1) The distance is (n + 5)/(n^2 + 1). (2) For n \ge 1: n + 5 \le 6n; n^2 < n^2 + 1 gives 1/(n^2 + 1) < 1/n^2; so the distance is < 6n/n^2 = 6/n, and 6/n \le 12/(n + 1) because n + 1 \le 2n. So the distance is < 12/(n + 1) for n \ge 1 (n_0 = 1; at n = 0 the term is 5). (3) Choose N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \varepsilon/12 for m \ge N; then N \ge 1 = n_0. (4) For n \ge N: n \ge 1 and n + 1 \ge N, so the distance is < 12/(n + 1) < \varepsilon. Where Archimedes is used: in step (3) only, both times. [B2] Prove that if a_n 	o a in F, then \abs{a_n} 	o \abs{a}. Show by an example that the converse fails, and prove that it holds when a = 0. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, and choose N with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon for n \ge N. By the reverse triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f)), for n \ge N,  igl\lvert \abs{a_n} - \abs{a}  igrvert \le \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon . So \abs{a_n} 	o \abs{a}, with the same N. The converse fails for a_n = (-1)^n and a = 1: \abs{a_n} = 1 for every n, a constant sequence, so \abs{a_n} 	o 1 = \abs{1} (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (a)); but (a_n) converges to nothing (part (d) of that example). For a = 0 the converse holds:  igl\lvert \abs{a_n} - \abs{0}  igrvert =  igl\lvert \abs{a_n}  igrvert = \abs{a_n} = \abs{a_n - 0}, by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), since \abs{a_n} \ge 0. So the two conditions coincide: a sequence is null if and only if its absolute values form a null sequence. [B3: Bounded but not convergent, in 
Q(t)] In the field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field, show that the sequence (n \cdot 1)_{n \in 
N} is bounded and does not converge. Is (n) bounded in 
Q? Bounded. By @exm-rational-function-field, t > n \cdot 1 for every n \in 
N. Also n \cdot 1 \ge 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), and 0 \cdot 1 = 0), so \abs{n \cdot 1} = n \cdot 1 < t. And t > 1 \cdot 1 = 1 > 0, so M \coloneqq t \in 
Q(t)_{>0} is a bound. Not convergent. Suppose n \cdot 1 	o a for some a \in 
Q(t). Take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1/2, which is positive (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)), and its N. With n \coloneqq N, both n and n + 1 are \ge N, and (n + 1) \cdot 1 - n \cdot 1 = 1 by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). The three-point triangle inequality gives 1 = \abs{(n + 1) \cdot 1 - n \cdot 1} \le \abs{(n + 1) \cdot 1 - a} + \abs{a - n \cdot 1} < 	frac12 + 	frac12 = 1 , against (O1). So the sequence diverges. In 
Q. No: by the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field, Archimedes puts some n above any proposed bound. The same sequence is bounded in one field and unbounded in another. Boundedness is a property of the sequence in F, like convergence. [B4: Prove or disprove] Let F be an ordered field and (a_n), (b_n) sequences in F. Prove each true statement from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field and refute each false one with a counterexample. 1. If a_n 	o a, then (a_{2n})_{n \in 
N} converges to a. 2. If (a_{2n})_n and (a_{2n+1})_n both converge, then (a_n) converges. 3. If (a_n) is null and \abs{b_n} \le \abs{a_n} for every n, then (b_n) is null. 4. If a_n 	o a, then (a_{n+1} - a_n) is null. 5. If (a_n b_n) is null, then (a_n) or (b_n) is null. 6. In F = 
Q: if a_n 	o a and every a_n is an integer, then there is N with a_n = a_N for every n \ge N. (a) True. Given \varepsilon, take the N of a_n 	o a. For n \ge N, 2n = n + n \ge n \ge N, so \abs{a_{2n} - a} < \varepsilon. (b) False. Take a_n = (-1)^n in 
Q. Then (-1)^{2n} = 1 and (-1)^{2n+1} = -1 for every n (induction, from (-1)^{k+2} = (-1)^k), so the two subsequences are constant, with limits 1 and -1; and (a_n) diverges (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)). (c) True. Given \varepsilon, take N with \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon for n \ge N; then \abs{b_n - 0} \le \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon for n \ge N. (d) True. Given \varepsilon, take N with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/2 for n \ge N. For n \ge N also n + 1 \ge N, and \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} \le \abs{a_{n+1} - a} + \abs{a - a_n} < \varepsilon. (e) False. In 
Q take a_n = (1 + (-1)^n)/2 and b_n = (1 - (-1)^n)/2. Since (-1)^n is 1 or -1 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)), their values are 1, 0, 1, \dots and 0, 1, 0, \dots, and a_n b_n = 0 for every n: the constant 0, which is null. Neither factor is null: for \varepsilon = 1 and any N, one of N, N + 1 is even and the other odd, and there \abs{a_n} = 1, resp. \abs{b_n} = 1. (f) True. Take N with \abs{a_n - a} < 1/2 for n \ge N. For n \ge N, k \coloneqq a_n - a_N is an integer with \abs{k} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a - a_N} < 1. If k > 0, then k \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c); the order of 
Q agrees with that of 
Z on integers, by the comparison formula of @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a) with denominators 1), against \abs{k} < 1; if k < 0, the same with -k. So k = 0, that is, a_n = a_N. C. Going deeper [C1: A positive limit keeps the terms positive] 1. Prove that if a_n 	o a in F and a > 0, then a_n > a/2 eventually; in particular a_n > 0 eventually. 2. Give a sequence in 
Q with a_n > 0 for every n whose limit is not positive. What does this say about the converse of (a)? (a) Let \varepsilon \coloneqq a/2, which lies in F_{>0} by @prp-ordered-field-halves (b), since a > 0. Choose N with \abs{a_n - a} < a/2 for every n \ge N. By @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), for such n, a_n > a -  rac{a}{2} =  rac{a}{2} > 0 , where a - a/2 = a/2 because a/2 + a/2 = a (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). So a_n > a/2 for every n \ge N. (b) a_n = 1/(n + 1): every term is positive, and the limit is 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). So “every term positive” does not give “limit positive”: the strict inequality is lost in the limit. What survives is the weak inequality a \ge 0, proved in Section 4.4. [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument for @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. Is the conclusion true? Is the argument correct? If not, name the line that fails, say what makes it illegal, and give a counterexample to the step. Then repair the argument. (1) Let a_n 	o a. (2) Take \varepsilon \coloneqq 1 in the definition of the limit, and let N be the index it provides. (3) Then for every n \in 
N, \abs{a_n} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a}. (4) So M \coloneqq 1 + \abs{a} is a bound for (a_n). The conclusion is true: it is @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. The argument is not correct. The failing line is (3). The first inequality is the triangle inequality and is fine. The second uses \abs{a_n - a} < 1 “for every n \in 
N”. Line (2) supplies it only for n \ge N: it is the bounded universal  orall n \in 
N \, (n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < 1). Instantiating it at n needs the line n \ge N (the bounded universal applies only to n \ge N), and for n < N no such line is available. Line (3) cites a line that is not there: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Counterexample to the step. In 
Q, let a_0 \coloneqq 5 and a_n \coloneqq 0 for n \ge 1, with a = 0. Then a_n 	o 0, and N = 1 is a legitimate choice in line (2) for \varepsilon = 1, since \abs{a_n - 0} = 0 < 1 for n \ge 1. At n = 0, line (3) claims \abs{a_0} < 1 + \abs{0} = 1, but \abs{a_0} = 5; and the M = 1 of line (4) is not a bound. No counterexample to the conclusion exists: 5 is a bound. Repair. Keep line (3) for n \ge N only, and take M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{a} + 1 \}, the finite maximum of the proof of @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and the argument is not correct. - 3: names line (3) and the use of \abs{a_n - a} < 1 for n < N, where the hypothesis does not apply. - 3: gives a convergent sequence and a legitimate N for which the step’s inequality fails at some n < N, and checks it. - 2: repairs the argument by a bound that also covers the finitely many terms before N (a finite maximum, or a finite sum of \abs{a_0}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}} and \abs{a} + 1). Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; offering a counterexample to the conclusion; blaming the triangle inequality.

title: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content:
The Algebra and Order of Limits So far every limit has been found by hand: we computed the distance from a_n to the candidate limit and bounded it, as in @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field and @exm-limit-from-definition. This section proves the rules that make most such work unnecessary. Sums, multiples, products and quotients of convergent sequences converge to the sum, multiple, product and quotient of the limits; limits respect \le; and a sequence trapped between two sequences with a common limit has that limit too. Everything holds in an arbitrary ordered field F. No result of this section uses the Archimedean property; only the examples in 
Q do, through @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b) or the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field. Throughout, F is an ordered field and F_{>0} its set of positive elements, as in Section 4.3. Two tools The first tool says that a small factor wins against a factor that merely stays bounded. [Null Times Bounded Is Null] Let (a_n) be a null sequence in F, and let (b_n) be a sequence with \abs{b_n} \le M for every n, where M \in F_{>0}. Then (a_n b_n) is null. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/M \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a) and (O4)). Since (a_n) is null, there is N with \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon/M for every n \ge N. For such n, by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), \abs{a_n b_n - 0} = \abs{a_n} \abs{b_n} \le \abs{a_n} M <  rac{\varepsilon}{M} \, M = \varepsilon , where the first inequality multiplies \abs{b_n} \le M by \abs{a_n} \ge 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d)), and the second multiplies \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon/M by M > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). For instance,  igl( (-1)^n/(n + 1)  igr) is null in 
Q: it is 1/(n + 1), null by @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b), times (-1)^n, bounded by 1. The bound M is fixed before \varepsilon and enters the tolerance \varepsilon/M. That is the pattern of the product law below. The second tool is the fact behind every division by b_n: if b_n 	o b
