Since a_n b_n - ab = a_n (b_n - b) + b (a_n - a) , the triangle inequality and \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y} give  egin{aligned} \abs{a_n b_n - ab} &\le \abs{a_n}\abs{b_n - b} + \abs{b}\abs{a_n - a} \ &\le M \abs{b_n - b} + (\abs{b} + 1)\abs{a_n - a} \ &<  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} where the second line uses 0 \le \abs{a_n} \le M and 0 \le \abs{b} \le \abs{b} + 1 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d)), and the third multiplies the two estimates by M > 0 and \abs{b} + 1 > 0. So for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0} there is N \in 
N with \abs{a_n b_n - ab} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N: a_n b_n 	o ab. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: fixes a bound M \in F_{>0} for one of the two factor sequences (say (\abs{a_n}); the mirror decomposition with (\abs{b_n}) is equally good), justified (convergent sequences are bounded), before \varepsilon. - 2: writes a_n b_n - ab as a sum of two terms, each with a factor tending to 0. - 3: chooses N_1, N_2 independent of n (N_1 from \varepsilon and M, N_2 from \varepsilon and b), with the case b = 0 handled, and N as their maximum. - 2: carries out the estimate with the triangle inequality and the product rule for \abs{\cdot}. - 1: concludes with the quantifiers in the order  orall \varepsilon \, \exists N \,  orall n \ge N. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a threshold or tolerance that depends on n; the bound “\abs{a_n} \le \abs{a} + 1 for every n” without the finite part for n < N; dividing by \abs{b} without b 
e 0. A route through @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field earns the same points, split as: bound fixed, 2; decomposition into two terms, 2; each product null by @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field (the constant factor bounded by \abs{b} + 1, or by \abs{b} with b = 0 handled separately), 3; sum of two null sequences proved from the definition, 2; null shift (@prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field) to conclude, 1. Citing @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field for the sum or for b(a_n - a) gets 0 for that step. A three-term route (a_n b_n - ab = (a_n - a)(b_n - b) + a(b_n - b) + b(a_n - a), with a tolerance such as \delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/(1 + \abs{a} + \abs{b})\} chosen from \varepsilon, a and b only) earns the same points: decomposition 2; the choice of \delta, independent of n and with \delta \le 1 controlling the product term (in place of the bound M), 2; a threshold N for both sequences at tolerance \delta (the case a = 0 or b = 0 covered by the 1 in the denominator) 3; the estimate 2; conclusion 1. [C2: Non-negative terms and reciprocals] Let a_n 	o a in F, with a_n \ge 0 for every n. 1. Prove that a \ge 0. 2. Suppose moreover a > 0. Prove that there is N_0 \in 
N with a_n > 0 for every n \ge N_0, and that the sequence (1/a_{n+N_0})_{n \in 
N} converges to 1/a. 3. Give an example in 
Q where a_n > 0 for every n and (1/a_n) does not converge. [Hint 1] For (a), compare with a constant sequence. For (b), which result keeps terms away from a non-zero limit? [Hint 2] For (b), start: “By @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field, since a > 0, there is N_0 with a_n > a/2 for every n \ge N_0.” (a) Since a_n \ge 0 for every n \ge 0, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (b) with c = 0 gives a \ge 0. (b) Since a > 0, @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field gives N_0 with a_n > a/2 > 0 for every n \ge N_0. The shifted sequence (a_{n+N_0})_n converges to a by @prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b), and each of its terms is non-zero. By @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (d), applied to the constant sequence 1 and to (a_{n+N_0})_n, whose limit a is non-zero, 1/a_{n+N_0} 	o 1/a. (c) a_n = 1/(n + 1): every term is positive, and 1/a_n = n + 1 is not bounded in 
Q: for any M \in 
Q_{>0}, the non-example after @def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field gives n with M < n < n + 1 = \abs{1/a_n}. So it does not converge (@prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field). The hypothesis a > 0 of (b) fails here: a = 0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a), by comparison with the constant sequence 0 (or by contradiction with \varepsilon = -a/2). - 3: (b), an index N_0 beyond which a_n is bounded away from 0, from a > 0. - 2: (b), 1/a_{n+N_0} 	o 1/a, either by the quotient law (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (d)) applied to the shift, with its convergence to a and a 
e 0 checked, or directly from \abs{1/a_{n+N_0} - 1/a} \le (2/a^2)\abs{a_{n+N_0} - a}, which uses a_{n+N_0} > a/2. - 2: (c), an example with the failure of convergence justified. Fatal errors (0 for the step): concluding a > 0 in (a) from a_n > 0; applying the quotient law without checking that the limit is non-zero.

title: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content:
Cauchy Sequences Every convergence proof so far began with the limit in hand: to show a_n 	o a we estimated \abs{a_n - a}, and the limit laws of Section 4.4 compute a new limit only from limits already known. That is no help for the sequence of Chapter 3 that closes in on the gap at \sqrt 2 (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2), whose terms 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots visibly settle down while no rational is available to be their limit. This section names a property that can be checked from the terms alone: eventually they are all close to each other. We prove the facts about it that Chapter 5 needs: convergent sequences have it, sequences with it are bounded and closed under sums and products, and, when such a sequence does not tend to 0, its terms eventually keep one sign and stay away from 0. Throughout, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), sequences are indexed by 
N (@def-sequence-ordered-field), and \varepsilon ranges over F_{>0}. Terms that agree with one another A limit relates a sequence to a point of F; boundedness (@def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field) is a property of the sequence alone. We want a second property of the sequence alone, saying “the terms settle down” without saying where. In 
Q the Newton terms satisfy 17/12 - 577/408 = 1/408, and the later terms are closer still to one another (Section 4.6 proves it). The way to say “settle down” without a target is to compare terms with terms: however small a tolerance is named, from some index on, any two terms differ by less than it. The terms eventually agree with one another to within any tolerance. [Cauchy Sequence] A sequence (a_n)_{n \in 
N} in F is a Cauchy sequence in F (or Cauchy) if for every \varepsilon \in F_{>0} there exists N \in 
N such that \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for all m, n \in 
N with m \ge N and n \ge N. In symbols:  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall m \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ &\qquad  igl( (m \ge N \wedge n \ge N) \Rightarrow \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . \end{aligned} In words: the tolerance is arbitrary and named first; the threshold comes after it, so it may depend on \varepsilon and on nothing else; and every pair of indices beyond the threshold, near or far apart, gives terms within \varepsilon of each other. Compared with @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, the point a has been replaced by a second index m. The tolerances are the elements of F_{>0}, so the field is part of the definition: for F = 
Q, “Cauchy in 
Q” is a statement about rationals only, as Chapter 5 needs. Since \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{a_n - a_m}, the roles of m and n are symmetric. Negate as in Logic and Proof, Chapter 6: each bounded quantifier flips (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation), the implication becomes a conjunction (@fd1:prp-negated-implication), and 
eg(x < \varepsilon) is x \ge \varepsilon. “(a_n) is not Cauchy” reads \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists m, n \in 
N \ \  igl( m \ge N \wedge n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_m - a_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . One tolerance is beaten beyond every threshold. Examples. A constant sequence. Let a_n = c for every n. Then \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{0} = 0 < \varepsilon for all m, n, so N = 0 works for every \varepsilon. This degenerate case matters: Chapter 5 represents each rational c by its constant sequence. The reciprocals in 
Q. Let a_n = 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \varepsilon. Let m, n \ge N. Then m + 1 > N and n + 1 > N, so 0 < 1/(m + 1) < 1/N and 0 < 1/(n + 1) < 1/N (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). Two elements of (0, 1/N) differ by less than 1/N, so \abs{a_m - a_n} < 1/N < \varepsilon. The threshold depends on \varepsilon only: for \varepsilon = 1/100, N = 101 works. Sequences with a limit. By the first result of the next subsection, the convergent sequences of Section 4.3 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field) are all examples. The definition earns its keep on sequences with no limit available, which Section 4.6 supplies. Non-example by a minimal change. Change the constant sequence 1 at every odd index: let a_n = 1 for even n and a_n = 0 for odd n. The sequence is still bounded, by 1, and every two terms still differ by at most 1. What fails is “for every \varepsilon”: take \varepsilon = 1. Whatever N is offered, the indices N and N + 1 are both \ge N, one even and one odd, and their terms differ by 1 
ot< 1. So the negation above holds with \varepsilon = 1, m = N, n = N + 1. Why this definition. Each clause is there for a reason. - Every pair, not only neighbors. Asking only that \abs{a_{n+1} - a_n} < \varepsilon for n \ge N is too weak: the example at the end of this section has consecutive differences tending to 0 and is not Cauchy. - The threshold after the tolerance. With the quantifiers swapped, “\exists N \  orall \varepsilon \  orall m, n \ge N”, the condition forces \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon, hence a_m = a_n for all m, n \ge N (the argument of @thm-limit-unique-ordered-field): only sequences that are eventually constant would qualify. - Tolerances from the field. 
Q(t) has the tolerance 1/t, below every positive rational; Exercise C2 of Section 4.6 shows a sequence of rationals that is Cauchy in 
Q and not in 
Q(t). The definition asks for one N that serves every pair m, n \ge N. A proof that checks only some pairs, say each n against n + 2, proves nothing: in the non-example above, a_{n+2} = a_n for every n, so those pairs pass every test, and the sequence still fails. Payoff. The tail-change principle extends at once. If a_n = b_n for every n \ge N_0 and (a_n) is Cauchy, then for \varepsilon \in F_{>0} and its threshold N for (a_n), every m, n \ge \max\{N, N_0\} give \abs{b_m - b_n} = \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon. So (b_n) is Cauchy, with thresholds \max\{N, N_0\}, as in @prp-tail-change-ordered-field. Convergent sequences are Cauchy, and Cauchy sequences are bounded The first result says the new property is no stronger than convergence: it is a necessary condition, one we can test without knowing the limit. [Convergent Sequences Are Cauchy] If a_n 	o a in F, then (a_n) is a Cauchy sequence in F. Two terms that are each within \varepsilon/2 of a are within \varepsilon of each other: insert the point a between them with the triangle inequality, and spend half the tolerance on each side. This is split \varepsilon, as in the uniqueness proof of Section 4.3, with the point a between the two terms; the threshold comes from the hypothesis, as in the limit laws. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Since a_n 	o a, there is N \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) with \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N. Let m, n \ge N. By the three-point triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) with a in the middle, \abs{a_m - a_n} \le \abs{a_m - a} + \abs{a - a_n} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , so (a_n) is Cauchy. The converse is the question of the chapter. In 
Q it fails (Section 4.6). Chapter 5 builds the field 
R, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 4 proves that it holds there. Is the sequence  igl( (-1)^n/(n + 1)  igr)_{n \in 
N} Cauchy in 
Q? Answer without estimating \abs{a_m - a_n}. Yes. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) is null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field), and ((-1)^n) is bounded by 1, since \abs{(-1)^n} = 1 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d)). So the product is null by @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field. A null sequence converges, to 0, so it is Cauchy by @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field. The second result is the Cauchy version of @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field. There the tail was trapped near the limit a; here no limit is available, so we trap the tail near one of its own terms. [Cauchy Sequences Are Bounded] Every Cauchy sequence in F is bounded. Apply the definition once, with the tolerance 1. It gives an index N beyond which every term is within 1 of the term a_N, a base point we can name. The finitely many terms before N are handled by a finite maximum, as for convergent sequences. Let (a_n) be Cauchy in F. Since 1 > 0, there is N \in 
N with \abs{a_m - a_n} < 1 for all m, n \ge N. For n \ge N, taking m = N and using the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), \abs{a_n} = \abs{(a_n - a_N) + a_N} \le \abs{a_n - a_N} + \abs{a_N} < 1 + \abs{a_N} . Let M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{a_N} + 1 \} , a finite maximum (@fd2:prp-finite-max, whose proof works in any totally ordered set; for N = 0 the set is \{ \abs{a_0} + 1 \}). Then M \ge \abs{a_N} + 1 \ge 1 > 0, so M \in F_{>0}. For n < N, \abs{a_n} \le M because \abs{a_n} is in the set; for n \ge N, \abs{a_n} < \abs{a_N} + 1 \le M. So \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N, and (a_n) is bounded (@def-bounded-sequence-ordered-field). The bound M depends on the whole sequence, not on any tolerance. That is what makes it usable in the next proof: it can be fixed before \varepsilon is named. Sums and products of Cauchy sequences Chapter 5 will add and multiply real numbers by adding and multiplying Cauchy sequences of rationals term by term. For that, sums and products of Cauchy sequences must again be Cauchy. The limit laws (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field) do not apply, since they need limits; the proofs below copy their estimates with a second index in place of the limit. Sums and Products of Cauchy Sequences Let (a_n) and (b_n) be Cauchy sequences in F, and let c \in F. 1. Every constant sequence and every null sequence in F is Cauchy. 2. The sequences (a_n + b_n), (c \, a_n), (-a_n) and (a_n - b_n) are Cauchy. 3. The sequence (a_n b_n) is Cauchy. (a) is @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field. For (b), split \varepsilon: give each of (a_n) and (b_n) the tolerance \varepsilon/2 and take the larger threshold. For (c), the difference a_n b_n - a_m b_m splits as a_n (b_n - b_m) + b_m (a_n - a_m). The factors a_n and b_m do not get small, but they are bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field). So bound, then shrink: replace each factor we cannot control by a bound fixed in advance, then make the other factor small enough to absorb the bound. (a) A constant sequence (c) converges to c, and a null sequence converges to 0 (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field, @def-null-sequence-ordered-field). Both are Cauchy by @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field. (b) Sums. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Since (a_n) is Cauchy, there is N_1 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_1; since (b_n) is Cauchy, there is N_2 with \abs{b_m - b_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, which depends only on \varepsilon. For m, n \ge N, we have (a_m + b_m) - (a_n + b_n) = (a_m - a_n) + (b_m - b_n), so the triangle inequality gives  egin{aligned} \abs{(a_m + b_m) - (a_n + b_n)} &\le \abs{a_m - a_n} + \abs{b_m - b_n} \ &<  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . \end{aligned} Multiples. The proof of @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b) carries over with a_m in place of a: for c 
e 0, the tolerance \varepsilon/\abs{c} for (a_n) gives \abs{c a_m - c a_n} = \abs{c}\,\abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for all m, n \ge N; for c = 0 it is the constant sequence 0, Cauchy by (a). Negatives and differences. Since -a_n = (-1) a_n, (-a_n) is the multiple with c = -1. Then a_n - b_n = a_n + (-b_n) is the sum of two Cauchy sequences. (c) By @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field, fix A, B \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le A and \abs{b_n} \le B for every n \in 
N; they depend on the two sequences only. Now let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then \varepsilon/(2A) and \varepsilon/(2B) are positive (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), so there are N_1 with \abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2A) for all m, n \ge N_1, and N_2 with \abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/(2B) for all m, n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, depending on \varepsilon, A, B, and let m, n \ge N. Expanding the right side shows a_n b_n - a_m b_m = a_n (b_n - b_m) + b_m (a_n - a_m) . By the triangle inequality and \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}, then @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) applied to 0 \le \abs{a_n} \le A and to 0 \le \abs{b_m} \le B,  egin{aligned} \abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} &\le \abs{a_n} \, \abs{b_n - b_m} + \abs{b_m} \, \abs{a_n - a_m} \ &\le A \abs{b_n - b_m} + B \abs{a_n - a_m} \ &< A \cdot  rac{\varepsilon}{2A} + B \cdot  rac{\varepsilon}{2B} = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} where the strict step multiplies by A > 0 and B > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and adds. So (a_n b_n) is Cauchy. The order of choices in (c) is the whole proof: A and B are chosen before \varepsilon, from the sequences alone, so that \varepsilon/(2A) is one fixed tolerance. Exercise C3 shows what goes wrong when the bound is skipped. Chapter 5 adds and multiplies classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals termwise; clauses (b) and (c) with F = 
Q keep the termwise results Cauchy. The sign of a Cauchy sequence that is not null A null sequence is the Cauchy analogue of 0. Chapter 5 must decide, for each Cauchy sequence of rationals that is not null, whether it represents a positive or a negative number, and it needs an inverse for it. Both rest on one fact: such a sequence eventually keeps one sign, at a definite distance from 0. [The Sign of a Non-Null Cauchy Sequence] Let (a_n) be a Cauchy sequence in F that is not null. Then there are c \in F_{>0} and N \in 
N such that either a_n \ge c \ 	ext{ for every } n \ge N , \qquad 	ext{or} \qquad a_n \le -c \ 	ext{ for every } n \ge N . The two alternatives do not both hold. Try it first (ten minutes): write “(a_n) is not null” in symbols. Which \varepsilon does it hand you, and what does the Cauchy condition do with it? “Not null” is the negation of @def-null-sequence-ordered-field: \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . The obvious attempt reads this as “\abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon for all large n”, and that is not what it says: it promises, beyond each threshold, one term at least \varepsilon from 0, and between such terms others might come near 0 or change sign. The Cauchy condition is what forbids that wandering. So fix the bad \varepsilon and keep it for the rest of the proof. Ask the Cauchy condition for a threshold N_0 with tolerance \varepsilon/2, and only then ask the negation for one term a_{n_0}, beyond N_0, with \abs{a_{n_0}} \ge \varepsilon. Every later term is within \varepsilon/2 of a_{n_0}, so it has the sign of a_{n_0} and size at least \varepsilon/2. Before reading on: where is n_0 \ge N_0 used? Negating @def-null-sequence-ordered-field (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication) gives \varepsilon \in F_{>0} such that for every N \in 
N some n \ge N has \abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon. Fix such an \varepsilon. Since (a_n) is Cauchy, there is N_0 \in 
N (depending only on the sequence, through \varepsilon) with \abs{a_m - a_n} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \quad 	ext{for all } m, n \ge N_0 . Applying the negation with N \coloneqq N_0 gives n_0 \in 
N with n_0 \ge N_0 and \abs{a_{n_0}} \ge \varepsilon. So a_{n_0} \ge \varepsilon or a_{n_0} \le -\varepsilon, according to the sign of a_{n_0} (@def-absolute-value-ordered-field). Let n \ge N_0. Since both n and n_0 are \ge N_0, \abs{a_n - a_{n_0}} < \varepsilon/2, that is, -\varepsilon/2 < a_n - a_{n_0} < \varepsilon/2 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). Case 1: a_{n_0} \ge \varepsilon. Adding a_{n_0} to the left inequality, a_n > a_{n_0} - \varepsilon/2 \ge \varepsilon - \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon/2. Case 2: a_{n_0} \le -\varepsilon. Adding a_{n_0} to the right inequality, a_n < a_{n_0} + \varepsilon/2 \le -\varepsilon + \varepsilon/2 = -\varepsilon/2. Let c \coloneqq \varepsilon/2 and N \coloneqq N_0. In Case 1, a_n \ge c for every n \ge N; in Case 2, a_n \le -c for every n \ge N. Finally, both alternatives cannot hold, even with different constants and thresholds: if a_n \ge c for n \ge N and a_n \le -c' for n \ge N', with c, c' \in F_{>0}, then n \coloneqq \max\{N, N'\} gives 0 < c \le a_n \le -c' < 0, a contradiction. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: n_0 \ge N_0 is used once, to apply the Cauchy estimate to the pair n, n_0. An n_0 taken before N_0 is known might lie below N_0 and say nothing about the tail. Both hypotheses are needed; the witnesses are in 
Q. - Not null. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) is Cauchy (the examples after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field) and null. For any c \in 
Q_{>0} and any N, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives an index n \ge N with 0 < 1/(n + 1) < c, so neither alternative holds. - Cauchy. The sequence ((-1)^n) is not null, since \abs{(-1)^n} = 1 \ge 1 for every n. Its terms alternate between 1 and -1, so neither alternative holds for any c > 0 and N: a_N and a_{N+1} have opposite signs. For a_n = (n - 3)/(n + 1) in 
Q, which alternative of @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign holds? Give a valid c and N. a_n = 1 - 4/(n + 1). For n \ge 7, n + 1 \ge 8, so 0 < 1/(n + 1) \le 1/8 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b), or equality at n = 7), hence 4/(n + 1) \le 1/2 and a_n \ge 1/2: the first alternative, with c = 1/2, N = 7. (At n = 6, a_6 = 3/7 < 1/2, so this N is least for this c; other pairs, such as c = 1/5, N = 4, work too.) Sign stability and reciprocals Two smaller results complete the toolkit: the sign found by @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign survives a null change of the sequence, and a sequence that stays away from 0 can be inverted. [Sign Stability under Null Differences] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be sequences in F such that (a_n - b_n) is null. If c \in F_{>0}, N \in 
N, and a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, then there is N' \in 
N with b_n \ge c/2 for every n \ge N'. Since (a_n - b_n) is null, there is N_1 (depending on c) with \abs{a_n - b_n} < c/2 for every n \ge N_1. Let N' \coloneqq \max\{N, N_1\} and n \ge N'. Then a_n - b_n < c/2, so b_n > a_n -  rac{c}{2} \ge c -  rac{c}{2} =  rac{c}{2} . In particular b_n \ge c/2. Neither sequence needs to be Cauchy here. Chapter 5 uses the proposition to show that being eventually \ge c for some c > 0 does not depend on which of two sequences with null difference represents a real number. [Reciprocals of Cauchy Sequences] Let (a_n) be a Cauchy sequence in F, and let c \in F_{>0} and N \in 
N be such that \abs{a_n} \ge c for every n \ge N. Define b_n \coloneqq  egin{cases} 1/a_n & 	ext{if } n \ge N , \ 1 & 	ext{if } n < N . \end{cases} Then (b_n) is a Cauchy sequence in F, and a_n b_n = 1 for every n \ge N. The difference of reciprocals is (a_m - a_n)/(a_n a_m); its numerator can be made small, and the denominator is at least c^2 in absolute value. So \abs{b_n - b_m} \le \abs{a_m - a_n}/c^2, and the tolerance c^2 \varepsilon for (a_n) gives the tolerance \varepsilon for (b_n). For n \ge N, \abs{a_n} \ge c > 0, so a_n 
e 0, and b_n = a_n^{-1} is defined, with a_n b_n = 1. For m, n \ge N, @lem-field-fraction-rules (c) gives b_n - b_m =  rac{1}{a_n} -  rac{1}{a_m} =  rac{a_m - a_n}{a_n a_m} . So \abs{b_n - b_m} = \abs{a_m - a_n} \cdot  igl(1/(\abs{a_n} \, \abs{a_m}) igr). From 0 < c \le \abs{a_n} and 0 < c \le \abs{a_m}, @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) gives c^2 \le \abs{a_n} \, \abs{a_m}, and then @prp-ordered-field-halves (c) gives 1/(\abs{a_n} \, \abs{a_m}) \le 1/c^2. Multiplying by \abs{a_m - a_n} \ge 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d), as 1/(\abs{a_n} \, \abs{a_m}) > 0) gives \abs{b_n - b_m} \le  rac{\abs{a_m - a_n}}{c^2} \quad 	ext{for all } m, n \ge N . Now let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Then c^2 \varepsilon > 0, so there is N_1 (depending on \varepsilon and c) with \abs{a_m - a_n} < c^2 \varepsilon for all m, n \ge N_1. Let N' \coloneqq \max\{N, N_1\}. For m, n \ge N', multiplying by 1/c^2 > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), \abs{b_n - b_m} \le  rac{\abs{a_m - a_n}}{c^2} <  rac{c^2 \varepsilon}{c^2} = \varepsilon . So (b_n) is Cauchy. The values b_n = 1 for n < N play no part; any values would do, by the tail-change remark after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field. The hypothesis “\abs{a_n} \ge c” cannot be weakened to “a_n 
e 0”. In 
Q, a_n = 1/(n + 1) is Cauchy and never 0, but 1/a_n = n + 1 is not bounded (for each M \in 
Q_{>0}, @thm-rationals-archimedean gives an n with n + 1 > M), so it is not Cauchy, by @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field. Combined with @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign, which supplies c and N for every Cauchy sequence that is not null, this proposition is how Chapter 5 inverts a non-zero real number. Small steps do not make a Cauchy sequence The commonest wrong proof that a sequence is Cauchy looks only at neighboring terms. “If a_{n+1} - a_n 	o 0, then (a_n) is Cauchy” is false. The next example gives a sequence of rationals whose steps shrink to 0 and whose terms do not settle down at all. [Shrinking Steps, Terms That Do Not Settle] Here is an argument for the false claim in the warning. “Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. Since a_{n+1} - a_n 	o 0, choose N with \abs{a_{k+1} - a_k} < \varepsilon for every k \ge N. Let m > n \ge N. Then a_m - a_n is the sum of the consecutive differences a_{k+1} - a_k for k = n, \dots, m - 1, and each of them is smaller than \varepsilon in absolute value. So \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon, and (a_n) is Cauchy.” In 
Q, let H_0 \coloneqq 0 and H_{n+1} \coloneqq H_n + 1/(n + 1) for n \in 
N. Show that H_{n+1} - H_n 	o 0, that H_{2n} - H_n \ge 1/2 for every n \ge 1, and that (H_n) is not Cauchy. Find the line of the argument that fails. The sequence. By @fd2:thm-recursion (read on 
N = \omega as @thm-omega-recursion, by @cor-omega-identification (b)), with X = 
Q, starting value 0 and g(n, s) \coloneqq s + 1/(n + 1), there is exactly one sequence (H_n) in 
Q with H_0 = 0 and H_{n+1} = H_n + 1/(n + 1). Its first terms are 0, 1, 3/2, 11/6, 25/12. Shrinking steps. H_{n+1} - H_n = 1/(n + 1), and (1/(n + 1)) is null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field). Long stretches. Fix n \ge 1. We show, by @fd1:ax-induction on k (through @cor-omega-identification (b)), that H_{n+k} - H_n \ge  rac{k}{n + k} \quad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N . Base P(0): both sides are 0. Step: assume it for k. Since n + k \ge 1, we have 0 < n + k < n + k + 1, so 0 < 1/(n + k + 1) < 1/(n + k) (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). With 0 \le k \le k, @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) gives k/(n + k + 1) \le k/(n + k). Hence, by the induction hypothesis,  egin{aligned} H_{n+k+1} - H_n &= (H_{n+k} - H_n) +  rac{1}{n + k + 1} \ &\ge  rac{k}{n + k + 1} +  rac{1}{n + k + 1} =  rac{k + 1}{n + k + 1} . \end{aligned} Taking k = n gives H_{2n} - H_n \ge n/(2n) = 1/2. Not Cauchy. We prove the negation displayed after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field with \varepsilon = 1/2. Let N \in 
N, and put n \coloneqq N + 1 and m \coloneqq 2n. Then m, n \ge N, n \ge 1, and \abs{H_m - H_n} = H_{2n} - H_n \ge 1/2. So no threshold works for the tolerance 1/2. The failing line. “Each of them is smaller than \varepsilon … so \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon.” A sum of m - n terms, each of absolute value below \varepsilon, is only below (m - n) \varepsilon (triangle inequality, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), applied m - n - 1 times). The number of summands m - n is not fixed: m is chosen after N, and the definition allows it to be as far beyond n as we like. To repair the line one would need each step below \varepsilon/(m - n), a tolerance that depends on m and n; no single N is promised for it. Section 4.6 goes further: its Exercise B2 shows H_{2^k} \ge 1 + k/2 for every k \in 
N, so (H_n) even grows without bound. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign and its proof. 1. Write “(a_n) is not null” in symbols, with every quantifier and its domain. 2. The proof asks the Cauchy condition for the tolerance \varepsilon/2. Why not \varepsilon itself? 3. Where is the inequality n_0 \ge N_0 used? 4. Run the proof in 
Q on a_n = 1/(n + 1) - 1 with \varepsilon = 1/2: check that this \varepsilon witnesses “not null”, give the least N_0 that the Cauchy condition with tolerance 1/4 allows, choose n_0, and state the c and N the proof produces. (a) \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \ \exists n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon): one tolerance and, beyond every threshold, some term at least that far from 0. (b) With tolerance \varepsilon, Case 1 would give only a_n > a_{n_0} - \varepsilon \ge \varepsilon - \varepsilon = 0: every later term is positive, but no positive c with a_n \ge c comes out, and the estimate a_n > 0 alone does not rule out terms approaching 0. Any tolerance strictly smaller than \varepsilon leaves a positive margin; \varepsilon/2 is the simplest. (c) In the line “since both n and n_0 are \ge N_0, \abs{a_n - a_{n_0}} < \varepsilon/2”: the Cauchy estimate holds only for pairs of indices beyond N_0. It is the reason N_0 is chosen first and the negation is applied at N_0. (d) Here \abs{a_n} = 1 - 1/(n + 1) = n/(n + 1), which is 0 at n = 0 and at least 1/2 for every n \ge 1 (as 2n \ge n + 1). So beyond any N the index n = N + 1 has \abs{a_n} \ge 1/2: \varepsilon = 1/2 witnesses “not null”. Next, \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{1/(m + 1) - 1/(n + 1)}. For m, n \ge 3, both reciprocals lie in (0, 1/4], so their difference is below 1/4, as in the examples after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field. For N_0 = 2 the pair m = 2, n = 11 gives 1/3 - 1/12 = 1/4 
ot< 1/4. So the least N_0 is 3. Take n_0 = 3 \ge N_0: a_3 = -3/4, \abs{a_3} = 3/4 \ge 1/2, Case 2. The proof gives a_n < a_3 + 1/4 = -1/2 \le -1/4 for n \ge 3, and it states the result as c = \varepsilon/2 = 1/4, N = 3: a_n \le -1/4 for every n \ge 3. (n_0 = 0 is not allowed: it is below N_0, and \abs{a_0} = 0 < 1/2.) B. Practice [B1] Determine which of the following sequences in 
Q are Cauchy. Justify your answers, and for the first one work directly from @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field. 1. a_n = (n + 1)/(n + 2). 2. a_n = (-1)^n. 3. a_n = n. (a) Cauchy. For every k \in 
N, (k + 1)/(k + 2) = 1 - 1/(k + 2), so \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{1/(n + 2) - 1/(m + 2)}. Let \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, and use @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon to choose N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \varepsilon. For m, n \ge N, both 1/(m + 2) and 1/(n + 2) lie in (0, 1/N), since m + 2, n + 2 > N (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). Two elements of (0, 1/N) differ by less than 1/N (as in the examples after the definition), so \abs{a_m - a_n} < 1/N < \varepsilon. (b) Not Cauchy. Take \varepsilon = 1. For any N, the indices N and N + 1 have a_{N+1} = -a_N and \abs{a_N} = 1, so \abs{a_N - a_{N+1}} = \abs{2 a_N} = 2 \ge 1. (c) Not Cauchy. If it were, it would be bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field): \abs{n} \le M for some M \in 
Q_{>0} and every n. By @thm-rationals-archimedean there is n \in 
N with M < n = \abs{n}, a contradiction. (Archimedes is used here; in the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of Section 4.2 the sequence (n \cdot 1) is bounded, by t, and the boundedness argument says nothing.) [B2] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be Cauchy sequences in F. Prove directly from @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field that (a_n - b_n) is Cauchy, naming the rule behind each step. Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. By @prp-ordered-field-halves (b), \varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0}. Since (a_n) is Cauchy, choose N_1 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_1; since (b_n) is Cauchy, choose N_2 with \abs{b_m - b_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\} (a maximum of two natural numbers; it depends only on \varepsilon). Let m, n \ge N; then m, n \ge N_1 and m, n \ge N_2. By the ring rules (@prp-ring-algebra), (a_m - b_m) - (a_n - b_n) = (a_m - a_n) +  igl(-(b_m - b_n) igr) . By the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)) and \abs{-x} = \abs{x} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), \abs{(a_m - b_m) - (a_n - b_n)} \le \abs{a_m - a_n} + \abs{b_m - b_n} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , adding strict inequalities by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) and using @prp-ordered-field-halves (b) for the equality. Since \varepsilon was arbitrary, (a_n - b_n) is Cauchy. [B3] Let a_n = 2 - 1/(n + 1) in 
Q. Show that (a_n) is Cauchy and not null, and find c \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N as in @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign. Then run the proof of the theorem with \varepsilon = 1 and the least admissible N_0: which c and N does it produce? Cauchy. (a_n) is the difference of the constant sequence 2 and the Cauchy sequence (1/(n + 1)) (examples after @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field), so it is Cauchy by @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b). Not null, and c, N directly. For every n, 0 < 1/(n + 1) \le 1, so a_n \ge 1. Then \abs{a_n} \ge 1 for every n, so \varepsilon = 1 witnesses “not null”, and c = 1, N = 0 satisfy the first alternative. (Any smaller positive c, for instance c = 1/2, works with N = 0 as well.) The proof run. With \varepsilon = 1, the Cauchy condition is asked for tolerance 1/2. Here \abs{a_m - a_n} = \abs{1/(n + 1) - 1/(m + 1)}; for m, n \ge 1 both reciprocals lie in (0, 1/2], so the difference is below 1/2, while N_0 = 0 fails (m = 0, n = 1: 1 - 1/2 = 1/2 
ot< 1/2). So N_0 = 1. Take n_0 = 1: a_1 = 3/2 \ge 1, Case 1. The proof gives c = 1/2, N = 1: a_n > 3/2 - 1/2 = 1 \ge 1/2 for every n \ge 1. C. Going deeper [C1] Let (a_n) be a Cauchy sequence in F and (b_n) a sequence in F such that (a_n - b_n) is null. Prove that (b_n) is Cauchy. Here is the beginning of a proof. Name the move, then complete it. “Let \varepsilon \in F_{>0}. For all m, n \in 
N, the triangle inequality (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), applied twice, gives \abs{b_n - b_m} \le \abs{b_n - a_n} + \abs{a_n - a_m} + \abs{a_m - b_m} . …” The move is split \varepsilon, now into three parts, one for each term on the right: two come from the null difference, one from the Cauchy condition. Completion. Let 3 \coloneqq 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 \cdot 1_F; then 3 > 0 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), so \varepsilon/3 \in F_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), and \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = 3 \cdot (\varepsilon/3) = \varepsilon: by (F5)–(F9), with 3 
e 0. Since (a_n - b_n) is null, choose N_1 with \abs{a_n - b_n} < \varepsilon/3 for every n \ge N_1. Since (a_n) is Cauchy, choose N_2 with \abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/3 for all m, n \ge N_2. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, which depends only on \varepsilon. For m, n \ge N, using \abs{b_n - a_n} = \abs{a_n - b_n} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), \abs{b_n - b_m} <  rac{\varepsilon}{3} +  rac{\varepsilon}{3} +  rac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon , adding three strict inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). So (b_n) is Cauchy. The split \varepsilon/4, \varepsilon/2, \varepsilon/4, which needs only halving, works as well. [C2: Exit check: the sign theorem] Let (a_n) be a Cauchy sequence in an ordered field F that is not null. Prove that there are c \in F_{>0} and N \in 
N such that either a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, or a_n \le -c for every n \ge N. “Null” means  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \exists N \in 
N \  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n} < \varepsilon). Its negation (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation (a), @fd1:prp-negated-implication, then (O1)) is \exists \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr) . Fix such an \varepsilon; it stays fixed from here on. Apply the Cauchy condition with the tolerance \varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)): there is N_0 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon/2 for all m, n \ge N_0. Apply the negation at N_0: there is n_0 \ge N_0 with \abs{a_{n_0}} \ge \varepsilon. By the definition of \abs{\cdot}, a_{n_0} \ge \varepsilon or a_{n_0} \le -\varepsilon. Let n \ge N_0. As n, n_0 \ge N_0, -\varepsilon/2 < a_n - a_{n_0} < \varepsilon/2 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). If a_{n_0} \ge \varepsilon, then a_n > a_{n_0} - \varepsilon/2 \ge \varepsilon/2. If a_{n_0} \le -\varepsilon, then a_n < a_{n_0} + \varepsilon/2 \le -\varepsilon/2. With c \coloneqq \varepsilon/2 and N \coloneqq N_0, the first case gives a_n \ge c and the second a_n \le -c, for every n \ge N. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: negates “null” correctly, with the quantifiers in order, and fixes one \varepsilon. - 2: applies the Cauchy condition with a fixed tolerance \delta such that 0 < \delta < \varepsilon (for example \delta = \varepsilon/2) to get N_0. - 2: obtains n_0 \ge N_0 with \abs{a_{n_0}} \ge \varepsilon from the negation applied at N_0. - 3: derives a one-signed bound a_n \ge c or a_n \le -c, with some c \in F_{>0} (for example c = \varepsilon - \delta), for every n \ge N_0, in both sign cases. - 1: names c and N and concludes. A proof by contraposition (assume neither alternative holds for any c, N; show the sequence null using the Cauchy condition at tolerance \varepsilon/2 and, beyond N_0, a term below \varepsilon/2 and a term above -\varepsilon/2) earns the same points, step for step: 2 for the negated conclusion, 2 for the Cauchy threshold, 2 for choosing the witnesses beyond N_0, 3 for the two-sided bound, 1 for concluding. A complete proof by contradiction likewise earns the same 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1. Fatal errors (0 for the step): an n_0 not known to satisfy n_0 \ge N_0, or “\abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon for all large n” read off “not null” alone. [C3: Find the error] Here is an argument that the product of two Cauchy sequences (a_n), (b_n) in F is Cauchy. “For all m, n, \abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} \le \abs{a_n} \, \abs{b_n - b_m} + \abs{b_m} \, \abs{a_n - a_m}. Given \varepsilon \in F_{>0}, choose N such that \abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) and \abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{b_m}) for all m, n \ge N. Then for m, n \ge N, \abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon.” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, and repair it. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (c). The argument does not prove it. The failing line is “choose N such that \abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) … for all m, n \ge N”. The tolerances \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) and \varepsilon/(2\abs{b_m}) depend on n and m, which are introduced after N. The definition of Cauchy supplies a threshold for one fixed tolerance \varepsilon' \in F_{>0}, named before the threshold; here the threshold is asked to serve a tolerance that changes with the very indices it controls. This is a witness depending on variables introduced later, entry (N2) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A counterexample to the step. The step gets one N for all the tolerances \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) from their being positive. In 
Q take the Cauchy sequence b_n = 1/(n + 1), the never-zero (but unbounded) a_n = n + 1, and \varepsilon = 1. For any N, n = N and m = 2N + 1 give \abs{b_n - b_m} =  rac{1}{N + 1} -  rac{1}{2N + 2} =  rac{1}{2(N + 1)} =  rac{\varepsilon}{2\abs{a_n}} , which is not smaller: no N works. Inside the exercise (a_n) is Cauchy, hence bounded, but the argument never uses that; the repair does. Repair. Fix bounds first: by @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field, choose A, B \in F_{>0} with \abs{a_n} \le A and \abs{b_n} \le B for every n, before \varepsilon is named. Then the fixed tolerances \varepsilon/(2A) \le \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n}) (when a_n 
e 0) and \varepsilon/(2B) give thresholds N_1, N_2, and N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\} works, as in the proof of @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (c).

title: 4.6 A Cauchy Sequence with No Rational Limit
content:
A Cauchy Sequence with No Rational Limit Section 4.5 proved that every convergent sequence is Cauchy (@prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field). In 
Q the converse fails, and the failure sits exactly at the hole Chapter 3 found at \sqrt 2: no rational squares to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two). This section proves that the rational sequence of Chapter 3 that closes in on that hole (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2) is Cauchy in 
Q and converges to no rational. Chapter 5 starts from this sequence and builds the number it is aiming at. The section ends by listing what the chapter has not proved, and why, in 
Q, it could not have. Throughout this section the field is F = 
Q: every tolerance \varepsilon is a positive rational, and “converges” means “converges in 
Q” (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field). The sequence again Recall the sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. For s \in 
Q_{>0} let t(s) \coloneqq (s^2 + 2)/(2s), the average of s and 2/s; let x_0 \coloneqq 2 and x_{n+1} \coloneqq t(x_n), and let e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2, the amount by which x_n^2 overshoots 2. The first terms are x_0 = 2 , \quad x_1 =  rac{3}{2} , \quad x_2 =  rac{17}{12} , \quad x_3 =  rac{577}{408} , with e_0 = 2 , \quad e_1 =  rac{1}{4} , \quad e_2 =  rac{1}{144} , \quad e_3 =  rac{1}{166464} . Chapter 3 proved, for every n \in 
N, the following facts, and we cite them from @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2 without proving them again:  egin{aligned} &x_n \in 
Q_{>0} , \qquad e_n > 0 \ \ (	ext{so } x_n^2 > 2) , \ &e_{n+1} =  rac{e_n^2}{4x_n^2} \le  rac{e_n^2}{8} , \qquad x_n - x_{n+1} =  rac{e_n}{2x_n} > 0 . \end{aligned} The second line says two things. The overshoot is roughly squared at each step, so it shrinks very fast; and the terms decrease. Section 4.5 asks for more than decrease: any two late terms must be close. The overshoot e_n measures how close, because every later term lies between 2/x_n and x_n, an interval of length e_n/x_n. For the proof we do not need the true speed of e_n. A crude bound is enough, as long as it can be pushed below every rational tolerance: e_1 =  rac{1}{4} , \quad e_2 =  rac{1}{144} \le  rac{1}{8} , \quad e_3 =  rac{1}{166464} \le  rac{1}{12} ; that is, e_n \le 1/(4n) for n = 1, 2, 3, and the theorem proves it for every n \ge 1. Archimedes then turns 1/(4n) into anything below a given \varepsilon. The theorem [The Newton Sequence Is Cauchy with No Rational Limit] Let (x_n)_{n \in 
N} and e_n = x_n^2 - 2 be as in @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. Then x_n > 1 for every n \in 
N, x_m \le x_n whenever m \ge n, and e_n \le 1/(4n) for every n \ge 1. The sequence (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence in 
Q, and there is no L \in 
Q with x_n 	o L. The first three clauses are part of the statement, rather than steps hidden in the proof, so that Chapter 5 can cite them. Cauchy. This keeps the shape of @exm-method-limit-from-definition, with a second index in place of the limit: bound \abs{x_m - x_n} by an expression in n alone, then let Archimedes push it below \varepsilon. For m \ge n, the later term x_m lies below x_n, since the terms decrease, and above 2/x_n, since x_m > 2/x_m \ge 2/x_n. So 0 \le x_n - x_m \le x_n - 2/x_n = e_n/x_n \le e_n. With e_n \le 1/(4n), every two terms beyond N differ by at most 1/(4N), and Archimedes makes 1/N smaller than any rational \varepsilon. No rational limit. Locate the missing limit: suppose x_n 	o L in 
Q and find out what L would have to satisfy. The limit laws turn x_n 	o L into x_n^2 	o L^2. But x_n^2 = 2 + e_n 	o 2, because e_n is squeezed between 0 and 1/(4n). Limits are unique, so L^2 = 2, and no rational satisfies that. Before reading on: which law turns x_n 	o L into x_n^2 	o L^2, and applied to which two sequences? We prove six facts, then the two claims. Induction is @fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b). (i), (ii), (iv) in part: cited. By @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, for every n \in 
N: (i) x_n \in 
Q_{>0}, e_n > 0 and x_n^2 > 2; (ii) e_{n+1} = e_n^2/(4x_n^2) \le e_n^2/8; and x_{n+1} < x_n. (iii) x_n > 1. Suppose x_n \le 1. Since x_n > 0 by (i), either x_n < 1, and then x_n^2 < 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), or x_n = 1 and x_n^2 = 1. Either way x_n^2 \le 1 < 2, a contradiction with x_n^2 > 2. So x_n > 1, by totality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). (iv) x_m \le x_n for m \ge n. Fix n. By induction on k, x_{n+k} \le x_n for every k \in 
N: the base P(0) is x_n \le x_n, and if x_{n+k} \le x_n, then x_{n+k+1} < x_{n+k} \le x_n. Every m \ge n in 
N is n + k for some k \in

Hence r_{n+1} - r_n = \Bigl( rac{r_n}{2} + 1\Bigr) - \Bigl( rac{r_n}{2} +  rac{r_n}{2}\Bigr) = 1 -  rac{r_n}{2} > 0 , and r_n < r_{n+1} by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). [R3] Say that a sequence (a_n) in an ordered field F eventually keeps one sign if there are c \in F_{>0} and N \in 
N such that either a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, or a_n \le -c for every n \ge N. Write this in symbols, and form its negation by moving 
eg inward one law at a time, naming each law. Then use the negation to show that a_n \coloneqq (-1)^n/(n + 1) in 
Q does not eventually keep one sign, and explain why this does not contradict the theorem that a Cauchy sequence that is not null eventually keeps one sign. “(a_n) eventually keeps one sign” is \exists c \in F_{>0} \ \exists N \in 
N \ \Bigl(  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N 	o a_n \ge c) \ \vee \  orall n \in 
N \ (n \ge N 	o a_n \le -c) \Bigr) . Negating, with the laws for bounded quantifiers (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation), De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan) and negated implication (@fd1:prp-negated-implication): 1.  orall c \in F_{>0} \ 
eg \exists N \in 
N \ (\dots), by (b) of the bounded law; 2.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \ 
eg  igl(  orall n \, (\dots) \vee  orall n \, (\dots)  igr), by (b) again; 3.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \  igl( 
eg  orall n \, (\dots) \wedge 
eg  orall n \, (\dots)  igr), by De Morgan (a) (and (b) for the converse); 4.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \  igl( \exists n \in 
N \ 
eg (n \ge N 	o a_n \ge c) \wedge \exists n \in 
N \ 
eg (n \ge N 	o a_n \le -c)  igr), by (a) of the bounded law, twice; 5.  orall c \in F_{>0} \  orall N \in 
N \  igl( \exists n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \wedge 
eg (a_n \ge c)) \wedge \exists n \in 
N \ (n \ge N \wedge 
eg (a_n \le -c))  igr), by @fd1:prp-negated-implication, twice; 6. and 
eg (a_n \ge c) is a_n < c, 
eg (a_n \le -c) is a_n > -c, by totality (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)). So the negation says: for every c \in F_{>0} and every N \in 
N, some n \ge N has a_n < c, and some n \ge N has a_n > -c. The example. Here (-1)^n is the power in 
Q (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field), so (-1)^{n+1} = -(-1)^n (@prp-ring-algebra (c)), and by induction (-1)^n is 1 or -1 for every n. Let c \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N. Of (-1)^N and (-1)^{N+1} = -(-1)^N, one is 1 and the other -1; call p the index among N, N + 1 with (-1)^p = 1, and q the other. Both are \ge N, and 1/(p + 1) > 0, 1/(q + 1) > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). So a_q = -1/(q + 1) < 0 < c and a_p = 1/(p + 1) > 0 > -c (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)). This is the negation, so (a_n) does not eventually keep one sign. No contradiction. \abs{a_n} = \abs{(-1)^n} \cdot \abs{1/(n + 1)} = 1/(n + 1) (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)), and (1/(n + 1)) is null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). So for each \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} the threshold that serves (1/(n + 1)) gives \abs{a_n - 0} < \varepsilon: the sequence (a_n) is null. It is Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), but the theorem (@thm-cauchy-not-null-sign) assumes “not null”, so it says nothing about (a_n). The example shows that this hypothesis cannot be dropped. [R4] Let (a_n) be a sequence in 
Q with a_n > 0 for every n and a_n^2 	o 2 in 
Q. Is (a_n) a Cauchy sequence in 
Q? Prove your answer. Yes. The tool is the factorization a_n^2 - a_m^2 = (a_n - a_m)(a_n + a_m), which turns closeness of the squares into closeness of the terms once the factor a_n + a_m is bounded below by a positive constant. A lower bound. By @lem-limit-bounded-away-ordered-field applied to a_n^2 	o 2 > 0, there is N_0 with a_n^2 > 2/2 = 1 for every n \ge N_0. For such n, a_n > 1: otherwise 0 < a_n \le 1 would give a_n^2 \le 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). So a_n + a_m > 2 for m, n \ge N_0, and 1/(a_n + a_m) < 1/2 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)). The estimate. For m, n \ge N_0, dividing the factorization by a_n + a_m 
e 0, \abs{a_n - a_m} =  rac{\abs{a_n^2 - a_m^2}}{a_n + a_m} \le  rac{\abs{a_n^2 - a_m^2}}{2} . The sequence (a_n^2) converges, so it is Cauchy (@prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field). Given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, choose N_1 with \abs{a_n^2 - a_m^2} < 2\varepsilon for all m, n \ge N_1, and let N \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1\}. For m, n \ge N, \abs{a_n - a_m} < 2\varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. So (a_n) is Cauchy. Why the look-alike tools fail. The limit laws would need a limit of (a_n), and there is none in 
Q: a_n 	o L would give a_n^2 	o L^2, so L^2 = 2, against @thm-no-rational-square-two. @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign and @prp-cauchy-reciprocal-ordered-field presuppose that (a_n) is Cauchy, which is what is asked. The Newton sequence of @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit is one such (a_n), so the question is not empty.

title: Constructing the Real Numbers from Cauchy Sequences
content:
Constructing the Real Numbers from Cauchy Sequences Chapter 4 ended at a hole. The Newton sequence 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408, \dots of Chapter 3 is Cauchy in 
Q, and no rational is its limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). Its terms crowd around a place where 
Q has no element. This chapter does not search for a number in the hole. It takes the sequence itself as the number. Many sequences crowd around the same hole: the decimal truncations 1, 7/5, 141/100, \dots approach it from below and never meet the Newton sequence. So two Cauchy sequences of rationals must count as one number when their difference dies out. That is an equivalence relation, and Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 knows what to do with one: take its classes. A real number is a Cauchy sequence of rationals, up to a null difference. The chapter defines the sum, product and order of these classes on representatives and proves each well defined. The laws of arithmetic are read off the laws of 
Q, one index at a time. The order needs a new idea, because comparing terms does not compare classes. The chapter then places 
Q inside the new field, proves it Archimedean with 
Q dense in it, and finds there a positive number whose square is 2. Until the field exists, every tolerance, margin and threshold is rational, so nothing about real numbers is assumed on the way to building them. Then comes completeness. A set of real numbers that is bounded above is trapped by halving intervals with rational ends; the ends form a Cauchy sequence of rationals, which is a real number, and that number is the least upper bound. So the constructed 
R is a complete ordered field. Chapter 6 shows that any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic, and Axiomatic Set Theory builds one from Dedekind cuts. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes the axioms of a complete ordered field as its starting point, and this chapter gives them a model. Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 builds the complex numbers on this 
R. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 5 repeats the construction for an arbitrary metric space. What you need. Chapter 4 above all, applied with F = 
Q and, once Section 5.3 has made 
R an ordered field, with F = 
R; Chapters 2 and 3; Chapter 1’s arithmetic and order of 
N; Sets and Functions, Chapters 2–6, chiefly Section 5.2; and Logic and Proof, Chapters 4 and 6. From Chapter 4: the rules of an ordered field and the absolute value (@prp-ordered-field-halves, @lem-field-fraction-rules, @def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field); the copy \iota_F of 
Q in an ordered field (@thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field); the Archimedean property in its reciprocal form, the integer part and density (@prp-archimedean-reciprocal, @prp-integer-part-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field); null sequences, tail changes, the limit laws, null times bounded, and limits preserving \le (@def-null-sequence-ordered-field, @prp-tail-change-ordered-field, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field, @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field); Cauchy sequences, their boundedness and algebra, the sign theorem and reciprocals (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field, @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field, @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field, @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign, @prp-cauchy-reciprocal-ordered-field); and the Newton sequence with no rational limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). From Chapters 2 and 3: the lemma on rules defined on classes (@thm-well-defined-on-classes); commutative rings, fields and ordered fields (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field, @prp-ordered-ring-rules); the order from a positive set (@prp-order-from-positives), used here a third time; least elements of sets of integers (@prp-integer-least-element); the Archimedean property of 
Q (@thm-rationals-archimedean); and the Newton sequence and the gaps (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, @thm-no-rational-square-two, @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). From Chapter 1: the arithmetic of 
N and its laws (@def-omega-arithmetic, @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws), its order and how the order meets the arithmetic (@thm-omega-order, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic), parity of powers (@prp-omega-powers-parity), and the citing rule by which induction and recursion apply to 
N (@cor-omega-identification (b)). From Sets and Functions: equivalence classes, quotient sets and the partition theorem (@fd2:def-equivalence-class, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition), with the method of checking a rule on representatives (@fd2:exm-method-well-definedness); the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion); suprema, with their uniqueness and the greatest element as supremum (@fd2:def-order-supremum, @fd2:prp-greatest-unique); and the axiom of choice (@fd2:ax-choice), named only to show that Section 5.5 does not use it. From Logic and Proof: induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the negation of bounded quantifiers (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation). Some exercises also draw on the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of Chapter 4, the fractions of Chapter 3, countability from Sets and Functions, Chapter 4, and the catalogue of what a proof may not do from Logic and Proof, Chapter 8. Nothing from Analysis on the Real Line is used, and no fact about 
R is assumed. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - Sequences That Should Converge. The Newton sequence and the decimal truncations, defined inside 
Q by a rule, as two sequences aimed at one hole; the set \sC of Cauchy sequences of rationals; the relation a \sim b when a - b is null, proved an equivalence relation; the truncations equivalent to the Newton sequence; and finite changes and shifts, which never change the class. - The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic. 
R defined as the quotient set \sC/{\sim}; sum, product and negative defined on representatives and proved well defined; the laws of a commutative ring read on representatives, one index at a time; and inverses through the sign theorem of Chapter 4, after the failed termwise reciprocal. - Positive Classes and the Order. Why termwise comparison defines no order on classes; positive sequences, eventually above a rational margin that is named before the index; positivity as a property of the class, which makes 
R an ordered field; and termwise \le passing to classes, which strict < does not. - The Rationals Inside the Reals. The map \kappa(q) = [(q)_n], which preserves the operations and the order and is Chapter 4’s embedding \iota_{
R}; 
R Archimedean, with 
Q dense in it by Chapter 4’s theorem; and the class of the Newton sequence, a positive real number whose square is 2. - Least Upper Bounds. Complete ordered fields; the bound 2^k \ge k + 1 in any ordered field; bisection with rational ends, whose right ends form a Cauchy sequence of rationals naming the supremum, so that 
R is complete; the bisection and the Newton sequence naming one number; and why no axiom of choice was needed. Named moves The first move was taught in Sets and Functions; the other two are method boxes of this chapter, cited from then on. - Representatives, then independence (@fd2:exm-method-well-definedness). To define an operation or a property on classes, state it on representatives, then show that the class of the answer survives replacing each input by an equivalent one. It proves the sum, product and negative well defined in Section 5.2 and positivity a property of the class in Section 5.3. The termwise reciprocal of Section 5.2 and the termwise order of Section 5.3 fail it. Exercise B2 of Section 5.2 and Exercise C1 of Section 5.3 leave the last step, and then the last half, to you. - Name the margin before the index (@exm-method-margin-before-index). To prove that a Cauchy sequence of rationals is positive, or that [a] < [b], first name a rational margin \delta from data that do not depend on n; only then ask the given sequences for thresholds at tolerances computed from \delta, and take the largest. (Section 5.3; used again in the proof that 
R is Archimedean in Section 5.4 and in Steps 4 and 5 of the completeness proof in Section 5.5; Exercise B4 (d) of Section 5.3 and Exercise C3 of Section 5.4.) - Bisect and keep the invariant (@exm-method-bisect-invariant). Start with a point that fails a test and one that passes it; halve by a rule that keeps one end on each side; prove the invariants and the length D/2^k by induction; make the lengths small by the Archimedean property; and spend one invariant on each half of the conclusion. (Section 5.5; Exercises C1 and C2 of Section 5.5.) Threads - The Newton class. Section 3.3 computes the Newton sequence and Section 4.6 proves it Cauchy with no rational limit; Section 5.1 shows the decimal truncations equivalent to it; Section 5.2 takes its class as a first real number; Section 5.4 proves that this class is positive with square 2 (@exm-sqrt2-class); the worked example of Section 5.5 finds the same number by bisection; and Chapter 6 returns to it when it proves that every non-negative element of a complete ordered field has a square root. - Archimedes. Chapter 3 proves the Archimedean property of 
Q from the construction; Section 4.2 defines it for any ordered field and derives the integer part and density; Section 5.4 proves it for 
R; Step 3 of the completeness proof in Section 5.5 uses it in 
Q, and density, which came from it in 
R, supplies the rational ends; Chapter 6 shows that a complete ordered field is always Archimedean. - Choice. Sets and Functions, Chapter 6 states the axiom of choice and asks every proof to name its rules; Section 5.1 defines the truncations by a rule, with no choices made; and the example on representatives in Section 5.5 shows that the completeness proof picks finitely many objects and defines the rest by recursion. Summary The set \sC of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences) carries the relation a \sim b, “a - b is null” (@def-cauchy-equivalent), which is an equivalence relation (@prp-cauchy-equivalent-relation), and a real number is one of its classes (@def-reals-cauchy-classes). The sum, product and negative defined on representatives are well defined (@thm-reals-operations-well-defined), the laws of 
Q applied index by index make 
R a commutative ring (@thm-reals-commutative-ring), and the sign theorem of Chapter 4 supplies inverses, so 
R is a field (@thm-reals-field). A Cauchy sequence of rationals is positive when its terms eventually stay above one rational margin (@def-positive-cauchy-sequence); positivity belongs to the class (@prp-positivity-well-defined), and the positive classes make 
R an ordered field (@thm-reals-ordered-field), in which termwise \le passes to classes (@lem-termwise-order). The map \kappa places a copy of 
Q in 
R that respects the operations and the order (@thm-rational-embedding); 
R is Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), 
Q is dense in it (@thm-constructed-rationals-dense), and the class of the Newton sequence is a positive real number whose square is 2 (@exm-sqrt2-class). Bisection with rational ends shows that every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound, so 
R is a complete ordered field (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), and the proof uses no axiom of choice (@exm-representatives-need-choice). What is open: is this the only complete ordered field? Other constructions give other sets, the cuts of Axiomatic Set Theory among them, and Chapter 6 proves that any two complete ordered fields are linked by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism. The sequence form of completeness, that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges, is proved in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 4. Terms - Cauchy sequences of rationals: the set \sC of sequences 
N 	o 
Q that are Cauchy in 
Q (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences). - Cauchy-complete: said of an ordered field in which every Cauchy sequence converges (@def-complete-ordered-field). - complete ordered field: an ordered field in which every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum (@def-complete-ordered-field). - copy of 
Q in 
R: \kappa(q) = [(q)_n], the class of the constant sequence (@def-rational-embedding). - equivalent (Cauchy sequences): a \sim b when a - b is null (@def-cauchy-equivalent). - integer part (in 
R): the one m \in 
Z with \kappa(m) \le x < \kappa(m + 1) (@prp-integer-part-ordered-field with F = 
R). - positive (Cauchy sequence): from some index on, every term is at least one fixed positive rational (@def-positive-cauchy-sequence). - real number: a class [a] of Cauchy sequences of rationals under \sim; 
R = \sC/{\sim} (@def-reals-cauchy-classes). - representative: any b \in [a] (@def-reals-cauchy-classes). - supremum: the least upper bound of a set, as defined in Sets and Functions (@fd2:def-order-supremum).

title: 5.1 Sequences That Should Converge
content:
Sequences That Should Converge Chapter 4 ended with a rational sequence that is Cauchy in 
Q and converges to no rational (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). Its terms crowd around a place where 
Q has a hole. This chapter builds the number that belongs in the hole, and the first step is to notice that many different sequences crowd around the same hole. This section sets up the raw material, the set \sC of Cauchy sequences of rationals, and the relation that will decide when two of them aim at the same number: their difference dies out. Nothing about real numbers is assumed. Every tolerance, bound and threshold in this section is a rational number. Two sequences aimed at one hole The first sequence is the Newton sequence of Chapter 3 (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2): x_0 \coloneqq 2 and x_{n+1} \coloneqq  rac{x_n^2 + 2}{2 x_n} =  rac{x_n}{2} +  rac{1}{x_n} \qquad (n \in 
N) , with error e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2. Its first terms are 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408. We shall use the following facts, each proved earlier, for every n \in 
N: 1. x_n \in 
Q_{>0}, and e_n > 0, that is, x_n^2 > 2 (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2); 2. x_n > 1, and e_n \le 1/(4n) when n \ge 1 (the first clauses of the statement of @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit); 3. (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence in 
Q, and there is no L \in 
Q with x_n 	o L (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). From (NS1) and (NS2), 0 < x_n^2 - 2 \le 1/(4n) for every n \ge 1. At n = 0 the expression 1/(4n) is not defined, and indeed x_0^2 - 2 = 2 is not small. The second sequence approaches the hole from below, by decimal truncation. To define it inside 
Q, without the school decimals, we need powers of ten. Powers of ten. For k \in 
N, 10^k is the power in the ordered field 
Q of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), with 10^0 = 1 and 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10. (Here 10 = 10 \cdot 1_{
Q}, by the identification 
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q of Chapters 2 and 3 and @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (d).) Two inductions, in the fold below, show that 10^k \in 
Z and 10^k \ge k + 1. In particular 10^k \ge 1 > 0, so 1/10^k > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), and @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), applied to 0 < k + 1 \le 10^k, gives 1/10^k \le 1/(k + 1). Together, 0 <  rac{1}{10^k} \le  rac{1}{k + 1} \qquad (k \in 
N) . {#eq-ten-power-reciprocal} The inequality is not strict at k = 0, where both sides are 1. We write 1/10^k throughout; negative powers have not been defined. Both are proved by induction (@fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N through @cor-omega-identification (b)) with base P(0). - 10^k \in 
Z. Base: 10^0 = 1 \in 
Z. Step: if 10^k \in 
Z, then 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10 is a product of two integers, and products of integers computed in 
Q are integers (@prp-integers-embed-rationals: j(m) j(n) = j(mn)). - 10^k \ge k + 1. Base: 10^0 = 1 = 0 + 1. Step: suppose 10^k \ge y, where y \coloneqq k + 1. Then y \ge 1 (@prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b)), and multiplying by 10 > 0 gives 10^{k+1} = 10^k \cdot 10 \ge 10y (by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) if 10^k > y; trivially if 10^k = y). Moreover 10y - (y + 1) = 9y - 1 \ge 9 - 1 > 0. So 10^{k+1} > y + 1 = k + 2, where (k + 1) + 1 = k + 2 is arithmetic in 
N (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws), carried into 
Q by the sum law of @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). The truncations. For k \in 
N, let m_k be the largest natural number m with m^2 \le 2 \cdot (10^k)^2 , and let d_k \coloneqq m_k / 10^k. In school terms, d_k is \sqrt 2 cut off after k decimal places; but the definition mentions only integers and the rational 10^k. That such a largest m exists, and is unique, is a fact about sets of integers (@prp-integer-least-element), checked in the fold below. Because exactly one number is described for each k, k \mapsto d_k is a function 
N 	o 
Q (@fd2:def-function), with no choices made. Let S_k \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z : m \ge 0 	ext{ and } m^2 > 2 \cdot (10^k)^2 \} . It is bounded below by 0, and it is non-empty: 2 \cdot 10^k is a non-negative integer, and (2 \cdot 10^k)^2 = 4 (10^k)^2 > 2 (10^k)^2 because (10^k)^2 > 0. By @prp-integer-least-element, S_k has a least element m^\ast. Since 0^2 = 0 \le 2 (10^k)^2, 0 
otin S_k, so m^\ast \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), hence m_k \coloneqq m^\ast - 1 \ge 0 is a natural number (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). It is not in S_k, being smaller than the least element, so m_k^2 \le 2 (10^k)^2. Every natural number m > m_k satisfies m \ge m^\ast (discreteness again), so m^2 \ge (m^\ast)^2 > 2 (10^k)^2 (by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) if m > m^\ast; trivially if m = m^\ast). So m_k is the largest natural number with m^2 \le 2 (10^k)^2, and there is exactly one. The first values are:  egin{array}{c|ccccccc} k & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \ \hline m_k & 1 & 14 & 141 & 1414 & 14142 & 141421 & 1414213 \end{array} For instance m_1 = 14, because 14^2 = 196 \le 200 = 2 \cdot 10^2 and 15^2 = 225 > 200. So d_0 = 1, d_1 = 7/5, d_2 = 141/100, d_3 = 707/500. Different sequences, one intended number. The two sequences never meet: x_k^2 > 2 \ge d_k^2 for every k, so x_k 
e d_k. They approach from opposite sides, and their differences x_1 - d_1 = 1/10, x_2 - d_2 = 1/150, x_3 - d_3 = 11/51000 shrink fast. Both “should” converge to the same number, and 
Q has no such number. The plan of the chapter is to make the sequences themselves into the numbers, and for that we must first say when two sequences count as one. Cauchy sequences of rationals The raw material is every sequence that behaves as if it had a limit. Cauchy Sequences of Rationals \sC is the set of all sequences a \colon 
N 	o 
Q (@def-sequence-ordered-field, F = 
Q) that are Cauchy sequences in 
Q (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field): for every \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} there is N \in 
N with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon for all m, n \ge N. In symbols, a \in \sC means  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall m \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ &\qquad  igl( (m \ge N \wedge n \ge N) \Rightarrow \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . \end{aligned} A sequence a of rationals is null if a_n 	o 0 in 
Q (@def-null-sequence-ordered-field, F = 
Q). We write a sequence as a single letter, a = (a_n)_{n \in 
N}, and do arithmetic on sequences termwise: a + b \coloneqq (a_n + b_n)_n, ab \coloneqq (a_n b_n)_n, -a \coloneqq (-a_n)_n and a - b \coloneqq (a_n - b_n)_n. For q \in 
Q, (q)_n is the constant sequence with every term q. Nothing is new here except the name: this is Chapter 4’s definition with F = 
Q, so every tolerance \varepsilon is rational. That is the point. The definition can be read by someone who knows only 
Q, and it will be used to build a larger field without assuming anything about it. Examples. Every constant sequence (q)_n is in \sC, with N = 0 for every \varepsilon. The sequence (1/(n + 1))_n is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), so it is in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)). The Newton sequence (x_n) is in \sC, by (NS3), and is not null, since x_n > 1 for every n. The sequence (n)_n is not in \sC: a Cauchy sequence is bounded (@prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field), and for every M \in 
Q_{>0} some n \in 
N has n > M (@thm-rationals-archimedean). The toolkit from Chapter 4, with F = 
Q. This chapter uses the following facts so often that we list them once. Each was proved in Chapter 4 for an arbitrary ordered field; here F =
