For k \ge N, both n_k \ge N and k \ge N, so \abs{a_{n_k} - a_k} < \varepsilon. So (a_{n_k} - a_k)_k is null, with the same thresholds, and (a_{n_k})_k \sim a. (b) By (a), (a_{n_k})_k \sim a and (b_{n_k})_k \sim b. The two subsequences are the same sequence, since a_{n_k} = b_{n_k} for every k. So a \sim (a_{n_k})_k = (b_{n_k})_k \sim b, using symmetry for the first step, and transitivity (@prp-cauchy-equivalent-relation) gives a \sim b. The hypothesis of (b) is that the sequences agree at infinitely many indices, n_0 < n_1 < \cdots, arbitrarily far out. In the warning, (0)_n and (1 - 1/(n + 1))_n agree only at n = 0. Agreement far out, along a whole subsequence, forces equivalence for Cauchy sequences; agreement at finitely many places says nothing. (For sequences that are not Cauchy, (b) fails: (1, 0, 1, 0, \dots) and (1)_n agree at every even index, and their difference is not null.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: proves n_k \ge k for every k, justifying the passage from n_{k+1} > n_k \ge k to the next whole number. - 3: shows (a_{n_k}) \in \sC, with one threshold that serves all j, k \ge N and with n_j, n_k \ge N justified from n_k \ge k. - 3: shows (a_{n_k} - a_k)_k is null by applying the Cauchy condition to the pair (n_k, k). - 2: deduces (b) by symmetry and transitivity of \sim. Fatal error (0 for the step): a threshold that depends on k.

title: 5.2 The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic
5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content:
Positive Classes and the Order Section 5.2 made 
R a field: its elements are classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals, added and multiplied through representatives. A field is not yet a number line. To compare two real numbers we need an order, and it must cooperate with the arithmetic: 
R should be an ordered field in the sense of @def-ordered-ring-and-field. Chapter 3 ordered 
Q in two steps. It first said which rationals are positive, and then let a < b mean that b - a is positive (@prp-order-from-positives). This section takes the same two steps for 
R. All the work is in the first: deciding which classes are positive, in a way that does not depend on the representative. Notation is that of Sections 5.1 and 5.2: \sC, \sim, [a], the operations of @def-reals-operations, 0_{
R} = [(0)_n], 1_{
R} = [(1)_n], and [a] - [b] = [a - b], used without comment. Until 
R has an order, every margin, tolerance and threshold is rational or natural: we may not measure with what we are building. Comparing terms does not compare classes The first idea is to compare two classes by comparing their terms. It fails, and the way it fails shows what the definition must contain. [Termwise Order Is Not an Order on Classes] Consider the rule [a] < [b] means that a_n < b_n for every n from some index on. Let a_n \coloneqq 0 and b_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1) for n \in 
N. Show that [a] = [b]. Then apply the rule to the classes [a] and [a] twice: once through the representatives a and a, once through a and b. Conclude that the rule does not define a relation on 
R. Both sequences are in \sC: a constant sequence and a null sequence are Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and (1/(n + 1)) is null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)). Termwise, b - a = (1/(n + 1)), which is null, so b \sim a, and [a] = [b] by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). Through the representatives a and a: the rule asks whether 0 < 0 from some index on, and 0 < 0 never holds. So the rule says that [a] < [a] is false. Through the representatives a and b, which name the same two classes, since b \in [b] = [a]: for every n, a_n = 0 < 1/(n + 1) = b_n. So the rule says that [a] < [a] is true. A relation on 
R must give one answer for each pair of classes. The rule gives two answers for the pair (0_{
R}, 0_{
R}), depending on the representatives, so it defines no relation on 
R. Worse, the second answer, 0_{
R} < 0_{
R}, is excluded by trichotomy (O1) in any ordered field. The trouble is that the gap between a_n and b_n is allowed to shrink to nothing, and a gap that shrinks to nothing is exactly what \sim ignores. A class that deserves to be called positive must have terms that stay above 0 by a fixed margin. Positive sequences We look for a property of a single sequence a \in \sC that says “the number a names is greater than 0”. The example shows that “eventually a_n > 0” is too weak, because a null sequence can have it. The repair is to name the margin first. Positive means: eventually above one fixed positive rational. [Positive Cauchy Sequence] A sequence a \in \sC is positive if there exist \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N such that a_n \ge \delta for every n \in 
N with n \ge N. In symbols, \exists \delta \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \ ( n \ge N \Rightarrow a_n \ge \delta ) . In words: the first quantifier names a margin \delta, a positive rational, before anything else is named; the second names a threshold; the third says that every term from the threshold on is at least the margin. Because \delta comes first, one margin serves all the late terms at once. The word “positive” describes the sequence as a name for a number, not its terms one by one: the terms before N may be negative, and, as the warning below shows, terms that are all > 0 are not enough. Compare the weaker condition \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \ ( n \ge N \Rightarrow a_n > 0 ) . There each late term clears 0 by its own amount, which may shrink with n; in the definition one margin is named before n, and that order of the quantifiers is the whole point. Examples. A positive constant. For q \in 
Q_{>0}, the constant sequence (q)_n is positive, with \delta = q and N = 0. This degenerate case is how Section 5.4 will see that the rational q, placed inside 
R, is greater than 0. The Newton sequence. Let (x_n) be the sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, which is in \sC by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit. The same theorem states that x_n > 1 for every n \in 
N. So (x_n) is positive, with \delta = 1 and N = 0. Late positivity. Let a_n \coloneqq 1 - 2/(n + 1). It is in \sC, as the difference of a constant sequence and a constant multiple of the null sequence (1/(n + 1)) (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)). Its first terms are -1, 0, 1/3, 1/2, so it is not positive “from the start”. For n \ge 3, n + 1 \ge 4, so 1/(n + 1) \le 1/4 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (c)), hence 2/(n + 1) \le 2/4 = 1/2 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (d), with 0 \le 2 \le 2), and a_n \ge 1/2. So a is positive, with \delta = 1/2 and N = 3. No smaller N works with this \delta, since a_2 = 1/3 < 1/2; the definition allows any finite stretch of bad terms. Non-example by a minimal change. Keep every term positive, but let the margin shrink: a_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1). Every term is > 0, so the weaker condition above holds with N = 0. What fails is the order of the quantifiers. The negation of the definition, by @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication, reads  orall \delta \in 
Q_{>0} \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \ ( n \ge N \wedge a_n < \delta ) , and it holds: given \delta and N, @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives n_0 \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \delta for every m \ge n_0. With n \coloneqq \max\{N, n_0\}, we have n \ge N, and m \coloneqq n + 1 \ge n_0, so a_n = 1/(n + 1) < \delta. Every margin is eventually undercut. Why this definition. Each clause has a job. - The margin \delta. Without it, the definition would be the weaker condition, and @exm-strict-termwise-order-fails shows the result: (1/(n + 1)) would be positive, while (0)_n, which names the same number 0_{
R}, is not. - A rational margin. The only positive numbers available are rationals. A real margin would use the order of 
R, which is what we are defining. - The threshold N. Changing finitely many terms does not change the class (@exm-finite-change-equivalent), so a definition meant for classes must ignore every finite stretch of terms. The late-positivity example needs N = 3. Either inequality would do: a_n \ge \delta gives a_n > \delta/2, and a_n > \delta gives a_n \ge \delta. We use \ge, the form in which @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign delivers its conclusion. “Every term of a is positive” does not make a positive. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) has every term > 0, and it is not positive (non-example above); its class is 0_{
R}. Let a \in \sC, with \delta ranging over 
Q_{>0}. Which of the two conditions 	ext{(A)} \ \exists \delta \ \exists N \  orall n \ge N \ \ a_n \ge \delta , \qquad 	ext{(B)} \ \exists N \  orall n \ge N \ \exists \delta \ \ a_n \ge \delta implies the other? Which of them says the same as “eventually a_n > 0”? (A) implies (B): the margin found once serves as the \delta for every late n. (B) does not imply (A): (1/(n + 1)) satisfies (B), with \delta \coloneqq 1/(n + 1) chosen after n, and fails (A). (B) says the same as “eventually a_n > 0”: if a_n > 0, take \delta \coloneqq a_n; if a_n \ge \delta > 0, then a_n > 0. So (A) is the definition of positive, and (B) is the weaker condition. Payoff: positivity belongs to the class. A definition about sequences says something about a class only if equivalent sequences agree on it. The proof shows the method of this section in its simplest form. [Positivity Is a Property of the Class] Let a, a' \in \sC with a' \sim a. If a is positive, then a' is positive. [Scratch work] The goal is an existence statement whose first quantifier is a margin. Name it first, from the data, before any index appears; then ask the given sequences for thresholds. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Givens Goal ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- a_n \ge \delta for n \ge N, with \delta \in 
Q_{>0}; a' - a null \exists \delta' \in 
Q_{>0} \ \exists N' \  orall n \ge N' \ \ a'_n \ge \delta' the margin comes first and may depend only on \delta: afford to lose half, \delta' \coloneqq \delta/2 \exists N' \  orall n \ge N' \ \ a'_n \ge \delta/2 nullity of a' - a at the tolerance \delta/2: a'_n - a_n is within \delta/2 of 0 for n \ge N'' the threshold N' \coloneqq \max\{N, N''\} for n \ge N': a'_n > a_n - \delta/2 \ge \delta - \delta/2 gap closed ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Fix \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N with a_n \ge \delta for every n \ge N. Then \delta/2 \in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). Since a' - a is null, fix N'' with \abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta/2 for every n \ge N'', and let N' \coloneqq \max\{N, N''\}. For n \ge N', @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d) gives -\delta/2 < a'_n - a_n, so a'_n > a_n - \delta/2 \ge \delta - \delta/2 = \delta/2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), @prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). So a' is positive, with margin \delta/2 and threshold N'. This is @prp-sign-stable-ordered-field with F = 
Q, written out because its order of choices is the method of this section. The margin halves, and that is harmless: the definition asks only for some margin. Exercise C2 shows a tempting proof of this proposition that keeps a margin of 0, and so does not prove it. [Method: name the margin before the index] Template. To prove that b \in \sC is positive, or that [a] < [b]: (1) name a margin \delta \in 
Q_{>0} from data that do not depend on n: a given margin, or a fraction (such as half) of a given margin or of a positive value the terms visibly approach; (2) only then ask the given sequences (Cauchy, null, positive) for thresholds at tolerances computed from \delta; (3) take the largest of these finitely many thresholds and check that the terms of the sequence to be shown positive (b, or b - a for [a] < [b]) are \ge \delta beyond it. When to use it. Whenever the goal reads \exists \delta \ \exists N \  orall n \ge N \ \ldots: positivity, a strict inequality between classes, a bound that must hold beyond one index. The usual failure. Proving “b_n > 0 for all large n” and calling b_n the margin: it depends on n (the Quick check above; Exercise C2). We can now name the set of positive real numbers. Let P \coloneqq \{ [a] : a \in \sC 	ext{ and } a 	ext{ is positive} \} \subseteq 
R . Chapters 2 and 3 built the positive sets P_{
Z} and P_{
Q}; P is the same step for 
R. For x \in 
R: x \in P \iff 	ext{some representative of } x 	ext{ is positive} \iff 	ext{every representative of } x 	ext{ is positive} . The first equivalence is the definition of P. For the second, every class has a representative (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (a)), which gives “every \Rightarrow some”. Conversely, if x = [a] with a positive and b \in x, then b \sim a (@fd2:def-equivalence-class), so b is positive by @prp-positivity-well-defined. Membership in P can therefore be tested on any representative we like. This is the well-definedness the termwise rule lacked. The positive classes Chapter 2’s recipe needs two facts about P: it is closed under sum and product, and it splits 
R into three parts, P, \{0_{
R}\} and the negatives of P. These are clauses (P1) and (P2) of @prp-order-from-positives. [The Positive Real Numbers] 1. For every x \in 
R, exactly one of x \in P, x = 0_{
R}, -x \in P holds. 2. If x \in P and y \in P, then x + y \in P and xy \in P. For (i), “at least one” is the sign theorem of Chapter 4: a Cauchy sequence that is not null is eventually above c or eventually below -c (@thm-cauchy-not-null-sign). A null representative gives 0_{
R}. “At most one” holds because a sequence cannot be eventually above a positive margin and also eventually below a negative one, or null. For (ii), add or multiply the two margins and take the later of the two thresholds. Let x \in 
R, and write x = [a] with a \in \sC. (i), at least one. Suppose first that a is null. Termwise a - (0)_n = a, so a \sim (0)_n and x = [(0)_n] = 0_{
R}. Suppose next that a is not null. By @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign with F = 
Q, there are c \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N such that either a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, or a_n \le -c for every n \ge N; fix them. In the first case a is positive, so x \in P. In the second case -a_n \ge c for every n \ge N (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), in each case of \le), so -a is positive and -x = [-a] \in P. (i), at most one. We exclude the three pairs. - x \in P and x = 0_{
R}. Then (0)_n is a representative of x, so it is positive, since every representative of an element of P is: some \delta \in 
Q_{>0} has 0 \ge \delta. This contradicts \delta > 0 by (O1) in 
Q. - -x \in P and x = 0_{
R}. Then -x = [-(0)_n] = [(0)_n] = 0_{
R}, and the previous case, applied to -x, excludes this. - x \in P and -x \in P. Then a and -a are both positive: a_n \ge \delta for n \ge N and -a_n \ge \delta' for n \ge N', with \delta, \delta' \in 
Q_{>0}. At n \coloneqq \max\{N, N'\}, \delta \le a_n \le -\delta' (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), in each case of \le), so 0 < \delta \le -\delta' < 0, against (O1) in 
Q. (ii) Let x, y \in P, and write x = [a], y = [b]. Both a and b are positive: there are \delta_a, \delta_b \in 
Q_{>0} and N_a, N_b \in 
N with a_n \ge \delta_a for n \ge N_a and b_n \ge \delta_b for n \ge N_b. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_a, N_b\} and n \ge N. Adding the two inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), a_n + b_n \ge \delta_a + \delta_b , and \delta_a + \delta_b > 0 + 0 = 0 by the same rule. Multiplying, by @prp-ordered-field-halves (d) applied to 0 \le \delta_a \le a_n and 0 \le \delta_b \le b_n, a_n b_n \ge \delta_a \delta_b , and \delta_a \delta_b > 0 by (O4). So a + b and ab are positive, with margins \delta_a + \delta_b and \delta_a \delta_b and the threshold N. Hence x + y = [a + b] \in P and xy = [ab] \in P (@def-reals-operations). The order of the reals With P in hand the definition is the one Chapters 2 and 3 used for 
Z and 
Q. [Order on the Reals] For x, y \in 
R, x < y means y - x \in P. As usual, x \le y means x < y or x = y, and y > x means x < y. In terms of representatives: [a] < [b] exactly when b - a is positive, that is, when b_n - a_n \ge \delta from some index on, for some margin \delta \in 
Q_{>0}. The terms of b must eventually overtake those of a by a fixed rational amount. Since 0_{
R} - x = -x and x - 0_{
R} = x, we have x > 0_{
R} if and only if x \in P, and x < 0_{
R} if and only if -x \in P. [The Reals Form an Ordered Field] With the operations of @def-reals-operations and the order of @def-reals-order, 
R is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), and its positive elements are exactly the elements of P. Each order axiom is a statement about one difference, and @thm-reals-positive-cone is exactly what @prp-order-from-positives asks for. (O1) is (i) applied to y - x, since -(y - x) = x - y. (O2) is closure under sums, since (z - y) + (y - x) = z - x. (O3) holds because (y + z) - (x + z) = y - x. (O4) is closure under products. By @thm-reals-field, 
R is a field, in particular a commutative ring (@def-commutative-ring-and-field). By @thm-reals-positive-cone, the subset P \subseteq 
R satisfies clause (P1) of @prp-order-from-positives (part (ii)) and clause (P2) (part (i)). That proposition then says that the relation “y - x \in P”, which is x < y of @def-reals-order, makes 
R an ordered commutative ring with P = \{ x \in 
R : x > 0_{
R} \}. An ordered commutative ring that is a field is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field). So 
R is an ordered field, and every result that Chapters 2 and 4 proved for an arbitrary ordered field holds in it. We write 
R_{>0} \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R : x > 0_{
R} \}, the set F_{>0} of Chapter 4 for F = 
R; by the theorem, 
R_{>0} = P. The rules for inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules), the rules for halves (@prp-ordered-field-halves), the absolute value (@def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), and limits, null sequences and Cauchy sequences with tolerances in 
R_{>0} (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field) are now available in 
R. From here on they may be applied with F = 
R. It pays to name the field at each such use, so that a tolerance in 
Q_{>0} is never confused with one in 
R_{>0}. One consequence deserves a line. In any ordered field, x \le y holds if and only if y < x fails: by (O1), exactly one of x < y, x = y, y < x holds. [A Margin Read Off the Limit] Let a_n \coloneqq (2n + 1)/(n + 3). Show that a \in \sC and [a] > 1_{
R}, and find a margin and a threshold. Since 2n + 1 = 2(n + 3) - 5, we have a_n = 2 - 5/(n + 3). The sequence (1/(n + 3))_n is the shift by 2 of the null sequence (1/(n + 1))_n (@prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b), @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), so a is a constant minus a multiple of a null sequence and lies in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)). By @def-reals-order we need a - (1)_n to be positive. Its terms are a_n - 1 =  rac{n - 2}{n + 3} = 1 -  rac{5}{n + 3} . Margin first. These terms approach 1, so we aim at half of it, \delta \coloneqq 1/2, before naming any index. Then the index. Multiplying by 2(n + 3) > 0, or by its reciprocal (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality as the other case),  rac{n - 2}{n + 3} \ge  rac{1}{2} \iff 2(n - 2) \ge n + 3 \iff n \ge 7 . So \delta = 1/2 and N = 7 work, and [a] > 1_{
R}. No smaller threshold works with this margin, since a_6 - 1 = 4/9 < 1/2. Any margin \delta < 1 works with a later threshold; \delta = 1 fails, since every a_n - 1 = 1 - 5/(n + 3) < 1. The tempting shortcut, “a_n - 1 > 0 for n \ge 3”, is the weaker condition and proves nothing about the class. Comparing classes through their terms The order is defined through margins, but in practice we usually know a termwise inequality and want an inequality between classes. The next lemma is the bridge, and the example at the start of the section shows its limit. [Termwise Inequalities Pass to Classes] Let a, b \in \sC and N_0 \in 
N. If a_n \le b_n for every n \ge N_0, then [a] \le [b]. Suppose instead that [b] < [a]. Then a - b is positive, so from some index on a_n exceeds b_n by a fixed margin; one index beyond both thresholds then contradicts a_n \le b_n. By trichotomy, “not [b] < [a]” is “[a] \le [b]”. Suppose that [b] < [a]. By @def-reals-order, [a] - [b] = [a - b] \in P, so a - b is positive, since every representative of an element of P is (@prp-positivity-well-defined). Fix \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N with a_n - b_n \ge \delta for every n \ge N. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N, N_0\}. Then a_n - b_n \ge \delta > 0. But n \ge N_0, so a_n \le b_n, that is, a_n - b_n \le 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), in each case of \le). These contradict (O1) in 
Q. Hence [b] < [a] is false. By (O1) in the ordered field 
R (@thm-reals-ordered-field), [a] < [b] or [a] = [b]; that is, [a] \le [b]. The strict version of the lemma is false. In @exm-strict-termwise-order-fails, a_n = 0 < 1/(n + 1) = b_n for every n, and yet [a] = [b], so [a] < [b] fails. A strict termwise inequality passes to classes only as \le. To get < between classes, show that the difference is eventually above a fixed margin. Most uses of the lemma compare a class with a constant: if a_n \le q for every n \ge N_0, then [a] \le [(q)_n]; and if a_n \ge q for every n \ge N_0, then [a] \ge [(q)_n]. Let a_n \coloneqq 1/(n + 1) - 1/(n + 1)^2. Every term satisfies a_n \ge 0. Is a positive? No. Here a_n = n/(n + 1)^2, so 0 \le a_n \le 1/(n + 1) for every n (as n \le n + 1). The lower sequence (0)_n and the upper sequence (1/(n + 1)) are null, so a is null by the squeeze, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) with F = 
Q; being null, a \in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)). Then [a] = 0_{
R}, as in the proof of @thm-reals-positive-cone (i), and 0_{
R} 
otin P by the same part. So a is not positive, although no term is negative. @lem-termwise-order gives only [a] \ge 0_{
R}, which is true. Since 
R is an ordered field, every x \in 
R has an absolute value \abs{x} (@def-absolute-value-ordered-field with F = 
R); Exercise C1 shows that it can be computed on representatives, \abs{[a]} = [(\abs{a_n})_n]. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In parts (a)–(d), decide for each sequence whether it is in \sC and whether it is positive; when it is positive, give a margin \delta and a threshold N. 1. a_n = 1 - 1/(n + 1). 2. a_n = 1/(n + 1). 3. a_k = d_k - 1, where (d_k) is the sequence of decimal truncations of @exm-truncations-equivalent. 4. a_n = (-1)^n. 5. Show from @def-reals-order and @def-positive-cauchy-sequence that 1_{
R} > 0_{
R}. Which result of Chapter 2 gives the same conclusion in every ordered field? 6. In the proof of @prp-positivity-well-defined, why is the tolerance for a' - a taken to be \delta/2 and not \delta? What would the proof give with \delta? (a) In \sC (a constant minus a null sequence, @thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)), and positive. For n \ge 1, n + 1 \ge 2, so 1/(n + 1) \le 1/2 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (c)) and a_n \ge 1/2. So \delta = 1/2, N = 1 work. (N = 0 fails for this \delta: a_0 = 0.) (b) In \sC, being null, and not positive: this is the non-example after @def-positive-cauchy-sequence. (c) In \sC, as the difference of (d_k) \in \sC (@exm-truncations-equivalent) and a constant, and positive. The first truncations are d_0 = 1 and d_1 = 7/5 (14 is the largest natural number whose square is at most 2 \cdot 10^2 = 200), and (d_k) is non-decreasing ((T1), stated before @exm-truncations-equivalent). So d_k \ge d_1 = 7/5 for every k \ge 1, and a_k \ge 2/5. So \delta = 2/5, N = 1 work. (N = 0 fails for every \delta > 0: a_0 = 0.) (d) Not in \sC: for every N, the indices N and N + 1 give terms differing by 2, so the tolerance 1 has no threshold. The question “positive?” does not arise; the definition applies only to members of \sC. (e) 1_{
R} - 0_{
R} = [(1)_n - (0)_n] = [(1)_n], and (1)_n is positive with \delta = 1, N = 0. So 1_{
R} - 0_{
R} \in P, that is, 0_{
R} < 1_{
R}. In every ordered commutative ring with 1 
e 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) gives 1 > 0; for 
R, 1_{
R} 
e 0_{
R} holds by @thm-reals-commutative-ring. (f) With the tolerance \delta the proof gives only a'_n > a_n - \delta \ge 0: terms above 0 with no margin, which is the weaker condition. The tolerance \delta/2 leaves the margin \delta/2, named before n. Any tolerance strictly between 0 and \delta would do. B. Practice [B1] Let a_n = 1 - 1/(n + 1) and b_n = x_n - 1, with (x_n) the Newton sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. Find margins and thresholds for a and b, and state the margins and threshold that the proof of @thm-reals-positive-cone (ii) produces for a + b and ab. Hint: for b, compare x_n with 7/5 by squaring. The example. For a, Exercise A1 (a) gives \delta_a = 1/2, N_a = 1. For b: x_n > 0 and x_n^2 > 2 for every n (@exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2), while (7/5)^2 = 49/25 < 2. Both 7/5 and x_n are \ge 0, so @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) turns (7/5)^2 < x_n^2 into 7/5 < x_n. Here b is in \sC, as the difference of (x_n), which is in \sC by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, and a constant (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)). From 7/5 < x_n, b_n = x_n - 1 > 2/5 for every n, and \delta_b = 2/5, N_b = 0 work. The proof then gives the threshold N = \max\{1, 0\} = 1, the margin 1/2 + 2/5 = 9/10 for a + b, and the margin (1/2)(2/5) = 1/5 for ab. [B2] Let a, b \in \sC. Prove that [a] < [b] if and only if there are \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N with b_n - a_n \ge \delta for every n \ge N. By @def-reals-order, [a] < [b] means [b] - [a] \in P. By @def-reals-operations, [b] - [a] = [b - a], where b - a \in \sC is the termwise difference (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (b)). An element of 
R lies in P if and only if one (equivalently, every) representative of it is positive, by the definition of P and @prp-positivity-well-defined. So [a] < [b] holds if and only if b - a is positive, which, by @def-positive-cauchy-sequence, is the condition stated, since the n-th term of b - a is b_n - a_n. [B3] 1. Let a \in \sC with 0 \le a_n \le 1 for every n \in 
N. Prove that 0_{
R} \le [a] \le 1_{
R}. 2. Give an example of a \in \sC with 0 < a_n < 1 for every n and [a] = 1_{
R}. What does your example show about part (a)? (a) The constant sequences (0)_n and (1)_n are in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)). By @lem-termwise-order with N_0 = 0, (0)_n \le a termwise gives 0_{
R} = [(0)_n] \le [a], and a \le (1)_n termwise gives [a] \le [(1)_n] = 1_{
R}. (b) Let a_n \coloneqq 1 - 1/(n + 2). For every n, n + 2 \ge 2 > 1, so 0 < 1/(n + 2) < 1 (@prp-reciprocal-order (b)), and 0 < a_n < 1. The sequence a - (1)_n = (-1/(n + 2)) is null: (1/(n + 2)) is the shift by one of the null sequence (1/(n + 1)) (@prp-tail-change-ordered-field (b)), and the negative of a null sequence is null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b)). So a = (1)_n + (-1/(n + 2))_n is in \sC, as the sum of a constant and a null sequence (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a), (b)). Since a - (1)_n is null, a \sim (1)_n and [a] = 1_{
R}. The example shows that part (a) cannot be sharpened to strict inequalities: a_n < 1 for every n, and still [a] = 1_{
R}. This is the warning after @lem-termwise-order once more. (Any a with 0 < a_n < 1 for all n and 1 - a_n null is a correct answer.) [B4: Prove or disprove] Let a, b \in \sC. Prove each statement or give a counterexample. 1. If a_n > 0 for every n, then [a] \ge 0_{
R}. 2. If a is positive and b \sim a, then b_n > 0 for every n. 3. If a 
ot\sim b, then a - b or b - a is positive. 4. If a is positive and b_n \ge a_n - 1/(n + 1) for every n, then b is positive. 5. If a and b are positive, then a - b or b - a is positive. (a) True. The constant (0)_n is in \sC (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and 0 \le a_n for every n, so @lem-termwise-order with N_0 = 0 gives 0_{
R} = [(0)_n] \le [a]. (b) False. Let b \coloneqq (-1, 1, 1, 1, \ldots), which agrees with (1)_n from index 1 on. Then b \in \sC and b \sim (1)_n (@exm-finite-change-equivalent (a)), and (1)_n is positive, with \delta = 1, N = 0. But b_0 = -1. (c) True. Since a 
ot\sim b, [a] 
e [b] (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)), so [a - b] = [a] - [b] 
e 0_{
R}. By @thm-reals-positive-cone (i), [a - b] \in P or -[a - b] = [b - a] \in P. Every representative of an element of P is positive (@prp-positivity-well-defined), so a - b or b - a is positive. (d) True, margin first. Fix \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N with a_n \ge \delta for every n \ge N, and name the margin \delta/2 \in 
Q_{>0} for b. Only then the index: @cor-rationals-archimedean-epsilon gives K \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/m < \delta/2 for every integer m \ge K. For n \ge \max\{N, K\}, n + 1 > K, so b_n \ge a_n -  rac{1}{n + 1} > \delta -  rac{\delta}{2} =  rac{\delta}{2} . So b is positive, with margin \delta/2 and threshold \max\{N, K\}. (e) False. Let a = b = (1)_n, both positive. Then a - b = b - a = (0)_n, which is not positive: no \delta \in 
Q_{>0} has 0 \ge \delta. C. Going deeper [C1, used later] 1. Show that the rule [a] \mapsto [(\abs{a_n})_n] is a well-defined function 
R 	o 
R. Here is the beginning of a proof. Name the move, then complete it. “Let a, a' \in \sC with a \sim a'. The sequences (\abs{a_n}) and (\abs{a'_n}) are in \sC: by the reverse triangle inequality in 
Q (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f)),  igl| \abs{a_m} - \abs{a_n}  igr| \le \abs{a_m - a_n}, so each has the thresholds of the original. …” 2. Prove that this function is x \mapsto \abs{x}: \abs{[a]} = [(\abs{a_n})_n] for every a \in \sC. (a) The move is representatives, then independence: the rule is defined on a representative, so we must show that replacing a by an equivalent a' gives the same output class. Then each class has exactly one output, and the rule is a function (@fd2:def-function). Completion. Let e_n \coloneqq \abs{a_n} - \abs{a'_n}. By the reverse triangle inequality in 
Q (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f)), 0 \le \abs{e_n} \le \abs{a_n - a'_n} \quad 	ext{for every } n \in 
N . The sequence (a_n - a'_n) is null, since a \sim a' (@def-cauchy-equivalent); so is (\abs{a_n - a'_n}), because  igl| \abs{a_n - a'_n} - 0  igr| = \abs{a_n - a'_n - 0} and the two sequences pass the same tests of @def-null-sequence-ordered-field. The squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) in 
Q, with lower sequence (0)_n and upper sequence (\abs{a_n - a'_n}), shows that (\abs{e_n}) is null. Then (e_n) is null, for the same reason as before: \abs{e_n - 0} =  igl| \abs{e_n} - 0  igr|. So (\abs{a_n}) \sim (\abs{a'_n}), and [(\abs{a_n})_n] = [(\abs{a'_n})_n] (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)). So the output depends only on the class [a], and the rule defines a function 
R 	o 
R. (b) Equality. We use three facts. A class [b] with b eventually equal to b' equals [b'] (@exm-finite-change-equivalent). A null sequence represents 0_{
R} (proof of @thm-reals-positive-cone (i)). And, in the ordered field 
R, \abs{x} = x for x > 0_{
R}, \abs{x} = -x for x < 0_{
R}, and \abs{0_{
R}} = 0_{
R} (@def-absolute-value-ordered-field). Case 1: a is null. Then [a] = 0_{
R}, so \abs{[a]} = 0_{
R}. The sequence (\abs{a_n}) is null too, since  igl| \abs{a_n} - 0  igr| = \abs{a_n} = \abs{a_n - 0} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a) and @def-absolute-value-ordered-field), so the two sequences pass the same tests of @def-null-sequence-ordered-field. Hence [(\abs{a_n})_n] = 0_{
R} = \abs{[a]}. Case 2: a is not null. By @thm-cauchy-not-null-sign with F = 
Q, fix c \in 
Q_{>0} and N \in 
N with a_n \ge c for every n \ge N, or with a_n \le -c for every n \ge N. If a_n \ge c for n \ge N, then a is positive, so [a] \in P and [a] > 0_{
R}, whence \abs{[a]} = [a]. For n \ge N, a_n > 0, so \abs{a_n} = a_n. The sequences (\abs{a_n}) and a agree from N on, so [(\abs{a_n})_n] = [a] = \abs{[a]}. If a_n \le -c for n \ge N, then -a is positive, so -[a] = [-a] \in P and [a] < 0_{
R}, whence \abs{[a]} = -[a] = [-a]. For n \ge N, a_n < 0, so \abs{a_n} = -a_n. The sequences (\abs{a_n}) and -a agree from N on, so [(\abs{a_n})_n] = [-a] = \abs{[a]}. Part (b) does not say that \abs{a_n} = a_n or -a_n for all n; a representative of a positive number may have negative terms early on, as the late-positivity example shows. It says that the class of (\abs{a_n}) is the right one, and classes do not see early terms. Marking scheme. Part (a), 10 points. - 2: names the move (representatives, then independence) and states the goal (\abs{a_n}) \sim (\abs{a'_n}). - 3: proves  igl| \abs{a_n} - \abs{a'_n}  igr| \le \abs{a_n - a'_n} for every n, citing the reverse triangle inequality in 
Q. - 3: from a \sim a' and the inequality of the previous step, shows that (\abs{a_n} - \abs{a'_n})_n is null. - 2: concludes [(\abs{a_n})_n] = [(\abs{a'_n})_n], so each class has one output and the rule is a function 
R 	o 
R. A direct \varepsilon–N proof of the third step, with no squeeze, earns its 3 points: given \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, take N for the null sequence (a_n - a'_n); then  igl| \abs{a_n} - \abs{a'_n}  igr| \le \abs{a_n - a'_n} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using \abs{x} on 
R, or citing part (b); proving only that the two output sequences are Cauchy, without proving them equivalent. Part (b) is not marked. [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument for @prp-positivity-well-defined. “Let a be positive and a' \sim a. Fix \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N with a_n \ge \delta for every n \ge N. Since a' - a is null, there is N' with \abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta for every n \ge N'. So, for n \ge \max\{N, N'\}, a'_n > a_n - \delta \ge 0. Hence a'_n > 0 for all large n. Therefore a' is positive.” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, give a counterexample to that step, and repair the argument. [Hint 1] Write out in symbols what “a' is positive” requires, and compare it with what the argument has when it reaches the last line. [Hint 2] “Positive” asks for one margin \delta' \in 
Q_{>0}, chosen before n, with a'_n \ge \delta' for all large n. Find the line where the argument should produce such a \delta', and ask what it produces instead. The conclusion is true: it is @prp-positivity-well-defined. The middle lines are correct. With the tolerance \delta and the strict inequality \abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta, we get a'_n > a_n - \delta \ge \delta - \delta = 0 for every n \ge \max\{N, N'\}. So the line “a'_n > 0 for all large n” is proved. The failing line is the last: “Therefore a' is positive.” What has been proved is \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \ge N \ \ a'_n > 0 , while “positive” (@def-positive-cauchy-sequence) is \exists \delta \in 
Q_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \ge N \ \ a'_n \ge \delta . To pass from the first to the second, one would take the margin \delta \coloneqq a'_n, which depends on n, and then claim one margin for all n. That swaps a “for every n, there is a margin” for a “there is a margin for every n”. It is the analogue, for a margin depending on n, of entry (N2) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, where a threshold depending on \varepsilon is treated as uniform. Counterexample to the step. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) has a'_n > 0 for all n, so it satisfies the premise of the last line, and it is not positive (the non-example after @def-positive-cauchy-sequence). So “eventually > 0” does not imply “positive”. The argument reached a true conclusion through a step that is not valid. Repair. Use the tolerance \delta/2 \in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)) instead of \delta. Since a' - a is null, choose N'' with \abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta/2 for every n \ge N''. For n \ge \max\{N, N''\}, a'_n > a_n -  rac{\delta}{2} \ge \delta -  rac{\delta}{2} =  rac{\delta}{2} . So a'_n \ge \delta/2 for every n \ge \max\{N, N''\}: one margin, \delta/2, fixed before n, and a' is positive. This is the proof of @prp-positivity-well-defined. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the conclusion is true, citing @prp-positivity-well-defined. - 3: identifies the last line as the failing one and names the quantifier swap (a margin depending on n treated as one margin for all n). - 2: a counterexample to the step: a sequence whose terms are eventually > 0 and which is not positive, such as (1/(n + 1)). - 3: a repair that produces one margin in 
Q_{>0} fixed before n (for instance the tolerance \delta/2 above; any tolerance strictly between 0 and \delta works equally well). Fatal errors (0 for the step): blaming one of the valid middle lines; a repair whose margin still depends on n.

title: 5.4 The Rationals Inside the Reals
content:
The Rationals Inside the Reals Section 5.3 made 
R an ordered field. We built it to enlarge 
Q, but 
Q is not yet inside it: a rational is a class of pairs of integers, a real number a class of sequences. This section places a copy of 
Q in 
R, preserved by the operations and the order; proves that 
R is Archimedean, so that Chapter 4’s theorems about Archimedean fields apply to it, density first; and meets the number that Chapter 4 promised, a positive real whose square is 2. Notation is as in Section 5.3: \sC is the set of Cauchy sequences of rationals, [a] is the class of a \in \sC, (q)_n is the constant sequence with value q, P = 
R_{>0} is the set of positive reals, and x < y means y - x \in P (@def-reals-order). By @thm-reals-ordered-field, the results of Chapters 2 and 4 for an arbitrary ordered field apply with F = 
R; we say “in 
R” where the context does not make the field clear. A copy of the rationals Section 5.2 already represented each rational q by the class of its constant sequence, as Chapter 4 said it would. We make that a map. [The Rationals in the Reals] For q \in 
Q, let \kappa(q) \coloneqq [(q)_n] \in 
R , the class of the constant sequence with value q. This defines a function \kappa \colon 
Q 	o 
R. The right side is in 
R because constant sequences are Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and \kappa is a function because each q determines one constant sequence and that sequence one class. In this notation 0_{
R} = \kappa(0) and 1_{
R} = \kappa(1) (@def-reals-operations). The letter \kappa is new on purpose: Chapter 2 used \iota and j for 
N 	o 
Z 	o 
Q, and Chapter 4 wrote \iota_F for the copy of 
Q in an ordered field F. Part (d) of the next theorem shows that \kappa is \iota_{
R}. The theorem says that \kappa carries everything we know how to do with rationals into 
R without change: sums, products, negatives, reciprocals, the order and the absolute value. [The Rationals Embed in the Reals] For all q, s \in 
Q: 1. \kappa(q + s) = \kappa(q) + \kappa(s), \kappa(qs) = \kappa(q) \kappa(s), \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} and \kappa(1) = 1_{
R}; 2. q < s if and only if \kappa(q) < \kappa(s); hence \kappa is injective; 3. \kappa(-q) = -\kappa(q), \kappa(\abs{q}) = \abs{\kappa(q)}, and, if q 
e 0, \kappa(q) 
e 0_{
R} and \kappa(1/q) = \kappa(q)^{-1}; 4. \kappa is the map \iota_{
R} of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field for the ordered field F = 
R; in particular \kappa(n) = n \cdot 1_{
R} for every n \in 
N (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field). Constant sequences add, multiply and negate termwise into constant sequences, so (a) and the first identity of (c) are the definitions of the operations. For (b), the difference of two constant sequences is constant, and a constant s - q > 0 is its own margin. The rest is algebra in a field: the absolute value by cases, reciprocals by uniqueness of inverses, and (d) by the uniqueness clause of Chapter 4’s embedding theorem. (a) By @def-reals-operations, \kappa(q) + \kappa(s) = [(q)_n + (s)_n] = [(q + s)_n] = \kappa(q + s), since the termwise sum of two constant sequences is the constant sequence of the sum. The product is the same with \cdot in place of +. The last two identities are the definitions of 0_{
R} and 1_{
R}. (c), first identity. By @def-reals-operations, -\kappa(q) = [-(q)_n] = [(-q)_n] = \kappa(-q). (b) (\Rightarrow) Let q < s. By (a) and the first identity of (c), \kappa(s) - \kappa(q) = \kappa(s) + \kappa(-q) = \kappa(s - q) = [(s - q)_n]. The constant s - q lies in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so the constant sequence (s - q)_n is positive, with margin \delta = s - q and threshold N = 0 (@def-positive-cauchy-sequence). Hence \kappa(s) - \kappa(q) \in P, that is, \kappa(q) < \kappa(s). (\Leftarrow) Let \kappa(q) < \kappa(s). By trichotomy in 
Q, q < s, q = s or s < q. If q = s, then \kappa(q) = \kappa(s); if s < q, then \kappa(s) < \kappa(q) by (\Rightarrow). Either contradicts \kappa(q) < \kappa(s) by (O1) in 
R (@thm-reals-ordered-field). So q < s. Injectivity: if q 
e s, then q < s or s < q, so \kappa(q) < \kappa(s) or \kappa(s) < \kappa(q), and in either case \kappa(q) 
e \kappa(s) by (O1). (c), the rest. If q > 0, then \kappa(q) > \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} by (b), so \abs{\kappa(q)} = \kappa(q) = \kappa(\abs{q}) (@def-absolute-value-ordered-field, in 
R and in 
Q). If q = 0, both sides are 0_{
R}. If q < 0, then \kappa(q) < 0_{
R} by (b), so \abs{\kappa(q)} = -\kappa(q) = \kappa(-q) = \kappa(\abs{q}). Now let q 
e 0. Then \kappa(q) 
e \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} by injectivity, and by (a), \kappa(q) \, \kappa(1/q) = \kappa(q \cdot (1/q)) = \kappa(1) = 1_{
R} . In the field 
R (@thm-reals-field), the inverse of \kappa(q) is the only element with this property (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)), so \kappa(1/q) = \kappa(q)^{-1}. (d) By @thm-reals-ordered-field, 
R is an ordered field, so @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field gives exactly one map \iota_{
R} \colon 
Q 	o 
R with \iota_{
R}(1) = 1_{
R} that preserves sums and products. By (a), \kappa is such a map, so \kappa = \iota_{
R}. The same theorem states that \iota_{
R}(n) = n \cdot 1_{
R} for every n \in 
N. By (d), part (b) and the injectivity of \kappa also follow from @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field with F = 
R; the direct proof of (b) shows a constant sequence as its own margin. Two more identities follow from (a) and (c):  egin{aligned} \kappa(q - s) &= \kappa(q) + \kappa(-s) = \kappa(q) - \kappa(s) , \ \kappa(q/s) &= \kappa(q) \, \kappa(1/s) = \kappa(q)/\kappa(s) \quad 	ext{for } s 
e 0 . \end{aligned} So any computation with rationals, done in 
Q and then moved into 
R by \kappa, gives the same answer as the computation done in 
R on the images. Part (b) adds that comparisons agree too. Archimedes in the reals Chapter 4 showed that an ordered field need not be Archimedean: in 
Q(t) the element t is larger than every n \cdot 1 (@exm-rational-function-field). So the Archimedean property of 
R has to be proved. It comes from 
Q, through the fact that a Cauchy sequence is bounded. [The Reals Are Archimedean] 
R is an Archimedean ordered field (@def-archimedean-ordered-field): for every x \in 
R there is n \in 
N with x < n \cdot 1_{
R}. A representative of x is a Cauchy sequence of rationals, so all its terms lie below one rational bound M. Archimedes in 
Q puts a natural number above M; one more unit gives a fixed margin above every term, and a fixed margin is what positivity asks for (@exm-method-margin-before-index). Let x \in 
R, and write x = [a] with a \in \sC. By @prp-cauchy-bounded-ordered-field with F = 
Q, there is M \in 
Q_{>0} with \abs{a_k} \le M for every k \in 
N. By @thm-rationals-archimedean, there is n \in 
N with M < n. For every k, (n + 1) - a_k \ge (n + 1) - M = (n - M) + 1 > 1 , since a_k \le \abs{a_k} \le M (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c)), so -M \le -a_k and then (n + 1) - a_k \ge (n + 1) - M (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), (b)), and n - M > 0. So the sequence ((n + 1) - a_k)_k is positive, with margin 1 and threshold 0. It represents \kappa(n + 1) - x, by @def-reals-operations. Hence x < \kappa(n + 1), and \kappa(n + 1) = (n + 1) \cdot 1_{
R} by @thm-rational-embedding (d). Since n + 1 \in 
N, this proves the theorem. Every result of Chapter 4 about Archimedean ordered fields now applies with F = 
R. Two of them are used at once. The integer part in 
R. By @prp-integer-part-ordered-field with F = 
R, and \iota_{
R} = \kappa (@thm-rational-embedding (d)), for every x \in 
R there is exactly one m \in 
Z with \kappa(m) \le x < \kappa(m + 1) . We call m the integer part of x. For a rational q, the integer part of \kappa(q) is the integer part  loor{q} of @prp-rational-integer-part, because \kappa preserves and reflects \le (@thm-rational-embedding (b)). The word “exactly” matters: an integer part is given by a rule, so a sequence of integer parts can be defined without choosing anything (Exercise B2). Between two reals there is a rational Chapter 4 proved that the rationals are dense in every Archimedean ordered field (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field), and 
R is one. [The Rationals Are Dense in the Reals] Let x, y \in 
R with x < y. Then there is q \in 
Q with x < \kappa(q) < y. By @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, 
R is an Archimedean ordered field, so @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field with F = 
R gives q \in 
Q with x < \iota_{
R}(q) < y; and \iota_{
R} = \kappa by @thm-rational-embedding (d). Density can also be seen directly from the representatives, with no appeal to Archimedes: write x = [a], y = [b], go far out, and take the midpoint of two late terms. Exercise C3 carries this out; it shows that in this construction the rationals are dense because each real number is made of rationals. Identification. From here on we write q for \kappa(q) when q \in 
Q, and 
Q \subseteq 
R. This is a convention about notation, of the kind Chapter 2 adopted twice, writing n for \iota(n) and m for j(m) (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals). It is safe because of @thm-rational-embedding: \kappa is injective and preserves sums, products, negatives, reciprocals, the order and the absolute value, so a statement about rationals means the same whether it is read in 
Q or, through \kappa, in 
R. It is not a set inclusion: the rational q is a class of pairs of integers, and \kappa(q) is a class of sequences of rationals, a different set. In this notation \kappa(1/n) is written 1/n, and @prp-archimedean-reciprocal in 
R says that for every \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0} some 1/n, n \in 
Z_{>0}, lies below \varepsilon. The square root of two Chapter 4 ended with the Newton sequence (x_n) of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, Cauchy in 
Q and with no limit in 
Q (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). Its class is the number it was aiming at. [The Class of the Newton Sequence] Let (x_n) be the Newton sequence of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, and let r \coloneqq [(x_n)] \in 
R. Show that r > 0, that r^2 = 2, that r 
e q for every q \in 
Q, and that r = [(d_k)], where (d_k) is the sequence of decimal truncations of @exm-truncations-equivalent. The sequence (x_n) is in \sC by @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, so r \in 
R. We use the facts x_n > 1 for every n \in 
N and e_n \le 1/(4n) for every n \ge 1, where e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2, stated in @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit, and e_n > 0 for every n \in 
N, proved in @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2. The first values are e_0 = 2 , \quad e_1 =  rac{1}{4} , \quad e_2 =  rac{1}{144} , \quad e_3 =  rac{1}{166464} , \quad e_4 =  rac{1}{221682772224} . r > 0. Since x_n > 1 for every n, the sequence (x_n) is positive, with margin 1 and threshold 0. So r \in P, that is, r > 0. By @lem-termwise-order, also r \ge 1. r^2 = 2. By @def-reals-operations, r^2 = r \cdot r = [(x_n^2)], and 2 = [(2)_n]. Termwise, (x_n^2) - (2)_n = (e_n). For n \ge 1, 0 < e_n \le  rac{1}{4n} \le  rac{1}{n + 1} , where the last step is @prp-ordered-field-halves (c), since 4n - (n + 1) = 3n - 1 > 0. The sequence (1/(n + 1)) is defined for every n \in 
N and null in 
Q (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)); so is (0)_n. The squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) in 
Q, with N_0 = 1, shows that (e_n) is null. (At n = 0 the bound 1/(4n) is undefined and e_0 = 2; the threshold N_0 = 1 skips it.) Hence (x_n^2) \sim (2)_n and r^2 = 2. r is not rational. Suppose r = \kappa(q) for some q \in 
Q. Then \kappa(q^2) = \kappa(q)^2 = r^2 = \kappa(2) by @thm-rational-embedding (a), so q^2 = 2 by injectivity. This contradicts @thm-no-rational-square-two. So r 
otin \kappa(
Q). r = [(d_k)]. By @exm-truncations-equivalent, (d_k) \sim (x_k), so the classes are equal. So 
R contains a positive element whose square is 2, and 
Q contains none. It is the number Chapter 4 promised, and the decimal truncations name the same number as the Newton sequence. r is not “the limit of (x_n) in 
Q”: there is no such limit (@thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit), and nothing in this section changes that. r is a new element, a class of sequences. Whether the x_n converge to it is a question about 
R, with tolerances in 
R_{>0}; Exercise B3 answers it. Find a rational number strictly between [(d_k)] and [(d_k + 1/(k + 1))]. There is none, and @thm-constructed-rationals-dense does not apply. The two sequences differ by (1/(k + 1)), which is null, so they are equivalent and the classes are equal. The hypothesis x < y fails, and no number lies strictly between a number and itself. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Show that \kappa(q^k) = \kappa(q)^k for every q \in 
Q and k \in 
N, the powers being those of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field in 
Q and in 
R. 2. Let r be as in @exm-sqrt2-class. Find the integer parts of r and of 10r, and justify each from the terms d_k: use d_1 = 7/5, d_2 = 141/100, and the bounds (T1) and (T2) stated before @exm-truncations-equivalent. 3. True or false: if a \in \sC, q \in 
Q and a_n < q for every n, then [a] < q. Give a reason or a counterexample. 4. Is \kappa \colon 
Q 	o 
R surjective? (a) By induction on k (@fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N through @cor-omega-identification (b)), applied to the property “\kappa(q^k) = \kappa(q)^k”. Base: \kappa(q^0) = \kappa(1) = 1_{
R} = \kappa(q)^0, by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) in 
Q and in 
R and @thm-rational-embedding (a). Step: if \kappa(q^k) = \kappa(q)^k, then \kappa(q^{k+1}) = \kappa(q^k q) = \kappa(q^k) \, \kappa(q) = \kappa(q)^k \, \kappa(q) = \kappa(q)^{k+1} , by the defining equation of powers, @thm-rational-embedding (a), and the induction hypothesis. In particular \kappa(q^2) = \kappa(q)^2, the step used in @exm-sqrt2-class. (b) By (T1) and (T2), stated before @exm-truncations-equivalent, (d_k) is non-decreasing, and d_j < d_k + 1/10^k whenever j \ge k. With k = 2: for every j \ge 2,  rac{7}{5} = d_1 \le d_j < d_2 +  rac{1}{100} =  rac{142}{100} =  rac{71}{50} . By @lem-termwise-order with N_0 = 2, and r = [(d_k)] (@exm-sqrt2-class), 7/5 \le r \le 71/50. Since 1 \le 7/5 and 71/50 < 2, 1 \le r < 2, so the integer part of r is 1. Multiplying by 10 > 0 in 
R (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed), 14 \le 10r \le 71/5 < 15, so the integer part of 10r is 14. (c) False. Take a_n \coloneqq q - 1/(n + 1). Here a \in \sC: (q)_n is constant and (1/(n + 1)) is null (@exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (b)), so both are Cauchy (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (a)), and so is their difference (@thm-cauchy-algebra-ordered-field (b)). Then a_n < q for every n, and a - (q)_n = (-1/(n + 1)) is null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b)), so [a] = \kappa(q), and [a] < \kappa(q) fails. The correct conclusion is [a] \le q (@lem-termwise-order); see the warning after it. (d) No. By @exm-sqrt2-class, r \in 
R is not \kappa(q) for any q \in 
Q. B. Practice [B1, used later: Rational tolerances suffice] Prove: 1. For every \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0} there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with \kappa(1/n) < \varepsilon for every n \in 
N with n \ge N. 2. Let (x_k)_{k \in 
N} be a sequence in 
R and x \in 
R. Then x_k 	o x in 
R (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field with F = 
R) if and only if, for every n \in 
Z_{>0}, there is K \in 
N with \abs{x_k - x} < \kappa(1/n) for every k \ge K. Likewise, (x_k) is Cauchy in 
R (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field with F = 
R) if and only if, for every n \in 
Z_{>0}, there is K \in 
N with \abs{x_j - x_k} < \kappa(1/n) for all j, k \ge K. (a) Let \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0}. Since 
R is Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), @prp-archimedean-reciprocal in 
R gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/(n \cdot 1_{
R}) < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. For such n, n 
e 0, n \cdot 1_{
R} = \kappa(n) (@thm-rational-embedding (d)) and 1/\kappa(n) = \kappa(1/n) (@thm-rational-embedding (c)). So \kappa(1/n) < \varepsilon. (b) (\Rightarrow) For n \in 
Z_{>0}, 1/n > 0 in 
Q (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), so \kappa(1/n) > \kappa(0) = 0_{
R} (@thm-rational-embedding (b)): it is one of the tolerances of the definition, which then supplies K. (\Leftarrow) Let \varepsilon \in 
R_{>0}. By (a), there is N \in 
Z_{>0} with \kappa(1/N) < \varepsilon. The hypothesis with n \coloneqq N gives K with \abs{x_k - x} < \kappa(1/N) for every k \ge K, and then \abs{x_k - x} < \varepsilon by (O2). So K serves for \varepsilon. The Cauchy version is the same argument with \abs{x_j - x_k} for j, k \ge K in place of \abs{x_k - x}. In practice: to prove a limit in 
R, fix n \in 
Z_{>0} and find a threshold for the rational tolerance 1/n. The threshold may depend on n, and on nothing chosen later. [B2, used later] Let x \in 
R. For k \in 
N, let m_k be the integer part of (k + 1)x, and q_k \coloneqq m_k/(k + 1) \in 
Q. Prove that q_k \le x < q_k + 1/(k + 1) for every k, and that q_k 	o x in 
R. Fix k \in 
N. By the definition of the integer part (after @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), m_k \le (k + 1)x < m_k + 1. Since k + 1 > 0, also 1/(k + 1) > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)), and multiplying by it in 
R preserves both inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed on the left): q_k =  rac{m_k}{k + 1} \le x <  rac{m_k + 1}{k + 1} = q_k +  rac{1}{k + 1} . So 0 \le x - q_k < 1/(k + 1) for every k. In 
R, the sequence (1/(k + 1)), that is (1/((k + 1) \cdot 1_{
R})) by @thm-rational-embedding (c), (d), is null, by @prp-reciprocals-null-iff-archimedean and @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean. The squeeze @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (c) in 
R, with lower sequence (0), gives that (x - q_k) is null. Then (q_k - x) is null (@thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (b)), so q_k 	o x (@prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field). Each q_k is given by a rule: the integer part of (k + 1)x is the only integer with the defining property, so nothing is chosen. [B3, used later: Put the proof in order] Let a \in \sC. We prove that \kappa(a_k) 	o [a] in 
R: a Cauchy sequence of rationals converges in 
R to its own class. The lines below, written with the identification (q for \kappa(q)), contain the proof, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Put the correct lines in order, and say what is wrong with each of the other two. 1. so \abs{[a] - a_k} = [(\abs{a_m - a_k})_m], by @exr-ordering-the-reals-c1 (b); 2. since a \in \sC, fix N with \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) for all m, k \ge N; 3. its terms are < 1/(2n) for m \ge N, so \abs{[a] - a_k} < 1/(2n); 4. so \abs{[a] - a_k} \le 1/(2n) < 1/n, and K = N serves; 5. let k \ge N; 6. let n \in 
Z_{>0}; by @exr-rationals-inside-the-reals-b1 (b), it suffices to find K with \abs{[a] - a_k} < 1/n for every k \ge K, since \abs{a_k - [a]} = \abs{[a] - a_k} (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)); 7. [a] - a_k is represented by (a_m - a_k)_m; 8. for each k, fix N_k with \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) for every m \ge N_k; 9. its terms are \le 1/(2n) for m \ge N, so \abs{[a] - a_k} \le 1/(2n), by @lem-termwise-order. Order: (vi), (ii), (v), (vii), (i), (ix), (iv). No other order is admissible: line (ii) introduces N, which line (v) needs; line (v) fixes the k that lines (vii), (i) and (ix) are about; line (i) rewrites the class that line (vii) names; line (ix) bounds that class; and line (iv) concludes from line (ix), so it comes last. Line (iii) uses the strict version of @lem-termwise-order, which is false: termwise < passes to classes only as \le (@exm-strict-termwise-order-fails). Concretely, for a_m = 1/2 - 1/(m+2), n = 1 and k = 0, every term \abs{a_m - a_0} is < 1/2, yet \abs{[a] - a_0} = 1/2. That is why the proof aims at 1/(2n) and then uses 1/(2n) < 1/n. Line (viii) claims a threshold N_k for every k, and the Cauchy property does not supply one for an early k: a_k can be far from all later terms. For a = (5, 0, 0, \dots) \in \sC, n = 1 and k = 0, \abs{a_m - a_0} = 5 for every m \ge 1, so no N_0 exists. The Cauchy property gives \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/(2n) only when both m and k are at least one N, which is why line (v) takes k \ge N. (If line (viii) did hold for every k, the remaining lines would give the bound for every k, so it is the claim that is unjustified, not the dependence on k.) Why 1/(2n) and not 1/n directly? The Cauchy property gives \abs{a_m - a_k} < 1/n, but @lem-termwise-order passes only the non-strict inequality to classes, so we would reach \abs{[a] - \kappa(a_k)} \le \kappa(1/n), one symbol short of the definition. Halving the tolerance first leaves room for the strict inequality. So every real number is a limit of rationals, namely of the terms of any of its representatives. Equivalent sequences have the same class, so their terms converge in 
R to the same number; by uniqueness of limits (@thm-limit-unique-ordered-field in 
R), that number is the only limit they have. A real number is what all its representatives converge to. C. Going deeper [C1] 1. Let x \in 
R with \abs{x} \le 1/n for every n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that x = 0. 2. Where does your proof use that 
R is Archimedean? Show that the statement of (a) fails in the ordered field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field. (a) Suppose that \abs{x} > 0. Since 
R is Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), @prp-archimedean-reciprocal in 
R with \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{x} gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/N < \abs{x}. The hypothesis with n = N gives \abs{x} \le 1/N. These contradict (O1). So \abs{x} > 0 is false. Since \abs{x} \ge 0 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a)), trichotomy leaves \abs{x} = 0, and then x = 0 by @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a). (b) @prp-archimedean-reciprocal applies to 
R because of @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean. In 
Q(t), @exm-rational-function-field shows 0 < 1/t < 1/(n \cdot 1) for every n \ge 1. So x \coloneqq 1/t satisfies \abs{x} = x \le 1/(n \cdot 1) for every n \ge 1, and x 
e 0. The statement of (a) is a form of the Archimedean property, and it fails without it. [C2] Let r be as in @exm-sqrt2-class. Prove that the set \{ x \in 
R : x 
otin \kappa(
Q) \} of irrational real numbers is dense in 
R: for all x, y \in 
R with x < y there is an irrational z with x < z < y. [Hint 1] Use @thm-constructed-rationals-dense, and the irrational number r. [Hint 2] Let q \in 
Q with x < q < y (@thm-constructed-rationals-dense). How small must r/k be for q + r/k to stay below y? Let x < y. By @thm-constructed-rationals-dense, fix q \in 
Q with x < q < y. Then y - q > 0, and r > 0 (@exm-sqrt2-class), so \varepsilon \coloneqq (y - q)/r \in 
R_{>0} (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)). By @prp-archimedean-reciprocal in 
R (Archimedean by @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), there is k \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/k < \varepsilon. Multiplying by r > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), r/k < y - q. Let z \coloneqq q + r/k. Since r/k > 0, x < q < z < q + (y - q) = y . If z were rational, z = p with p \in 
Q, then r = k(p - q) would be rational, since \kappa preserves differences and products (the identities after @thm-rational-embedding, and its part (a)); this contradicts @exm-sqrt2-class. So z is irrational, and lies strictly between x and y. The same argument works with r replaced by any positive irrational number. Between any two reals there are therefore both rationals and irrationals. [C3: Density from the representatives] 1. Let x = [a] and y = [b] with a, b \in \sC and x < y. Prove, without @thm-constructed-reals-archimedean or @thm-rationals-archimedean, that there is q \in 
Q with x < \kappa(q) < y. 2. Which hypothesis does your proof use that the proof of @thm-constructed-rationals-dense in the text does not, and conversely? [Hint 1] Name the margin first: b - a is positive. Then take the midpoint of a_N and b_N for one large N. [Hint 2] Fix \delta and N_1 with b_n - a_n \ge \delta for n \ge N_1, and thresholds N_2, N_3 for a and b at the tolerance \delta/4. (a) Write x = [a] and y = [b] with a, b \in \sC. By @def-reals-order, y - x = [b - a] \in P, so b - a is positive (@prp-positivity-well-defined). Fix \delta \in 
Q_{>0} and N_1 \in 
N with b_n - a_n \ge \delta \quad 	ext{for every } n \ge N_1 . Then \delta/4 = (\delta/2)/2 \in 
Q_{>0} (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b), twice). Since a and b are Cauchy in 
Q, fix N_2 with \abs{a_m - a_n} < \delta/4 for all m, n \ge N_2, and N_3 with \abs{b_m - b_n} < \delta/4 for all m, n \ge N_3. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2, N_3\} , \qquad q \coloneqq  rac{a_N + b_N}{2} \in 
Q . Let n \ge N. Expanding the right sides shows  egin{aligned} q - a_n &= (a_N - a_n) +  rac{b_N - a_N}{2} , \ b_n - q &= (b_n - b_N) +  rac{b_N - a_N}{2} . \end{aligned} Since n, N \ge N_2, a_N - a_n > -\delta/4 (@prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)); since N \ge N_1, b_N - a_N \ge \delta, and multiplying by 1/2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b) with \varepsilon = 1) gives (b_N - a_N)/2 \ge \delta/2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed). Adding (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), q - a_n > - rac{\delta}{4} +  rac{\delta}{2} =  rac{\delta}{4} . In the same way, since n, N \ge N_3, b_n - b_N > -\delta/4, and b_n - q > \delta/4. So the sequences (q - a_n)_n and (b_n - q)_n are positive, each with margin \delta/4 and threshold N. By @def-reals-operations they represent \kappa(q) - x and y - \kappa(q). Hence x < \kappa(q) and \kappa(q) < y. The rational q depends on the representatives a, b and on the constants fixed in the proof; nothing makes it the “best” rational, and a different run of the proof may give a different q. (b) The proof in the text uses that 
R is Archimedean, through @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field, and knows nothing of representatives. Your proof in (a) uses the Cauchy property of a and b and positivity of b - a, and no Archimedean property of 
Q or 
R. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the margin \delta from positivity of b - a, named before any index. - 3: Cauchy thresholds at a tolerance small enough for the estimates (relative to \delta), and one N beyond every threshold used. - 3: both estimates q - a_n > \delta/4 and b_n - q > \delta/4 for every n \ge N. - 2: the estimates read as positivity of two representatives, of \kappa(q) - x and y - \kappa(q). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a midpoint of a_n and b_n with n varying; q compared only with a_N and b_N, not with every later term.

title: 5.5 Least Upper Bounds
content:
Least Upper Bounds Section 5.4 made 
R an Archimedean ordered field with 
Q dense in it. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 starts from a property of sets: every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound. In 
Q it fails (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). This section names the property for an arbitrary ordered field and proves that the constructed 
R has it. The proof halves intervals with rational ends. Their right ends form a Cauchy sequence of rationals, which is a real number by definition, and that number is the least upper bound. The sequence form of completeness, that every Cauchy sequence of reals converges, is proved from this one in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 4. Throughout, F is an ordered field (@def-ordered-ring-and-field). Its order \le is a total order (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)), so the words “upper bound”, “bounded above” and “supremum” of Sets and Functions, Section 5.3 apply to subsets of F (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum). When F = 
R, we keep the identification of Section 5.4, writing q for \kappa(q). Complete ordered fields Section 3.3 found a gap in 
Q without any sequence: the set A = \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} is non-empty and bounded above in 
Q, and among its rational upper bounds there is no least one (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). The upper bounds crowd down toward a place where 
Q has no element. A field without such gaps is one in which every set that could have a least upper bound does have one. Every non-empty set that is bounded above has a least upper bound. [Complete Ordered Field] An ordered field F is complete if every non-empty subset A \subseteq F that is bounded above in (F, \le) (@fd2:def-order-bounds) has a supremum in F (@fd2:def-order-supremum). In symbols, writing \mathrm{ub}(u) for  orall a \in A \ \ a \le u,  egin{aligned} & orall A \subseteq F \ \  igl( (A 
e \emptyset \wedge \exists u \in F \ \mathrm{ub}(u)) \Rightarrow \ &\qquad \exists s \in F \  igl( \mathrm{ub}(s) \wedge  orall u \in F \ (\mathrm{ub}(u) \Rightarrow s \le u)  igr)  igr) . \end{aligned} An ordered field in which every Cauchy sequence (@def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field) converges is called Cauchy-complete. In words: the hypothesis asks for a set with at least one element and at least one upper bound in F; the conclusion asks for an element s of F that is an upper bound, clause (S1), and lies below every upper bound, clause (S2). The supremum need not belong to A. Well-definedness. A set has at most one supremum, since a supremum is a least element of the set of upper bounds (Sets and Functions, Section 5.3, the remark after @fd2:def-order-supremum, by @fd2:prp-greatest-unique). So “the supremum of A”, written \sup A, names one element when it exists. Examples. The negative elements. In every ordered field, A \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x < 0 \} has supremum 0. It is non-empty (-1 \in A). The element 0 is an upper bound. If an upper bound b had b < 0, then b < b/2 < 0 (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)), so b/2 \in A lies above b, which is impossible. So every upper bound b satisfies b \ge 0, and \sup A = 0 
otin A. No completeness was needed: some sets have suprema in every ordered field. The rationals. 
Q is not complete: @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 exhibits a non-empty subset bounded above with no supremum in 
Q. The constructed reals. 
R is complete; this is the main theorem of the section. A singleton. \sup \{a\} = a, in every ordered field, since a greatest element is the supremum (the same remark of Sets and Functions, Section 5.3). This degenerate case matters below: a set may be bounded above by its own element. Drop “non-empty”: the empty set is bounded above by every element of F, so its upper bounds are all of F, and F has no least element (x - 1 < x). Drop “bounded above”: F itself has no upper bound (x < x + 1), so no supremum. With either clause removed, no ordered field at all would be complete. Why this definition. It asks about suprema, not maxima: the set of negative elements has no greatest element in any ordered field, since x < x/2 < 0 for x < 0, and asking for maxima would make no field complete. It asks about sets, not sequences, the form Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes as its axiom. “Complete” alone always means this property; the sequence property is “Cauchy-complete”. The supremum of a set is an upper bound not necessarily in the set, and “complete” is not “every non-empty bounded set has a largest element”: the set of negative elements above has supremum 0 and no largest element. A proof that ends “so \sup A \in A” needs a reason, such as A being finite. So 
Q is not complete. The rest of the section proves that 
R is. Powers of two in an ordered field The bisection below halves an interval at each step, so after k steps its length is the first length divided by 2^k. We need 2^k to grow at least as fast as k + 1, here in 
Q; the induction is the one for 10^k in Section 5.1. [A Lower Bound for Powers of Two] Let F be an ordered field, and let (2 \cdot 1_F)^k be the power in F of @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). Then (2 \cdot 1_F)^k \ge (k + 1) \cdot 1_F \qquad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N . In particular (2 \cdot 1_F)^k \ge 1_F > 0. Induction on k. Multiplying by 2 doubles the right side, (k + 1) + (k + 1), and doubling gains at least 1, which is all the step needs. We use @fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N through @cor-omega-identification (b), for P(k): (2 \cdot 1_F)^k \ge (k + 1) \cdot 1_F. Base P(0). (2 \cdot 1_F)^0 = 1_F by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), and (0 + 1) \cdot 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F = 0 \cdot 1_F + 1_F = 1_F by (a) of that definition, since 0 + 1 = 1 (@def-omega-arithmetic (c)). Equality holds. Step. Assume P(k), and let y \coloneqq (k + 1) \cdot 1_F. By @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a) and @def-omega-arithmetic (c), 2 \cdot 1_F = 1 \cdot 1_F + 1_F = 1_F + 1_F, which is positive (@prp-ordered-field-halves (b)). By @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b), P(k), and @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (or equality, if P(k) holds with equality), (2 \cdot 1_F)^{k+1} = (2 \cdot 1_F)^k (2 \cdot 1_F) \ge y (1_F + 1_F) = y + y , the last step by distributivity (F9) and (F7). Since k + 1 \ge 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)), @prp-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) gives y \ge 1_F, so y + y \ge y + 1_F (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). Finally y + 1_F = ((k + 1) + 1) \cdot 1_F by @def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a). Hence (2 \cdot 1_F)^{k+1} \ge ((k + 1) + 1) \cdot 1_F, which is P(k + 1).
