title: The Complete Ordered Field Is Unique
content:
The Complete Ordered Field Is Unique Chapter 5 ended with one complete ordered field, whose elements are classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals. Axiomatic Set Theory builds another, whose elements are sets of rationals, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 builds none: it assumes that a complete ordered field exists and calls it 
R. Are these the same 
R? The axioms of an ordered field alone do not decide it. The field 
Q(t) of rational functions of Chapter 4, ordered by leading coefficients, satisfies all of them and has an element above every natural number; the field 
Q(\sqrt 2) is even Archimedean, and still 3 has no square root in it. This chapter proves that completeness is the property that pins 
R down: any two complete ordered fields are linked by an order-preserving field isomorphism, and by only one. So “the” real numbers are well defined, and no theorem about them depends on how they were built. The tool is one idea. In an Archimedean ordered field an element is determined by the rationals below it, and a map that respects sums, products, 1 and the order must send each element to one with the same rationals below it. In a complete field the supremum of the copies of those rationals is such an element. So from an Archimedean field into a complete one there is exactly one order-preserving field map, and each identity it satisfies is checked by comparing rationals below the two sides, with no arithmetic of suprema. When both fields are complete, maps run both ways, and the word “exactly” makes them inverse to each other without a computation. The same uniqueness leaves a complete ordered field no symmetry: a map of it to itself that respects only sums, products and 1 is the identity, because there the positive elements are the non-zero squares. Without the order, a field like 
Q(\sqrt 2) does have a symmetry that breaks it; that example belongs to Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 2, and this chapter only points to it. The chapter, the last of the volume’s main line, ends by comparing the two ways to begin analysis, assuming the axioms or building a model, and by listing what Analysis on the Real Line takes from this volume. What you need. Chapters 4 and 5 above all, with Chapters 2 and 3; Sets and Functions, Chapters 1, 2, 4 and 5, chiefly Section 5.3; and Logic and Proof, Chapters 2 and 6, with Chapters 5 and 7 for one remark. From Chapter 4 of this book: the rules of an ordered field and the absolute value (@prp-ordered-field-halves, @lem-field-fraction-rules, @def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field); powers and the one copy \iota_F of 
Q in an ordered field, with its uniqueness clause (@def-naturals-in-ordered-field, @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field); the Archimedean property, density of 
Q, and the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) (@def-archimedean-ordered-field, @prp-archimedean-reciprocal, @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field, @exm-rational-function-field); and, in Section 6.3 and its exercises, limits and Cauchy sequences (@def-sequence-limit-ordered-field, @exm-first-sequences-ordered-field, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field, @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field, @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field, @prp-convergent-cauchy-ordered-field, @thm-sqrt2-cauchy-no-rational-limit). From Chapter 5: complete ordered fields (@def-complete-ordered-field); the Cauchy model 
R, its classes and its order (@def-rational-cauchy-sequences, @def-cauchy-equivalent, @def-reals-cauchy-classes, @thm-reals-ordered-field, @lem-termwise-order); the theorems that it is a complete ordered field (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field) and Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean); the map \kappa = \iota_{
R} (@def-rational-embedding, @thm-rational-embedding); and the class of the Newton sequence, a positive real number whose square is 2 (@exm-sqrt2-class). From Chapter 3: 
Q as classes of pairs (@def-rationals-as-classes, @prp-rational-pairs-equivalence), 
Q Archimedean (@thm-rationals-archimedean), reciprocals and the order (@prp-reciprocal-order), no rational square equal to 2 (@thm-no-rational-square-two, @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2), and the countability of 
Q (review exercise R2 of Section 3.3). From Chapter 2: the axioms (F1)–(F9) and (O1)–(O4) (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @def-ordered-ring-and-field) and their rules (@prp-ring-algebra, @prp-ordered-ring-rules). Chapter 1 supplies one analogy (@thm-peano-categoricity) and, in Exercise C3 of Section 6.3, induction and the order arithmetic of 
N (@thm-omega-induction, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic). From Sets and Functions: proving uniqueness, Section 1.4 (@fd2:exm-method-uniqueness); injective and bijective maps, compositions and two-sided inverses, Sections 2.2 and 2.4 (@fd2:def-injective, @fd2:def-bijective, @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @fd2:exm-method-construct-and-verify); countable sets, Section 4.2, for exercises of Section 6.3 (@fd2:thm-countable-characterizations, @fd2:prp-countable-image); equivalence relations and well-definedness, Section 5.2 (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:exm-method-well-definedness); and upper bounds and suprema, Section 5.3 (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum). From Logic and Proof: the contrapositive, Chapter 2 (@fd1:prp-contrapositive); the negation of quantifiers, unbounded and bounded, Chapter 6 (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation); and, for the remark on what an isomorphism carries in Section 6.3, first-order formulas and their invariance under isomorphism, Chapters 5 and 7 (@fd1:def-first-order-formula, @fd1:thm-isomorphism-invariance). Time. About 15 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 25 hours for everything. Roadmap - What Completeness Gives at Once. Order-preserving field maps, which reflect the order and fix the rationals; the theorem that a complete ordered field is Archimedean, by a supremum of the copy of 
N that cannot exist; the rationals below an element, 
Q_F(x), which determine x when F is Archimedean (rationals separate); and square roots in a complete ordered field, built as a supremum and unique. - Building the Map from the Rationals Below. The rationals below a sum, and below a product of positive elements, computed from those below each term; and the main theorem in its one-sided form: from an Archimedean ordered field F into a complete one L there is exactly one order-preserving field map, which sends x to the supremum in L of the copies of the rationals below x. - Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism. Any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism, with the inverse obtained from the uniqueness clause instead of computed; every complete ordered field a copy of the Cauchy model, and a Dedekind cut read as a set of rationals below; the automorphisms of a complete ordered field, of which there is one, the identity, even among the maps that respect only sums, products and 1; what an isomorphism carries (limits, as the worked case) and what it does not (a model whose zero is the empty set); and the two ways to begin analysis, with a table of what Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 assumes and where this series supplies it. The review exercises return to Chapter 5’s real numbers, to well-definedness on 
Q as a set of classes of pairs, and to countability and the density of the elements of a complete ordered field that are not rational. Named moves - Rationals separate (@lem-cof-rationals-separate). To show a = b in an Archimedean ordered field, show that the same rationals lie below each; otherwise a rational would lie strictly between them. It is proved in Section 6.1 and then proves every equation between elements of the complete field in the main theorem of Section 6.2 (Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7); the exit check C1 of Section 6.2 runs it alone. In 
Q(t), where Archimedes fails, t and t + 1 have the same rationals below them (the fold in Section 6.1). - Construct a point as a supremum (@exm-method-point-as-supremum). To produce an element you cannot name, take the supremum of a well-chosen set and refute the two wrong cases of trichotomy, one with an element of the set above the supremum, the other with a smaller upper bound. It builds square roots in Section 6.1 and the map of Section 6.2. Exercise B2 of Section 6.2 (cube roots) leaves the last step to you, and Exercise C3 of Section 6.3 (a bounded increasing sequence converges to the supremum of its terms) the last half. - Uniqueness gives inverses (@fd2:exm-method-uniqueness). If the only order-preserving field map F 	o F is the identity, then two maps F 	o L 	o F compose to the identity without computing anything. It proves in Section 6.3 that the map between two complete ordered fields is bijective, and the same uniqueness clause shows there that a complete ordered field has no order-preserving automorphism except the identity; once square roots recover the order, also no field automorphism. Threads - Rationals below an element. The copy \iota_F of 
Q in an ordered field and density (Chapter 4) are what let Section 6.1 define 
Q_F(x); Section 6.2 turns it into a map, and Section 6.3 into the uniqueness theorem. - Square roots. Chapter 3 shows that 2 has no square root in 
Q, Chapter 5 builds one in 
R (@exm-sqrt2-class), and Section 6.1 proves that every positive element of a complete ordered field has one; Section 6.3 uses them to recover the order from the arithmetic. - Categoricity. Section 1.4 proved that any two Peano systems are isomorphic by exactly one isomorphism; Section 6.3 proves the same for complete ordered fields, with the same shape: existence by a recursion or a supremum, uniqueness by induction or by rationals separate. - Two ways to begin analysis. Section 1.5 says where 
N comes from, Chapter 5 builds 
R on it, and Section 6.3 compares that route with assuming the axioms, as Analysis on the Real Line does. Summary An order-preserving field map between ordered fields fixes the rationals and reflects the order (@def-cof-order-preserving-map, @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals). A complete ordered field is Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), and in an Archimedean ordered field an element is determined by the set of rationals below it (@def-cof-rationals-below, @lem-cof-rationals-separate). Every positive element of a complete ordered field has a square root (@prp-cof-square-roots). From an Archimedean ordered field into a complete one there is exactly one order-preserving field map, which sends x to the supremum of the copies of the rationals below x (@thm-cof-embedding-into-complete). Hence any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic by exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism (@thm-cof-uniqueness), every complete ordered field is a copy of the Cauchy model (@cor-cof-isomorphic-to-cauchy-reals), and a complete ordered field has no order-preserving automorphism but the identity (@cor-cof-order-automorphism-identity), nor any field automorphism (@thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity). What is open: 
R is now one structure, and nothing here says anything about its sequences, series or continuous functions. Analysis on the Real Line starts there, from the axioms this volume has shown to describe exactly one thing. Terms - order-preserving field map: a map \chi \colon F 	o L of ordered fields that respects sums, products and 1 and is strictly increasing (@def-cof-order-preserving-map). - rationals below an element: 
Q_F(x) = \{ q \in 
Q : \iota_F(q) < x \} in an ordered field F (@def-cof-rationals-below). - complete ordered field: an ordered field in which every non-empty set bounded above has a supremum (@def-complete-ordered-field). - isomorphic complete ordered fields: linked by an order-preserving field isomorphism, which is unique (@thm-cof-uniqueness).

title: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content:
What Completeness Gives at Once Chapter 5 ended with one complete ordered field, the classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). Axiomatic Set Theory builds another from Dedekind cuts, and Analysis on the Real Line simply assumes that one exists. This chapter asks whether these are the same field. Before that question can be asked we need a precise meaning for “the same”: a map between ordered fields that respects everything. This section fixes that meaning, and then collects what completeness gives at once: the Archimedean property, a way to tell elements apart by the rationals below them, and square roots. Standing setting. Throughout the chapter, F and L are ordered fields (@def-ordered-ring-and-field), so \le is a total order on each (@prp-ordered-field-halves (a)) and upper bounds and suprema in the sense of Sets and Functions, Section 5.3 apply to their subsets (@fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum). “Complete” is always the property of @def-complete-ordered-field: every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum. We do not redefine it. Each ordered field F carries its own copy of 
Q: the map \iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field, the only map with \iota_F(1) = 1_F that preserves sums and products. It is injective, strictly increasing and reflects order, and \iota_F(n) = n \cdot 1_F for n \in 
N. For the constructed reals, \iota_{
R} is the map \kappa of Chapter 5 (@thm-rational-embedding (d)). When only one field is in play, a proof may write q for \iota_F(q), as Chapter 4 did; statements keep \iota_F visible, and so does every argument that moves between two fields. Maps that respect everything To say that two ordered fields are “the same”, we want a dictionary between them: a map that turns sums into sums, products into products, 1 into 1, and smaller into smaller. A map that respects addition, multiplication, the unit and the order. [Order-Preserving Field Map] Let F and L be ordered fields. A map \chi \colon F 	o L is an order-preserving field map if, for all a, b \in F, \chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(ab) = \chi(a)\, \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(1_F) = 1_L , and a < b implies \chi(a) < \chi(b). An order-preserving field isomorphism is an order-preserving field map that is bijective (@fd2:def-bijective). An order-preserving field automorphism of F is an order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o F. No other order is admissible: each line uses the one before it ((iii) needs the bound of (v) for the supremum to exist, (viii) needs s, (vi) unpacks (viii), (i) uses the n of (vi), and (iv) is the contradiction with (i)). The contradiction in (iv) refutes (v), so \iota_F(
N) is not bounded above; unpacked with the negation laws, as at the end of the proof of @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, that is the statement of (b). Line (vii) is wrong: a supremum need not belong to the set (in every ordered field, the set of negative elements has supremum 0, which is not negative: the first example after @def-complete-ordered-field). Line (ii) has the wrong quantifier: “s - 1 is not an upper bound” gives some n with \iota_F(n) > s - 1, by @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, not every n (and for n = 0 it may be false). B. Practice [B1] Let F be a complete ordered field. Prove that \inf\{ \iota_F(1/n) : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} = 0. Let T \coloneqq \{ \iota_F(1/n) : n \in 
Z_{>0} \}. For n \in 
Z_{>0}, 1/n > 0 in 
Q, so \iota_F(1/n) > 0: 0 is a lower bound of T. Let c be a lower bound of T, and suppose, for contradiction, that c > 0. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, F is Archimedean, so @prp-archimedean-reciprocal (with \varepsilon \coloneqq c, applied at n = N) gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/(N \cdot 1_F) < c. Since \iota_F preserves products and \iota_F(N) = N \cdot 1_F, we have \iota_F(1/N) \cdot (N \cdot 1_F) = \iota_F(1) = 1_F, so \iota_F(1/N) = 1/(N \cdot 1_F) by uniqueness of inverses (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). So the element \iota_F(1/N) of T lies below c, against c being a lower bound. Hence every lower bound c satisfies c \le 0, and 0 is the greatest lower bound (@fd2:def-order-supremum). [B2] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field and x \in F. Prove that the set \iota_F(
Q_F(x)) = \{ \iota_F(q) : q \in 
Q_F(x) \} has supremum x in F. Upper bound. Every element \iota_F(q) of the set satisfies \iota_F(q) < x by the definition of 
Q_F(x). Least. Let u be an upper bound, and suppose u < x. By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is q \in 
Q with u < \iota_F(q) < x. Then q \in 
Q_F(x), so \iota_F(q) is in the set and exceeds u, against u being an upper bound. So x \le u by totality, for every upper bound u. Hence x = \sup \iota_F(
Q_F(x)). No completeness was used: the supremum exists because we exhibited it. [B3: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one. Throughout, F is a complete ordered field and rationals stand for their copies \iota_F(q). 1. Every a > 0 in F has exactly two elements b with b^2 = a. 2. In every Archimedean ordered field, every element a \ge 0 has a square root. 3. If S \subseteq F is non-empty and bounded above, then \sup S \in S. 4. For every a > 0 in F there is x > 0 with x^2 + x = a. 5. If S \subseteq F is non-empty, c \in F, and y < c for every y \in S, then \sup S < c. (a) True. Let r \coloneqq \sqrt a (@prp-cof-square-roots). Then r 
e 0, since a 
e 0; so r > 0 > -r (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)) and r 
e -r, and both square to a. Conversely, let b^2 = a. If b \ge 0, then b = r by the uniqueness clause. If b < 0, then -b > 0 and (-b)^2 = b^2 = a, so -b = r and b = -r. So the two elements are r and -r. (b) False. 
Q is Archimedean (@thm-rationals-archimedean), and 2 has no square root in it (@thm-no-rational-square-two). (c) False. S \coloneqq \{ 1 - 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} has supremum 1 (@exm-cof-sup-one-minus-reciprocals), and 1 
otin S, since every element is strictly below 1. (d) True. Complete the square: x^2 + x = (x + 1/2)^2 - 1/4. So put x \coloneqq \sqrt{a + 1/4} - 1/2, which exists because a + 1/4 > 0. Then x^2 + x = (a + 1/4) - 1/4 = a. And x > 0: a + 1/4 > 1/4 = (1/2)^2, and both \sqrt{a + 1/4} and 1/2 are non-negative, so \sqrt{a + 1/4} > 1/2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). (e) False. Take S as in (c) and c \coloneqq 1: every element of S is below 1, and \sup S = 1. The true statement is \sup S \le c, by (S2), since c is an upper bound of S. C. Going deeper [C1: An Archimedean field is no larger than the subsets of the rationals] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field. Prove that the map F 	o \powerset{
Q}, x \mapsto 
Q_F(x), is injective. What does this say about the size of F? Let x, y \in F with 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_F(y). By @lem-cof-rationals-separate, x = y. So the map is injective (@fd2:def-injective). An injection F 	o \powerset{
Q} says that F has at most as many elements as \powerset{
Q}, in the sense of Sets and Functions, Chapter 4. In particular every Archimedean ordered field, and so (by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean) every complete ordered field, is no larger than the set of all sets of rationals. The non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) shows that the hypothesis is needed for injectivity: t and t + 1 have the same image. [C2: Find the error] Here is a “proof” that a complete ordered field F is Archimedean. Suppose that \iota_F(
N) is bounded above, and let s be its supremum. Since s is the least upper bound of \iota_F(
N), it is the largest element of \iota_F(
N), so s = \iota_F(m) for some m \in 
N. But \iota_F(m + 1) > s, a contradiction. Is the conclusion true? Find the line that fails, give a counterexample to that line, and repair the proof. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. The illegal step is “the least upper bound of a set is its largest element”. A supremum is an upper bound that lies below every other upper bound (@fd2:def-order-supremum); nothing says it belongs to the set. Counterexample to the step: in the constructed 
R, A \coloneqq \{ 1 - 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} has supremum 1 by @exm-cof-sup-one-minus-reciprocals, with F = 
R (a complete ordered field, @thm-reals-complete-ordered-field) and 1 - 1/n read as \iota_{
R}(1 - 1/n), and 1 
otin A, since every element is < 1. So the step fails for this set, though the theorem’s conclusion is not affected. Repair: replace the second and third sentences by the argument of the proof of @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. Since s - 1 < s, s - 1 is not an upper bound, so \iota_F(n) > s - 1 for some n; then \iota_F(n + 1) = \iota_F(n) + 1 > s, against s being an upper bound. The repair uses that s is least only through “s - 1 is not an upper bound”, which hands us an element of the set just below s, not s itself. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: says the conclusion is true, with the reason (the theorem). - 3: names the line “the supremum is the largest element” and says which property of suprema it wrongly assumes. - 2: a counterexample to that step: a set whose supremum is not an element of it, with the supremum verified. - 2: a correct repair that uses that s is least, without assuming s lies in the set: for example, s - 1 is not an upper bound, so some \iota_F(n) > s - 1 and then \iota_F(n + 1) > s; or, equivalently, if \iota_F(n + 1) \le s for all n then s - 1 is a smaller upper bound (the case n = 0 uses 1 \le s). Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; a counterexample to the theorem rather than to the step.

title: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content:
Building the Map from the Rationals Below Section 6.1 gave every element x of an ordered field F a record, the set 
Q_F(x) of rationals below it, and showed that in an Archimedean field the record determines the element (@lem-cof-rationals-separate). This section turns the record into a map. Given an Archimedean field F and a complete field L, we send x \in F to the element of L with the same record. The result is the main theorem of the chapter in its one-sided form: there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o L. Section 6.3 applies it twice, in both directions, to compare two complete ordered fields. Two fields are in play throughout, so every proof here keeps \iota_F and \iota_L visible. Only the two lemmas, each about one field, write q for \iota_F(q). What the map must be Suppose \varphi \colon F 	o L is an order-preserving field map (@def-cof-order-preserving-map). By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals it fixes the rationals, \varphi(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q), and it preserves and reflects order. So for q \in 
Q and x \in F, \iota_F(q) < x \iff \varphi igl(\iota_F(q) igr) < \varphi(x) \iff \iota_L(q) < \varphi(x) . In the notation of Section 6.1: 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x). The image of x has exactly the rationals below it that x has. That already shows there can be at most one such map when L is Archimedean: two candidates for \varphi(x) would have the same rationals below them, and rationals separate. For existence, we need an element of L with a prescribed set of rationals below it. When L is complete there is a natural candidate: the least element of L that lies above all the copies \iota_L(q), q \in 
Q_F(x), that is, their supremum. The check that this candidate respects sums and products goes through the record, not through suprema. For that we need to know how the rationals below a + b and below ab are made from those below a and b. Let \varphi \colon 
Q 	o L be an order-preserving field map into an ordered field L. Which rationals lie below \varphi(1/2)? Those q < 1/2: \varphi(1/2) = \iota_L(1/2) (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals with \iota_{
Q} = \id_{
Q}), and \iota_L preserves and reflects order. Sums and products, measured by rationals A rational q lies below a + b exactly when it splits into a rational below a and a rational below b. [Rationals below a Sum] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, a, b \in F and q \in 
Q. Then \iota_F(q) < a + b if and only if there is r \in 
Q with \iota_F(r) < a \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \iota_F(q - r) < b . In other words, q \in 
Q_F(a + b) \iff \exists r \in 
Q \  igl( r \in 
Q_F(a) \wedge q - r \in 
Q_F(b)  igr). One direction is addition of inequalities. For the other, split q as r + (q - r) with r a rational just below a: we need r in the gap between q - b and a, which is non-empty exactly because q < a + b, and density supplies it. We write q for \iota_F(q); since \iota_F preserves sums, it preserves differences, so \iota_F(q - r) = q - r in F. (\Leftarrow) If r < a and q - r < b, then q = r + (q - r) < a + b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). (\Rightarrow) Let q < a + b. Then q - b < a (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)). By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is r \in 
Q with q - b < r < a. Then r < a, and q - r < b by the same rule. For products the same idea works for positive elements and positive rationals, with q/r in place of q - r. [Rationals below a Product] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, a, b \in F with a > 0 and b > 0, and q \in 
Q with q > 0. Then \iota_F(q) < ab if and only if there is r \in 
Q with r > 0 , \qquad \iota_F(r) < a \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \iota_F(q/r) < b . For q \le 0, \iota_F(q) < ab holds always. In words: below a product of positives, a positive rational splits as a product of a rational below each factor. Exercise B1 asks for the proof; the fold below has it. As for sums, with division in place of subtraction: split q as r \cdot (q/r) with r a rational in the gap between q/b and a, a gap of positive elements. We write q for \iota_F(q); since \iota_F preserves products and \iota_F(r) 
e 0 for r 
e 0, it preserves quotients, so \iota_F(q/r) = q/r in F. If q \le 0, then q \le 0 < ab by (O4). Let q > 0. (\Leftarrow) Let r > 0 with r < a and q/r < b. Since q/r > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) gives q = r \cdot (q/r) < a \cdot (q/r); since a > 0, it gives a \cdot (q/r) < ab. So q < ab. (\Rightarrow) Let q < ab. Multiplying by b^{-1} > 0 (by the same two rules) gives q/b < a, and q/b > 0 by (O4). By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is r \in 
Q with q/b < r < a. Then r > q/b > 0, so r > 0 in 
Q, since \iota_F reflects order. Multiplying q/b < r by b > 0 gives q < rb, and multiplying by r^{-1} > 0 gives q/r < b. In F = 
Q, with a \coloneqq 3/4, b \coloneqq 1/2 and q \coloneqq 1, find a rational r as in @lem-cof-below-sum. Which rationals r work? We need r < 3/4 and 1 - r < 1/2, that is, 1/2 < r < 3/4. For example r = 2/3: then 1 - 2/3 = 1/3 < 1/2. Exactly the rationals of the open gap between q - b = 1/2 and a = 3/4 work, as the proof predicts. The map into a complete field Here is the theorem. Its proof is the first key proof of the chapter. [Embedding an Archimedean Field in a Complete One] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field and L a complete ordered field. Then there is exactly one order-preserving field map \varphi \colon F 	o L. It is given by \varphi(x) \coloneqq \sup
olimits_L \, \{ \iota_L(q) : q \in 
Q_F(x) \} \qquad (x \in F) , the supremum taken in L, and it satisfies 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x) igr) = 
Q_F(x) \qquad 	ext{for every } x \in F . 	ag{$\star$} Try it first (ten minutes): if \varphi exists and fixes 
Q, which element of L must \varphi(x) be? The natural first attempt defines \varphi on the copy of 
Q, by \varphi(\iota_F(q)) \coloneqq \iota_L(q), and then tries to “extend”. It stalls at once: an element x \in F that is not a rational has no formula, and nothing in F names it. What we do know, from the opening of this section (“What the map must be”), is its record: \varphi(x) must have exactly the rationals 
Q_F(x) below it. So we construct a point as a supremum (@exm-method-point-as-supremum): \varphi(x) is the least upper bound in L of the copies of those rationals, and (\star) says the construction has the right record. After that, sums, products and uniqueness are checked the same way: compute the record of both sides (for sums and products by the two lemmas) and let rationals separate in L. Monotonicity needs only one rational between x and y. ① \varphi(x) exists; ② (\star); ③ \varphi fixes the rationals; ④ \varphi is strictly increasing; ⑤ sums; ⑥ products and the unit; ⑦ uniqueness. Before reading on: where is completeness of L used, and where the Archimedean property of F? By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, L is Archimedean. The rules of an ordered field are used without comment. So @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field, @lem-cof-rationals-separate, @lem-cof-below-sum and @lem-cof-below-product apply in L as well as in F. For x \in F write A_x \coloneqq \{ \iota_L(q) : q \in 
Q_F(x) \} \subseteq L. Step 1: \varphi(x) is defined. Let x \in F. Since F is Archimedean, there is n \in 
N with -x < n \cdot 1_F, so \iota_F(-n) = -(n \cdot 1_F) < x, and -n \in 
Q_F(x): the set A_x is non-empty. Applied to x, the Archimedean property gives m \in 
N with x < m \cdot 1_F = \iota_F(m). For q \in 
Q_F(x), \iota_F(q) < x < \iota_F(m), so q < m because \iota_F reflects order, and \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(m). So \iota_L(m) is an upper bound of A_x. Since L is complete, A_x has a supremum in L, and it is unique; \varphi(x) is that supremum. So \varphi \colon F 	o L is a function. Step 2: (\star). Let x \in F and q \in 
Q. (\subseteq) Let q \in 
Q_F(x). By density in F there is r \in 
Q with \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) < x. Then r \in 
Q_F(x), so \iota_L(r) \in A_x and \iota_L(r) \le \varphi(x), since \varphi(x) is an upper bound. Also q < r (reflection in F), so \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) \le \varphi(x), and q \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)). (\supseteq) Let \iota_L(q) < \varphi(x). Since \varphi(x) is the least upper bound of A_x, \iota_L(q) is not an upper bound, so there is r \in 
Q_F(x) with \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) (totality). Then q < r (reflection in L), so \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) < x, and q \in 
Q_F(x). Step 3: \varphi fixes the rationals. Let r \in 
Q. By (\star) and the first example after @def-cof-rationals-below, used in F and in L, 
Q_L igl(\varphi(\iota_F(r)) igr) = 
Q_F igl(\iota_F(r) igr) = \{ q \in 
Q : q < r \} = 
Q_L igl(\iota_L(r) igr) . By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \varphi(\iota_F(r)) = \iota_L(r). In particular \varphi(0_F) = 0_L and \varphi(1_F) = 1_L. Step 4: \varphi is strictly increasing. Let x < y in F. By density in F there is r \in 
Q with x < \iota_F(r) < y. Then r 
otin 
Q_F(x) (by (O1)), so r 
otin 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) by (\star), and \varphi(x) \le \iota_L(r) by totality. And r \in 
Q_F(y) = 
Q_L(\varphi(y)), so \iota_L(r) < \varphi(y). Hence \varphi(x) \le \iota_L(r) < \varphi(y). Step 5: sums. Let x, y \in F and q \in 
Q. Then  egin{aligned} q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x + y) igr) &\iff q \in 
Q_F(x + y) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q \  igl( r \in 
Q_F(x) \wedge q - r \in 
Q_F(y)  igr) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q \  igl( r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) \wedge q - r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(y))  igr) \ &\iff q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x) + \varphi(y) igr) , \end{aligned} by (\star), @lem-cof-below-sum in F, (\star) twice, and @lem-cof-below-sum in L. By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \varphi(x + y) = \varphi(x) + \varphi(y). Step 6: products and the unit. First let x > 0 and y > 0. By Steps 3 and 4, \varphi(x) > \varphi(0_F) = 0_L and \varphi(y) > 0_L; and xy > 0, \varphi(x)\varphi(y) > 0 by (O4). Let q \in 
Q. If q \le 0, then q \in 
Q_F(xy) = 
Q_L(\varphi(xy)), and q \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)\varphi(y)), by the last clause of @lem-cof-below-product in F and in L. If q > 0, then  egin{aligned} q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(xy) igr) &\iff q \in 
Q_F(xy) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q_{>0} \  igl( r \in 
Q_F(x) \wedge q/r \in 
Q_F(y)  igr) \ &\iff \exists r \in 
Q_{>0} \  igl( r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) \wedge q/r \in 
Q_L(\varphi(y))  igr) \ &\iff q \in 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x)\varphi(y) igr) , \end{aligned} by (\star), @lem-cof-below-product in F, (\star) twice, and @lem-cof-below-product in L (with \varphi(x), \varphi(y) > 0). By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) for x, y > 0. Now the signs. By Steps 5 and 3, \varphi(x) + \varphi(-x) = \varphi(0_F) = 0_L, so \varphi(-x) = -\varphi(x). If x = 0 or y = 0, both sides of \varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) are 0_L (Step 3). If x < 0 < y, then -x > 0 and xy = - igl((-x)y igr), so \varphi(xy) = -\varphi igl((-x)y igr) = - igl(\varphi(-x)\varphi(y) igr) = - igl(-\varphi(x) igr)\varphi(y) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y) . The case x > 0 > y follows by commutativity, and if x, y < 0, then xy = (-x)(-y) and \varphi(xy) =  igl(-\varphi(x) igr) igl(-\varphi(y) igr) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y). Finally \varphi(1_F) = 1_L by Step 3. With Steps 4 and 5, \varphi is an order-preserving field map. Step 7: uniqueness. Let \chi \colon F 	o L be any order-preserving field map, and let x \in F, q \in 
Q. By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, \chi(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q). If \iota_F(q) < x, then \iota_L(q) = \chi(\iota_F(q)) < \chi(x). If \iota_L(q) < \chi(x), that is, \chi(\iota_F(q)) < \chi(x), then \iota_F(q) < x, because \chi reflects order (the remark after @def-cof-order-preserving-map). So 
Q_L igl(\chi(x) igr) = 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_L igl(\varphi(x) igr) , the second equality by (\star). By @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L, \chi(x) = \varphi(x). Since x was arbitrary, \chi = \varphi. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Completeness of L is used in Step 1, where the supremum must exist, and in Step 2 (\supseteq), where its leastness turns “below \varphi(x)” into “below some \iota_L(r)”. The Archimedean property of F is used in Step 1 for the bounds -n and m, in Steps 2 and 4 through density in F, and in Steps 5 and 6 through the two lemmas applied in F. Completeness of L is used a third time, indirectly: it makes L Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), which Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 need for rationals to separate in L and for the lemmas in L. Step 7 is the whole of “uniqueness”. Its idea, comparing the rationals below two candidate values, needs only that L is Archimedean, not that it is complete: Exercise C1 runs it for any two order-preserving field maps F 	o L, with no appeal to (\star). Section 6.3 leans on the uniqueness clause throughout: to show that the maps between two complete fields are inverse to each other, that the isomorphism they give is the only one, and that a complete ordered field has no order-preserving field automorphism other than the identity. Neither hypothesis can be dropped from the existence half. Without completeness of L: take F = 
R, which is Archimedean (@thm-constructed-reals-archimedean), and L = 
Q. An order-preserving field map \varphi \colon 
R 	o 
Q would fix 2 (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals), so for \sqrt 2 \in 
R (Section 6.1), \varphi(\sqrt 2)^2 = \varphi((\sqrt 2)^2) = \varphi(2) = 2 in 
Q, against @thm-no-rational-square-two. Without the Archimedean property of F: take F = 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field and any complete L. An order-preserving field map \varphi would fix each n \cdot 1 and be strictly increasing, so n \cdot 1_L = \varphi(n \cdot 1) < \varphi(t) for every n \in 
N, against the Archimedean property of L (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean). The supremum in the definition of \varphi is taken in L, of the copies \iota_L(q). In 
Q it may not exist: 
Q_{
R}(\sqrt 2) has the same upper bounds in 
Q as \{ p \in 
Q : p^2 < 2 \}, which has no least one (@thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2). In F it always exists and is x itself (Exercise B2 of Section 6.1): an element of the wrong field. Take L \coloneqq F, a complete ordered field. Which map F 	o F does @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete produce, and why, without computing a single supremum? The identity. The theorem says there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o F (F is Archimedean by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean), and \id_F is one (the first example after @def-cof-order-preserving-map). So \varphi = \id_F. This is the argument Section 6.3 builds on. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete. 1. Which steps use that L is complete, and which that F is Archimedean? Which steps use that L is Archimedean, and where does that come from? 2. Run the definition of \varphi with F = 
Q and L = 
R, the constructed reals. What is \varphi? 3. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 4. Why may Step 1 not define \varphi(x) as a supremum taken in F? (a) L complete: Step 1 (the supremum exists) and Step 2 (\supseteq) (its leastness). F Archimedean: Step 1 (the bounds -n, m), Steps 2 and 4 (density in F), and Steps 5 and 6 (@lem-cof-below-sum and @lem-cof-below-product applied in F). L Archimedean: Steps 3, 5, 6 and 7, through @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L and the two lemmas in L. It comes from the completeness of L, by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean. (b) \varphi = \iota_{
R} = \kappa. By Step 3, \varphi(\iota_{
Q}(r)) = \iota_{
R}(r) for every r \in 
Q, and \iota_{
Q} is the identity (Chapter 4, after @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field). So \varphi(r) = \iota_{
R}(r), which is \kappa(r) by @thm-rational-embedding (d). Concretely, \varphi(r) is the supremum in 
R of \{ \kappa(q) : q < r \}, and that supremum is \kappa(r). (c) An order-preserving map that fixes the rationals must send x to an element with the same rationals below it, and in a complete L the supremum of their copies is such an element. Every field identity for \varphi is then checked by comparing the rationals below the two sides, which the sum and product lemmas compute, and rationals separate in L. (d) In F the supremum of \iota_F(
Q_F(x)) always exists, since F is Archimedean, and it is x itself (Exercise B2 of Section 6.1): an element of F, not of L. So it does not give a map into L. The supremum must be of the copies \iota_L(q), taken in L. B. Practice [B1] Prove @lem-cof-below-product: let F be an Archimedean ordered field, a, b \in F with a, b > 0, and q \in 
Q with q > 0; show that \iota_F(q) < ab if and only if some rational r > 0 has \iota_F(r) < a and \iota_F(q/r) < b. Show also that \iota_F(q) < ab for every rational q \le 0. Hint: imitate the proof of @lem-cof-below-sum, with division in place of subtraction. Write q for \iota_F(q). Since \iota_F preserves products, \iota_F(r)\,\iota_F(r^{-1}) = \iota_F(1) = 1 for r 
e 0, so \iota_F(r^{-1}) = \iota_F(r)^{-1} (@lem-field-fraction-rules (a)) and \iota_F(q/r) = q/r in F. If q \le 0, then q \le 0 < ab by (O4). Let q > 0. (\Leftarrow) Let r > 0, r < a, q/r < b. Then q/r > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a), (O4)), so @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) gives q = r(q/r) < a(q/r), and, as a > 0, a(q/r) < ab. Hence q < ab. (\Rightarrow) Let q < ab. Since b^{-1} > 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) gives q/b < a, and q/b > 0. By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field there is r \in 
Q with q/b < \iota_F(r) < a. Then \iota_F(r) > 0 = \iota_F(0), so r > 0 since \iota_F reflects order. From q/b < r and b > 0, q < rb; multiplying by r^{-1} > 0, q/r < b. This r is as required. [B2: Cube roots] Let F be a complete ordered field and a \in F with a > 0. Let S \coloneqq \{ y \in F : y \ge 0 	ext{ and } y^3 < a \}. The following steps prove that some s \in F has s^3 = a. 1. S is non-empty (0 \in S) and bounded above by 1 + a: if y > 1 + a, then y > 1, so y^3 > y > a. Let s \coloneqq \sup S. Then s > 0, since m \coloneqq \min\{1, a/2\} has 0 < m \le 1, so m^3 \le m \le a/2 < a, and m \in S. 2. For y, z \in F, z^3 - y^3 = (z - y)(z^2 + zy + y^2) and z^2 + zy + y^2 = (z + y/2)^2 + (3/4)y^2, which is > 0 unless y = z = 0 (if y 
e 0, then (3/4)y^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c) and the square is \ge 0, so the sum is positive by (b); if y = 0 and z 
e 0, the expression is z^2 > 0 by (e)). Hence y < z \iff y^3 < z^3, for all y, z \in F. 3. The case s^3 < a is impossible. Let h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^3)/(2(3s^2 + 3s + 1))\} > 0. Since 0 < h \le 1 and s \ge 0, (s + h)^3 = s^3 + 3s^2h + 3sh^2 + h^3 \le s^3 + h(3s^2 + 3s + 1) \le s^3 + (a - s^3)/2 < a, so s + h \in S, against s being an upper bound. 4. The case s^3 > a is impossible. Name the move, then complete it. 5. Hence s^3 = a. Then explain how to get a cube root of a = 0 and of a < 0, and why every a \in F has exactly one cube root. The move is construct a point as a supremum: s is built as \sup S, and each of the two wrong cases of trichotomy is refuted by exhibiting a point that contradicts one clause of the supremum. In step (3) it was an element of S above s, against (S1). In step (4) it is an upper bound below s, against (S2). (4) Suppose s^3 > a. Let h \coloneqq (s^3 - a)/(3s^2); it is positive, since s > 0 by (1). Also h < s: this says s^3 - a < 3s^3, which holds because a > 0 and 2s^3 > 0. So s - h > 0, and (s - h)^3 - a = (s^3 - a) - 3s^2h + 3sh^2 - h^3 = h^2(3s - h) > 0 , since 3s^2 h = s^3 - a, h^2 > 0 and 3s - h > 2s > 0. Let y > s - h. By (2), y^3 > (s - h)^3 > a, so y 
otin S. Hence every element of S is \le s - h, and s - h is an upper bound of S smaller than s, against s being the least upper bound. (5) Steps (3) and (4) leave only s^3 = a, by trichotomy (O1). For a = 0, 0^3 = 0. For a < 0, -a > 0 has a cube root c by the above, and (-c)^3 = -c^3 = a (@prp-ring-algebra (c)). Uniqueness: if b^3 = c^3, then neither b < c nor c < b can hold, since by (2) either would make the cubes differ; so b = c. So every element of a complete ordered field has exactly one cube root. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: at most one map into an Archimedean field] Let F and L be Archimedean ordered fields, and let \chi_1, \chi_2 \colon F 	o L be order-preserving field maps. Prove that \chi_1 = \chi_2. [Hint 1] Compare the rationals below \chi_1(x) and below \chi_2(x). [Hint 2] By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, \chi_i(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q) for i = 1, 2 and every q \in 
Q. Let x \in F and i \in \{1, 2\}. By @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals (which needs no order hypothesis), \chi_i(\iota_F(q)) = \iota_L(q) for every q \in 
Q. Since \chi_i is strictly increasing and reflects order (the remark after @def-cof-order-preserving-map), \iota_F(q) < x \iff \chi_i igl(\iota_F(q) igr) < \chi_i(x) \iff \iota_L(q) < \chi_i(x) . So 
Q_L(\chi_1(x)) = 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_L(\chi_2(x)). Since L is Archimedean, @lem-cof-rationals-separate gives \chi_1(x) = \chi_2(x). As x was arbitrary, \chi_1 = \chi_2. (This is Step 7 of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete with \chi_2 in place of \varphi; completeness of L is not needed, and neither is the Archimedean property of F.) Why L must be Archimedean (remark, not proved here). The last step separates \chi_1(x) from \chi_2(x) by a rational strictly between them, which is density of \iota_L(
Q) in L, and density needs Archimedes (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). In the non-Archimedean field 
Q(t) of @exm-rational-function-field, the elements 1/t and 2/t are different and have the same rationals below them, namely all q \le 0: a positive rational q has q > 1/n in 
Q for some n \in 
Z_{>0} (@thm-rationals-archimedean), so \iota_{
Q(t)}(q) > \iota_{
Q(t)}(1/n) = 1/(n \cdot 1) > 2/t, because t > 2n \cdot 1 (@exm-rational-function-field). So the separating step fails in such a field. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: each \chi_i fixes 
Q, with the reason (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, or directly: induction for 
N, then negatives and quotients). - 3: links the rationals below x to those below \chi_i(x), using that \chi_i fixes 
Q and reflects order. Either gives the full equivalence \iota_F(q) < x \iff \iota_L(q) < \chi_i(x), or, for the squeeze route of the next item, applies reflection by \chi_1 and \chi_2 to a rational strictly between \chi_1(x) and \chi_2(x). - 3: concludes \chi_1(x) = \chi_2(x) by rationals separating, or by a rational strictly between the two, invoking the Archimedean property of L. - 2: states the conclusion for every x \in F. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using density in L without a hypothesis that gives it; assuming \chi_i surjective. [C2: Dense image, and when the map is onto] Let F be an Archimedean ordered field, L a complete ordered field, and \varphi \colon F 	o L the map of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete. 1. Prove that \varphi(F) is dense in L: for all u < v in L there is x \in F with u < \varphi(x) < v. 2. Prove that if F is complete, then \varphi is surjective. 3. Prove that if \varphi is surjective, then F is complete. [Hint 1] For (b), given y \in L, look at the set S \coloneqq 
Q_L(y) and its copy \iota_F(S) in F. [Hint 2] For (b): \iota_F(S) is non-empty and bounded above in F; let x \coloneqq \sup_F \iota_F(S), and show 
Q_F(x) = S. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, L is Archimedean. (a) Let u < v in L. By @thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field in L there is q \in 
Q with u < \iota_L(q) < v. By Step 3 of the proof of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, \iota_L(q) = \varphi(\iota_F(q)), so x \coloneqq \iota_F(q) works. (b) Let F be complete and y \in L. Let S \coloneqq 
Q_L(y). Since L is Archimedean, there are n, m \in 
N with -y < \iota_L(n) and y < \iota_L(m). So -n \in S, and every q \in S has \iota_L(q) < y < \iota_L(m), hence q < m and \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(m). So \iota_F(S) is non-empty and bounded above in F, and x \coloneqq \sup_F \iota_F(S) exists. We show 
Q_F(x) = S. (\supseteq) Let q \in S. By density in L there is r \in 
Q with \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) < y; then r \in S and q < r, so \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) \le x. (\subseteq) Let \iota_F(q) < x. Then \iota_F(q) is not an upper bound of \iota_F(S), so \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(r) for some r \in S; hence q < r and \iota_L(q) < \iota_L(r) < y, so q \in S. By (\star), 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x) = S = 
Q_L(y), so \varphi(x) = y by @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L. (c) Let \varphi be surjective. It is injective (strictly increasing), so bijective, with an inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon L 	o F (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Let A \subseteq F be non-empty with an upper bound b. Then \varphi(A) is non-empty and bounded above by \varphi(b), since a \le b gives \varphi(a) \le \varphi(b). As L is complete, s \coloneqq \sup \varphi(A) exists; let c \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}(s). Upper bound: for a \in A, \varphi(a) \le s = \varphi(c), so a \le c, because \varphi reflects order (and is injective, for the case of equality). Least: if u is an upper bound of A, then \varphi(u) is an upper bound of \varphi(A), so \varphi(c) = s \le \varphi(u), and c \le u as before. So c = \sup A (@fd2:def-order-supremum), and F is complete. So \varphi is an order-preserving field isomorphism exactly when F is complete. Section 6.3 reaches the “if” direction by a different route, which computes no supremum at all. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) L is Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), so some \iota_L(q) lies strictly between u and v, and \iota_L(q) = \varphi(\iota_F(q)) (Step 3). - 2: (b) \iota_F(S) is non-empty and bounded above in F (Archimedes in L, transferred through \iota_F), so x = \sup_F \iota_F(S) exists by completeness of F. - 2: (b) 
Q_F(x) = S, both inclusions; (\supseteq) uses density in L. - 1: (b) 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x) = 
Q_L(y) by (\star), hence \varphi(x) = y by @lem-cof-rationals-separate in L. - 3: (c) for non-empty A \subseteq F bounded above by b, \varphi(A) is bounded above by \varphi(b), and \varphi^{-1}(\sup \varphi(A)) is an upper bound of A and the least one, both using that \varphi reflects order and is bijective. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using density of \iota_L(
Q) in L without the Archimedean property of L; in (b), taking a supremum in F before checking that the set is non-empty and bounded above; in (c), assuming \varphi^{-1} preserves order without justification.

title: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content:
Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism Section 6.2 built, from an Archimedean ordered field F into a complete one L, exactly one order-preserving field map \varphi, and it keeps the rationals below each element: 
Q_L(\varphi(x)) = 
Q_F(x) (property (\star) of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete). This section takes both fields complete. Then maps run both ways, and the word “exactly” makes them inverse to each other. So any two complete ordered fields are copies of each other, by one isomorphism; the only symmetry of a complete ordered field is the identity; and every first-order statement about sums, products and order has the same truth value in all of them. The section ends with what this means for the two ways to begin analysis. The uniqueness theorem Section 6.2 gave us, for complete F and L, a map \varphi \colon F 	o L. It did not say that \varphi is onto. A map can preserve everything in sight and still miss most of its target: the map \iota_{
R} \colon 
Q 	o 
R preserves sums, products and order (@thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field), and the real number r of @exm-sqrt2-class, whose square is 2, is not in its image. What rules this out when the source is complete as well? [Uniqueness of the Complete Ordered Field] Let F and L be complete ordered fields (@def-complete-ordered-field). Then there is exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o L (@def-cof-order-preserving-map). It is the map \varphi of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete. Section 6.2 runs in both directions. Since F is complete, it is Archimedean (@thm-cof-complete-archimedean), so it is a legal source; since L is complete, it is a legal target. That gives \varphi \colon F 	o L. Swapping the roles gives \psi \colon L 	o F. To show that \psi undoes \varphi, we could try to compute \psi(\varphi(x)) from the two suprema. We do not have to. The composite \psi \circ \varphi \colon F 	o F is again an order-preserving field map, and so is the identity of F. The uniqueness clause of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, applied with F as source and as target, says there is only one such map. So the two are equal. Uniqueness gives inverses. (This is the pattern of @fd2:exm-method-uniqueness: two objects with the same defining property are equal.) Before reading on: self-explain why \psi \circ \varphi is order-preserving. Which of the four conditions of @def-cof-order-preserving-map needs more than one line? Let F and L be complete ordered fields. By @thm-cof-complete-archimedean, each of them is Archimedean. The two maps. Since F is Archimedean and L is complete, @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete gives an order-preserving field map \varphi \colon F 	o L. Since L is Archimedean and F is complete, the same theorem, with the roles of the two fields exchanged, gives an order-preserving field map \psi \colon L 	o F. The composite \psi \circ \varphi is an order-preserving field map F 	o F. For a, b \in F, additivity of \varphi and then of \psi gives \psi(\varphi(a + b)) = \psi(\varphi(a) + \varphi(b)) = \psi(\varphi(a)) + \psi(\varphi(b)) , and the same two steps with products give \psi(\varphi(ab)) = \psi(\varphi(a)) \, \psi(\varphi(b)). Also \psi(\varphi(1)) = \psi(1) = 1. If a < b, then \varphi(a) < \varphi(b), since \varphi is strictly increasing, and then \psi(\varphi(a)) < \psi(\varphi(b)), since \psi is. The composite is the identity. The identity map \id_F is an order-preserving field map F 	o F: each of the four conditions reads u = u or a < b \Rightarrow a < b. Now apply @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete with source F, which is Archimedean, and target F, which is complete: there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o F. Both \psi \circ \varphi and \id_F are such maps, so \psi \circ \varphi = \id_F. Exchanging the roles of F and L, the same argument gives \varphi \circ \psi = \id_L. Existence. So \psi is a two-sided inverse of \varphi, and \varphi is bijective by @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Hence \varphi is an order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o L. Uniqueness. Let \chi \colon F 	o L be any order-preserving field isomorphism. Forgetting that it is bijective, \chi is an order-preserving field map F 	o L, and by the uniqueness clause of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete there is only one such map. Hence \chi = \varphi. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: each of the four conditions passes through a composite in one line, the order condition in two (a < b gives \varphi(a) < \varphi(b), which \psi accepts). The weight of the proof sits in the uniqueness clause, used three times: for \psi \circ \varphi, for \varphi \circ \psi, and for \chi. A direct proof that \varphi is onto, computing a supremum in F, is Exercise C2 of Section 6.2. Why could the proof not simply define \psi \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}, instead of building \psi from @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete? The inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon L 	o F exists only if \varphi is bijective (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse), and bijectivity is what the theorem is trying to prove. Section 6.2 gives \varphi as an injective map (it is strictly increasing), with no claim that it is onto. The map \psi is built independently of \varphi, and only afterwards shown to be its inverse. Each hypothesis has a job. Completeness of L makes it a target, so \varphi exists; completeness of F makes it a target, so \psi exists; and completeness of each gives the Archimedean property that makes it a source. Drop the completeness of F, and the conclusion fails: for F = 
Q, L = 
R, the only order-preserving field map is \iota_{
R}, which is not onto. One real line The theorem says that two complete ordered fields have the same shape, with a unique dictionary between them. We want a short way to write the first half of that sentence. Two ordered fields are the same up to relabeling when an order-preserving bijection respects the arithmetic. For ordered fields F and L, write F \cong L when there is an order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o L (@def-cof-order-preserving-map). Read it “F is isomorphic to L”, with “as ordered fields” understood. Examples. - 
R \cong 
R, by \id_{
R}. Any ordered field is isomorphic to itself in the same way. - F \cong 
R for every complete ordered field F, where 
R is the field of Chapter 5. This is the corollary below. - 
Q 
ot\cong 
R. An isomorphism \chi \colon 
Q 	o 
R would fix the rationals (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals, with \iota_{
Q} = \id_{
Q} by the uniqueness clause of @thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field), so \chi = \iota_{
R}, and \iota_{
R} is not onto (@exm-sqrt2-class). [Every Complete Ordered Field Is a Copy of the Reals] Let F be a complete ordered field, and let 
R be the field of Chapter 5. Then F \cong 
R: there is exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o 
R. By @thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, 
R is a complete ordered field. Apply @thm-cof-uniqueness with L = 
R. So “the real numbers” names one ordered field up to a unique relabeling. A statement about sums, products and order is then true in F exactly when it is true in 
R; the subsection What the isomorphism carries below makes this precise for first-order statements and shows it at work on limits. On any set \mathcal S of ordered fields, \cong is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation): it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. No proof in this subsection uses its symmetry or transitivity; this paragraph records that the word “isomorphic” behaves as the word “equal” suggests. The symmetric clause is used below: the inverse of the isomorphism of @thm-cof-uniqueness is again one. Reflexive. \id_F is an order-preserving field isomorphism F 	o F. Symmetric. Let \chi \colon F 	o L be an order-preserving field isomorphism, and let \chi^{-1} \colon L 	o F be its two-sided inverse (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse); it is bijective by the same theorem. For u, v \in L, additivity of \chi gives \chi igl( \chi^{-1}(u) + \chi^{-1}(v)  igr) = \chi(\chi^{-1}(u)) + \chi(\chi^{-1}(v)) = u + v = \chi igl( \chi^{-1}(u + v)  igr) , and since \chi is injective, \chi^{-1}(u + v) = \chi^{-1}(u) + \chi^{-1}(v). The same lines with products give \chi^{-1}(uv) = \chi^{-1}(u) \chi^{-1}(v), and \chi(1) = 1 gives \chi^{-1}(1) = 1. Finally, let u < v. Then \chi(\chi^{-1}(u)) < \chi(\chi^{-1}(v)), and since \chi reflects order, \chi^{-1}(u) < \chi^{-1}(v). Transitive. If \chi \colon F 	o L and \chi' \colon L 	o M are order-preserving field isomorphisms, then \chi' \circ \chi is bijective (@fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective), and it is an order-preserving field map by the computation in the proof of @thm-cof-uniqueness for \psi \circ \varphi, which used nothing but the four conditions for each factor. [Two Models, One Square Root of Two] Let M be any complete ordered field (for instance the one Axiomatic Set Theory builds, whose elements are sets of rationals). Let \varphi \colon 
R 	o M be the isomorphism of @thm-cof-uniqueness and r the real number of @exm-sqrt2-class (r > 0, r^2 = 2). Find \varphi(r) in terms of M alone, and describe 
Q_M(\varphi(r)). The image of r. Since \varphi is multiplicative and fixes the rationals (@prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals), \varphi(r)^2 = \varphi(r^2) = \varphi(\iota_{
R}(2)) = \iota_M(2). Since \varphi is strictly increasing and r > 0, \varphi(r) > \varphi(0) = 0 (\varphi fixes the rational 0, @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals). By @prp-cof-square-roots in the complete field M, there is exactly one b \ge 0 in M with b^2 = \iota_M(2). So \varphi(r) is that b: the square root of 2 in M, however M was built. The rationals below it. By (\star) of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete, 
Q_M(\varphi(r)) = 
Q_{
R}(r). By @exm-cof-rationals-below-sqrt2 this is the set of rationals q with q < 0, or with q \ge 0 and q^2 < 2. The same set of rationals sits below \sqrt 2 in both models. The set 
Q_F(x) of an element x of an Archimedean ordered field F always has four properties. It is non-empty: some n \in 
N has -x < n \cdot 1_F, so -n \in 
Q_F(x). It is not all of 
Q: some m has x < m \cdot 1_F, so m 
otin 
Q_F(x). It is closed downward (Section 6.1). It has no largest element: for q \in 
Q_F(x), density (@thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field) gives p \in 
Q with \iota_F(q) < \iota_F(p) < x. A set of rationals with these four properties is called a Dedekind cut. Axiomatic Set Theory, Chapter 1 takes the cuts themselves as the real numbers, proves that they form a complete ordered field, and shows that there the rationals below a cut c are exactly the elements of c. By @thm-cof-uniqueness that field is one more copy of 
R; by (\star) the copy of a real number y has the same rationals below it as y, so the copy of y is the cut 
Q_{
R}(y). Automorphisms An isomorphism from a field to itself is a symmetry: a relabeling that leaves the arithmetic unchanged. The uniqueness theorem rules out every symmetry of a complete ordered field that respects the order; the theorem after it rules out every symmetry. [A Complete Ordered Field Has Only the Trivial Order Automorphism] Let F be a complete ordered field. The only order-preserving field automorphism of F is \id_F. In particular, this holds for the field 
R of Chapter 5. F is Archimedean by @thm-cof-complete-archimedean and complete by hypothesis, so by @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete with source and target F there is exactly one order-preserving field map F 	o F. The identity is one, and every order-preserving field automorphism is one. So every such automorphism is \id_F. For 
R, use @thm-reals-complete-ordered-field. The corollary assumes that the map respects the order. Can a map that only respects the arithmetic move anything? [Field Maps of a Complete Ordered Field to Itself] Let F be a complete ordered field, and let \sigma \colon F 	o F satisfy, for all a, b \in F, \sigma(a + b) = \sigma(a) + \sigma(b) , \qquad \sigma(ab) = \sigma(a) \sigma(b) , \qquad \sigma(1) = 1 . Then \sigma = \id_F. No order condition and no bijectivity is assumed. Try it first (ten minutes): why must such a \sigma send positive elements to positive elements? Look for a description of “positive” that uses only multiplication. The order condition has to be recovered from the arithmetic. In a complete ordered field, positivity has a description in terms of multiplication alone: an element is positive exactly when it is a non-zero square (@prp-cof-square-roots gives the square root). A map that respects products sends squares to squares, and squares in an ordered field are never negative. Then additivity turns “positives go to positives” into “\sigma is strictly increasing”, and the uniqueness clause of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete finishes, as in the corollary’s proof (which never uses bijectivity). Plan: ① positive to positive, through a square root; ② strictly increasing, through differences; ③ the uniqueness clause. Before reading on: which line of the proof below needs completeness, and which would work in any ordered field? Step 1: \sigma sends positive elements to positive elements. Let a \in F with a > 0. By @prp-cof-square-roots there is b \in F with b \ge 0 and b^2 = a. Then b 
e 0, since 0^2 = 0

title: Axiom 1.1.1 (The Natural Numbers)
page: 1.1 Peano's Axioms and Induction
content: There is a Peano system.

title: Definition 1.1.1 (Peano system)
page: 1.1 Peano's Axioms and Induction
content: A Peano system \((M, e, s)\) consists of a set \(M\) , an element \(e \in M\) , and a function \(s \colon M \to M\) , such that: (P3) \(s(x) \ne e\) for every \(x \in M\) ; (P4) \(s\) is injective; (P5) every subset \(A \subseteq M\) with \(e \in A\) and \(s(x) \in A\) for every \(x \in A\) is equal to \(M\) .

title: Example (Method: induction through a closed subset)
page: 1.1 Peano's Axioms and Induction
content: Template. (1) Name \(A \coloneqq \{ x \in M : P(x) \}\) . (2) Show \(e \in A\) . (3) Take \(x \in A\) and show \(s(x) \in A\) , using \(P(x)\) if needed. (4) Conclude \(A = M\) by (P5). If \(P\) fails at \(e\) , carry “ \(x = e\) or \(P(x)\) ” (the shape of @fd2:lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)). When to use it. A statement about every element of a Peano system whose elements are not known one by one: an abstract \((M, e, s)\) , the image of a map out of \(\nN\) , a set of pairs. The usual failure. A property false at \(e\) . Closure checked only for elements of a special form ( \(x = s(y)\) ), forgetting \(e\) . (P5) applied to a set that is not a subset of \(M\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 1.3 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Here is an attempted proof that any two natural numbers are comparable. The proof is meant to replace the totality step in the proof of @thm-omega-order , so it may cite only results stated before that theorem. Is the conclusion true? Is the proof correct? If not, give the first line that fails, the error, and a counterexample to the step. Claim. For all \(m, n \in \nN\) : \(m \le n\) or \(n \le m\) . Fix \(m\) ; we use @thm-omega-induction (b) on \(n\) , for the property “ \(m \le n\) or \(n \le m\) ”. (2) For \(n = 0\) : \(0 \le m\) , since \(m = 0 + m\) . (3) Suppose that \(m \le n\) or \(n \le m\) . (4) If \(n = m + j\) , then \(n + 1 = m + (j + 1)\) , so \(m \le n + 1\) . (5) If \(n \le m\) , then \(n + 1 \le m\) , because \(n < n + 1\) and nothing lies strictly between \(n\) and \(n + 1\) . (6) So \(m \le n + 1\) or \(n + 1 \le m\) . (7) By induction, the claim holds.

title: Theorem 1.4.1 (Categoricity of the Peano Axioms)
page: 1.4 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be a Peano system. There is exactly one function \(\varphi \colon \nN \to M\) with \(\varphi(0) = e\) and \(\varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n))\) for every \(n \in \nN\) . This \(\varphi\) is a bijection. For any two Peano systems \((M, e, s)\) and \((M', e', s')\) there is exactly one bijection \(\psi \colon M \to M'\) with \(\psi(e) = e'\) and \(\psi(s(x)) = s'(\psi(x))\) for every \(x \in M\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Functions on Classes)
page: 2.2 Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) , and \(\approx\) an equivalence relation on a set \(Y\) . Classes are taken for \(\sim\) in \(X\) and for \(\approx\) in \(Y\) . Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function such that, for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(x \sim x'\) implies \(f(x) \approx f(x')\) . Then there is exactly one function \(F \colon X/{\sim} \to Y/{\approx}\) with \(F([x]) = [f(x)]\) for every \(x \in X\) . Let \(g \colon X \times X \to X\) be a function such that, for all \(x, x', y, y' \in X\) , \[ \begin{aligned} x \sim x' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) , \\ y \sim y' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x, y') . \end{aligned} \] Then there is exactly one function \(G \colon (X/{\sim}) \times (X/{\sim}) \to X/{\sim}\) with \(G([x], [y]) = [g(x, y)]\) for all \(x, y \in X\) . Let \(S \subseteq X\) be such that, for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(x \sim x'\) and \(x \in S\) imply \(x' \in S\) . Let \(\bar S \coloneqq \{ [x] : x \in S \} \subseteq X/{\sim}\) . Then, for every \(x \in X\) , \([x] \in \bar S\) if and only if \(x \in S\) .

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Commutative Ring, Field)
page: 2.3 Commutative Rings; the Integers Are One
content: A commutative ring is a set \(R\) with two functions, addition \(+ \colon R \times R \to R\) and multiplication \(\cdot \colon R \times R \to R\) (written \(a \cdot b = ab\) ), such that clauses (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of the following list hold; clause (F8) is used only for fields. \(a + b = b + a\) for all \(a, b \in R\) . \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . There is an element \(0 \in R\) with \(a + 0 = a\) for every \(a \in R\) . For every \(a \in R\) there is an element \(-a \in R\) with \(a + (-a) = 0\) . \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in R\) . There is an element \(1 \in R\) with \(a \cdot 1 = a\) for every \(a \in R\) . For every non-zero \(a \in R\) there is an element \(a^{-1} \in R\) with \(a a^{-1} = 1\) . \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . A field is a commutative ring in which, in addition , \(1 \ne 0\) and (F8) holds. We write \(a - b \coloneqq a + (-b)\) , and in a field \(a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1}\) for \(b \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 2.4.1 (Ordered Ring, Ordered Field)
page: 2.4 Ordered Rings and the Rules for Inequalities
content: An ordered commutative ring is a commutative ring \(R\) ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ) together with a relation \(<\) on \(R\) such that, for all \(a, b, c \in R\) : (trichotomy) exactly one of \(a < b\) , \(a = b\) , \(b < a\) holds; (transitivity) if \(a < b\) and \(b < c\) , then \(a < c\) ; (addition) if \(a < b\) , then \(a + c < b + c\) ; (multiplication) if \(0 < a\) and \(0 < b\) , then \(0 < ab\) . An ordered field is a field that is an ordered commutative ring. We write \(b > a\) for \(a < b\) , and \(a \le b\) for “ \(a < b\) or \(a = b\) ” (likewise \(b \ge a\) ). An element \(a\) is positive if \(a > 0\) , negative if \(a < 0\) , and non-negative if \(a \ge 0\) .

When to use it. Any rule for inequalities; comparisons in \(\nZ\) and, later, in every ordered field. The usual failure. Expanding, \(p'^2 - 2q'^2 = 2q^2 - p^2 = 0\) , so \(p'^2 = 2q'^2\) . \(q < p\) , since \(p \le q\) would give \(2q^2 = p^2 \le q^2\) , that is, \(q^2 \le 0\) .

title: Definition 4.1.1 (Absolute Value in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field. For \(x \in F\) , the absolute value of \(x\) is \[ \abs{x} \coloneqq \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 , \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 . \end{cases} \] For \(x, y \in F\) , the element \(\abs{x - y}\) is the distance from \(x\) to \(y\) .

title: Lemma 4.1.1 (Fraction Rules in a Field)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content:
Let \(F\) be a field ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ), and let \(a, b, c, d \in F\) with \(b 
e 0\) and \(d 
e 0\) . \(b^{-1}\) is the only element \(y\) with \(b y = 1\) , and \((b^{-1})^{-1} = b\) . Moreover \(bd 
e 0\) and \((bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}\) . \(\dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad + bc}{bd}\) and \(\dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}\) . \(\dfrac{1}{b} - \dfrac{1}{d} = \dfrac{d - b}{bd}\) . For all \(x, y \in F\) : if \(xy = 0\) , then \(x = 0\) or \(y = 0\) .

title: Proposition 4.1.3 (Rules for the Absolute Value)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field, and let \(x, y, z, r \in F\) . \(\abs{x} \ge 0\) , and \(\abs{x} = 0\) if and only if \(x = 0\) . \(\abs{-x} = \abs{x}\) , \(\abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}\) and \(\abs{x}^2 = x^2\) ; if \(x \ne 0\) , then \(\abs{1/x} = 1/\abs{x}\) . \(-\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}\) . \(\abs{x} \le r\) if and only if \(-r \le x \le r\) ; and \(\abs{x} < r\) if and only if \(-r < x < r\) . (Triangle inequality.) \(\abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) , and \(\abs{x - z} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y - z}\) . (Reverse triangle inequality.) \(\bigl| \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr| \le \abs{x - y}\) .

title: Proposition 4.1.2 (Halves and Comparisons in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.1 Working in an Ordered Field
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field. \(\le\) is a total order on \(F\) ( @fd2:def-partial-order ), and its strict part is \(<\) . \(2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 > 0\) . For every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) , \[ 0 < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < \varepsilon \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon . \] For all \(a, b \in F\) with \(a < b\) , \(a < \dfrac{a + b}{2} < b\) . For \(a, b \in F_{>0}\) : if \(a \le b\) , then \(\dfrac{1}{b} \le \dfrac{1}{a}\) . For \(a, b, c, d \in F\) : if \(0 \le a \le b\) and \(0 \le c \le d\) , then \(ac \le bd\) .

title: Definition 4.2.2 (Archimedean Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: An ordered field \(F\) is Archimedean if for every \(x \in F\) there is \(n \in \nN\) with \(x < n \cdot 1_F\) . In symbols, \[ \forall x \in F \ \ \exists n \in \nN \ \ x < n \cdot 1_F . \]

title: Definition 4.2.1 (Natural Numbers and Powers in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property

N . \]

title: Proposition 4.2.3 (Small Reciprocals in an Archimedean Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
In an Archimedean ordered field \(F\) , for every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) there is \(N \in 
Z_{>0}\) such that \(1/(n \cdot 1_F) < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge N\) . In symbols, \[  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
Z_{>0} \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \ \Bigl( n \ge N \Rightarrow  rac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon \Bigr) . \]

title: Proposition 4.2.4 (Integer Part in an Archimedean Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: Suppose that the ordered field \(F\) is Archimedean. Then for every \(x \in F\) there is exactly one \(m \in \nZ\) with \[ \iota_F(m) \le x < \iota_F(m + 1) . \]

title: Proposition 4.2.1 (The Natural Numbers inside an Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
Let \(F\) be an ordered field, and let \(m, n, k \in 
N\) . \((m + n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F\) and \((mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)\) . If \(m < n\) , then \(m \cdot 1_F < n \cdot 1_F\) . Hence \(n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F\) is injective, and \(n \cdot 1_F \ge 1_F > 0\) whenever \(n \ge 1\) . \((n^k) \cdot 1_F = (n \cdot 1_F)^k\) . In particular \((2^k) \cdot 1_F = (2 \cdot 1_F)^k\) , the \(k\) -th power in \(F\) of \(2 = 1 + 1\) . In \(
Q\) , \(n \cdot 1_{
Q} = j(\iota(n))\) , the image of \(n\) under the embeddings @prp-naturals-embed-integers and @prp-integers-embed-rationals . With the identifications \(
N \subseteq 
Z \subseteq 
Q\) , this says \(n \cdot 1_{
Q} = n\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.5 (The Rationals Are Dense in an Archimedean Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: In an Archimedean ordered field \(F\) , for all \(x, y \in F\) with \(x < y\) there is \(q \in \nQ\) with \(x < \iota_F(q) < y\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.2 (The Rationals Embed in Every Ordered Field)
page: 4.2 The Rationals inside an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
Let \(F\) be an ordered field. There is exactly one map \(\iota_F \colon 
Q 	o F\) such that, for all \(x, y \in 
Q\) , \[  egin{gathered} \iota_F(1) = 1_F , \ \iota_F(x + y) = \iota_F(x) + \iota_F(y) , \qquad \iota_F(xy) = \iota_F(x)\, \iota_F(y) . \end{gathered} \] It satisfies \(\iota_F(n) = n \cdot 1_F\) for every \(n \in 
N\) . It is injective and strictly increasing ( \(x < y\) implies \(\iota_F(x) < \iota_F(y)\) ), and it reflects order : \(\iota_F(x) < \iota_F(y)\) implies \(x < y\) .

title: Definition 4.3.4 (Bounded Sequence)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: A sequence \((a_n)\) in \(F\) is bounded if there exists \(M \in F_{>0}\) with \(\abs{a_n} \le M\) for every \(n \in \nN\) . Such an \(M\) is a bound for \((a_n)\) .

title: Definition 4.3.3 (Null Sequence)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: A sequence \((a_n)\) in \(F\) is null if \(a_n \to 0\) .

title: Definition 4.3.2 (Limit of a Sequence in an Ordered Field)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) and \(a \in F\) . The sequence converges to \(a\) in \(F\) , written \(a_n 	o a\) , if for every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) there exists \(N \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge N\) . In symbols, \[  orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \Rightarrow \abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon  igr) . \] Then \(a\) is a limit of \((a_n)\) . The sequence is convergent if it converges to some \(a \in F\) , and divergent otherwise.

title: Definition 4.3.1 (Sequence; Eventually)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
A sequence in \(F\) is a function \(a \colon 
N 	o F\) ( @fd2:def-function ). Its value at \(n\) is written \(a_n\) and called the \(n\) -th term ; the sequence is written \((a_n)_{n \in 
N}\) , or \((a_n)\) , and \(\{ a_n : n \in 
N \}\) is its set of values. A property \(P(n)\) of natural numbers holds eventually if there is \(N_0 \in 
N\) such that \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in 
N\) with \(n \ge N_0\) .

title: Example (First Limits)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Decide, from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field , which of these converge, and to what. A constant sequence \(a_n = c\) in any ordered field \(F\) . \(a_n = 1/(n + 1)\) in \(\nQ\) . \(a_n = (n + 1)/(n + 2)\) in \(\nQ\) . \(a_n = (-1)^n\) in any ordered field \(F\) .

page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Prove from the definition that \(a_n = \dfrac{2n + (-1)^n}{n + 1} \to 2\) in \(\nQ\) .

page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Prove from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field that \(a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{n^2 + 1}{2n^2 + 3} \to \dfrac{1}{2}\) in \(\nQ\) .

title: Example (Method: proving a limit from the definition)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Template. (1) Bring the distance \(\abs{a_n - a}\) to one fraction. (2) Bound it, for all \(n \ge n_0\) , by \(C/(n + 1)\) with \(C \in F_{>0}\) , enlarging numerators and shrinking denominators. (3) If \(F\) is Archimedean, take \(N'\) from @prp-archimedean-reciprocal with \(1/m < \varepsilon/C\) for \(m \ge N'\) , and let \(N \coloneqq \max\{N', n_0\}\) . (4) Write forwards: let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) ; let \(N\) be as in (3); let \(n \ge N\) ; then \(\abs{a_n - a} \le C/(n + 1) < \varepsilon\) . When to use it. The candidate limit is known, the distance has a formula, and \(F\) is Archimedean (as \(\nQ\) is, @thm-rationals-archimedean ); in a general \(F\) , step (3) needs another source of thresholds (Section 4.4). The usual failure. Writing the backward computation as the proof: that proves the converse, entry (N5) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue . Choosing \(N\) before \(\varepsilon\) , or letting it depend on \(n\) .

content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \((a_n)\) , \((b_n)\) sequences in \(F\) . Prove each true statement from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field and refute each false one with a counterexample. page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Here is an argument for @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field . Is the conclusion true? Is the argument correct? If not, name the line that fails, say what makes it illegal, and give a counterexample to the step. Then repair the argument. Let \(a_n \to a\) . (2) Take \(\varepsilon \coloneqq 1\) in the definition of the limit, and let \(N\) be the index it provides. (3) Then for every \(n \in \nN\) , \(\abs{a_n} \le \abs{a_n - a} + \abs{a} < 1 + \abs{a}\) . (4) So \(M \coloneqq 1 + \abs{a}\) is a bound for \((a_n)\) .

title: Proposition 4.3.5 (Convergent Sequences Are Bounded)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Every convergent sequence in \(F\) is bounded.

title: Proposition 4.3.3 (Limits Through Null Sequences)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: For a sequence \((a_n)\) in \(F\) and \(a \in F\) : \(a_n \to a\) if and only if the sequence \((a_n - a)\) is null.

title: Proposition 4.3.1 (Archimedes as a Null Sequence)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: The sequence \(\bigl( 1/((n + 1) \cdot 1_F) \bigr)_{n \in \nN}\) is null in \(F\) if and only if \(F\) is Archimedean.

title: Proposition 4.3.2 (Only the Tail Matters)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content:
Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be sequences in \(F\) , and \(a \in F\) . If there is \(N_0 \in 
N\) with \(a_n = b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a_n 	o a\) if and only if \(b_n 	o a\) ; in particular \((a_n)\) is null if and only if \((b_n)\) is; and \((a_n)\) is bounded if and only if \((b_n)\) is. For \(k \in 
N\) , the shifted sequence \((a_{n+k})_{n \in 
N}\) converges to \(a\) if and only if \((a_n)\) does.

title: Theorem 4.3.4 (Uniqueness of Limits)
page: 4.3 Sequences and Limits in an Ordered Field
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) and \(a, b \in F\) . If \(a_n \to a\) and \(a_n \to b\) , then \(a = b\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: These questions are about the proof of the product law, @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field (c). Why is \(M\) fixed before \(\varepsilon\) , and what does it depend on? Which hypothesis supplies \(N_1\) , which supplies \(N_2\) , and which supplies \(M\) ? Why does the proof use \(\abs{b} + 1\) rather than \(\abs{b}\) ? State the idea of the proof in two sentences. Run the proof in \(\nQ\) on \(a_n = 1 + 1/(n + 1)\) , \(b_n = 2\) and \(\varepsilon = 1/10\) : give a valid \(M\) , the least \(N_1\) , the least \(N_2\) , and \(N\) .

page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Find the following limits in \(\nQ\) by the limit laws, naming the result used at each step. \(\dfrac{n + 2}{3n + 1}\) . \(\dfrac{n^2 + 1}{(n + 1)^2}\) . \(\Bigl( \dfrac{1}{n + 1} - 2 \Bigr) \Bigl( 3 + \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n + 1} \Bigr)\) . title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Here are lines of the proof of @prp-limit-preserves-order-ordered-field (a), shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Recall the hypotheses: \(a_n \to a\) , \(b_n \to b\) , and \(a_n \le b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) . Write the seven lines of a correct proof in a correct order, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Let \(n \coloneqq \max\{N_0, N_1, N_2\}\) . Let \(\varepsilon \coloneqq a - b\) , which lies in \(F_{>0}\) . Choose \(N_2\) with \(\abs{b_n - b} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_2\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(b < a\) . This contradicts \(a_n \le b_n\) ; so \(b < a\) is false, and \(a \le b\) by trichotomy. Let \(\varepsilon \coloneqq (a - b)/2\) , which lies in \(F_{>0}\) by @prp-ordered-field-halves . Let \(n \coloneqq N_1\) . Then \(a_n > a - \varepsilon = (a + b)/2 = b + \varepsilon > b_n\) . Choose \(N_1\) with \(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) .
