page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(a_n \to a\) in \(F\) , and let \((b_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) such that \((b_n - a_n)\) is null. Prove that \(b_n \to a\) . Here is the start of a proof. Let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) . Then \(\varepsilon/2 \in F_{>0}\) . Since \(a_n \to a\) , choose \(N_1\) with \(\abs{a_n - a} < \varepsilon/2\) for every \(n \ge N_1\) . Since \((b_n - a_n)\) is null, choose \(N_2\) with \(\abs{b_n - a_n} < \varepsilon/2\) for every \(n \ge N_2\) . Let \(N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}\) . … Name the move, then complete it.

page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Prove, from @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field , that if \(a_n \to a\) and \(b_n \to b\) in an ordered field \(F\) , then \(a_n b_n \to ab\) . You may use that convergent sequences are bounded ( @prp-convergent-bounded-ordered-field ), the rules for the absolute value ( @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field ), @prp-limit-null-shift-ordered-field and @prp-null-times-bounded-ordered-field , but not @thm-limit-laws-ordered-field .

page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content:
Let \(a_n 	o a\) in \(F\) , with \(a_n \ge 0\) for every \(n\) . Prove that \(a \ge 0\) . Suppose moreover \(a > 0\) . Prove that there is \(N_0 \in 
N\) with \(a_n > 0\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , and that the sequence \((1/a_{n+N_0})_{n \in 
N}\) converges to \(1/a\) . Give an example in \(
Q\) where \(a_n > 0\) for every \(n\) and \((1/a_n)\) does not converge.

title: Lemma 4.4.2 (Terms Near a Non-zero Limit)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(b_n \to b\) in \(F\) with \(b \ne 0\) . Then there is \(N_0 \in \nN\) with \(\abs{b_n} > \abs{b}/2\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) . If \(b > 0\) , then moreover \(b_n > b/2\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) .

title: Proposition 4.4.4 (Limits Preserve Weak Inequalities)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(a_n \to a\) and \(b_n \to b\) in \(F\) , and let \(N_0 \in \nN\) . If \(a_n \le b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a \le b\) . In particular, for \(c \in F\) : if \(a_n \le c\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a \le c\) ; and if \(a_n \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(a \ge c\) . (Squeeze.) Let \((c_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) . If \(a = b\) and \(a_n \le c_n \le b_n\) for every \(n \ge N_0\) , then \(c_n \to a\) .

title: Proposition 4.4.1 (Null Times Bounded Is Null)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a null sequence in \(F\) , and let \((b_n)\) be a sequence with \(\abs{b_n} \le M\) for every \(n\) , where \(M \in F_{>0}\) . Then \((a_n b_n)\) is null.

title: Theorem 4.4.3 (Limit Laws)
page: 4.4 The Algebra and Order of Limits
content: Let \(a_n \to a\) and \(b_n \to b\) in \(F\) , and let \(c \in F\) . Then: \(a_n + b_n \to a + b\) ; \(c a_n \to c a\) ; in particular \(-a_n \to -a\) and \(a_n - b_n \to a - b\) ; \(a_n b_n \to a b\) ; if \(b \ne 0\) and \(b_n \ne 0\) for every \(n\) , then \(a_n / b_n \to a / b\) .

title: Definition 4.5.1 (Cauchy Sequence)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content:
A sequence \((a_n)_{n \in 
N}\) in \(F\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) (or Cauchy ) if for every \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) there exists \(N \in 
N\) such that \(\abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon\) for all \(m, n \in 
N\) with \(m \ge N\) and \(n \ge N\) . In symbols: \[  egin{aligned} & orall \varepsilon \in F_{>0} \ \ \exists N \in 
N \ \  orall m \in 
N \ \  orall n \in 
N \ &\qquad  igl( (m \ge N \wedge n \ge N) \Rightarrow \abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon  igr) . \end{aligned} \]

title: Example (Shrinking Steps, Terms That Do Not Settle)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Here is an argument for the false claim in the warning. “Let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) . Since \(a_{n+1} - a_n \to 0\) , choose \(N\) with \(\abs{a_{k+1} - a_k} < \varepsilon\) for every \(k \ge N\) . Let \(m > n \ge N\) . Then \(a_m - a_n\) is the sum of the consecutive differences \(a_{k+1} - a_k\) for \(k = n, \dots, m - 1\) , and each of them is smaller than \(\varepsilon\) in absolute value. So \(\abs{a_m - a_n} < \varepsilon\) , and \((a_n)\) is Cauchy.” In \(\nQ\) , let \(H_0 \coloneqq 0\) and \(H_{n+1} \coloneqq H_n + 1/(n + 1)\) for \(n \in \nN\) . Show that \(H_{n+1} - H_n \to 0\) , that \(H_{2n} - H_n \ge 1/2\) for every \(n \ge 1\) , and that \((H_n)\) is not Cauchy. Find the line of the argument that fails.

title: Exercise (C1)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) and \((b_n)\) a sequence in \(F\) such that \((a_n - b_n)\) is null. Prove that \((b_n)\) is Cauchy. Here is the beginning of a proof. Name the move, then complete it. “Let \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) . For all \(m, n \in \nN\) , the triangle inequality ( @prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), applied twice, gives \[ \abs{b_n - b_m} \le \abs{b_n - a_n} + \abs{a_n - a_m} + \abs{a_m - b_m} . \] …”

title: Exercise (C2: Exit check: the sign theorem)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in an ordered field \(F\) that is not null. Prove that there are \(c \in F_{>0}\) and \(N \in \nN\) such that either \(a_n \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N\) , or \(a_n \le -c\) for every \(n \ge N\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Find the error)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Here is an argument that the product of two Cauchy sequences \((a_n)\) , \((b_n)\) in \(F\) is Cauchy. “For all \(m, n\) , \(\abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} \le \abs{a_n} \, \abs{b_n - b_m} + \abs{b_m} \, \abs{a_n - a_m}\) . Given \(\varepsilon \in F_{>0}\) , choose \(N\) such that \(\abs{b_n - b_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{a_n})\) and \(\abs{a_n - a_m} < \varepsilon/(2\abs{b_m})\) for all \(m, n \ge N\) . Then for \(m, n \ge N\) , \(\abs{a_n b_n - a_m b_m} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon\) .” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, and repair it.

title: Proposition 4.5.2 (Cauchy Sequences Are Bounded)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Every Cauchy sequence in \(F\) is bounded.

title: Proposition 4.5.6 (Reciprocals of Cauchy Sequences)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) , and let \(c \in F_{>0}\) and \(N \in \nN\) be such that \(\abs{a_n} \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N\) . Define \[ b_n \coloneqq \begin{cases} 1/a_n & \text{if } n \ge N , \\ 1 & \text{if } n < N . \end{cases} \] Then \((b_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) , and \(a_n b_n = 1\) for every \(n \ge N\) .

title: Proposition 4.5.1 (Convergent Sequences Are Cauchy)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: If \(a_n \to a\) in \(F\) , then \((a_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) .

title: Proposition 4.5.5 (Sign Stability under Null Differences)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be sequences in \(F\) such that \((a_n - b_n)\) is null. If \(c \in F_{>0}\) , \(N \in \nN\) , and \(a_n \ge c\) for every \(n \ge N\) , then there is \(N' \in \nN\) with \(b_n \ge c/2\) for every \(n \ge N'\) .

title: Theorem 4.5.3 (Sums and Products of Cauchy Sequences)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) and \((b_n)\) be Cauchy sequences in \(F\) , and let \(c \in F\) . Every constant sequence and every null sequence in \(F\) is Cauchy. The sequences \((a_n + b_n)\) , \((c \, a_n)\) , \((-a_n)\) and \((a_n - b_n)\) are Cauchy. The sequence \((a_n b_n)\) is Cauchy.

title: Theorem 4.5.4 (The Sign of a Non-Null Cauchy Sequence)
page: 4.5 Cauchy Sequences
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) that is not null. Then there are \(c \in F_{>0}\) and \(N \in \nN\) such that either \[ a_n \ge c \ \text{ for every } n \ge N , \qquad \text{or} \qquad a_n \le -c \ \text{ for every } n \ge N . \] The two alternatives do not both hold.

title: Definition 5.2.1 (The Real Numbers)
page: 5.2 The Real Numbers and Their Arithmetic
content: The set of real numbers is the quotient set ( @fd2:def-quotient-set ) \[ \nR \coloneqq \sC/{\sim} \] of the set \(\sC\) of Cauchy sequences of rationals ( @def-rational-cauchy-sequences ) by the relation \(\sim\) of @def-cauchy-equivalent . Its elements are the classes \([a] = \{ b \in \sC : b \sim a \}\) for \(a \in \sC\) ( @fd2:def-equivalence-class ), and any \(b \in [a]\) is a representative of \([a]\) .

title: Definition 5.3.2 (Order on the Reals)

content: For \(x, y \in \nR\) , \(x < y\) means \(y - x \in P\) . As usual, \(x \le y\) means \(x < y\) or \(x = y\) , and \(y > x\) means \(x < y\) .

title: Example (Method: name the margin before the index)
page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content: Template. To prove that \(b \in \sC\) is positive, or that \([a] < [b]\) : (1) name a margin \(\delta \in \nQ_{>0}\) from data that do not depend on \(n\) : a given margin, or a fraction (such as half) of a given margin or of a positive value the terms visibly approach; (2) only then ask the given sequences (Cauchy, null, positive) for thresholds at tolerances computed from \(\delta\) ; (3) take the largest of these finitely many thresholds and check that the terms of the sequence to be shown positive ( \(b\) , or \(b - a\) for \([a] < [b]\) ) are \(\ge \delta\) beyond it. When to use it. Whenever the goal reads \(\exists \delta \ \exists N \ \forall n \ge N \ \ldots\) : positivity, a strict inequality between classes, a bound that must hold beyond one index. The usual failure. Proving “ \(b_n > 0\) for all large \(n\) ” and calling \(b_n\) the margin: it depends on \(n\) (the Quick check above; Exercise C2).

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 5.3 Positive Classes and the Order
content: Here is an argument for @prp-positivity-well-defined . “Let \(a\) be positive and \(a' \sim a\) . Fix \(\delta \in \nQ_{>0}\) and \(N\) with \(a_n \ge \delta\) for every \(n \ge N\) . Since \(a' - a\) is null, there is \(N'\) with \(\abs{a'_n - a_n} < \delta\) for every \(n \ge N'\) . So, for \(n \ge \max\{N, N'\}\) , \(a'_n > a_n - \delta \ge 0\) . Hence \(a'_n > 0\) for all large \(n\) . Therefore \(a'\) is positive.” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, say why, give a counterexample to that step, and repair the argument.

title: Definition 5.5.1 (Complete Ordered Field)
page: 5.5 Least Upper Bounds
content: An ordered field \(F\) is complete if every non-empty subset \(A \subseteq F\) that is bounded above in \((F, \le)\) ( @fd2:def-order-bounds ) has a supremum in \(F\) ( @fd2:def-order-supremum ). In symbols, writing \(\mathrm{ub}(u)\) for \(\forall a \in A \ \ a \le u\) , \[ \begin{aligned} &\forall A \subseteq F \ \ \bigl( (A \ne \emptyset \wedge \exists u \in F \ \mathrm{ub}(u)) \Rightarrow \\ &\qquad \exists s \in F \ \bigl( \mathrm{ub}(s) \wedge \forall u \in F \ (\mathrm{ub}(u) \Rightarrow s \le u) \bigr) \bigr) . \end{aligned} \] An ordered field in which every Cauchy sequence ( @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field ) converges is called Cauchy-complete .

title: Example (Method: bisect and keep the invariant)
page: 5.5 Least Upper Bounds
content: Template. (1) Start with two points on opposite sides of a test (here: not an upper bound, an upper bound). (2) Define the step by a rule that applies the test to the midpoint and keeps one end on each side; the recursion theorem then builds the sequence with no choice. (3) Prove the invariants and the length \(D/2^k\) by induction. (4) Make \(D/2^k\) small, by Archimedes, to get Cauchy sequences. (5) Spend one invariant on each half of the conclusion. When to use it. The point you want is the boundary between two kinds of points, and one test decides the kind of each point. The usual failure. A step that “takes some point of \(A\) above the midpoint” with no rule. A starting left end that may itself be an upper bound ( \(l_0 = a_0\) for \(A = \{a_0\}\) ). Asserting \(1/2^k \to 0\) without Archimedes.

title: Definition 6.1.1 (Order-Preserving Field Map)
page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be ordered fields. A map \(\chi \colon F \to L\) is an order-preserving field map if, for all \(a, b \in F\) , \[ \chi(a + b) = \chi(a) + \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(ab) = \chi(a)\, \chi(b) , \qquad \chi(1_F) = 1_L , \] and \(a < b\) implies \(\chi(a) < \chi(b)\) . An order-preserving field isomorphism is an order-preserving field map that is bijective ( @fd2:def-bijective ). An order-preserving field automorphism of \(F\) is an order-preserving field isomorphism \(F \to F\) .

title: Example (Method: construct a point as a supremum)
page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once
content: Template. To produce an element with a property \(P\) in a complete ordered field: (1) choose a set \(S\) of elements that should lie below it; (2) check that \(S\) is non-empty and bounded above; (3) let \(s \coloneqq \sup S\) ; (4) prove \(P(s)\) . An inequality \(y \le s\) for \(y \in S\) is (S1). An inequality \(s \le u\) follows once \(u\) is shown to be an upper bound of \(S\) (S2). An equation is proved by refuting both strict cases: one by an element of \(S\) above \(s\) , the other by an upper bound of \(S\) below \(s\) . When to use it. When the element has no formula but the elements below it can be described: a square root, an element between two sets, the value \(\varphi(x)\) in Section 6.2, the limit of a bounded increasing sequence (Exercise C3 of Section 6.3). It is @fd2:exm-method-construct-and-verify with the construction step done by completeness. The usual failure. Taking the supremum before checking (2); assuming \(s \in S\) ; choosing \(h\) that depends on something other than \(s\) and the data.

page: 6.1 What Completeness Gives at Once

title: Exercise (B1)
page: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content: Prove @lem-cof-below-product : let \(F\) be an Archimedean ordered field, \(a, b \in F\) with \(a, b > 0\) , and \(q \in \nQ\) with \(q > 0\) ; show that \(\iota_F(q) < ab\) if and only if some rational \(r > 0\) has \(\iota_F(r) < a\) and \(\iota_F(q/r) < b\) . Show also that \(\iota_F(q) < ab\) for every rational \(q \le 0\) . Hint: imitate the proof of @lem-cof-below-sum , with division in place of subtraction.

title: Exercise (B2: Cube roots)
page: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field and \(a \in F\) with \(a > 0\) . Let \(S \coloneqq \{ y \in F : y \ge 0 \text{ and } y^3 < a \}\) . The following steps prove that some \(s \in F\) has \(s^3 = a\) . \(S\) is non-empty ( \(0 \in S\) ) and bounded above by \(1 + a\) : if \(y > 1 + a\) , then \(y > 1\) , so \(y^3 > y > a\) . Let \(s \coloneqq \sup S\) . Then \(s > 0\) , since \(m \coloneqq \min\{1, a/2\}\) has \(0 < m \le 1\) , so \(m^3 \le m \le a/2 < a\) , and \(m \in S\) . For \(y, z \in F\) , \(z^3 - y^3 = (z - y)(z^2 + zy + y^2)\) and \(z^2 + zy + y^2 = (z + y/2)^2 + (3/4)y^2\) , which is \(> 0\) unless \(y = z = 0\) (if \(y \ne 0\) , then \((3/4)y^2 > 0\) by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c) and the square is \(\ge 0\) , so the sum is positive by (b); if \(y = 0\) and \(z \ne 0\) , the expression is \(z^2 > 0\) by (e)). Hence \(y < z \iff y^3 < z^3\) , for all \(y, z \in F\) . The case \(s^3 < a\) is impossible. Let \(h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^3)/(2(3s^2 + 3s + 1))\} > 0\) . Since \(0 < h \le 1\) and \(s \ge 0\) , \((s + h)^3 = s^3 + 3s^2h + 3sh^2 + h^3 \le s^3 + h(3s^2 + 3s + 1) \le s^3 + (a - s^3)/2 < a\) , so \(s + h \in S\) , against \(s\) being an upper bound. The case \(s^3 > a\) is impossible. Name the move, then complete it. Hence \(s^3 = a\) . Then explain how to get a cube root of \(a = 0\) and of \(a < 0\) , and why every \(a \in F\) has exactly one cube root.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: at most one map into an Archimedean field)
page: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be Archimedean ordered fields, and let \(\chi_1, \chi_2 \colon F \to L\) be order-preserving field maps. Prove that \(\chi_1 = \chi_2\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Dense image, and when the map is onto)
page: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content: Let \(F\) be an Archimedean ordered field, \(L\) a complete ordered field, and \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) the map of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete . Prove that \(\varphi(F)\) is dense in \(L\) : for all \(u < v\) in \(L\) there is \(x \in F\) with \(u < \varphi(x) < v\) . Prove that if \(F\) is complete, then \(\varphi\) is surjective. Prove that if \(\varphi\) is surjective, then \(F\) is complete.

title: Lemma 6.2.2 (Rationals below a Product)
page: 6.2 Building the Map from the Rationals Below
content: Let \(F\) be an Archimedean ordered field, \(a, b \in F\) with \(a > 0\) and \(b > 0\) , and \(q \in \nQ\) with \(q > 0\) . Then \(\iota_F(q) < ab\) if and only if there is \(r \in \nQ\) with \[ r > 0 , \qquad \iota_F(r) < a \qquad \text{and} \qquad \iota_F(q/r) < b . \] For \(q \le 0\) , \(\iota_F(q) < ab\) holds always.

title: Corollary 6.3.3 (A Complete Ordered Field Has Only the Trivial Order Automorphism)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field. The only order-preserving field automorphism of \(F\) is \(\id_F\) . In particular, this holds for the field \(\nR\) of Chapter 5.

title: Example (Limits Are Carried Across)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence in \(F\) and \(a \in F\) . Show that \(a_n \to a\) in \(F\) ( @def-sequence-limit-ordered-field ) if and only if \(\varphi(a_n) \to \varphi(a)\) in \(L\) .

title: Example (Two Models, One Square Root of Two)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(M\) be any complete ordered field (for instance the one Axiomatic Set Theory builds, whose elements are sets of rationals). Let \(\varphi \colon \nR \to M\) be the isomorphism of @thm-cof-uniqueness and \(r\) the real number of @exm-sqrt2-class ( \(r > 0\) , \(r^2 = 2\) ). Find \(\varphi(r)\) in terms of \(M\) alone, and describe \(\nQ_M(\varphi(r))\) .

title: Example (A Complete Ordered Field Whose Zero Is the Empty Set)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Find a complete ordered field whose zero element is \(\emptyset\) .

title: Exercise (A2)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Throughout, \(F\) and \(L\) are complete ordered fields and \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) is the order-preserving field isomorphism. For each statement, decide whether its truth could depend on which complete ordered field is taken as \(\nR\) , and justify your answer: (i) \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 > 3\) ; (ii) the zero element is the empty set; (iii) \(\nR\) is uncountable. Which step of @exm-cof-limits-carried-across uses that \(\varphi\) is onto? Why does a model of the axioms, built inside set theory, show that the axioms of a complete ordered field cannot contradict each other unless that set theory does?

content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be complete ordered fields, \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) the isomorphism of @thm-cof-uniqueness , and \((a_n)\) a sequence in \(F\) . Prove that \((a_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(F\) ( @def-cauchy-sequence-ordered-field ) if and only if \((\varphi(a_n))\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(L\) .

title: Exercise (B2)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be complete ordered fields, and \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) the isomorphism of @thm-cof-uniqueness . Let \(A \subseteq F\) be non-empty and bounded above. Prove that \(\varphi(A) \coloneqq \{ \varphi(a) : a \in A \}\) has a supremum in \(L\) and that \(\varphi(\sup A) = \sup \varphi(A)\) ( @fd2:def-order-supremum ).

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: field maps of a complete ordered field)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field and \(\sigma \colon F \to F\) a map that respects sums and products and has \(\sigma(1) = 1\) . Using only @prp-cof-square-roots , @prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals , @lem-cof-rationals-separate , @thm-cof-complete-archimedean and @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete (and the rules of an ordered field), prove that \(\sigma = \id_F\) . Write the proof without looking at the one in this section.

title: Exercise (R1)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(q_n \coloneqq (n + 1)/(n + 2) \in \nQ\) . Show that \((q_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence of rationals and that \([(q_n)] = 1\) in \(\nR\) . Every \(q_n\) is less than \(1\) . title: Theorem 6.3.4 (Field Maps of a Complete Ordered Field to Itself)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(F\) be a complete ordered field, and let \(\sigma \colon F \to F\) satisfy, for all \(a, b \in F\) , \[ \sigma(a + b) = \sigma(a) + \sigma(b) , \qquad \sigma(ab) = \sigma(a) \sigma(b) , \qquad \sigma(1) = 1 . \] Then \(\sigma = \id_F\) . No order condition and no bijectivity is assumed.

title: Theorem 6.3.1 (Uniqueness of the Complete Ordered Field)
page: 6.3 Two Complete Ordered Fields, One Isomorphism
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be complete ordered fields ( @def-complete-ordered-field ). Then there is exactly one order-preserving field isomorphism \(F \to L\) ( @def-cof-order-preserving-map ). It is the map \(\varphi\) of @thm-cof-embedding-into-complete .
